PM-DOS - Protected Mode DOS, a 32-bit DOS kernel
================================================
Started 2026-08-06.  Version 0.62.

The VDM - running 16-bit DOS programs
-------------------------------------
Started 2026-08-08.  IO\VM86.INC (the monitor) and DOS\VDM.INC (the
DOS side).  First 16-bit instructions executed 2026-08-08: a
hand-assembled real-mode program doing INT 21h AH=09h and AH=4Ch, its
output printed by the 32-bit kernel, verified in DOSBox.

WHERE THE SPLIT IS.  The monitor lives in PMIO, because it is about
the CPU - a TSS, an IOPL, a fault handler - and PMIO is where the
hardware lives.  The DOS side lives in PMDOS, because it is about
INT 21h.  They meet at one service, IOS_V86RUN, and the shape of it is
a VM exit loop: hand over a context, get it back when the guest does
something that needs answering, answer it, hand it over again.  The
monitor deals with CLI, STI, PUSHF, POPF, IRET and with reflecting
untrapped interrupts into the guest's own IVT, and never troubles the
caller with any of them.  A bitmap in the context says which vectors
the caller wants; PM-DOS claims 20h-2Fh and lets INT 10h and INT 16h
reflect to the BIOS.

"WHICH IS HOW THEY WORK WITH NO CODE AT ALL" is how that sentence used
to end, and it was half true for two years.  Reflecting a BIOS call
costs no code, but it only WORKS if the state the ROM reads is still
being kept up - and this kernel owns IRQ 1, so nothing was filling the
keyboard buffer the ROM's INT 16h looks at.  See v0.34.  The general
form is worth having in mind before the next reflected vector is
added: reflection hands the work to the ROM, and the ROM's handler is
only half of what the ROM did.  The other half was its INTERRUPT, and
that half is ours.

THREE THINGS MAKE V86 GO, and the third is not in the manuals'
introductions:
  - A TSS.  V86 runs at CPL 3, so every fault switches stacks through
    SS0:ESP0.  Without a loaded task register the first INT a DOS
    program executes triple-faults the machine.
  - IOPL 0 in the guest's flags.  THAT is the mechanism - it is what
    makes INT, IRET, CLI, STI, PUSHF and POPF fault into the monitor
    instead of running for real.  A guest at IOPL 3 dispatches its own
    interrupts through the IVT and the monitor never sees them.
  - An 8K I/O permission bitmap of zeros in the TSS.  In V86 mode IOPL
    does NOT govern IN and OUT; only the bitmap does.  All-zeros gives
    the guest every port, so it can drive hardware with no emulation
    at all.  Individual bits get set when a device needs virtualising,
    and that is the hook the whole device story will hang off.

THE INTERRUPT FLAG IS VIRTUAL.  The guest always runs with the real IF
set, because a DOS program must not be able to stop the system timer;
its CLI and STI move a flag of ours, and PUSHF, POPF and IRET are
doctored to show it that flag instead of the real one.

CONVENTIONAL MEMORY, THE PSP AND THE .COM LOADER came next, and on
2026-08-08 a real 16-bit .COM read off the disk ran to completion.
DOS\LOWMEM.INC is the arena a DOS program can see: genuine 16-byte
MCBs, 'M' blocks ending in a 'Z', owner = PSP segment, length in
paragraphs, first fit, coalescing on free.  It is deliberately NOT
the kernel's own arena (ARENA.INC, above 2MB, 32-bit, owner-id based)
because programs WALK this chain - MEM does, installers do - so it
has to be the real article rather than a convenient approximation.
Its constants are RMCB_* because ARENA.INC already owns MCB_*.

THE BRIDGE IS THE INTERESTING PART, and the decision worth recording
is that a V86 guest's INT 21h is served by THE KERNEL'S OWN HANDLERS -
the same i21_table the 32-bit side dispatches through.  DOS is not
reimplemented for 16-bit callers.  All that stands between them is
translation: the guest says DS:DX, the kernel wants one flat address,
so the bridge multiplies the segment by sixteen and hands the same
handler the same request.  k21 manufactures the frame those handlers
read their registers out of - pushad's eight dwords, the saved EBP,
then EIP/CS/FLAGS, forty-eight bytes - which makes the whole DOS API
callable from anywhere in the kernel, and the loader uses it too.
A table says which register holds a pointer for each function; that
table is the entire 16-bit-to-32-bit impedance match.
The pay-off is that file handling, searches and the long-name calls
worked the day the bridge did, because they are code that was already
there and already tested.

Some things cannot be passed through, and they are exactly the places
where "a program" means something different on each side: 48h/49h/4Ah
(the guest's memory is the DOS arena below 1MB, not the kernel's),
00h/4Ch/31h (terminate ends the VM), 62h (a PSP is a segment here),
2Fh (the DTA is a far pointer) and 4Bh (refused until a VM can nest -
which it can since v0.25).
On the way out the guest's handles are swept and its memory reclaimed
by PSP segment - it gets its own owner id for the purpose, or its open
files would belong to the shell and outlive it.

TWO MORE JOINED THAT LIST when the .EXE loader went in, and both would
have been quiet, expensive bugs:

  25h/35h, set and get an interrupt vector.  The kernel's 25h installs
  a 32-bit protected-mode IDT gate.  A guest calling it would point a
  gate at a real-mode segment:offset pair, and the next interrupt of
  that number would jump into nowhere in ring 0.  What a guest means
  by a vector is a slot in the real-mode IVT at 0:0 - which is where
  the monitor reflects untrapped interrupts - so that is where these
  two now read and write.  Hooking 24h, 1Bh, 23h or the timer is
  ordinary behaviour for a DOS program; it has to work.

  42h, seek.  CX:DX in and DX:AX out are each ONE 32-bit number split
  across two registers, and the kernel's own 42h takes the whole
  offset in ECX (see the 32-bit API notes below).  The generic path
  would have passed CX alone and returned the low half twice, so any
  file over 64K would have seeked to the wrong place and read the
  wrong bytes without ever reporting an error.

The proof is TOOLS\HELLO.ASM, an ordinary real-mode .COM that knows
nothing about any of this: it prints, asks 30h for the version, 62h
for its PSP, shrinks itself with 4Ah, allocates with 48h, frees with
49h, and opens and reads README.TXT.  Its output is arithmetic that
can be checked: PSP at 3701, shrink to 1000h paragraphs, and 48h
answers 4702 - 3701 + 1000h + one paragraph for the new MCB header.
"48h refused" before the 4Ah was added was not a bug either: a .COM
is handed every free paragraph, so allocation MUST fail until it
gives some back, which is what DOS did and what programs expect.

THE .EXE LOADER followed the same day.  It is arithmetic and one loop:
work out how much of the file is program, find somewhere to put it,
read it in, then walk the fixup table adding the load segment to every
segment word the linker could not know the value of.  CS:IP and SS:SP
in the header get the same treatment.

WHICH KIND OF PROGRAM IT IS COMES OUT OF THE FILE, NOT THE NAME.  DOS
always worked that way and it matters: LINK will happily produce an
.EXE called SOMETHING.COM, several utilities shipped exactly like
that, and a loader that trusts the extension runs the MZ header as
code.  vdm_load reads the first 28 bytes, looks for the signature, and
lets the answer decide; the extension is a hint for humans.

Three details in the header are easy to get wrong and all three cost
something silent if they are:

  CBLP is the number of valid bytes in the LAST page, and ZERO MEANS
  THE LAST PAGE IS FULL, not empty.  Read it as "empty" and every
  program that happens to end on a page boundary loses 512 bytes.

  MAXALLOC is 0FFFFh in nearly every .EXE ever linked, so allocating
  it always fails.  The loader is really driven by MINALLOC: ask for
  the maximum, take the largest run there is when that fails, and
  refuse only if even the minimum will not fit.

  THE LOAD MODULE STARTS AT PSP + 10h, and that is what every fixup is
  relative to.  Get it wrong by one paragraph and the program runs for
  a while and then dies somewhere unrelated - the worst kind of wrong.

TOOLS\HELLOX.ASM is the proof, and it was deliberately made harder
than the first draft.  That draft had a far call inside its only code
segment; the assembler quietly made it near, the file came out with a
single fixup, and the fixup loop was barely exercised.  The version
that ships has four segments - two code, one data, one stack - a far
call to the SECOND code segment (a real 9Ah with a segment fixup), and
a table of four far pointers it walks at run time.  Seven fixups in
two different segments, and a 64-byte header rather than a 48-byte
one.  Its output is checkable arithmetic again: PSP 0D01, load segment
0D11 = PSP + 10h, code segment 0D4A = 0D11 + the header's relative CS
of 0039, and all four pointers followed.

PMIO MOVED ABOVE 1MB next, which is what the 588K in the map is.  The
mechanism is worth recording because it needed no boot-sector change
at all.  A 512-byte boot sector can do one simple thing - read the
file into one segment - so it still drops all of PMIO.SYS at 2000:0000
and jumps there.  The stub then puts ITSELF where it wants to be: it
copies its own 8K down to 0B00:0000 and far-jumps to the copy, and
once unreal mode is up it blits its protected-mode half from 22000h to
200000h and enters protected mode there.  Everything before the
self-copy is position independent - a near jump, CS-relative data, and
nothing else - which is the only thing that has to be true for it to
work.  The IDT, the kernel stack and the TSS went up with it.

THE TRAP THAT WOULD HAVE EATEN IT: FL_FATBUF was at 0000B000h and
FL_DIRBUF at 0000D000h - the boot loader's FAT window and directory
sector - which is exactly where the relocated stub and the first page
of the DOS box now live.  The FAT window would have overwritten the
very code reading it, on the first cluster of the first file.  They
moved to 1000h/1400h, under a real-mode stack that is entered at 7C00h
and never comes within twenty kilobytes of them.  Both boot paths were
re-checked afterwards, floppy and hard disk, because BOOT2.BIN embeds
FATLOAD and therefore changed with them.

v0.22 - THE VDM IS WIRED INTO COMMAND.COM (2026-08-08)
------------------------------------------------------
Typing the name of a 16-bit program at the prompt now runs it.  Until
today the VDM_TEST self-test was the only way in; the DOS box existed
but nothing could ask for one.

THE FORK IS IN 4Bh, NOT IN THE SHELL, and that is the whole design.
COMMAND.COM was not taught anything about 16-bit programs - it asks
for HELLO.COM exactly as it asks for MEM.EXE, and the kernel decides.
exec_kind opens the file, reads the first eight bytes (four before
0.29, which put a 16-bit jump in front of the magic), and answers
EK_D32 or EK_16BIT; a D32 image goes the path it always did, anything
else goes to vdm_exec.  Putting the decision in the shell would have
meant every other program that ever calls 4Bh - a batch file, an
installer, INSTALL= later - having to make the same decision again,
and getting it wrong differently.  THE EXTENSION DECIDES NOTHING.
The one change in COMMAND.COM is a pointer to its environment in the
EXEC parameter block, which had been a documented "(ignored)" field.

THE 16-BIT PATH RETURNS, and that is why it is a tenth of the size of
the 32-bit one.  A D32 EXEC has to park the occupant of the transient
slot, count depth, switch to the kernel stack and never come back
(the child's 4Ch unwinds into the parent's frame).  A DOS box lives
below 1MB, so it disturbs nothing above it: the caller stands exactly
where it was, vdm_exec returns, and there is nothing to put back.  A
16-bit program does not count against EXEC_MAX either.

exec_kind ANSWERS WITH A VALUE, NOT A FLAG, and the reason is worth
keeping: the natural test - CMP against the signature - sets the carry
flag on its own account, so a "could not open the file" answer riding
in CF would be forged by any 16-bit program whose bytes at the magic's
offset sort below D32_MAGIC.  A file that will not open is deliberately NOT
reported by exec_kind at all; it goes down the D32 path, which is the
one that knows how to say "no such program".  That also stops COMMAND
trying four extensions in turn from building and tearing down three
DOS boxes before it finds the right one.

WHAT A PROGRAM IS HANDED, all of which only exists once a shell is
doing the starting:

  THE COMMAND TAIL, copied into PSP+80h from the same buffer 4Bh
  already copies for the 32-bit side.

  THE TWO FCBs at 5Ch and 6Ch, parsed out of that tail, and the two
  result codes in AX at entry: FFh if the argument named a drive that
  does not exist, 01h if it holds a wildcard, 00h otherwise.  This is
  furniture from 1981 that programs still read.  SIXTEEN BYTES EACH,
  NOT THE THIRTY-SEVEN AN OPEN FCB OCCUPIES - the two in a PSP are
  sixteen apart and the second ends four bytes short of the tail, so
  zeroing a whole FCB would wipe the tail it was parsed from.

  THE ENVIRONMENT, as a block of its own below 1MB: the shell's
  strings copied in, an empty string to end them, a word 0001h, and
  the program's own fully-qualified path.  That last is where argv[0]
  comes from in every C runtime of the era.  It goes through truename
  (21h/7160h) rather than being copied as typed, so "ARGS" at the
  prompt arrives as C:\ARGS.COM.  The block is ALLOCATED BEFORE THE
  PROGRAM'S OWN, and the order is not arbitrary: a .COM is handed
  every free paragraph there is, so anything allocated after it would
  find nothing left.  Ownership is handed to the PSP once there is
  one, so the exit sweep takes both with one call.

  THE DTA, set to PSP+80h as DOS does.  Without this a guest's
  directory searches would fill the DTA of whoever started it - which
  is COMMAND.COM, possibly in the middle of a FOR loop.

^C AND ABORT BOTH ARRIVE AS 32-BIT CODE INSIDE A CALL THE GUEST MADE,
and neither has a sensible value to return.  ctrl_break raises INT 23h
and COMMAND's handler issues 4Ch; an Abort at the critical-error
prompt does the same.  Both are several frames above the monitor, in
the middle of k21.  So fn4C checks whether a VM is running and, if it
is, longjmps: vdm_abort puts the kernel stack back to what it was when
vdm_run started and falls into the ordinary exit path, which closes
the guest's handles and gives its memory back exactly as a 4Ch would.
It is the same manoeuvre COMMAND makes with cmd_gohome and for the
same reason - the thing being abandoned is not the caller of that
code, it is the code itself.  WITHOUT IT, ANSWERING ABORT WOULD HAVE
TERMINATED THE SHELL, which is merely waiting in its EXEC call, and
taken AUTOEXEC.BAT round again.  f4C_vdm clears crit_busy first, for
the reason cmd_gohome does: a longjmp out of a critical-error handler
carries the kernel's "a handler is running" lock away with it, after
which every critical error quietly answers itself.

The VM flag is cleared FIRST in the exit path, before the handle
sweep.  The sweep flushes the guest's files, a flush can raise a
critical error, and Abort at that prompt comes back to the same exit
path - which with the flag still set is a loop rather than an exit.

TWO MORE CALLS JOINED THE INTERCEPTED LIST: 51h, which is 62h under
its undocumented name and would otherwise have handed a guest the
32-bit PSP address; and 50h, which sets the current PSP.  50h moves
what 51h and 62h answer AND NOTHING ELSE - the block the VM gives back
at the end is the one it was given, so a TSR swapping PSPs cannot make
the cleanup free somebody else's memory.

A LEAK AND A BUG FOUND WHILE RESTRUCTURING THE FAILURE PATHS: the
.COM loader's out-of-memory exit returned without closing the file it
had open, which mattered little when the self-test was the only caller
and matters a great deal when COMMAND tries four extensions for every
command typed.  Every failure exit now goes through one place that
closes the file and gives back both allocations.

STILL MISSING, and worth being honest about: a guest that hooks INT
23h does not get to see the ^C.  Real DOS would run its handler and
carry the interrupted call on if it returned, which means running V86
code from inside a kernel call the guest is already inside - the
monitor has no way to nest that yet.  Same for a guest's own INT 24h
handler.  Nesting a VM inside a VM is still refused at the guest's
4Bh, so a 16-bit program cannot yet start another one.

The proof is TOOLS\ARGS.ASM and DISK\VDMTEST.BAT.  ARGS prints its
tail, its FCBs, its entry AX, its environment and its own path, and
exits with an ERRORLEVEL taken from its tail so a batch file can
prove exit codes come back through EXEC; /W waits for a key so there
is something for ^C to interrupt, and /B touches a drive that is not
there so there is something to answer Abort to.  Verified on DOSBox
floppy and 86Box FAT16/ATA: tail and FCBs (including AX=FF01 for a
bad drive and a wildcard), the environment with COMSPEC/PROMPT and
the truename path, ERRORLEVEL 3, a guest redirected into a file, a
guest piped into SORT, ^C killing only the DOS box, Abort killing
only the DOS box, and MEM reading 587K free before and after - the
same number, so nothing leaks.

IN PROGRESS - WHAT MEM READS (2026-08-17)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Taken up because v0.35 shipped MEM half-fixed: the lockup was gone and
the numbers were wrong, which is a reporting bug rather than a stopped
machine but is still a machine describing itself incorrectly.  Four
faults found and fixed and one hypothesis killed; MEM's summary is now
correct, and what is left of it is written up at the end.

AND THE THING THAT ACTUALLY SOLVED IT WAS THE SOURCE.  Half a day of
black-box work here - a filtered call trace, a new test, two real
fixes - had ruled things out and moved two numbers, and had not
touched the headline symptom.  Charlie then mentioned he had an early
MS-DOS 6.0 source tree at S:\DOS6SRC, MEM.EXE's C source included,
and the question was answered in about ten minutes by reading
cmd\mem\membase.c.  THE LESSON IS ABOUT WHEN TO ASK: the evidence
being read here was a program's OUTPUT, and no amount of it says what
the program READ.  It is the same shape as v0.35's watch sampler - a
guest that spins says nothing - one level further out.  If the thing
you are debugging has published source anywhere in reach, that comes
before the third experiment, not after the tenth.

FIRST, A TOOL, because the fault trace could not answer this.
V86_TRACE prints every fault a guest takes, which for a program that
prints anything is one line per character, so the handful of calls
where a program asks the machine a QUESTION scroll off the top before
they can be read.  BUILD calls is that trace with the noise removed:
software interrupts only, not the ones that are output, and - the
part that mattered - THE SAME CALL TWICE RUNNING IS ONE LINE.  MEM
asks 21h/38h for the country before every number it prints, forty
times, which pushed everything else off the screen until repeats were
folded.  Run the guest with its own output redirected and what is
left on the screen is the whole conversation.

It said immediately what MEM asks about memory: INT 12h, INT 15h/88h,
2Fh/4300h and 4310h for XMS, 2Fh/4309h for the XMS handle table,
2Fh/4A01h for the HMA, 21h/5802h for the UMB link state, 52h for the
list of lists - and then it walks the MCB chain by hand, which no
trace can see.

THE COUNTRY BLOCK WAS INNOCENT, and proving it took a test.  Every
figure MEM prints comes out with only its first group of digits -
"1K" where it means 1,048,576 - and a formatter that stops at the
thousands separator is a formatter given a bad separator.  It was not:
CTRYTEST.COM asks 38h and 65h/01h the way MEM does and reads back a
comma and a NUL at offset 7, the right decimal, date, time and list
separators, and a case-map pointer that can be CALLED and returns.
6/6.  The value of that is not the pass - it is that a whole family
of "the numbers look wrong" suspicions is now answerable in four
seconds instead of an afternoon.

THE DOCUMENTED TAIL OF THE LIST OF LISTS WAS UNDER THE DEVICE CHAIN.
The structure did not stop at the JOIN count in DOS 5, and this one
did: CON's header began at LoL+3Ah, on top of eight fields MS-DOS 5.0
and 6.x publish at fixed offsets.  A program reading the boot drive
from LoL+43h got the high byte of CON's interrupt entry; one reading
the extended memory size from LoL+45h read the word "ON" out of
'CON     ' - 20,047 KB on a machine with 131,072.  MEM was reading
it: putting the field where DOS puts it moved MEM's Extended row from
19K to 64K, which is how we know.  So the tail now exists - unused
word, SETVER pointer, copy-protection fixup, A20 PSP, buffer counts,
boot drive, the 386 dword-move flag and the extended memory size -
and OURS moved past it: the RETF, the media byte, the DBCS table and
all three device headers.  An offset DOS defines is not ours to
spend.  Buffers answer 0 and that is the true answer rather than a
modest one: a DOS buffer is 528 bytes of conventional memory that
BUFFERS= sizes, and PM-DOS caches clusters and FAT windows above 1MB
instead, so a program costing the arena out finds none down there
because none of it is down there.

AND THE ONE THAT IS NOT ABOUT MEM AT ALL: THE ARENA RAN PAST THE END
OF CONVENTIONAL MEMORY.  lm_init ended it at a hardcoded 640K.  That
is right on a 1985 machine and wrong on nearly everything since,
because a BIOS with an EXTENDED BIOS DATA AREA takes the top kilobyte
or two for itself and says so in the word at 40:13 - the 486 and the
86Box machine here both report 639.  So the last kilobyte of the
arena was memory the BIOS owned: a program that allocated that high
would overwrite the EBDA, where the mouse driver's state and the PS/2
handler's stack live, and the damage would appear somewhere else
entirely and later.  Nothing here had ever allocated that high, which
is the only reason it had not been seen - it wants a program asking
for 600K and getting it.  lm_init now takes the top from 40:13,
clamps it to 640K, refuses a BIOS that says something useless, and
every walk in LOWMEM.INC and fn F1h/AL=8 measures against lm_top
rather than the constant.

MCBTEST HAD THE SAME ASSUMPTION AND SO PASSED THE BUG.  Its check 4 -
"the blocks tile the arena exactly" - compared the end of the chain
against a hardcoded 0A000h, and the chain really did reach 0A000h,
so the test agreed with the fault because it shared it.  It asks INT
12h now, and reports 9FC0/9FC0 on this machine.  A TEST THAT SHARES
THE CODE'S ASSUMPTION CANNOT SEE THE CODE'S MISTAKE, which is the
v0.32 lesson - a limit no test can reach is not covered by having
tests - from the other end: a test can reach the limit and still be
looking at the wrong number.

THE TWO REGIONS WERE ONE UNINITIALISED WORD.  membase.c, thirteen
lines in:

    FP_SEG(UMB_Head_ptr) = SegRegs.es;    /* what 52h answered */
    FP_OFF(UMB_Head_ptr) = 0x8c;          /* ptr to UMB_HEAD in DOS Data */
    UMB_Head = (*UMB_Head_ptr) & 0xFFFF;

and then, for every block in the chain, "if (addr < UMB_Head)" is
conventional memory and everything else is upper.  UMB_HEAD is a WORD
AT A FIXED OFFSET IN THE DOS DATA SEGMENT - 8Ch from the segment 52h
returns in ES, nothing to do with the pointer it returns in BX - and
it is not part of the list of lists at all.  PM-DOS left those two
bytes as whatever the paragraph held, and so the ENTIRE arena was
classified as upper memory, conventional showed not one free byte,
and the largest executable program size on a machine with 600K free
was reported as nothing.  Every absurd figure in the report came from
that one word.
  The value is not a guess either: the kernel's own alloc.asm tests
  "cmp ax,0ffffh ; Q: is umb_head initialized", so FFFFh is DOS's way
  of saying there is no upper memory.  No segment can be at or above
  it, every block is therefore conventional, and it agrees with what
  58h/02h and XMS function 10h have always said here.  Three ways of
  asking one question, and now they answer the same.
  The block is zeroed before it is filled now, too.  The general rule
  the bug is an instance of: A FIXED OFFSET IN A SEGMENT WE PUBLISH IS
  A FIELD WHETHER WE MEAN IT TO BE OR NOT.  What is not written is not
  "unused", it is whatever was in the RAM, and somebody's program is
  reading it as an answer.

AND THE LIST OF LISTS WAS IN THE WRONG PLACE ENTIRELY.  It was
allocated out of the arena, five paragraphs above the first MCB.  No
real DOS does that - MS-DOS's data segment is BELOW the transient
program area - and MEM sizes the DOS data area by subtracting:

    Out_Var2 = (AddressOf(ThisArenaPtr) - FP_SEG(SysVarsPtr))*16L - 16L;

With the list of lists above the first MCB that goes NEGATIVE, and
MEM takes it as an unsigned length: a four-gigabyte block enters its
table, the detail listing floods the screen padding a field to a
nonsense width, and MEM takes a BOUND - an index out of range - in its
own bounds check.  So there is a DOS data segment now, 256 bytes at
00004000h with the arena starting at 00004100h, exactly where DOS
keeps its own.  It costs a quarter of a kilobyte of a DOS box's
memory and it means every tool that computes a size by subtraction
gets a positive one.  (BOUND is vector 05, which on a PC is ALSO the
ROM's print-screen service, so a failed BOUND lands in the
print-screen routine, makes no progress, and v0.35's stuck-handler
guard ends the box.  Correct behaviour; it looks like a screen full
of garbage.)

WHERE IT STANDS.  MEM's summary is right: one region, Conventional
639K total / 17K used / 622K free, Upper and Reserved 0K, largest
executable program size 622K - which is the machine, and agrees with
PM-DOS's own MEM to the kilobyte.  Two things are still not right and
neither is a stopped machine:
  - MEM /C still floods and takes its BOUND, and a second pass with
    the source narrowed it without closing it.  WHAT IS KNOWN NOW:
    MEM finishes its walk and gets as far as PRINTING - piping it
    through MORE shows the header and the first module row, which is
    where it dies - and that row already says MSDOS is using 1,703,7xx
    bytes, more than the whole of low memory, against about 17K by
    hand from MEM's own five fixed rows plus our three system blocks.
    So the aggregate is wrong before any printing starts.  The call
    trace says the last sane thing MEM does is 21h/38h - it dies
    FORMATTING A NUMBER, which is what the country call is for - and
    then the ROM's print-screen handler starts making INT 17h calls,
    which is the BOUND being reflected.  After that MEM issues a 38h
    with DS:DX = 0000:00FC and PM-DOS dutifully writes 34 bytes over
    IVT entries 3Fh-45h; that is a corrupt guest scribbling on its own
    machine and real DOS would do it too, but it is why the box is
    strange afterwards and why MORE stops taking keys.
    Checked and NOT the cause: the MCB name field (fixed anyway, see
    below), the PSP (ours is zeroed, so MEM's GetFromArgvZero scan -
    which starts at the PSP, not the environment, and is unbounded -
    stops harmlessly), the device-driver chain walk, and the DOS data
    size subtraction.  mem.h is NOT in the 6.0 tree, so MEM's SYSVARS
    and ARENA struct offsets could not be checked against ours; that
    and the 1.7MB aggregate are where to start
  - AND ONE FIX THAT CAME OUT OF LOOKING: PM-DOS never wrote the
    EIGHT-BYTE NAME at MCB+8.  DOS 4 and later put the program's name
    there and every memory reporter prints it, so our listings named
    whichever program had last owned that memory.  lm_alloc clears it
    and lm_setname stamps the base name at load.  It did not fix /C
    and it was still wrong.
    The first version of it zeroed EAX to clear the field - the
    register holding the segment lm_alloc was about to RETURN - so
    every allocation came back as segment zero and the machine died on
    the first write through it.  Exactly the shape of the v0.30 3Ch
    that returned a timestamp for a handle: THE RETURN VALUE IS SET
    EARLY AND THE REGISTER LOOKS FREE
  - figures of a thousand or more print only their first group
    ("65,535K" as "65K", "(637,120 bytes)" as "(637 bytes)").  The
    country block is innocent (CTRYTEST), and the 6.0 source builds
    those particular strings with sprintf, which has no separator at
    all - so the shipped 6.22 differs from this source there and the
    answer is in msgserv.asm's $M_CONVERT2ASC or in a 6.22-only
    routine.  Cosmetic, and last in the queue
  Three things were ruled out by experiment and are not worth
  repeating: the country block, the EBDA kilobyte, and the size of
  the machine (16MB reports the same shape as 128MB).
  THE REFERENCE IS WORTH KEEPING: MEM622 runs under DOSBox's own DOS
  if it is told "ver set 6 22" and writes its output to a mounted
  host directory, so a known-good report - with UMBs and without -
  can be diffed against ours without an emulator screenshot at all.
  A no-UMB machine says Conventional 640K, Upper 0K, Reserved 384K,
  and "No upper memory available" to MEM /F.

IRQ 1 INTO THE DOS BOX - AND THE DEVICE BEHIND IT (2026-08-18)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
MSD takes a keystroke.  That was the pass/fail the roadmap named for
this piece and it is met: MSD comes up, probes the mouse, gets past
the empty floppy, opens its Memory panel from the keyboard, closes it
with Esc and quits with F3.

THE INTERRUPT WAS THE EASY HALF.  A guest that hooks INT 09h needs a
hardware interrupt delivered into V86, which is what v86_intctx
already does for a software one; the only new questions are WHEN and
WHOSE.

WHEN is three places, and it has to be all three:
  - THE IRQ ITSELF, when it interrupted the guest.  The frame the CPU
    pushed IS the guest's, VM bit and all, so rewriting CS:IP in it
    sends the guest to its handler instead of back where it was.  This
    is the case that matters: a program spinning on a flag its own
    handler sets makes no faults and no calls, so it is never seen
    anywhere else.  irq_common does it on the way out, with EBP set
    four bytes low so the existing FR_* offsets land on a frame that
    has no error code in it.
  - A RESUME OUT OF THE MONITOR.  This is how a key gets in promptly
    after a CLI has been holding it off, because the STI that ends the
    critical section is itself a fault and this runs on the way out of
    it.
  - AN ENTRY TO v86_run, for the interrupt that arrived while the DOS
    side had the CPU and there was no guest to interrupt at all.
And in all three the GUEST'S OWN interrupt flag decides, not the real
one - which is the whole reason IF is virtualised.

WHOSE is one comparison, made when the interrupt arrives: has this box
hooked INT 09h?  The ROM's vector is captured at boot, before anything
can have changed it.  If the slot still holds it, nothing changes at
all - the driver decodes the key into the buffer at 40:1E exactly as
v0.34 left it, which is every case that already worked.  If it does
not, the scan code is QUEUED instead and the interrupt is delivered,
and the guest's chain owns the whole keystroke: its handler reads port
60h, and if it chains on to the ROM's the ROM fills the ring.  ONE
CONSUMER PER KEYSTROKE, decided once.  Two decoders would produce two
keys, and the ring is shared with the shell.

THE LATCH IS THE PART THAT HAD TO BE RIGHT.  A real 8042 holds one
byte and goes on holding it: reading it does not take it away.  That
is not a detail, it is what makes a chained handler possible - the
resident program reads 60h, then jumps to the handler it replaced,
which reads 60h again and must get the SAME byte.  So the queue is
emptied one code per INT 09h DELIVERED, at the moment of delivery,
which is when the hardware would have latched it; everything the guest
reads between one interrupt and the next is that latch, as often as it
likes.  The status bit follows the same rule: set on delivery, cleared
by the read, because a careful handler checks there is a byte before
taking one.

AND THEN THE 8042 TURNED OUT TO BE THE REST OF THE JOB.  The first
version delivered the interrupt correctly and killed the keyboard -
not the box's, THE MACHINE'S, shell included.  The ROM's INT 09h does
not merely read the scan code, it TALKS BACK: it sends the lock lights
their command whenever the shift state changes.  Those writes went to
the real controller, the one this kernel is taking scan codes off and
standing in for on port 60h, so the two halves of one conversation
were happening on different devices.  The keyboard stopped scanning to
wait for a byte nobody was going to send it.

  THE GENERAL FORM, and it is the third time this project has met it:
  OWNING AN INTERRUPT MEANS OWNING THE DEVICE, NOT JUST THE VECTOR.
  v0.32 learned it for IRQ 0 and paid in the floppy motor and the tick
  count; v0.34 learned it for IRQ 1 and paid in the keyboard buffer.
  This is the same sentence one layer down: the buffer was the ROM's
  BOOKKEEPING, and the controller is the ROM's CONVERSATION, and
  taking the interrupt takes both.

The fix that followed was too broad by exactly one device.  Swallowing
every write to port 64h stops the keyboard being disturbed - and MSD
asks the ROM whether there is a PS/2 mouse, and the ROM answers by
sending D4h and then FFh, "reset, and that byte is for the AUXILIARY
device".  A monitor that treats every write to 60h as a keyboard
command replies with the keyboard's ACK to a question the mouse was
asked; the BIOS then waits for a self-test result that is never
coming, in a loop with no DOS call in it, and the box is gone.

  WHAT FOUND IT WAS A TRANSCRIPT.  Nothing else could have.  The call
  trace goes silent at exactly the moment the interesting thing starts
  - a guest spinning on a status bit issues no interrupts - and the
  spin sampler never fires either, because a loop full of IN
  instructions faults constantly and looks busy.  BUILD kbio prints
  the guest's side of the controller: writes as they come, reads only
  when the answer CHANGES.  Ten lines of it said D4h, FFh, and an ACK
  that came from the wrong device.
  (Its first version printed the port number as the value, because
  con_str and con_hex both work in EAX and the byte had not been put
  down first.  A trace that lies is worse than none; check a new one
  against something already known before believing it.)

SO THE LINE IS DRAWN COMMAND BY COMMAND: the keyboard is the kernel's
and the rest of the controller is still the box's.  Three refusals -
ADh and AEh, because a box may not switch the machine's keyboard off
any more than it may stop the machine's timer, and F0h-FFh, which
pulse the output lines and include the one that resets the CPU.  The
command byte goes through with IRQ 1 forced on and the keyboard-
disable bit forced off.  Everything else - the self tests, the aux
interface, D4h and its data byte - goes to the hardware it was
addressed to, and a reply the guest asked for comes back from the real
port rather than from our latch.

AND ONE MORE, WHICH ONLY EXISTS BECAUSE THE MOUSE NOW WORKS.  The 8042
has ONE output buffer and two devices behind it.  A mouse byte nobody
reads sits in it for ever with every scan code queued up behind it,
and IRQ 1 simply stops - PM-DOS masks IRQ 12 and has no use for mouse
packets, so once MSD had woken the mouse up, the next click killed the
keyboard.  The timer tick drains them now, only the ones flagged as
the auxiliary device's, in a bounded loop.  It is the same tick that
winds down the floppy motor, and for the same reason: this kernel took
the interrupts, so it inherited the housekeeping.

WHAT ELSE CHANGED, both small and both found on the way:
  - A HLT WITH INTERRUPTS ON IS NOT A STOPPED PROGRAM, it is one
    waiting for an interrupt - which is the canonical way to wait for
    a key without spinning.  vdm_halt ended the box for it, which was
    a defensible answer while there was nothing to wait FOR and is a
    poor joke now.  It idles and resumes past the HLT.  IF clear is
    still the end, and that is the honest end: an 8086 that halts with
    no way to be interrupted has genuinely stopped.
  - irq_common trusted EBX to survive the handler it called when it
    decided which PIC to acknowledge.  irq_keyboard does not preserve
    it - it leaves a scan code there - so "is this IRQ 8 or above" was
    really "was the last key pressed above 08h", and half the
    keystrokes on the machine were sending an EOI to a slave PIC with
    nothing in service.  Harmless, and wrong, and now read back off
    the stack.

INT9TEST.COM is new and asks the four separable questions: did the
handler run at all, was the scan code a real one, does reading port
60h twice give the same byte, and did the chain still fill 40:1E
afterwards.  It hooks and chains the way a resident program does, so
it is testing the arrangement and not just the delivery.  Interactive
and tick-bounded, like KBTEST, because the failure it exists for is a
program that sits there.

VERIFIED on 86Box: INT9TEST 4/4 with a clean run of make and break
codes (1E 9E 30 B0 2E AE 01 for a, b, c, Esc); KBTEST 5/5, unchanged;
MSD's full lifecycle; VDMTEST end to end; A20TEST and XMSTEST, which
matter because the A20 gate is reached through the ports this rewrote;
MCBTEST 5/5 and MEM 6.22 still reporting 639K/17K/622K on a fresh
boot.  Noticed here and fixed next: MSD leaves conventional memory
fragmented behind it, 604K free with a largest block of 309K.

A BLOCK OWNING ITSELF (2026-08-18)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
That fragmentation was a leak, and it was every 21h/48h a DOS box had
ever made.

lm_alloc leaves each block OWNING ITSELF.  For the case it was written
for that is exactly right: a program's own block has its PSP in the
first paragraph, so "owner = block + 1" IS the PSP.  But that is a
CONSEQUENCE of where the PSP happens to sit, and the code had it as
the rule - so memory a program merely ASKS for was stamped the same
way.  vdm_cleanup frees by PSP; a self-owned block never matches the
PSP that is terminating; the block stands there for the rest of the
session with nobody left who could free it.

The environment block has been corrected since the loader was written
- vdm_psp hands it to the PSP the moment there is one, with a comment
saying why - and THAT CORRECTION BEING INLINE AND UNNAMED is the whole
reason the identical one was never made for 48h.  A fix that is three
instructions in the middle of another routine teaches nobody.  It is
lm_setown now, so there is one place that says what owning means, and
both callers reach it by name.

The same three instructions were missing from DPMI 0100h, which is the
call a client makes for memory real-mode code can see.  Same shape,
same fix, found by looking rather than by failing.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, and it is worth the four lines.  MEM said 604K free
with a largest block of 309K, which reads like a memory-REPORTING bug
and was very nearly filed as one.  MCBTEST printed the chain and two
blocks were sitting in the middle of it that no program owned - and
they had EMPTY NAME FIELDS, which said immediately that they had not
come from the loader, because the loader stamps a name.  The MCB name
field was added on 2026-08-17 for MEM's sake and had not been thought
of as a diagnostic; it answered this in one screen.  (MCBTEST prints
it now.  It was printing segment, signature, owner and length, and the
owner word alone cannot answer "whose is this" for a block whose
program has gone: the number points at nothing.)

  THE OTHER HALF IS WHY NOBODY NOTICED FOR ELEVEN RELEASES.  A LEAK IS
  NOT AN ERROR MESSAGE.  Nothing fails, nothing prints, every test
  passes; it is a largest-free-block that quietly gets smaller, and it
  only becomes visible when some later program needs a big one and is
  told no.  The tests could not see it because each one runs on a
  freshly booted machine, which is the state where the bug has not
  happened yet.

TOOLS\ALLOCTST.ASM is the permanent answer to that.  It asks in ONE
run by being both halves: the parent measures the largest free block,
EXECs ITSELF with a tail saying "be the child", and measures again.
The child allocates two blocks and exits without freeing either, which
is what every real program does.  The two measurements must match.
Measuring is 48h with BX=FFFFh - the one call in DOS whose FAILURE is
the answer, since it cannot succeed and reports the largest run there
is.  Check 1 is the plain one it would be wrong to leave out: a block
asked for and freed by the SAME program comes back, which separates
"the sweep is broken" from "free is broken", two things that look
identical from outside.

  A trap the test walked into first: its child is a .COM, so DOS gives
  it every free paragraph, so its 48h was asking for memory it already
  held and was correctly refused.  The child shrinks with 4Ah first,
  as the parent already did for a different reason.  A test that fails
  because the TEST is wrong costs the same as a real failure and
  teaches less.

VERIFIED on 86Box: ALLOCTST 2/2; the MCB chain after MSD now identical
to a fresh boot, five blocks tiling to 9FC0; MEM 6.22 after MSD back
to 639K/17K/622K with 622K largest executable, which was 604K/309K;
the chain after DPMITEST clean too; VDMTEST end to end; XMSTEST;
MCBTEST 5/5.  And the one that matters in the other direction -
TSRTEST twice, where the resident copy's block must NOT be swept: it
survives, still owned by its PSP and still named, because vdm_cleanup
skips a program that went resident.

A REGISTER NOBODY RETURNS (2026-08-19)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
MEM /C works.  So does /D, and /F, and the thousands groups in every
figure MEM has ever printed here.  All of it was ONE missing
instruction, and it was not in the memory code at all.

    vdm_country loads EAX, EBX and EDX out of the guest's context
    before calling the kernel's 38h, and does not load ECX.

vdm_result copies EAX, EBX, ECX and EDX back into the guest.  So a
register that is not LOADED is not "left alone" - it is handed back
holding whatever the kernel last had in it, and the last thing to
touch ECX before the frame is built is the `rep movsb` that copies the
country block.  Every 21h/38h a DOS box made came back with CX = 0.

THAT IS WHY MEM'S NUMBERS WERE WRONG, and the path from one to the
other is worth writing down because nothing about it is guessable.
MS-DOS's message service formats a figure by dividing it down, pushing
the digits on the STACK, and counting them in CX - and $M_CONVERT2ASC
does not zero CX, it adds to whatever is there.  It also calls 38h for
the thousands separator on the way past.  So the count arrived
poisoned; the collector popped words that were never digits; and the
separator logic, which counts characters to decide where a comma goes,
placed them for a number two digits longer than the one it had.

  MSDOS      1,703,7[15][00]  and then four thousand NUL bytes

is 17,037 - the correct answer, which had been there all along - with
two stack words on the end of it and the commas at the positions of a
seven-digit number.  The four thousand NULs are the same count used as
a field width.  THE OTHER SYMPTOM, filed separately for two releases
as "cosmetic and unexplained" - 65,535K printing as 65K, (637,120
bytes) as (637 bytes) - is the same poisoned count landing the other
way, and it went out with the same instruction.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, because the route matters more than the fix:

  THE COUNTRY BLOCK WAS EXONERATED PROPERLY THIS TIME.  CTRYTEST
  checks the fields a program is documented to read and says ok six
  times, which is a test of what its author thought of.  TOOLS\
  CTRYDMP.ASM prints the block and NOTHING ELSE, so it can be run
  under DOSBox with "ver set 6 22" and under PM-DOS and diffed.  The
  two are identical through offset 23 - date format, the comma at 7,
  the full stop at 9, the currency symbol, the lot.  Only our own
  case-map pointer differs, and that we zero the reserved tail where
  real DOS leaves it untouched.
  So it printed the REGISTERS too, seeded with AA55h so that
  "untouched" is visible rather than inferred.  Real DOS came back
  AX=0001 BX=0001 CX=AA55; PM-DOS came back AX=3800 BX=0001 CX=0000.
  Two lines of output, and the question was answered.

  THE ARITHMETIC SAID SO FIRST AND I NEARLY THREW IT AWAY.  Adding up
  what MEM should attribute to PSP 8 by hand gives 17,037, and the
  screen said 1,703,7xx - the same five digits.  That looked too much
  like a coincidence to trust and too exact to ignore, and the thing
  that settled it was reading the FILE rather than the screen: the
  field is eight characters wide and ours fills it completely, where
  the reference has three spaces of padding.  A screenshot cannot show
  you a NUL.

THE GENERAL RULE, and it is the third form of a lesson this project
keeps meeting: A REGISTER THE SPECIFICATION CALLS UNDEFINED IS STILL
THE SAME VALUE EVERY TIME ON REAL DOS, AND SOMEBODY HAS BUILT ON IT.
"Undefined" describes the contract, not the machine.  PM-DOS is only
allowed to differ where real DOS differs from itself.

Two more of the same shape were fixed by looking rather than by
failing: 1Bh, 1Ch and 63h go through vd_go, which loaded only EAX and
EDX - 1Bh and 1Ch answer IN CX so the handler overwrites it, but 63h
does not, and a guest calling it was having its CX taken away by a
routine with no interest in it.  And 38h now returns the country code
in AX as well as BX, which is what 6.22 does; the books say "AX
destroyed", and what real DOS destroys it with is the answer.

TOOLS: scratchpad\fatget.ps1 reads a named file out of a FAT16 PM-DOS
image from the HOST, with no emulator running.  A guest that dies
mid-print has still written the file - PM-DOS closes a dead guest's
handles on cleanup - and eight kilobytes of output with control
characters in it is not something a scrolling TYPE can show.  It is
how the NULs were found.  (Watch the shell: a PowerShell function
named RD collides with the alias for Remove-Item.)

VERIFIED on 86Box: MEM 6.22 /C prints MSDOS 17,037 (17K) and Free
637,184 (622K) with the summary in full figures; /D prints all eleven
regions with the right names and sizes, agreeing with the hand
computation term by term; /F lists the three free blocks and says no
upper memory, as the DOSBox reference does.  No flood, no BOUND, and
the keyboard is alive afterwards - that symptom was the crash, not a
second bug.  Regressions: CTRYTEST 6/6, APITEST, DEVTEST, VDMTEST end
to end with DPMITEST, MCBTEST 5/5, ALLOCTST 2/2, INT9TEST 4/4, and
PM-DOS's own MEM unchanged.


THE REST OF THE CD-ROM LIST, EXCEPT EL TORITO (2026-09-12)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie asked for everything still open on the CD to be finished with
El Torito left for later, so this is the other five items and a bug
that only the finishing found.  They have nothing in common except
where they are, which is worth saying because it is the opposite of
the previous release: multi-session, Rock Ridge and CD audio were one
idea seen three ways, and these are five separate pieces of work.

150Fh - GET DIRECTORY ENTRY, AND THE SHAPE WAS READ OUT OF MSCDEX.EXE
ITSELF.  The note left last release said this call was chained on
purpose, because it is a FILESYSTEM question and a second reader of
its own is how two answers about one disc start to disagree.  That
argument was right and is still right, so what changed is the
implementation and not the reasoning: the path is resolved by THE SAME
resolve_parent and fat_search that 3Dh and 4Eh use, on the same
mounted volume, and the record handed back is the one that walk kept
in iso_lastrec.  There is still one reader; this call is a second
SHAPE for what it found.

  THE ABI WAS NOT REMEMBERED, IT WAS DISASSEMBLED.  A structure a
  program parses is not a place to be approximately right, and what
  was to hand is a real MSCDEX - 25,473 bytes of it in the PRESARIO
  backups.  TOOLS\UNDIS.PL disassembles a window of a raw binary, and
  the dispatch table for AH=15h gave itself away by its own
  repetitions: seventeen entries where 02h, 03h and 04h share one
  handler, and 06h and 07h share another, which is exactly the shape
  of "the three identifier fields" and "debugging on and off".  Its
  0Fh handler then says, in its own instructions, that the drive is in
  CL ALONE - CH is a flag on this call and a whole-CX read would
  refuse every letter - that the path is at ES:BX, that the buffer is
  at SI:DI with SI the SEGMENT, and that the answer is 3Bh bytes of
  fixed fields plus the system use area, with the both-endian pairs
  collapsed to their little halves and the version after the ';'
  lifted out into a word of its own.  Two fields could not be
  established from the binary and are written as zero rather than
  guessed at.  Errors are DOS's own numbers: 15 for the drive, 21 for
  not ready, and 2 and 3 for the file and the path.

ISO_FL_MULTI - A FILE IN MORE THAN ONE PIECE.  A file too big for one
extent is written as several directory records in a row, all with the
same name, the flag set on every one but the last.  The walk joins
them in iso_dirnext now, and THE RULE IS THE RECORDS' ORDER AND NOT
THEIR NAMES: the standard says the pieces follow each other, so "keep
going while the last record had the flag" needs no name comparison and
cannot be fooled by two files whose names match after a Joliet or Rock
Ridge rewrite.  The size is added up ONLY WHILE THE PIECES ARE
CONTIGUOUS and stops at the first gap, because everything above this
layer reads a file by running forward from one block: a total that
counted a piece somewhere else would be a promise the read path cannot
keep, and the file would read as whatever was recorded after the first
piece.

  THE TEST DISC HAD TO BE WRITTEN FOR IT, because the real article is
  over four gigabytes and nothing here would build one.  TOOLS\MKCD.PL
  grew a "split" attribute: the same structure at a size a test disc
  can hold, three extents of one file with the flag on the first two.
  bsdtar reads it as one file of 4159 bytes and so does PM-DOS, and
  the last line of the file is in the third extent, so a TYPE that
  reaches it has read all three.

RAW READS, AND THE BEST CHECK IN THE WHOLE CD-ROM TEST SET.  A raw
read hands back the 2352-byte FRAME - twelve bytes of sync, the header
that says which sector this is, the user data, and the error
correction behind it - and no block read can express one, so it is
built as a READ CD packet in MSCD001.INC.  What makes the test good is
that it needs to trust nothing: CDATEST reads THE SAME SECTOR twice,
cooked and raw, and checks that the frame begins with the sync pattern
that is on every disc ever pressed AND that the 2048 bytes at offset
16 of the frame are the cooked sector byte for byte.  A driver that
quietly served a cooked read when asked for a raw one fails both; one
that returned the right length of the wrong data fails the second.

THE DISC'S CATALOGUE NUMBER, which is the barcode on the back of a
pressed disc recorded in the Q sub-channel.  The drive answers with
thirteen ASCII digits and the control block wants packed BCD, so this
is a conversion rather than a copy - and most discs have none, which
the drive says in MCVal and which comes back as a field of zeros.
That is a pass and not a failure: it is what "there is not one" looks
like in a field that is always fourteen digits long.

THE R-W SUB-CHANNELS ARE STILL REFUSED, and the reason is the one
thing on this list that could not be grounded: MSCDEX passes IOCTL
input 13 through to the driver without reading it, so its own binary
does not describe the control block either, and no drive in reach
answers a request for de-interleaved R-W data.  A guessed structure
that a program writes its graphics into is worse than a refusal.

A REAL CODEPAGE TABLE, which the old note asked for in one line and
which turned out to matter more than it sounds.  A Joliet name is
UCS-2 and a Rock Ridge name is UTF-8, and both can say things this
machine's screen can show; folding everything above 7Eh to '_' threw
away the half that WAS spellable.  There is no arithmetic between
Unicode and codepage 437 above 7Eh - the 128 characters are four
alphabets, a currency set and the box drawing, in the order IBM put
them in a ROM in 1981 - so the mapping is a table and the lookup is a
scan.  The UTF-8 path decodes the whole character first, so one
character costs one output byte whether 437 can spell it or not.

  IT IS EXACT AND NOT APPROXIMATE, which is the one decision in it.
  "é" is 82h because 437 has an é at 82h; "ę" is not in 437 at all and
  stays an underscore.  A table that stripped accents to reach a
  letter would make two different files on one disc list under one
  name.  On the test disc: "café menu.txt", "naïve résumé ½.txt",
  "straße _uro.txt" - the sharp s is in 437 and the euro sign is not -
  and "α__ and ∞.txt", where alpha and infinity are in 437 and
  lower-case beta and gamma are not.  THE 8.3 FIELD STAYS ASCII: an
  alias exists to be TYPED, and this kernel's case folding is ASCII
  (cfg_upcase), so a high byte in an alias would be a name the user
  could not reliably reproduce.  (MS-DOS 6's own tables, in
  S:\DOS6SRC\dos\dostab.asm, DO fold the high half - 82h upcases to
  'E' - and answering 65h's table subfunctions with them is a separate
  job worth doing one day.)

UDF, WHICH IS A THIRD FILESYSTEM AND COST MORE THAN THE OTHER FOUR
TOGETHER.  DOS\UDF.INC, and the arrangement is the point: ISO9660
FIRST AND UDF ONLY WHEN THERE IS NO CD001, so every disc this kernel
has ever read is read by the code that read it before and the new path
is reached only by a disc the old one refused.

  WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE FROM ABOVE IS NOTHING.  The whole output of the
  file is the same thirty-two byte FAT directory entry ISO9660.INC
  synthesises, in the same buffer, through the same iso_entry
  dir_seek calls; vol_fs still says FS_ISO, because to the block layer
  that is exactly what this is - a read-only volume of 2048-byte
  blocks through IOS_CDREAD.  One flag says which of the two directory
  formats is underneath and it is read in three places.
  iso_label and iso_mkboth were lifted out of ISO9660.INC so both
  filesystems share them: reading the NAME is what the two disagree
  about, and everything after that is the same question.

  THE MOUNT IS FOUR POINTERS IN A ROW: the volume recognition sequence
  at block 16 says NSR02 or NSR03 where ISO9660 says CD001; the anchor
  at block 256 says where the volume descriptors are; the descriptors
  say where the PARTITION starts - every block number after this is
  counted from there - and where the FILE SET is; and the file set
  says which File Entry is the root directory.

  AND THE PART THAT IS GENUINELY DIFFERENT: A DIRECTORY RECORD DOES
  NOT DESCRIBE THE FILE.  It carries a name and a pointer to a File
  Entry somewhere else, and the size, the dates and the extents are
  all in that - so listing thirty files reads thirty extra blocks.
  That is not a shortcut this reader is missing, it is what the format
  is.  Two more differences worth writing down: a record MAY CROSS A
  BLOCK BOUNDARY, which is the exact opposite of ISO9660's rule and
  the trap waiting for anyone who writes the second reader with the
  first one's habits (the walk keeps a two-block window); and there
  are no "." and ".." records at all, so a subdirectory's first two
  entries are synthesised, one from the directory itself and one from
  the parent record UDF does keep.

  A UDF NAME IS A d-STRING whose FIRST byte says how wide its
  characters are - 8 for one byte, 16 for two, big-endian like Joliet
  - and Windows writes 16 for every name whatever is in it, so both
  forms have to be read.  Both go through the same iso_lchar and the
  same 437 table as everything else.

  WHAT IS REFUSED, and each refusal is in the file: virtual, sparable
  and metadata partition maps, which remap blocks through a table this
  reader does not have; allocation descriptors of the extended form;
  and EMBEDDED DATA - a file small enough to live inside its own File
  Entry - which is listed with a size of zero, because there is no
  block to give and a wrong one would read somebody else's bytes.

  THE TEST DISC IS NOT MINE, and that is deliberate.  TOOLS\MKUDF.PS1
  drives IMAPI2FS - Windows' own image builder, the thing that burns a
  disc from Explorer - with FileSystemsToCreate = 4, which is UDF and
  nothing else, so there is no ISO9660 bridge to fall back on.  The
  disc is therefore written by somebody other than the person who
  wrote the reader, which is the whole argument for an oracle, and
  Windows will mount it back: Mount-DiskImage says fs=UDF and lists
  the names and sizes PM-DOS has to match.  It does match, file for
  file and byte for byte.

AND THE BUG THE SECOND DRIVE FOUND, which is older than any of this.
ONE READER, MANY LETTERS: fat_ok and the rest of vol_state are kept
per letter and swapped, but ISO9660.INC's own state - the root extent,
the volume name, the session base, and now which directory format the
disc carries - is ONE SET OF GLOBALS.  It describes whichever CD
letter was touched last.  Nothing had ever shown it because this
machine has only ever had one CD-ROM drive; the moment there were two,
DIR H:, DIR I:, DIR H: listed the SECOND disc under the FIRST letter,
volume label and all, because fat_ok said H: was mounted and it WAS -
just not by the reader that was loaded.  iso_chkmedia now compares the
letter's ATAPI unit with the one the reader holds and re-mounts when
they differ, which costs a few block reads when a program alternates
between two discs.

  THE TEST RIG IS THE FIX'S OWN EVIDENCE and is worth keeping: a
  second CD-ROM in 86box.cfg on IDE 1:1, with a UDF disc in one drive
  and an ISO9660 one in the other.  Two filesystems, two letters, one
  boot, and switching between them in either direction.  It also
  turned the GUI disc-swap harness into an unnecessary risk - changing
  the disc under a running guest needs the mouse released from the
  emulator first (the middle button), which is a thing worth knowing
  and not a thing worth relying on.

VERIFIED ON 86Box, all of it:
  - CDATEST 00 failures on a mixed-mode disc AND on the UDF disc:
    tracks, play, the Q channel moving, stop and resume, the strategy
    and interrupt entries called directly, the catalogue number, the
    raw frame against the cooked sector, and 150Fh on the root and on
    a path that is not there
  - 150Fh's answer cross-checked against the host: the root's extent
    came back 00000123h, and the host-side dump of UDFTEST.ISO says
    the root directory's data is at block 291
  - DIR of the UDF disc matches Windows' own listing of it: seven
    entries, the same long names, the same sizes, "café menü.txt"
    spelled, a subdirectory walked into and a 14,576-byte file read to
    its last line
  - the split file lists ONCE at 4159 bytes on two different discs and
    TYPEs through to its third extent
  - the Rock Ridge disc still shows its real names, RR_MOVED still
    hides its relocated copy, and the two-session disc still reads
    session one's data through session two's directory
  - regressions: CDXTEST (now reporting two drives), IDETEST all
    checks with both packet devices on bus-master DMA mode 42,
    APITEST, LFNAPI


MULTI-SESSION, ROCK RIDGE AND CD AUDIO: THE CD-ROM AS A DISC RATHER
THAN AS A FILESYSTEM (2026-09-11)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Three things asked for together, and they turned out to be one piece
of work seen from three sides: everything left on the CD-ROM list
except El Torito needed the driver to know what a DISC is, rather than
what a filesystem on one is.

MULTI-SESSION, AND WHY THE BOOK'S ANSWER IS THE WRONG ONE HERE.  The
note this release started from said what every book says: READ
TOC/PMA/ATIP with format 1 answers "where does the last session
begin", so ask it and start the descriptor walk there.  The trouble is
what a drive that does not think in sessions answers - format 1 comes
back saying ONE session, track one, and says it in exactly the way a
disc that really has one session does.  86Box answers precisely that
for a disc it reports three tracks for in format 0.  A reader built on
format 1 alone is therefore correct on paper and wrong on the machine
it is being tested on, which is the worst of the two available ways to
be wrong.

So iso_findbase asks the question that was actually meant: WHERE IS
THE NEWEST ISO9660 VOLUME ON THIS DISC.  Read the whole table of
contents, walk the tracks BACKWARDS, skip the ones carrying music, and
take the first one with CD001 sixteen blocks into it.  On an ordinary
disc that is track one and the answer is zero - the same read every
disc got before.  On a disc appended to twice it is the last session.
On a CD Extra, whose first session is audio and whose block 16 is
therefore music, it is the data track a reader starting at 16 could
never see at all.  It is also more honest than format 1 in a way worth
keeping: a last session holding no filesystem is skipped rather than
mounted as nothing.

MEASURED, on the two-track disc TOOLS\MKCD.PL builds:

  Volume in drive is SESSION TWO
  BOTH.TXT  237   NEW.TXT  189   NEWDIR <DIR>

GONE.TXT, which exists only in session one, is correctly absent - that
is how a listing alone says which session is being read.  And TYPE
H:\BOTH.TXT prints session ONE's text through session TWO's directory,
which is the one fact the whole feature rests on: THE EXTENTS IN A
LATER SESSION ARE ABSOLUTE FROM THE START OF THE DISC, not relative to
the session.  A reader that quietly made them relative would produce
garbage rather than an error.  The second session sits at LBA 11425 -
past a real recorder's 11400-block lead-out, lead-in and pregap - so
the number cannot have been arrived at by accident.

ROCK RIDGE, WHICH IS ONE ROUTINE AND ONE PLACE TO PUT IT.  Names come
from iso_rawname and always did, so iso_susp reads the system use area
behind each directory record and iso_rawname prefers what it finds.
Joliet still wins where a disc has both, because that is the tree
Windows reads and the names a DOS user has seen for that disc; Rock
Ridge is the answer for the discs that have no Joliet at all.

What it does: NM names, including the ones split across several NM
entries AND continued into a CE area somewhere else on the disc; the
CL, RE and PL markers that say the tree was rearranged to fit inside
ISO9660's eight levels; and a character map, because a Rock Ridge name
is a UNIX name and may contain the characters DOS keeps for its own
syntax.  A UTF-8 character becomes ONE underscore rather than one per
byte.  RE is honoured by marking the synthesised entry E5h - every
walker above this layer already skips a deleted FAT entry, so a
relocated directory disappears from the listing without teaching any
of them what Rock Ridge is.

MEASURED, on RRTEST.ISO - the aliases with their real names beside
them, which is what the LFN layer gives for nothing:

  ARATHE~3.TXT   A Rather Long Unix File Name, With Spaces And ...
  CAF_ME~4.TXT   caf_ menu.txt
  MAKEFILE       Makefile
  SRCWIT~9 <DIR> src with spaces
  WHAT_~10.TXT   what_ and _.txt

The first of those is 230 characters and arrives in several NM entries
with the tail in a continuation area; the second is the UTF-8 fold.
On the shallow-relocation disc, DIR of ...\THREE shows FOUR as a
DIRECTORY although the record on the disc is a file record (that is
CL), walking into it lists its file, and \RR_MOVED shows only "." and
".." (that is RE).

PL IS HONOURED AND CANNOT CURRENTLY BE OBSERVED, which is worth
writing down rather than claiming as tested: resolve_core folds ".."
textually before any directory is read, so the ".." record's extent is
never followed by this kernel.  The entry is applied in iso_entry
anyway, for the day something does follow it.

CD AUDIO, AND THE DEVICE THAT HAD TO EXIST BEFORE IT COULD.  Every
audio call a DOS program makes - play, stop, resume, where is the
head, what is on this disc - is an MSCDEX 1510h request aimed at a
DEVICE DRIVER.  There is no other route to audio: the audio API IS the
device interface.  So the gap MSCDEX.INC left deliberately open a
release ago had to be closed first, and closed the way that note said:
a real character device named MSCD001, served by the kernel, linked
into the chain behind NUL.

HOW A GUEST REACHES 32-BIT CODE is the only new machinery in it, and
it is not new at all: the header's strategy and interrupt entries are
two bytes each of guest memory holding HLT and RETF, recognised by
ADDRESS in the VM loop exactly as the XMS entry point and the DPMI
mode switch have been for releases.  A program that finds the driver
through 1501h and calls it directly is served; 1510h is answered by
running the same handler without the round trip, which is what MSCDEX
itself did.

PMIO CARRIES PACKETS AND PMDOS DECIDES WHAT THEY SAY.  IOS_CDPKT is a
passthrough: AL a unit, ESI twelve bytes, EDI a buffer.  Everything a
CD needs beyond reading blocks - the table of contents, playing audio,
the Q channel, locking the tray, the audio volume - is a SCSI command
block and nothing else, and the code that knows WHY it is asking is
the device over in PMDOS.  It is always PIO: every reply that comes
that way is tens of bytes, and arming a bus master to move them costs
more than moving them.  The block reads worth a DMA transfer still go
through IOS_CDREAD, which decides per transfer.

THE TRAP THAT CAME WITH IT, and it would have been a quiet one.  A
drive reports "the medium may have changed" exactly ONCE, as a sense
condition on the next command it is given, and being told CLEARS it.
While the volume layer was the only thing that ever spoke to a CD that
was safe by luck.  It is not safe now: a program polling the Q channel
through the MSCDEX API can easily be the command the drive reports the
change on, and the volume layer would carry on using the extents of a
disc that is no longer in the drive.  So the report is caught in
atapi_note, where every failed command passes, and kept as ONE BIT PER
LISTENER until that listener asks - IOS_CDCHG now takes a CDL_ bit in
AH saying who is asking.  PMIO does not know who the listeners are; it
keeps the bits and hands each one back once.

MEASURED, by TOOLS\CDATEST.ASM on the mixed-mode disc - data track
first and music after, which is what a game with CD music is:

  1501h  driver list says MSCD001: ok
  15h/06 device status:   00000312 ok
  15h/07 sector size:     2048 ok
  15h/10 tracks:          01-03  lead-out 00:39:23 ok
    track 01 00:02:00 data / 02 00:04:23 audio / 03 00:24:23 audio
  play   audio track 02: ok
  15h/12 Q channel: 00:04:23 ... a second later: 00:04:38 ok
  status busy while playing: ok
  133 stop, then paused: ok    136 resume, and moving: ok
  133x2 stopped for good: ok
  device strategy+interrupt called directly: ok

The Q channel moving is the only check there that a merely polite
driver cannot pass: the drive has to be really playing for the
position to advance.

THE TEST DISCS HAD TO BE BUILT, and that is TOOLS\MKCD.PL - an
ISO9660 writer, because nothing on this machine can make any of the
three discs this release needed.  IMAPI2FS (which MKISO.PS1 uses, and
which is the right tool for a Joliet disc) has never written Rock
Ridge; a second session is a property of the DISC rather than of a
file, so no .iso writer can express one; and an audio track is not a
filesystem at all.  It writes Rock Ridge, relocation, multi-session
tracks with the real 11400-block gap, audio tracks as raw PCM, and
.CUE sheets so 86Box can mount a disc with more than one thing on it.

THE ORACLE IS NOT THAT SCRIPT.  Windows ships bsdtar as tar.exe and
libarchive reads Rock Ridge - names, continuations, relocation - so
"tar -tvf" over the image is an independent reading of it, the same
discipline TOOLS\ISODUMP.PL provides on the ISO9660 side.  It earned
its keep immediately: the first RRTEST.ISO listed its MANGLED 8.3
names under bsdtar, because the writer put PX before SP in the root's
"." record.  SP MUST BE THE FIRST SYSTEM USE ENTRY THERE - it is the
whole protocol's handshake, and an SP written second is an SP that is
never found.  The reader then made the same mistake from the other
end, looking for SP one byte late: a pad byte follows an identifier of
EVEN length, and the root's is one byte long.  Two independent
one-byte mistakes about the same handshake, found by two independent
readers, which is the argument for having both.

TWO BUGS FOUND THAT WERE NOT IN THIS WORK.

COMMAND.COM COULD NOT CHANGE TO THE CD'S OWN LETTER.  Typing H: said
"Bad command or file name" while DIR H: worked perfectly, and the
reason was four: "cmp dl,4", written when four letters was all there
were.  LASTDRIVE has been 16 since the CD-ROM release.  The letter was
never the thing to check - 21h/0Eh mounts the volume or leaves the
current drive alone and 19h says which happened, which is the check
that was already there underneath it.

DIR OF A DIRECTORY EIGHT COMPONENTS DEEP FAILS, and this one is NOT
fixed.  MAX_DEPTH is 8 and resolve_core enforces it correctly, but DIR
appends its own "*.*" as a ninth component, so the effective limit for
a listing is seven directories.  It is exactly where ISO9660's own
eight-level limit puts a relocated directory, which is why the CL
markers had to be tested on a disc that relocates at the fourth level
instead.  Worth raising MAX_DEPTH one day; it is a FAT-side limit and
nothing to do with CD-ROM.

REGRESSIONS after all of it: CDXTEST every check (the MSCDEX API is
unchanged by the session base on a single-session disc - 1505h and
1508h still agree byte for byte), LFNAPI all probes, APITEST all
checks, IDETEST all checks including "packet 2: bus-master DMA, mode
42", and DIR of the Joliet disc unchanged.

IN PROGRESS - THE MSCDEX API WITHOUT MSCDEX, AND A DISK WHOSE ROOT IS
ONLY PM-DOS
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Two things, and the first one was a question Charlie asked rather than
a bug report: "are we telling external applications that MSCDEX is
loaded so that the user doesn't try to load it again?"  We were not.

DO WE NEED OUR OWN MSCDEX.EXE?  No, and writing one would be a step
backwards.  MSCDEX is a REDIRECTOR CLIENT: it exists because DOS had
no way to put a non-FAT filesystem behind a drive letter, so the
letter had to be faked by the network layer.  This kernel's founding
idea is that a letter is a VOLUME and vol_fs says which filesystem is
behind it, so the CD already has a real drive letter with no
redirector anywhere.  Building MSCDEX.EXE would mean building the
redirector interface we deliberately do not have, in order to route
around machinery that already works.

WHAT PROGRAMS NEED IS THE API, NOT THE PROGRAM.  A DOS-box game or
installer does not care how the letter came to exist; it asks INT 2Fh
AX=1500h whether a CD driver is loaded, and if nobody answers it
concludes the machine has no CD-ROM and refuses to install.  So
DOS\MSCDEX.INC answers the family out of the volume table the scan
already built, from inside the V86 monitor's own 2Fh chain, next to
the XMS and DPMI handlers.

AND THE ANSWER WAS ALREADY CORRECT BY ACCIDENT, which is worth
recording because it is the third time this tree has found that shape.
The installation check is "set BX to zero, call, and read installed
from BX having CHANGED"; 2Fh is in vdm_stublist, so it landed on an
IRET, so BX stayed zero, so every guest correctly concluded there was
no CD driver.  Right answer, no reason.  The same was true of Windows'
1600h/160Ah/4680h/1680h before WINDOWS.INC claimed them, and the
argument for claiming them is the same: the answer stops depending on
the stub still being an IRET, and a guest TSR that hooked 2Fh cannot
answer on PM-DOS's behalf and get it wrong.

WHAT IS ANSWERED:

    1500h  how many CD letters, and the first one
    1502h  copyright file name        \  the three 37-byte identifier
    1503h  abstract file name          }  fields at the end of a
    1504h  bibliographic file name    /   primary volume descriptor
    1505h  read a volume descriptor by index
    1506h  debugging on   \  no-ops that report success: there is no
    1507h  debugging off  /  driver, so there is no debugging in it
    1508h  absolute sector read
    1509h  absolute sector WRITE - refused, as every real MSCDEX
           refused it on every drive anybody ever had
    150Bh  is this drive one of ours?  BX=ADADh either way
    150Ch  version - 2.25, the last one and the one every program was
           written against
    150Dh  the drive letters, one byte each

WHAT IS CHAINED, AND THE LINE IS DRAWN ON PURPOSE: 1501h (the device
driver header list), 150Fh (get directory entry) and 1510h (send a
device request).  All three hand the caller a DEVICE DRIVER to talk
to, and there is not one.  A SYNTHETIC HEADER WOULD BE WORSE THAN
SILENCE: it invites a program to CALL a strategy and interrupt routine
that do not exist, and a request packet that is never marked done
hangs the caller in a wait loop rather than failing.  Chaining leaves
the IRET stub to answer, which is the same "no" the machine gave
before, and the program falls back to file calls on the drive letter -
which work perfectly here.

The right way to close that gap is a REAL character device named
MSCD001 in the device chain DEVLOAD.INC already has, served by the
kernel; then 1501h has a genuine header to hand out and 1510h has
somewhere to send a packet.  That is a piece of work, not a patch.

  [SUPERSEDED 2026-09-11.  It was done, because CD AUDIO could not be
  done without it - the audio API IS the device interface.  1501h and
  1510h are answered now and only 150Fh still chains.  See the
  multi-session/Rock Ridge/CD audio entry above.]

IF THERE ARE NO CD LETTERS WE ARE NOT MSCDEX and every call chains.
One test at the top, and it is the honest answer: a machine with no
CD-ROM has no CD-ROM extensions on it either.

TWO DETAILS WORTH KEEPING.  The guest's CARRY is cleared ONCE, before
the dispatch, rather than in each answer - this family reports failure
in CF the way a DOS call does, and a subfunction that succeeds without
clearing it hands back whatever flag the caller arrived carrying.
And 1508h's count is checked against the BUFFER and not against the
disc, which is buf_ok's lesson from another direction: the guest is
naming a length, and a guest that names a big one while pointing
somewhere legal is exactly the case a check on the pointer alone lets
through.  It is capped at 32 blocks, which is all an ES:BX buffer can
hold before BX wraps.

PROVED BY TOOLS\CDXTEST.ASM, which is SIXTEEN-BIT ON PURPOSE and that
is the whole point of it: the API is answered out of the V86 monitor's
2Fh chain, so a 32-bit native program cannot reach that path at all
and a guest is the only place it can be asked from.  Nine checks, in
the order a real installer makes them, and two of them are the ones
that matter:

  - 150Bh ON C:, which must answer ADADh AND NO.  A shim that said
    yes to every letter would pass every other check in the program
  - 1505h AND 1508h COMPARED BYTE FOR BYTE.  Block 16 is both "the
    first volume descriptor" and "sector 16", so the two calls have to
    return identical buffers; if they do not then one of them is
    addressing the disc wrongly and it does not matter which

All nine pass on the 86Box machine with a disc in the drive: one
drive at H:, version 2.25, C: correctly not a CD, both reads
identical, the write refused.


THE DISK'S ROOT IS NOW ONLY PM-DOS
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie asked for BIN\ to be cleaned up "for use with actual programs
that we will include in PM-DOS", with the test programs somewhere
else.  Both halves were done, and the disk half matters more than it
sounds: the root of a PM-DOS disk had about sixty files in it and
fewer than fifteen of them were PM-DOS.

    BIN\           what a PM-DOS disk is MADE OF - the boot sectors,
                   the kernel, COMMAND.COM, and the commands
    BIN\TESTS\     everything written to prove one thing about it

THE SPLIT IS BY WHAT SHIPS, NOT BY WHAT MOVES, and that is deliberate:
the list in the build names the twenty-five things that STAY, so a new
test program added next month lands in TESTS by default - the safe
direction to be wrong in - and adding a new COMMAND means having to
say so.

MKDISK.EXE GREW A "-dir NAME" SWITCH to do the same on the images.
Everything after it in the file list lands in that subdirectory; one
level only, because nesting wants a stack and nothing here needs one.
Both the floppy and the hard-disk builders have it, and both allocate
the directory's clusters CONTIGUOUSLY even under -frag - -frag exists
to make a loader that reads straight through instead of following the
chain produce garbage, and a directory is not what that test is about.

Two things stay in the root whatever -dir was last set: CONFIG.SYS and
AUTOEXEC.BAT, because DOS looks for them there, and the long-named LFN
fixtures, because LFNTEST.BAT does.

C:\TESTS WENT ON THE PATH, so every test still runs by bare name and
none of the commentary in AUTOEXEC.BAT had to change.  What did have
to change is the handful of places that named a moved file with an
EXPLICIT path - BATTEST's "CALL \SUB.BAT", BIG16's "C:\HELLOX.EXE",
AUTOEXEC's "PARKTEST \RMFIND.COM", and the three commented DEVICE= and
INSTALLHIGH= lines in CONFIG.SYS.

DIR C:\ now prints fifteen files: COMMAND.COM, the seven commands,
RMDOS.SYS, README.TXT, CONFIG.SYS, AUTOEXEC.BAT, TESTS <DIR> and the
two long-named fixtures.  PMIO.SYS and PMDOS.SYS are there and hidden,
which is what the system attribute is for.

ONE TRAP WORTH RECORDING, because it cost a restore-from-backup: the
script that reordered the file lists looked for "TOOLS\MKDISK.EXE"
anywhere, and MKHD.CMD has "if not exist TOOLS\MKDISK.EXE goto
nobuild" forty lines above the real invocation.  It treated the guard
as the start of a command and folded every line between it and the
first "|| goto" into one.  ONLY A COMMAND AT THE START OF A LINE IS A
COMMAND, and a script that rewrites build files has to know that.

Regressions after the split: APITEST every check, IDETEST all checks,
LFNAPI all six probes, CDXTEST all nine - every one of them run from
\TESTS through the PATH.

AND THEN DRIVES.EXE WENT WITH THEM, because Charlie read the list and
said he had not planned on having it.  He is right, and the reason is
worth writing down rather than just doing: PM-DOS SHIPS WHAT DOS
SHIPPED, and DOS never had a DRIVES.  It was written to check the
volume table while the volume table was being written, which makes it
a DIAGNOSTIC, and diagnostics live in \TESTS.

What it prints is not lost.  The DISK-side view of the same facts is
FDISK /L, which is a real DOS command and already lists the partitions
with the letter each one became.  What DRIVES adds is the LETTER-side
view and the letters no partition table explains - a CD-ROM, a RAM
disk a block driver made, a floppy - plus the FAT the volume really
turned out to be against the type byte that claims it.  That is a
diagnostic's question, so it is a diagnostic's program.

MKDISK.EXE WAS NEVER IN THE DISTRIBUTION AT ALL, which is the other
half of the same reading.  It is a HOST program - wcl386 -bt=nt, a
Win32 console tool in TOOLS\ next to MKMULTI and FSIZE - and it is the
