thing that BUILDS the images.  It appears in BUILD.CMD and MKHD.CMD as
the command being run, never in a file list, so nothing ever copied it
onto a PM-DOS disk.  Worth being able to say quickly: what ships is
BIN\ plus what the "-dir TESTS" switch puts in TESTS, and TOOLS\ is the
workshop.

Verified on the machine after the move: DIR C:\ lists fifteen files
with no DRIVES.EXE among them, DRIVES still runs by bare name out of
\TESTS through the PATH and prints all eight letters including the
CD-ROM at H:, and FDISK /L prints both disks and the extended chain.

AND THE IMAGES WENT OUT OF BIN\ TOO (2026-09-11), which finishes the
same reading rather than adding a new one.  BIN\ is what a disk is
MADE OF; a disk image is not an ingredient of anything, it is the
FINISHED MEDIA - and eight of them, 300MB, were sitting in a directory
whose other twenty entries are all a few kilobytes.  They live in
IMAGES\ now:

    IMAGES\PMDOS.IMG      the bootable 1.44M floppy (BUILD.CMD) - and
    IMAGES\TESTS.IMG      the tests, on a floppy of their own since
                          2026-10-08 (BUILD.CMD too)
    IMAGES\HD16.IMG       32MB FAT16, bootable      \
    IMAGES\HD32.IMG       40MB FAT32, bootable       } MKHD.CMD
    IMAGES\MULTI.IMG      the multi-partition disk  /
    IMAGES\HDBIG.IMG      80MB/16K clusters - the FAT16 ceiling disk
    IMAGES\BLANK16.IMG    formatted, empty, kept to copy from
    IMAGES\BLANK32.IMG       "       "      "    "   "     "
    IMAGES\PMDOSFDD.IMG   a BUILD fdd floppy, kept for the 486

THE ONE THING THAT HAD TO BE ADDED RATHER THAN RENAMED is the mkdir.
MKDISK.EXE and MKMULTI.EXE write the file they are given and do not
create its directory, and IMAGES\ is in .gitignore like BIN\ is, so a
fresh clone has no such directory and the first build would have
failed on a path rather than on anything real.  Both scripts make it,
because MKHD.CMD is run on its own as often as after a BUILD.

Everything else was a path in a comment or an echo.  Entries dated
before today say BIN\HD16.IMG and BIN\PMDOS.IMG and mean IMAGES\; the
layout section near the end of this file has been corrected, and so
have the imgmount recipes and the 86Box "copy it into the VM
directory" trap, because those are read as INSTRUCTIONS rather than as
history.  CD images are not in here: MKCD.PL's discs and the ISOs live
in S:\Software\PMDOSCD because that is where the emulator's config
points at them, outside the tree entirely.


IN PROGRESS - FDISK: A PARTITION EDITOR THAT CAN RESIZE AND MOVE, AND
THE TWO BUGS THE PORT FOUND IN THE ENGINE IT WAS PORTED FROM
---------------------------------------------------------------------

CMD\FDISK.ASM, and it is the first PM-DOS program that can destroy the
machine it runs on.  Charlie asked for it with two requirements up
front: it must RESIZE, EXTEND and MOVE partitions and refuse anything
that would violate the rules of the filesystem inside, and EVERYTHING
IS TO BE PORTED TO 32-BIT.  The engine already existed - SAFEPART at
S:\CPP\NEWDEV\SAFEPART, RELOCATE.CPP and FATVOL.CPP, 16-bit DOS C++
for Open Watcom 1.9 - and the decision on 2026-09-08 was to build on
it rather than write fresh, because its being runtime-untested is a
reason to test it.

Which is exactly what happened.  See "WHAT THE PORT FOUND" below.

THE KERNEL HAD NO WAY TO REACH A DISK, and that is the first thing
this needed.  INT 25h and 26h exist and are the obvious answer and are
the wrong one: they address a DRIVE LETTER, which in this kernel means
a VOLUME, and the sector a partition editor most needs - LBA 0, the
table itself - lies outside every letter on the machine.  An API that
begins by naming a volume cannot reach the thing volumes live on.  So
three new subfunctions, all in the F1h family where the kernel's own
reports live:

    F1h AL=0Ch  DL = a BIOS drive, EDI -> a DSK_LEN record.  That
                PHYSICAL DISK - its CHS geometry, its true capacity,
                and how far CHS can reach on it.  ECX = how many disks
                there can be
    F1h AL=0Dh  DL = drive, EBX = LBA, ECX = sectors, EDI -> buffer.
                Raw sectors off it, LBA 0 included
    F1h AL=0Eh  the same registers, written back

DSK_CHS AND DSK_TOTAL ARE BOTH REPORTED and that is not redundancy.
They agree on a small disk and part company on a large one, and a
partition table built from the wrong one is a table the BIOS cannot
boot.  IOS_DRVGEO already answered one and IOS_DRVPARM the other; what
was missing was a way for a program at ring 3 to ask either.

The count is capped at ABS_MAXSEC and measured with cbuf_ok, which is
the buf_ok lesson again from a new direction: the pointer is checked
by r3_xlat and the LENGTH is the hole.  A caller may point somewhere
perfectly legal and ask for thirty-two megabytes of it.

A LETTER'S CACHED STATE IS NOT INVALIDATED by any of the three, and
must not be.  F1h AL=2 already exists for that and takes a letter,
which is the right granularity: a raw write cannot know which volumes
the sector belonged to, and guessing would either throw away every
mounted volume in the machine for a write to unallocated space or miss
the one that mattered.  FDISK says REBOOT, because a partition table
change means the drive letters themselves are wrong.

WHAT IT DOES
---------------------------------------------------------------------

    FDISK           every disk's partition table
    FDISK /L        ...and the logical drives in the extended chain
    FDISK /P d:p    one partition: its BPB, what is stored in it, and
                    how far it can be shrunk, grown or moved
    FDISK /M d:p n  move it so that it starts at sector n
    FDISK /S d:p n  resize it to n sectors, or n MB written 40M
    ...add /W       and it happens

NOTHING IS WRITTEN WITHOUT /W - SAFEPART's DiskArmWrites gate, kept,
and worth more here than there.  A run without it walks every check,
prints exactly what it would have done, and is physically unable to
touch a sector because the write path refuses unarmed.  That is what
made it possible to develop this against real partition tables at all.

THE EXTENDED CHAIN WALK is the fiddly half of the report and the
reason /L is a switch rather than the default.  The two start fields
in an extended boot record are relative to DIFFERENT THINGS: slot 0's
is relative to the record holding it, slot 1's - the pointer to the
next record - is relative to the FIRST extended record, the one the
MBR named.  Getting that wrong produces a walk that drifts a little
further each step and eventually reads a sector belonging to nobody.
It was checked against MKMULTI.EXE's own printed numbers: 91854,
124173 and 156492, all three exact, and the hidden volume correctly
given no drive letter because hiding one is a request.

THE SAFETY MODEL, AND THE ONE DELIBERATE DEVIATION
---------------------------------------------------------------------

SAME-LAYOUT means the cluster size and the FAT width are unchanged, so
CLUSTER NUMBERS SURVIVE.  Cluster 5000 is still cluster 5000 when the
volume has finished moving, so every chain in the FAT is still right,
every directory entry's starting cluster is still right, and not one
byte of file data or directory content has to be rewritten or even
understood.  The engine moves three regions and lays down a new BPB.

The other regime - where the cluster size must change - renumbers
everything and would have to rebuild every chain and rewrite every
directory entry recursively.  SAFEPART has that code and refuses to
run it against a live volume because it has never been proven against
images.  This port does not carry it at all: rl_plan answers RL_REMAP
and says what it would take.

AND HERE IS THE DEVIATION.  SAFEPART always PREFERS the smallest
cluster size, which means nearly every resize it plans lands in the
remap regime - and then RelocExecute refuses that regime.  So the
answer to "shrink this by 100MB" is usually "not supported" even
though a perfectly safe same-layout shrink was available the whole
time.  Its fallback only fires when the remap engine declines with
NEED_DEFRAG, not when the regime is refused outright.

Here the preference is INVERTED: keep the volume's current cluster
size whenever it is still legal and the data still fits, because that
is the regime in which nothing has to be rewritten.  The smallest-
cluster geometry is still computed and still REPORTED, as information
about what a rebuild would achieve.  It is not what the executor is
pointed at.

THE ORDER OF THE THREE REGIONS is the whole correctness argument for a
resize, because the new positions overlap the old ones - the volume
starts in the same place and only the FAT changed length, so
everything after it slides.

    GROWING: the data moves RIGHT into space being freed behind it, so
    it is copied BACK-TO-FRONT and BEFORE the FATs, which grow
    rightward over sectors the old data still occupies
    SHRINKING: everything moves LEFT, so the FATs go down FIRST - they
    now end to the left of where the old root began - and the root and
    data follow, FRONT-TO-BACK

rl_copy picks its direction from the sign of the move, so each of
those is one call.  A move AND resize at once whose ranges overlap is
REFUSED rather than attempted: SAFEPART hands that case to a simulator
that walks the whole copy against a bitmap of already-written sectors,
and a refusal that is understood is worth more than a rebuild that is
hoped for.  Two steps do it.

WHAT THE REFUSALS ARE, because they are the feature Charlie asked for:

    TOOSMALL   something is stored above the proposed new end.  NOT
               "the volume is too full" - the question is where the
               LAST occupied cluster is, so a volume one percent full
               with one file at the top cannot shrink at all
    REMAP      the new size cannot be expressed at this cluster size
    FATTYPE    the cluster count would cross FAT12/FAT16
    OVERLAP    it would run into the partition next to it
    BOUNDS     off the disk, or over the master boot record

Every one of them prints what to do next.  "Cannot shrink" tells
somebody they are stuck; "something is stored above the new end, and
/P says how far down it goes" tells them to defragment and retry.

WHAT THE PORT FOUND - TWO BUGS IN SAFEPART'S GEOMETRY
---------------------------------------------------------------------

THE SECTORS-PER-FAT ESTIMATE IS WRONG FOR BOTH FAT WIDTHS, and it was
found by shrinking a real volume and reading the number back.

The FAT specification's formula is

    TmpVal1 = DskSize - (ResvdSecCnt + RootDirSectors)
    TmpVal2 = (256 * SecPerClus) + NumFATs
    if (FAT32) TmpVal2 = TmpVal2 / 2
    FATSz   = ceil( TmpVal1 / TmpVal2 )

and THE HALVING IS FAT32'S, NOT FAT16'S: the 256 is already 512/2, one
sector's worth of two-byte entries.  SAFEPART halves it for FAT16,
which doubles the FAT.  On a 40000-sector volume that is 156 sectors
where 78 is right.

WHICH IS HOW IT WAS NOTICED.  A SHRINK MOVED ITS DATA REGION TO THE
RIGHT.  Shrinking 67536 sectors to 40000 should make the FAT smaller
and pull everything left; instead the FAT went from 132 sectors to
156, the data region moved right, and the screen printed the GROWING
order - data, root, FATs - for an operation called a shrink.  The
volume that resulted was internally consistent and perfectly readable,
because an oversized FAT is legal and the cluster count derived from
it is honest.  It simply wasted 156 sectors and moved data that had no
need to move.  Corrected: 19827 clusters became 19905, and the order
became FATs, root, data.

FAT12 IS WRONG THE SAME WAY.  Setting FATSz*(512/1.5)*spc = t1 -
nfats*FATSz gives FATSz = 3*t1 / (1024*spc + 3*nfats).  SAFEPART uses
(256*spc + nfats)*2/3, about half the divisor, so its FAT12 FAT comes
out roughly twice the size as well.  Checked against MKMULTI's FAT12
volume: 16128 sectors, spc=4, and the corrected form gives 12 sectors
per FAT, which is what is on the disk.

THE ESTIMATE IS AN APPROXIMATION AND NOTHING CHECKED IT.  The
specification says as much, and an approximation that lands one sector
SHORT is a FAT with no room for its own last entries - which is not
waste, it is corruption.  So fg_forspc now SETTLES: it derives the
cluster count from the FAT it estimated, asks how many sectors that
count really needs (clusters PLUS TWO, because entries 0 and 1 are the
media byte and the end-of-chain marker and are not clusters), and if
the FAT is short it grows it to exactly that and derives again.
Growing shrinks the count, which shrinks the requirement, so it cannot
oscillate - and it is bounded anyway, because a loop deciding how big
to make a FAT is not a loop to leave unbounded.

AND A THIRD, SMALLER ONE: t1 = tot - (reserved + root) is computed in
unsigned arithmetic with nothing checking that tot is the larger.  A
target smaller than the volume's own fixed overhead makes it negative,
negative is enormous, and the estimate comes back as a FAT of hundreds
of thousands of sectors that every check downstream passes.  Guarded.

ONE MORE DEVIATION, DELIBERATE: MbrPack repacks all four table
entries' CHS fields from the geometry.  This port rewrites only the
entry it was asked about.  A partition editor that quietly "corrects"
a neighbour's bytes as a side effect of touching this one has done
something the user cannot see and did not ask for.

WHAT WAS PROVED, AND HOW
---------------------------------------------------------------------

MULTI.IMG, the second disk in the 86Box machine: two primaries, a
Linux partition, and an extended chain with two logical drives and a
hidden one.  MKHD.CMD rebuilds it from scratch, so anything done to it
is undone by a rebuild - which is what makes it the thing to practise
on.

D: was filled with real files first - COMMAND.COM, PMDOS.SYS, MEM.EXE
and MKMULTI's own PRIM1.TXT, 184153 bytes - because a resize engine
tested on an empty volume has not been tested.  Then, each with a
reboot and a re-read in between:

    SHRINK   67536 -> 40000 sectors.  Four files intact, byte counts
             identical, PRIM1.TXT still reads, and the type byte
             correctly changed 06h -> 04h, which is the rule that a
             FAT16 volume under 32MB carries 04h and one over it 06h.
             A BIOS that meets a type byte promising CHS addressing
             for sectors CHS cannot reach will read the wrong place
             and be certain it is right
    MOVE     start 63 -> 20000, 40000 sectors copied in 313 chunks.
             Still mounts as D:, still labelled PRIMARY-ONE, all four
             files intact, PRIM1.TXT still reads
    GROW     40000 -> 47000 sectors, sectors/FAT 78 -> 92, free space
             up from 20196352 to 23766016 bytes.  Same four files

So the volume was moved, shrunk and grown in three separate
operations, rebooted between each, and read correctly every time.

The limits /P reports were checked by hand: with 364 sectors in use at
2 sectors a cluster it says the volume can shrink to 399 sectors,
which is 1 reserved + 2 FATs of 1 + 32 root + 364 data, and 364/2 is
the 182 clusters that are needed.  Room at the new start is 47599,
which is 67599 - 20000 - the next partition, not the end of the disk.

Regressions: APITEST every check, IDETEST all checks with both disks
on bus-master DMA mode 42 and 32-bit PIO and the packet device with
them, LFNAPI all six probes.

WHAT IS NOT DONE
---------------------------------------------------------------------

* [DONE 2026-09-20 - CREATE and DELETE, /C and /D, and SET ACTIVE
  with /A.  Cylinder alignment came with them: the start goes up to a
  boundary and the end goes down to one, with the first track's
  exception.  See the v0.60 entry, and FDTEST.BAT.]
* [DONE 2026-09-21 - CYLINDER ALIGNMENT IS REPORTED NOW as well as
  written: a star in the report for a partition that does not begin
  and end on a boundary, with the two exceptions nobody chose.  It
  corrects nothing.]
* [DONE 2026-09-21 - /MBR, and it writes 440 bytes rather than 446 so
  that the disk identity at 1B8h survives.]
* [DONE 2026-09-21 - LOGICAL DRIVES ARE EDITED: created, deleted,
  moved and resized, numbered 5 and up.  The four-way surgery turned
  out to be one sector for a delete and two for a create, because the
  head of the chain is made to STAY rather than move.]
* [DONE 2026-09-21 - FAT32, and the note it replaces was wrong about
  why it would be hard.  A region of no sectors is a region that does
  not move; the relocator already handled it, and what was actually
  needed was the sectors-per-FAT field at 24h, a masked FAT scan, the
  backup boot sector and the FSInfo free count.]
* [DONE 2026-09-21 - AN INTERACTIVE MENU, /I, and it was an afternoon
  on top of a proven engine, exactly as the old note said.  It echoes
  the command line it built, and it can be typed at by a file, which
  is how it is tested.]
* the cluster REMAP regime, refused by design and documented above -
  and now the only thing on this list

IN PROGRESS - FINISHING THE CD-ROM: DMA, LONG NAMES, AND A DISC THAT
CHANGES WHILE THE MACHINE IS RUNNING
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Four things, and one of them turned out to be a design that had never
worked.

THE DEFAULT LETTER WAS ALREADY RIGHT AND NOBODY COULD SEE IT.  With no
CDROM= line the drive takes the letter after the last hard disk -
drv_addcds has done that since it was written - but DRIVES.EXE knew
nothing about DRVF_CDROM and rendered a CD as a hard disk with no
partition table, no size and a filesystem it could not read, so the
letter LOOKED wrong wherever it landed.  DRIVES now has a row of its
own for a packet device:

  H:  cd0     -- CD-ROM            -    0 MB  ISO9660

DRV_BIOS is printed as the ATAPI unit it is rather than as a BIOS
drive; the type byte and the start LBA are dashes, because a CD-ROM is
not a partition on anything; and the size comes from 21h/36h, which is
also the test of whether there is a disc in it - a drive with none
says "(no disc)" where the filesystem goes.  The general lesson is
about diagnostics rather than about CDs: A TOOL THAT READS A KERNEL
TABLE AND DOES NOT KNOW ONE OF ITS FLAGS DOES NOT REPORT LESS, IT
REPORTS SOMETHING FALSE, and a false report is what sends the next
hour after a bug that is not there.

BUS-MASTER DMA ON A PACKET DEVICE is four lines of new decision and
one routine.  ata_identify never reached ata_pickbm and ata_pickdma
for a packet device - it branches away at the signature - so the CD
had no engine and no mode recorded, which is why it was still on PIO.
Calling both from atapi_ident is the whole of the policy work: a
packet device answers IDENTIFY words 49, 63 and 88 exactly as a disk
does, so IDEDMA= in CONFIG.SYS applies to a CD-ROM with nothing said
about CDs anywhere.  atapi_dmapkt is a disk's sequence with one step
in the middle: arm the engine, issue PACKET, hand over the twelve-byte
command block, and only THEN start the engine - because a packet
command has a PIO phase whatever its data phase is, and the engine
must not be running while the command block goes out through the same
data port.  The byte count limit in LBA1/LBA2 is meaningless in a DMA
transfer and is written as zero: there are no bursts to announce
because the drive is not talking to the processor at all.

atapi_xfer decides, per transfer and not per device, exactly as
ata_rw does, and for the same reason - two of the conditions are about
WHERE THE BUFFER IS and that changes call by call.  The fourth
condition is ours rather than the hardware's: ata_dmaok and
ata_prdbuild count in 512-byte sectors because everything else that
calls them is a disk, so a transfer has to be a whole number of them.
A 2048-byte CD block is four, so every read qualifies; an eight-byte
status reply does not, which is the right answer for a second reason,
that arming an engine to move eight bytes costs more than moving them.

A FAILURE IS SORTED THE SAME WAY A DISK'S IS.  ata_dmarun already
says whose fault it was, and the answer is acted on identically: a
drive that failed has really failed, and a bus master that has got one
transfer wrong is not trusted with the retry - that device drops to
PIO for the rest of the session and the same read is done again the
slow way.

AND ONE BUG FOUND BY READING RATHER THAN BY RUNNING: ata_init never
reset atapi_count.  ata_config re-runs the whole probe whenever
IDEDMA= or IDE32= changes a policy - deliberately, and it says so - so
a CONFIG.SYS with either line in it would have counted the CD-ROM
twice and drv_addcds would have given the machine two CD letters, one
of them pointing at a unit that does not exist.  A probe that is
DOCUMENTED as idempotent has to stay idempotent in every counter it
touches, not just the one it was written around.

VERIFIED, and the distinction matters: IDETEST now reports the packet
device (it used to skip it, because ATDF_PRESENT is deliberately
withheld) and says "packet 2: bus-master DMA, mode 42", which is a
claim about the MODE SELECTED.  BUILD ata says

  ATAPI units=0001 cap=00000024/0800 pvd=CD001 by DMA

and "by DMA" is the other claim - that atapi_xfer's four questions all
answered yes and the block really came off the disc through the
engine.  The two are not the same statement and only the second one is
about the transfer.

LONG NAMES, AND THE ONE IDEA THAT MADE THEM CHEAP.  A Joliet
identifier is UCS-2 and there is no length limit worth the name, so
the old iso_jolname folded it down to 8.3 and threw the rest away -
which turned "Setup Files" into the eleven bytes "SETUP FI   ", a
field with a SPACE in the middle of the base that nothing can type and
name83_str renders as "SETUP".  The fix is to stop making the 8.3 name
out of the disc and start making it out of the NAME: iso_rawname reads
the identifier once, in full, into lfn_buf, and iso_mk83 derives the
eleven bytes from that.  THAT IS THE ORDER VFAT ITSELF WORKS IN, and
it is why the two can never disagree about what a file is called.

iso_mk83 answers in three grades - the field IS the name, only the
case differs, or something had to be thrown away - and the third grade
is the only one that gets a ~N alias.  A name that differs only in
case keeps its plain 8.3, exactly as VFAT does; a name that loses
spaces, a second dot, or its ninth character does not.

THE NUMBER IN THE ALIAS IS THE RECORD'S POSITION IN ITS DIRECTORY, and
that is the decision here worth defending.  VFAT numbers its aliases
1, 2, 3 by searching the directory for what is already taken, which
costs a whole directory walk for every entry listed to produce a
number whose only job is to be different from the others.  A READ-ONLY
FILESYSTEM CAN HAVE THAT FOR NOTHING: what an alias has to be is
unique and stable, and a record's position in its own directory is
both, because two entries can no more share a position than they can
share a name.

The seam into the rest of the kernel is ONE ROUTINE.  lfnw_seal is
what fat_search and 714Fh call at every real entry to ask "did a
long-name chain land on this one" - so on an ISO volume it answers
from [iso_lname] instead, which iso_dosname has already set.  There
are no 0Fh fragments on a disc, but THE QUESTION THE KERNEL ASKS IS
THE SAME QUESTION, so it is answered in the same place and every
consumer of lfn_ok and lfn_buf works on a CD unchanged: DIR's long
column, 714Eh/714Fh, 7160h, and opening a file by a name its 8.3 field
cannot spell.

VERIFIED against a disc built for it - TOOLS\MKISO.PS1 makes
S:\Software\lfntest.iso, because every disc already here is
pre-Windows-95 and every name on all of them already fits 8.3, which
proves Joliet is being FOUND and proves nothing about what happens to
a name that is not:

  Directory of H:\
  README.TXT       50
  README~4.TXT     66   Read Me First.txt
  README~5.TXT     60   Read Me Second.txt
  SETUPF~6      <DIR>   Setup Files
  WIN31         <DIR>
  LOWER.TXT        58   lower.txt
  NOTETX~9.TXT     40   note.txt.backup.txt

Every alias is unique, every long name is right, the two entries whose
8.3 field IS their name have no long name at all, and the numbers 4,
5, 6 and 9 are the records' own positions.  DIR H:\SETUPF~6 and
DIR H:\Setup Files both work, and so does TYPE on either spelling.

ONE BUG, AND IT WAS IN A LINE WRITTEN FOR A DIFFERENT REASON.  "." and
".." came out as "~1" and ".".  ISO9660 stores a file with no
extension as "READ.;1" - the separator is not optional in the grammar
- so iso_rawname strips one trailing dot, and it stripped the dot
entries too: ".." became "." and "." became the empty string, which
iso_mk83 called unspellable and iso_alias then named "~1".  The two
dot branches now jump past the strip.  A RULE THAT IS RIGHT ABOUT
NAMES IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY RIGHT ABOUT THE TWO ENTRIES THAT ARE NOT
NAMES.

AND THE DISC CHANGE, WHICH HAD NEVER WORKED AND COULD NOT HAVE.  The
design was that there is no change line on an ATAPI drive, so the
failed read IS the notification: iso_rdblk would clear iso_ok and
fat_ok on any failure and vol_select would mount again.  It was
written down as implemented-but-unverified, and the first time it was
actually tested it did nothing at all, for a reason that is obvious
once seen: AFTER A SWAP, NOTHING READS.  A CD's root directory is one
block and it is sitting in iso_buf; fat_ok still says mounted; so DIR
answers out of the cache and the drive is never spoken to.  A CACHE IS
EXACTLY THE THING THAT STOPS A CHANGE BEING NOTICED, and a scheme that
waits for an I/O error to tell it about a swap is waiting for I/O that
its own cache has made unnecessary.

So the check moved from where a volume is READ to where a volume is
ENTERED.  vol_select calls iso_chkmedia, which - only for a mounted
ISO volume - asks IOS_CDCHG, and atapi_chkchg issues TEST UNIT READY
ONCE.  The failure is the answer: the drive reports "not ready to
ready transition, medium may have changed" as a sense condition on the
next command it is given, and that command fails.

THE RETRY IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN THAT ROUTINE, and this is the part
that is easy to get wrong twice.  atapi_ready asks up to sixteen times
because a drive with a disc newly inserted spends a second or two
saying "becoming ready", and giving up on that would report an empty
drive.  But asking again also CLEARS the condition - the drive reports
it exactly once - so a retry is a second question whose answer the
first question has already destroyed.  atapi_chkchg asks once.  The
waiting moved to the other end: iso_mount now calls IOS_CDINFO before
it reads block 16, which is TEST UNIT READY with retries followed by
READ CAPACITY, so the mount that follows an invalidation waits for the
drive to spin the new disc up instead of reading nothing and calling
it an unreadable disc.  Without that line the swap was detected and
the re-mount then failed, which on screen is "Invalid drive
specification" - a right diagnosis reported as a wrong one.

The cost is one TEST UNIT READY per DOS call that names a CD letter,
which is what MSCDEX paid for the same guarantee: the redirector asked
it to check the media on every request.  Reads inside an already-open
file do not come through vol_select and pay nothing.

VERIFIED AT RUNTIME AT LAST, and the harness is now able to do it:
TOOLS\SWAPTEST.PS1 boots the machine, drives 86Box's Media menu with
the mouse (Media -> CD-ROM 1 -> Image...), types the new path into the
file dialog, and releases a PAUSE in the guest.  The guest listed
LFNTEST, the disc became offnt42.iso underneath it, and the next
DIR H:\ said

  Volume in drive is OFFNT42

with the new disc's six entries, twice running.  TWO THINGS ABOUT
DRIVING 86Box FROM A SCRIPT, both of which cost a while to find:
Alt+M does not open the menu - the emulator has the keyboard - but a
MOUSE CLICK on the menu bar does; and SendKeys does not reach the
guest at all, while keybd_event with a real scancode does, after one
click inside the video area.

AND A TEST THAT WAS WRONG RATHER THAN A KERNEL THAT WAS.  LFNAPI's
first probe, 71A0h, failed with "access denied" - and the kernel was
right.  71A0h asks about a VOLUME and DS:DX is which one; the probe
never set EDX, and r3_xlat validates every pointer a call DECLARES
before the handler runs, so it refused the call on whatever happened
to be in the register.  The general shape is worth keeping: A CALL
THAT IGNORES ONE OF ITS POINTER REGISTERS STILL HAS TO BE GIVEN A
VALID ONE, because the validation happens at the door and the door
does not know which handler will read what.

REGRESSIONS: APITEST passes every check, including 5Bh create and 60h
TRUENAME; LFNAPI passes all six of its probes on FAT (71A0h, 7147h,
7160h both ways, 716Ch create and reopen, 43h, 7141h), which is the
one that matters most because lfnw_seal is now shared between the two
filesystems; IDETEST passes including its "DMA implies an engine and a
mode" check, now extended to packet devices.

TODO - MOUNTING AN IMAGE FILE AS A DRIVE LETTER (Charlie, 2026-09-08).
The same machinery that makes a CD a drive letter should make a FILE
one: an .ISO given a letter and read as ISO9660, and an .IMG, .IMA or
.DSK given a letter and read as FAT.  What makes this cheap NOW and
would not have been before is that vol_state already says a letter is
a VOLUME rather than a disk, and vol_fs already says which filesystem
is behind it: what a mounted image needs is a third kind of backing
store under fat_readclus and disk_read - neither a BIOS drive nor an
ATAPI unit but an open file handle and an offset - and the drive table
has the room to say so.  Worth doing after FDISK, and worth doing
before any of the MSCDEX work, because it is the piece that would let
the machine test disk layouts without a host tool writing images.

IN PROGRESS - A CD-ROM IS A DRIVE LETTER
---------------------------------------------------------------------

On 86Box with offnt42.iso in the drive and CDROM=M in CONFIG.SYS:

  Directory of M:\
  EXCEL.NT       <DIR>   11-19-1994  03:51
  MOM.16         <DIR>   11-19-1994  03:51
  OFREADME.HLP   17865   10-02-1994  07:00
  POWERPNT.16    <DIR>   11-19-1994  03:51
  README.TXT      2778   10-02-1994  07:00
  WORD.NT        <DIR>   11-19-1994  03:51
        6 file(s)  20643 bytes
                       0 bytes free

DIR walks into M:\EXCEL.NT, and TYPE M:\README.TXT prints the file.
Those names are the JOLIET ones - the ISO9660 tree on that disc calls
them EXCEL_NT, MOM_16, POWERPNT and WORD_NT - so the supplementary
descriptor is being found and used.

THE DESIGN, AND IT IS ONE IDEA.  Everything above the directory layer
in this kernel - walk_to, resolve_parent, 4Eh/4Fh, open, the LFN
wrapper - consumes a pointer to a THIRTY-TWO BYTE FAT DIRECTORY ENTRY
and reads DE_ATTR, DE_CLUSTER and DE_SIZE off it.  Rather than teach
all of that about ISO9660, ISO9660 ANSWERS IN THEIR SHAPE: iso_entry
translates a directory record into a FAT entry, putting the extent
where the start cluster goes and the file flags where the attributes
go.  dir_seek branches to it on vol_fs and nothing above dir_seek ever
finds out which filesystem it is reading.

That left four seams and no more:

  ctx_root / ctx_chain   the directory context is an extent and a
                         length rather than a cluster chain
  dir_seek               produce an entry
  fat_next               "the next cluster" is the next block, because
                         AN ISO9660 FILE IS ONE CONTIGUOUS EXTENT and
                         there is no table to consult
  fat_readclus           read that block through IOS_CDREAD

file_chunk - the whole file-reading path - needed NOTHING, and the
reason is a coincidence worth writing down: fat_spc is set to 4 for an
ISO volume, so a "cluster" is 4 * 512 = 2048 bytes, which is exactly a
CD block.  The arithmetic that finds an offset within a cluster is
already the arithmetic that finds an offset within a block.

vol_fs lives in vol_state, out of padding that was already there, so
VOL_STATE_SIZE did not move.

WHAT A DIRECTORY LENGTH COSTS.  A FAT directory ends when its cluster
chain does, so nothing needs to know how long it is.  An ISO directory
is a number of bytes, and for a SUBDIRECTORY that number is written
down in the parent's record - which ctx_chain no longer has, because
all it was handed was an extent.  The way out is that the disc records
it twice: the first record of every directory is its own "." entry,
and that entry carries the directory's size.  iso_dirlen reads one
block and takes it from there.

THE ROOT IS INDEXED DIFFERENTLY FROM EVERY OTHER DIRECTORY, twice
over, and both are about looking like FAT:

  - entry zero is a SYNTHETIC VOLUME LABEL.  ISO9660 keeps the volume
    name in the primary descriptor; FAT keeps it in a root entry with
    ATTR_VOLUME, and that is where COMMAND.COM's DIR looks for it with
    a 4Eh search.  Synthesising one means the label is found by the
    code that already knows how to find a label.
  - "." and ".." are SKIPPED in the root, because a FAT root has
    neither.  A subdirectory keeps its own, exactly as FAT does.

CDROM= IN CONFIG.SYS, and the awkwardness it exposed.  disk_scan runs
long before CONFIG.SYS is read, so the statement cannot influence the
first pass; it sets cd_letter and calls drv_addcds AGAIN, which is why
that routine clears the CD slots and recomputes drv_count before it
places anything.  It is idempotent on purpose.  A letter already held
by a hard disk is not stolen - the drive falls back to where the scan
would have put it - because a CONFIG.SYS line should not be able to
make a partition unreachable.

LASTDRIVE WENT FROM 8 TO 16 AND HAD TO.  Two disks with a handful of
partitions between them used A: to H: exactly, so there was no letter
left and drv_addcds silently placed nothing - correct behaviour for a
full table and useless on a machine with a drive in it.  The cost is
drv_tbl, the parked volume states (arena-allocated, so nothing in the
image), and 8 * (VOL_LEN + CDS_LEN) = 944 bytes of RMDOS, which is the
only one of the three with a hard ceiling and has 64K.

DISC CHANGE, and why the trigger is a FAILURE.  There is no change
line on an ATAPI drive the way there is on a floppy controller: the
drive reports "medium may have changed" as a sense condition on the
next command, and that command fails.  So the failed read IS the
notification.  iso_rdblk clears iso_ok and fat_ok on any failure, and
vol_select mounts again the next time the letter is touched.  It is
deliberately not clever - a read can also fail because the tray is
open or the disc is scratched, and re-mounting is the right answer to
all three.  IMPLEMENTED BUT NOT RUNTIME-VERIFIED: swapping media
underneath a running guest is not something this harness can do yet.

  [AND IT WAS WRONG.  When the harness could finally do it, this
  scheme did nothing at all: after a swap NOTHING READS, because the
  root directory is one block sitting in iso_buf and fat_ok still says
  mounted.  The check moved from where a volume is read to where it is
  ENTERED - vol_select asks IOS_CDCHG, one TEST UNIT READY with no
  retry - and is verified at runtime now.  See "FINISHING THE CD-ROM"
  above.]

JOLIET is a supplementary descriptor whose escape sequence at offset
88 is %/@, %/C or %/E - UCS-2 levels 1, 2 and 3 - and whose directory
tree is a parallel copy under the real names.  iso_joliet walks the
descriptor list a second time and, if it finds one, replaces the root.
iso_jolname reads the identifiers two bytes to a character, BIG-endian,
and keeps the low byte: a disc whose names are plain ASCII in UCS-2
clothing, which is nearly all of them, comes out with those names, and
anything that will not fit becomes '_'.  A full long-name path would
hand the whole thing to the LFN layer and that is still to do.

TWO BUGS, AND BOTH WERE INSERTION MISTAKES RATHER THAN LOGIC.

  A LABEL IS NOT A BARRIER.  The guard that stops a CD volume reaching
  the 512-byte block layer was written as "dio_nocd: stc / ret" and
  put immediately before dio_done - where nothing jumps to it and
  EVERYTHING FALLS INTO IT.  Every disk transfer returned straight
  into stc/ret with five registers still pushed, and the machine went
  into a loop of CPU exception 0C.  The routine was correct; the place
  it was put was not.  It lives after a ret now.  This is the v0.54
  "rr_strfull fell through past a comment block into rr_exec" trap
  arriving from the other direction: there, code fell into a routine;
  here, a routine was placed where code would fall into it.

  AND THE FREE-SPACE LINE AT THE BOTTOM OF DIR.  The listing was
  right and then DIR ended with "Not ready reading drive A" on a
  machine whose floppy drive was empty.  fat_freecount walks the FAT
  through disk_read, which addresses fat_drive - and on an ISO volume
  fat_drive holds an ATAPI UNIT NUMBER, so unit 0 went out as BIOS
  drive 0.  A CD has no free space and no FAT to count it in; saying
  so is one comparison.  The general shape is worth keeping: WHEN TWO
  KINDS OF DEVICE SHARE A FIELD, THE INDEX FOR ONE IS A VALID INDEX
  FOR THE OTHER, and the failure is not an error but a wrong device.

REGRESSIONS.  APITEST passes every check on the release build -
including 5Bh create, which writes to a FAT volume through the guarded
disk_write, and 60h TRUENAME and the 44h drive subfunctions.  DIR and
TYPE on FAT volumes are unchanged.

WHAT IS LEFT HERE:  [all but one of these are DONE - see "FINISHING
THE CD-ROM" above, which is the entry that closed them]
  - a full long-name path for Joliet, through the LFN layer, instead
    of folding UCS-2 down to 8.3                              [DONE]
  - DMA.  The transport is still PIO; ATA.INC's bus-master engine is
    built and a packet transfer uses it the same way          [DONE]
  - the MSCDEX API (INT 2Fh AH=15h)                          [DONE]
    Answered by the kernel, not by a program - DOS\MSCDEX.INC.
    TOOLS\CDXTEST.ASM proves it from inside a DOS box, which is the
    only place it can be asked from
  - DRIVES.EXE renders a CD as a broken hard disk, because it does not
    know DRVF_CDROM.  Cosmetic, and it is the only program that reads
    the drive table directly                                  [DONE]
  - runtime proof of the disc-change path                     [DONE,
    and it disproved it: the path did not work]


IN PROGRESS - THE ISO9660 READER
---------------------------------------------------------------------

PM-DOS reads a CD-ROM.  On 86Box with win16ddk.iso in the drive,
BUILD iso says:

  ISO9660: 123volume "WIN16DDK" root: .   ..   VISUALC   WIN31

and a host-side parser of the same image, written independently in
perl, says volume "WIN16DDK", root extent 32, length 146, entries
".  ..  VISUALC  WIN31".  The two agree entry for entry, which is the
check worth having: the kernel's answer compared against something
that is not the kernel.

DOS\ISO9660.INC, and it is the SECOND FILESYSTEM THIS KERNEL HAS and
the first that is not FAT.  iso_mount walks the descriptor list from
block 16 rather than assuming the primary is first (a disc with a boot
record in front of it is legal), checks CD001, refuses a logical block
size that is not 2048 rather than reading it wrongly, and copies the
root directory record out whole - because the block it sits in is
about to be replaced by the first directory read.  iso_diropen/
iso_dirnext walk a directory; iso_name83 turns "README.TXT;1" into the
eleven bytes DOS wants, and knows that the one-byte identifiers 00h
and 01h are "." and "..".

THE TWO FACTS ABOUT THE FORMAT THAT SHAPE THE CODE are worth stating
because neither is guessable from a FAT background.  EVERY MULTI-BYTE
NUMBER IS STORED TWICE, little-endian then big-endian, so a dword
field is eight bytes and a word field is four - which is why the
offsets look oddly spaced.  And A DIRECTORY IS A FLAT RUN OF
VARIABLE-LENGTH RECORDS THAT NEVER CROSS A BLOCK: a zero length byte
means "nothing more in THIS block", not "the end", and a walker that
stops there reads the first 2048 bytes of a directory and calls it
the whole thing.

TWO NEW SERVICES, IOS_CDREAD AND IOS_CDINFO, and they are not
IOS_RDBLK for a reason worth keeping: a packet device has no BIOS
drive number by design, and its block is 2048 bytes rather than 512.
A CD arriving down the ordinary block path would read a quarter of
what was asked for AND REPORT SUCCESS.  Two calls of their own,
indexed by ATAPI unit, keep the two block sizes from ever meeting.
IOS_CDINFO fills in the unit count even when it fails, so "how many CD
drives are there" is one call with AL = 0 rather than a special case.

THE CASE-FOLDING TRAP, AGAIN, AND IT IS WRITTEN DOWN IN THIS FILE
ALREADY.  iso_blksize (a dword of state) and ISO_BLKSIZE (the equate
2048) differ only in case, wasm folds case, so they were ONE symbol
and the constant won in silence.  v0.48 recorded this exact trap -
"a label and a constant that differ only in case are one symbol, and
the constant wins IN SILENCE" - and this release walked into it
anyway, on the first file where the natural name for the state and
the natural name for the constant were the same word.  Renamed
iso_lbsize, with the reason at the declaration.  The lesson the v0.48
entry drew was that no assembly-time check exists and the rule has to
be kept by naming; what this adds is that the rule is hardest to keep
exactly where it matters most, because a filesystem's block size is
going to be both a constant and a variable in any reader anybody
writes.

AND THE ONE THAT COST THE RUNS: A POP WITH NOTHING OF ITS OWN LEFT TO
TAKE.  iso_name83 kept the start of the eleven-byte field on the
stack, and the extension branch popped it a SECOND time to get back to
the beginning:

        pushad
        push    edi             ; the field start
        ...
        pop     edi             ; balanced - the stack is level again
        ...
  in8_dot:
        pop     edi             ; ...and this one takes pushad's EDI
        push    edi             ; ...and puts a different value back

The depth stayed balanced, so it assembled and it ran.  What it did
was lift pushad's saved EDI off the stack and push the field start in
its place, so popad restored a register the caller never passed.  The
machine did not hang: IT RESET, AND REBOOTED, AND RESET AGAIN, and the
screen the harness photographed was a FRESH BOOT each time - which is
why three runs in a row showed "Starting PM-DOS..." and nothing else,
including runs where the reader had already printed its answer and
lost it to the reset half a second later.

  THAT IS THE MEASUREMENT LESSON AND IT IS BIGGER THAN THE BUG.  A
  hang and a reset loop look identical through a screenshot taken once
  a second.  The thing that separated them was a marker character
  printed at the call site: the run that printed "<" and then nothing
  would have proved a hang, and the run that printed the whole answer
  proved the reset.  One character per step turns "it stopped
  somewhere in here" into a location, and it is the cheapest
  instrument in this project.

Nothing needs the stack there - EBP is dead in that routine and popad
puts it back - so the field start lives in EBP now.

WHAT IS NEXT, and the first of them is the big one:
  - A DRIVE LETTER.  The volume table has to accept a volume whose
    filesystem is not FAT, which it has never had to do, and every
    INT 21h path that reaches a file goes through resolve_core ->
    vol_select -> the FAT code with no branch in it for anything else.
    That is a bigger change than the reader was, and it is where the
    design thinking goes next: either a filesystem vector per volume,
    or a second walk_to that ISO paths take
  - reading a FILE, not just a directory.  The extent and length are
    already parsed; what is missing is the path walk and a read
  - Joliet, for long names - the supplementary descriptor this code
    already knows the type number of.  A disc of this era has 8.3
    names in the base tree, so this is not urgent
  - disc-change invalidation.  iso_forget exists and nothing calls it;
    ATAPI reports a change as a sense condition rather than a change
    line, so the trigger has to come from a failed command
  - DMA.  The transport is PIO only; ATA.INC's bus-master engine is
    already built and a packet transfer uses it the same way


IN PROGRESS - CD-ROM, AND WHY IT IS NOT THE REDIRECTOR
---------------------------------------------------------------------

THE ROUTE WAS CHOSEN BEFORE ANY CODE WAS WRITTEN, and the entry above
about ATAPI had it wrong.  It said the hard half of CD-ROM support was
that "MSCDEX is not a block driver but a network-REDIRECTOR client,
and that is an interface PM-DOS does not have at all" - which is true,
and which only matters IF YOU WANT TO RUN MSCDEX.  PM-DOS has its own
32-bit block layer and a volume table whose founding idea is already
that a letter is a volume rather than a disk.  It can read ISO9660
itself and never involve a real-mode redirector.

The redirector was looked at first and has a prerequisite that had not
been noticed: GLOL_CDS is deliberately FFFF:FFFF, with a comment in
PMDOS.INC saying that inventing plausible structures would be worse
than saying no because a tool would follow them.  But the current
directory array is exactly where a real-mode redirector plants itself
- MSCDEX and every network client find a free CDS entry and set the
network bit in it.  No CDS array, no redirector.  So that route starts
by reversing a deliberate decision, then routes about twenty INT 21h
functions through a V86 excursion per file operation.

Decision (Charlie, 2026-09-08): NATIVE.  ATAPI and ISO9660 in the
32-bit kernel, a drive letter out of the volume table, no excursion
and no invented DOS structures.  What that does not buy is network
drives and the MSCDEX API - a program calling INT 2Fh AH=15h will not
find one, and a shim for that can come later if something asks.

[AND IT DID, 2026-09-09.  Charlie asked whether anything was telling
programs that MSCDEX was loaded, and nothing was.  The last sentence
above is now wrong in a way worth leaving visible: the shim exists,
it is DOS\MSCDEX.INC, and it did NOT need a redirector or an
MSCDEX.EXE - the API is answered out of the volume table the scan
already built.  What the paragraph got right is the important half:
the API is a separate thing from the mechanism, and this kernel was
never going to need the mechanism.]

DONE SO FAR: THE PACKET TRANSPORT, IO\ATAPI.INC.  An ATAPI device is
an ATA device that takes SCSI command blocks instead of ATA commands,
so everything underneath - port layout, select, the status waits, the
400ns settle - is ATA.INC's, used unchanged.  What is new above it is
the command layer, and one thing that has no ATA analogue: THE DEVICE
DECIDES HOW MUCH IT SENDS.  A disk read moves exactly the sectors
asked for; a packet command comes back in bursts whose size the drive
announces in LBA1/LBA2 as each one starts, and the host keeps taking
them until DRQ stays low.  So the data loop is driven by the drive
rather than by a count, and a burst longer than the caller's buffer is
DRAINED rather than abandoned - data left sitting in the drive wedges
the next command on that channel, and the next command is usually
REQUEST SENSE asking what went wrong.

A CD-ROM IS NOT A BIOS DRIVE HERE, and that is the one design point
worth writing down.  ata_slot hands out 80h, 81h and so on in probe
order to everything carrying ATDF_PRESENT, so giving a CD-ROM that
flag would renumber the hard disks behind it - a machine with the CD
on the primary slave would find its second disk had moved.  An ATAPI
unit gets ATDF_ATAPI and NOT ATDF_PRESENT: ata_slot, ata_count and the
whole INT 13h path carry on seeing exactly the disks they saw before,
and atapi_slot indexes the packet devices separately.

MEASURED on 86Box (Pentium II 450 / 440BX), BUILD ata, with
S:\Software\win16ddk.iso in the emulated drive on the secondary
master:

  ATAPI units=0001 cap=00039B1B/0800 pvd=CD001

Three questions in the order a driver has to ask them, each reachable
only if the one before it worked.  READ CAPACITY says the packet
transport carries a reply: last block 39B1Bh, block size 800h, and the
ISO is 483,975,168 bytes = 236,316 blocks, so the last one is 236,315
= 39B1Bh exactly.  READ(10) of block 16 says the data path carries a
whole 2048-byte block: 16 is where ISO9660 puts its primary volume
descriptor and bytes 1 through 5 of it are the letters CD001.

THE BUG IN THE MIDDLE OF IT WAS ONE INSTRUCTION AND IT WAS NEW CODE'S,
not the old code's.  The first boot said "ATAPI units=0000" with the
probe stage stuck at 'P' - the new signature test.  Rather than guess,
the signature was printed, and it was 14EBh: exactly the value being
compared against.  The compare was:

        or      al,ah                   ; are both bytes zero?
        jz      aid_nosig
        cmp     ax,ATAPI_SIG

"or al,ah" is how the original asked whether the drive had signed
anything at all, and IT ASKS BY WRITING AL.  By the time the cmp ran,
AX was 14FFh.  The signature had been right from the first boot and
the test destroyed it before reading it.  cmp leaves the register
alone, so the order is inverted now: signature first, zero test after.

This is the sibling of a trap already in this file - "an 8-bit move
into AL silently corrupts a 32-bit value you were about to use" - and
the general form is worth stating once: A FLAG-SETTING INSTRUCTION
THAT ALSO HAS A RESULT IS NOT A TEST.  The old code was correct
because it never looked at AX again; the new code inherited an
idiom whose precondition it had quietly broken.

WHAT IS NEXT, in order:
  - ISO9660: the primary volume descriptor, the root directory record,
    the directory walk and a file read.  Joliet after that, because a
    disc of this era has 8.3 names in the base tree anyway
  - a drive letter.  The volume table has to accept a volume whose
    filesystem is not FAT, which is the first time it has had to, and
    that is a bigger change than the reader is
  - READ CAPACITY is asked once at probe time now; a disc CHANGE has
    to invalidate whatever the volume layer cached.  ATAPI reports it
    as a sense condition rather than a change line
  - DMA.  The transport is PIO only so far.  ATA.INC's bus-master
    engine is already built and a packet transfer uses it the same
    way, so this is a contained addition once the reader works

v0.60 - A FILE IS A DRIVE LETTER, A PATH IS THIRTY-TWO DEEP, EVERY
        COMMAND ANSWERS /?, THERE IS A MOVE, AND THE VERSION IS THE
        ONE THE MACHINE SAYS (2026-09-19)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Three things Charlie asked for together, and one bug underneath the
largest of them that is the entry worth reading - then /? on every
command and MOVE.COM, asked for afterwards, each of which had a bug of
its own worth the same attention.  MOVE's was in the KERNEL and had
been there all along: nothing before it had ever asked 56h to rename
between two volumes.


THE VERSION EQUATE HAD BEEN STALE FOR TWO RELEASES.

INC\PMDOS.INC said PMDOS_MINOR = 57 while NOTES.TXT, the release and
everything written about it said 0.59.  v0.58 and v0.59 were built,
tested and committed that way, so VER - the only thing a user can ask
- named the wrong kernel for two releases running, and a bug report
from either of those builds would have been filed against the wrong
one.

NOTHING WAS BROKEN, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHY NO TEST COULD HAVE CAUGHT IT.
COMMAND.COM compares its own build's PMDOS_MINOR against the kernel's
and warns when they differ - but both come from the same equate, so
they agreed with each other and were wrong together.  A test can only
ask whether two things match; it cannot ask whether they match the
world.

So the guard is not a test.  BUILD.CMD now prints the equate's line
before it assembles anything:

    === version ===
    ---------- INC\PMDOS.INC
    PMDOS_MINOR     EQU     60

FIND rather than FOR /F, because NT 3.51's cmd.exe has no FOR /F and
does not say so - it expands the tokens to literal text and carries
on.  The number is now in front of whoever is building, every time,
which is the only kind of guard that works on a fact nobody checks.


DIR OF A DIRECTORY EIGHT DEEP, AND THE MEASURE THAT WAS A GUESS.

MAX_DEPTH was 8 and had been since the path resolver was written.  The
bug it produced was not in a deep tree at all:

    MD \D1\D2\D3\D4\D5\D6\D7\D8     worked
    CD \D1\D2\D3\D4\D5\D6\D7\D8     worked
    DIR \D1\D2\D3\D4\D5\D6\D7\D8    "Path not found"

DIR APPENDS ITS OWN "*.*" AND THE WILDCARD IS A COMPONENT, so the
eighth level was the last place a user could stand and the first place
they could not look.  It is also exactly where ISO9660 puts a
relocated directory - the standard allows eight levels and Rock
Ridge's CL/RE move the rest - so the one filesystem guaranteed to
produce a path this long was the one the kernel had just learnt to
read.

MAX_DEPTH is 32 now.  cwd_names is inside vol_state, so VOL_STATE_SIZE
went 8884 -> 9148 and the assert at vol_state_end says so out loud.

THE OTHER HALF OF THE FIX IS THE ONE WORTH KEEPING: 32 IS A COUNT AND
THE REAL LIMITS ARE LENGTHS.  cwd_install used to refuse a current
directory by computing "components times thirteen" - twelve characters
plus a separator, the worst a component can be - and comparing it with
63.  That made the ceiling FOUR directories deep whatever they were
called: \A\B\C\D\E renders to nine characters and was refused as
sixty-five.  There is now names_len, which measures what names_string
WOULD write, and three callers ask it:

  - cwd_install, against 63, because 47h promises 64 bytes
  - fn60, against 124, because "D:\" plus the text plus a NUL is the
    128 that TRUENAME promises
  - imm_savepath in IMAGE.INC, for its own field

MEASURE WHAT YOU HAVE; ESTIMATE ONLY WHAT YOU CANNOT SEE.  A worst
case is the right measure when the buffer is being written now and the
contents are not known yet.  Here the contents were sitting in
rp_names the whole time, and the only reason to estimate was that
nothing had been written to measure them.

AND RAISING THE DEPTH EXPOSED SOMETHING THAT WAS ALREADY WRONG.
path_render - 7147h and 7160h, the long-name TRUENAME and get-current-
directory - writes into the caller's buffer and had NEVER CHECKED how
much it was writing.  Those calls render LONG names, up to 259
characters each, into a buffer the LFN API says is 260 for the whole
path: eight of them was already four times the buffer.  Nothing found
it because nobody nests long names deeply.  Raising the depth to 32
would have turned a latent overrun of somebody else's memory into a
likely one, so it is closed rather than made larger: prd_lim is one
past the last byte the text may occupy, and the four places that write
check it.

The failure path restores ESP from prd_sp, because the checks sit at
three different stack depths - inside the pushad, inside a "push edi",
and inside "push edi / push esi" - and a bound that has to be unwound
three different ways is a bound that will be got wrong the next time a
branch is added.  A path too long to NAME is refused; the same file
can still be opened.  The limit belongs to the call's buffer, not to
the filesystem.

DEEPTEST.BAT is the proof: ten levels built, DIR of the eighth and the
tenth, CD down and back up through "..\..\..\..\..", and the tree
removed again.


A FILE GIVEN A DRIVE LETTER OF ITS OWN: DOS\IMAGE.INC AND MOUNT.EXE.

    MOUNT E: C:\IMAGES\DISK.IMG
    MOUNT E: C:\CD.ISO /R
    MOUNT /U E:
    MOUNT                       what is mounted now

WHAT IS IN THE FILE DECIDES HOW IT IS READ, NOT WHAT IT IS CALLED.
img_sniff reads block 16 and takes CD001, BEA01, NSR02 or NSR03 as an
optical filesystem; failing that it reads sector 0 and asks bpb_looks;
failing that it looks for a master boot record and takes the first FAT
partition in it.  The order is the order of how sure each test is - a
five-byte signature at a fixed place, then three plausibility tests on
fields that could be anything, then two bytes of signature that a FAT
boot sector's tail can resemble.  A file named the wrong way round
still works, which is the point of looking rather than guessing.

A PARTITION INSIDE AN IMAGE COST NOTHING, and that is the volume
table's doing rather than this file's: DRV_START already says where a
volume begins and has never cared whether the number came from a
disk's partition table or from anywhere else.

AN EXTENT MAP, NOT AN OPEN HANDLE, and this is the design decision the
rest follows from.  The roadmap's note said "an open file handle and
an offset".  That is wrong here for three reasons and the third
decided it:

  RE-ENTRANCY.  Serving a sector for E: by reading a file on C: means
  calling vol_select in the middle of an operation standing on E:'s
  volume state - and this kernel keeps ONE volume loaded and swaps the
  others in and out of it.  The caller's filesystem would be pulled
  out from under it while it was using it.

  THE CRITICAL ERROR PATH.  disk_read may call INT 24h, whose handler
  may call INT 21h.  A backing store that is itself an INT 21h file
  operation puts a DOS call inside a DOS call inside a DOS call.

  THE CACHE, WHICH IS THE ONE THAT DECIDED IT.  The disk cache is
  keyed by PHYSICAL DRIVE AND ABSOLUTE LBA.  An image's sectors ARE
  real sectors, on a real disk, at real LBAs - so if the translation
  happens ABOVE the cache, the image's blocks and the host file's
  blocks are THE SAME BLOCKS.  Coherency between the two views comes
  free, and it comes free because there is only one view.  A
  handle-based reader would have needed a second cache and then a rule
  for keeping the two honest, which is the bug nobody finds until a
  file written through E: reads back stale through C:.

So the cluster chain becomes a list of runs once, at mount time, and
every transfer after that is a lookup plus an ordinary transfer to the
host's drive.  Two passes - count, allocate, fill - so the arena is
asked for what the map needs rather than for a ceiling: an image
written by MKDISK, by FORMAT, or copied onto a fresh volume is
contiguous, and a contiguous image has a map of twelve bytes.  The
test image mounts with ONE extent.

THE MAP BELONGS TO THE KERNEL AND NOT TO WHOEVER TYPED MOUNT.
arena_alloc stamps every block with [cur_own] and 4Ch sweeps the arena
for the exiting program's blocks, so a map bought while MOUNT.EXE is
running is freed the moment MOUNT.EXE ends - with the image still
reading it.  This is v0.59's cache bug exactly, four lines of
push/zero/allocate/pop, and it is written out again in IMAGE.INC
rather than cross-referenced because the next thing that allocates
from inside a program will need telling a third time.

THE PRICE, STATED PLAINLY: THE FILE MAY NOT MOVE WHILE IT IS MOUNTED.
Three refusals guard the ways this machine could do it - 41h delete,
3Ch's truncate-in-place, and open_core for any WRITE mode - all
through img_locked, which compares the host volume and the FIRST
CLUSTER rather than the name, because a name can be reached by more
than one path and the damage happens at the cluster level.  A file
already mounted cannot be mounted a SECOND time either: two letters
over one set of sectors means two FAT caches, two free-cluster hints
and two ideas of the directory, and the second writer wins silently.
Reading the image file while it is mounted IS allowed - the two views
are the same blocks in the same cache, which is the whole argument
above.  A host volume that is itself a mounted image is refused:
stacking would work arithmetically and would corrupt itself at once,
because img_iobody's working variables are single and not a stack.

WHERE THE FLAG HAD TO BE NAMED.  DRVF_IMAGE changes what DRV_BIOS
means, and there are four such flags now:

  fat_mount     which filesystem to mount it with
  dio_try       the translation, ABOVE the cache
  dio_raw       and again below it, for VERIFY's read-back and 25h/26h
  cd_read       a new single door for every 2048-byte read, because
                five places called IOS_CDREAD directly and every one
                of them would otherwise have had to learn what a
                mounted .ISO is
  iso_mount     skip the drive handshake: no tray, nothing to become
                ready, and no ATAPI unit to ask
  iso_chkmedia  skip the change check for the same reason - but KEEP
                the "one reader, many letters" test, which applies to
                an image and a disc alternating exactly as it did to
                two discs
  cd_readtoc    refuse, which iso_findbase already reads as "it starts
                at block zero" - the multi-session walk is skipped
                with no special case anywhere
  drv_tbl/park  see below
  DRIVES, FDISK the diagnostics

AND THAT LIST CAUGHT AN OLDER BUG OF THE SAME SHAPE.  park_fillhdr
zeroes the flags for a DRVF_DRIVER row, with a comment saying a number
that names a real disk by accident is worse than nothing - and it did
not name DRVF_CDROM.  DRV_BIOS on a CD-ROM row is an ATAPI UNIT, and
unit 0 handed to RMDOS as a BIOS drive is THE FIRST FLOPPY.  Exactly
the accident the comment was written about, one flag short of being
caught by it.  Fixed with DRVF_CDROM and DRVF_IMAGE added to the same
test.  The general form, since this is the second time: A FLAG THAT
CHANGES WHAT DRV_BIOS MEANS HAS TO BE NAMED EVERYWHERE THAT READS
DRV_BIOS.

DRIVES got a row for an image and, on the way, a false report fixed.
F1h AL=1 answers 12, 16 or 32 for a FAT volume and 0 for one that is
not - and 0 fell off the end of the comparisons and printed as FAT32.
It never showed, because until a file could be mounted the only
non-FAT volume was a CD-ROM and a CD-ROM had a row of its own that
never reached that code.  A mounted .ISO comes through the ordinary
path and would have been labelled FAT32.  Same lesson as DRVF_CDROM
cost this same program a release ago: A TOOL THAT DOES NOT KNOW ONE OF
THE KERNEL'S ANSWERS DOES NOT REPORT LESS, IT REPORTS SOMETHING FALSE.


AND THE BUG UNDERNEATH ALL OF IT, WHICH IS THE ONE TO REMEMBER:

A NEW INT 21h SUBFUNCTION THAT TAKES A POINTER HAS TO BE REGISTERED IN
vdm_flags, OR A NATIVE PROGRAM'S POINTER NEVER GETS FLATTENED.

The symptom: MOUNT.EXE said "Cannot mount C:\TESTS\TESTIMG.IMG: no
such file" about a file that DIR listed, DEL deleted and TYPE printed.

r3_xlat converts a ring-3 program's offsets into flat addresses on the
way into the kernel, and r3_unxlat puts them back on the way out - but
only for the registers a per-function table names.  vdm_subptr has a
row per F1h subfunction: 03h, 06h, 08h, 0Bh, 0Ch, 0Dh, 0Eh.  The new
0Fh and 11h had none, so img_mount received OFFSET arg_path raw and
resolved whatever sat at that flat address - which, in MOUNT.EXE's own
image, was the middle of its usage text.  rp_cnt came back as 1 or 2,
resolve_parent succeeded, and fat_search honestly could not find it.

WHAT COST THE TIME, AND IT IS A LESSON ABOUT PROBES RATHER THAN ABOUT
POINTERS.  MOUNT was made to open the same path with 3Dh immediately
before the mount, using the same register with the same value.  It
worked - "PROBE: 3Dh opened it" - and that was read as "the pointer is
good", which sent the next hour into img_mount's own code.  It proved
no such thing: 3Dh IS in the table.  A CONTROL THAT GOES THROUGH
DIFFERENT MACHINERY IS NOT A CONTROL, and "the same pointer" was the
one thing about the two calls that was genuinely identical.

What ended it was the kernel saying what it had received, rather than
the program saying what it had sent.  BUILD img (-dIMG_DEBUG) prints
the pointer AND the bytes at it, and the two lines together are the
whole diagnosis:

    PROBE: arg_path at 000024E2
    IMG path: 000024E2 ted
      MOUNT d: file        mount that file as drive d:

Same address, different bytes: the program and the kernel were not
looking at the same memory.  Keep that build target.


WHAT THE TESTS SAY.  IMGTEST.BAT, in DOSBox 0.74 against HD16.IMG with
C:\TESTS\TESTIMG.IMG - a 1.44M FAT12 image that BUILD.CMD makes with
MKDISK and then carries onto the hard disk as ordinary content:

  - mounts on E:, one extent, 1440 KB, and MOUNT lists it
  - DIR E: reads the files inside it, long names and all
  - COPY and MD write to it; unmount and mount again and the writes
    are still there, so they reached the host's platter and not just a
    cache that went away with the volume
  - DEL of the image file says "Access denied", COPY over it says
    "Unable to create destination", and a second MOUNT of it is
    refused
  - DIR of the image AS A FILE, while mounted, sees the volume's own
    writes - one cache, one truth

DEL SAYING "ACCESS DENIED" IS NEW AND WAS A FALSE REPORT BEFORE.
cmd_del counted successes and printed "File not found" whenever there
were none - about a file its own find had just matched, which is a
statement the program had disproved a moment earlier.  It keeps the
last error now and says which it was.  The old message stays for the
case it was always right about: nothing matched the pattern.

STILL TO DO HERE: an .ISO mounted from a file is read-only and always
will be, but nothing yet mounts an image held on a CD or inside
another image (both refused honestly); there is no CONFIG.SYS line to
mount one at boot; and a fragmented image is capped at 4096 extents
and refused above it with "defragment the volume" rather than being
made to work.


FDISK CREATES AND DELETES NOW, WHICH IS WHAT FDISK IS FOR.

    FDISK /C d:p        create a partition filling the largest free gap
    FDISK /C d:p n      ...n sectors of it, or n MB written 40M
    FDISK /C d:p n tt   ...and tt as the type byte, in hex
    FDISK /D d:p        delete one
    FDISK /A d:p        make one the active - bootable - one

All three are dry runs without /W, like everything else in this
program: they walk every check, print exactly what would have
happened, and cannot touch a sector because dk_write refuses unarmed.

THE ARITHMETIC IS THE WORK, not the writing.  Creating a partition is
sixteen bytes; deciding WHICH sixteen is fd_gap and the two alignment
routines.

  THE FIRST TRACK IS NEVER FREE.  It holds the master boot record,
  and every DOS that partitioned a disk started the first partition
  at the beginning of the SECOND track - which is why a 63-sector
  disk's first partition starts at LBA 63.

  THE START GOES UP TO A CYLINDER BOUNDARY AND THE END GOES DOWN TO
  ONE, with that first sector as the single exception.  The test is
  built on a number chosen to catch it: MULTI.IMG's third partition
  starts at 83727, which is 83 cylinders of 1008 sectors plus 663 -
  not a boundary.  Delete it and create in the space and the answer
  has to be 84672 + 7056, seven whole cylinders inside a gap of
  eight.  If the report says 83727 the alignment is not happening,
  and the report would otherwise look perfectly reasonable.

  THE TYPE BYTE IS A PROMISE ABOUT ADDRESSING, which is rl_typebyte's
  argument applied to empty space: 06h says "FAT16 reachable by CHS",
  and a BIOS meeting it on a partition that ends past the CHS line
  will read the wrong sector and be certain it is right.  So the END
  decides between the CHS spellings and the LBA ones, and the size
  decides the width.  fd_newtype differs from rl_typebyte in what it
  can know - that one asks a FAT layout that exists, this one is
  predicting - which is why the type can be given explicitly.

THE REFUSALS, WHICH ARE AGAIN THE HALF WORTH HAVING:

  - creating into an occupied slot.  Overwriting the entry would be a
    delete nobody asked for, and that entry is the only record of
    where the partition was
  - deleting an EXTENDED CONTAINER THAT STILL HAS LOGICAL DRIVES IN
    IT.  Their EBRs would stay on the disk, chained to each other,
    described by nothing.  fd_chainbusy reads one sector to decide,
    and treats an unreadable container as busy: "I could not tell"
    and "it is empty" must not come back as the same answer when the
    consequence is orphaning somebody's volumes
  - a gap that is shorter than one cylinder once aligned
  - a size larger than the gap, which says how big the gap is

THE CHAIN WAS NOT EDITED YET WHEN THAT WAS WRITTEN, and the reason
stood until the next entry did it properly: a half-implemented chain
editor leaves a disk whose table walks a little further each time,
which is the one failure a partition editor must not have.  An
extended container could be created, and deleted while it was empty,
and nothing could empty it.  See the entry below.

FDTEST.BAT does all of it against MULTI.IMG as the second disk, which
MKHD rebuilds every time - so everything the test does is undone by
the next build.  Verified 2026-09-20 in DOSBox: the four refusals, the
dry runs, set-active moving the flag from slot 1 to slot 2, a delete,
a create that aligned to 84672 + 7056, a second create of an explicit
2016 sectors with an explicit type 04, and the extended chain read
back intact underneath all of it.


AND THEN FDISK WAS FINISHED (2026-09-21): THE CHAIN IS EDITED, FAT32
RESIZES, THERE IS A /MBR AND THERE IS A MENU.

Everything the entry above listed as still to do, and the list it was
on is empty now.  Four features, two bugs in code that was already
here and believed, and one fifteen-line refactor that turned out to be
the whole of what "logical drives too" cost.

    FDISK /D d:5        delete a logical drive - the chain is EDITED
    FDISK /C d:8        create one, in the largest free run inside
                        the extended container
    FDISK /P /M /S d:5  and plan, move and resize one
    FDISK /MBR d        put the standard boot code back
    FDISK /I            a menu
    ...and FAT32 volumes move and resize like any other

d:p NAMES 5 AND UP FOR LOGICAL DRIVES, counting on from the four
primary slots, which is the numbering every tool has used since the
1990s and - more to the point - the numbering FDISK /L now prints.
The report lists a logical drive as an ordinary row with a number in
it rather than an "L" in the margin, so the number on the screen is
the number to type back.


THE CHAIN.  A logical drive is not a table entry, it is a LINK: a
boot record of its own, a volume one track behind it, and a pointer
to it in the record before.  Adding or removing one is surgery on a
singly linked list written across the very space it describes.

THE HEAD OF THE LIST CANNOT MOVE, and that is the whole reason this
is harder than it sounds.  The master boot record names the sector
the chain starts at, and every slot-1 offset in every record of the
chain is measured from THAT sector - so moving the head means
rewriting every link in the list.  Both operations below are arranged
around not doing that.

  DELETING ANY LINK BUT THE FIRST: the record in front of it takes
  over its slot 1, VERBATIM.  Those sixteen bytes are already
  measured from the container and already describe the link that is
  about to become the next one, so copying them is not a shortcut -
  it is the exactly correct answer, and it preserves whatever
  convention the tool that built the chain used for the length field.

  DELETING THE FIRST: the head record STAYS and takes over the second
  link instead.  Slot 0 is rewritten to describe the second volume -
  from this record now, so the offset changes - and slot 1 is copied
  verbatim.  The second record becomes an abandoned sector inside the
  free space, which is what it was going to be anyway.

  DELETING THE LAST ONE THERE IS: both entries go to zero, leaving a
  container with one empty record in it - which is exactly what
  fd_chainbusy has always called free, so the container can then be
  deleted too.  That was the refusal the previous release could only
  apologise for.

  CREATING: two writes, and THE ORDER IS THE ARGUMENT.  The new
  record goes down first, while it is still a sector nothing refers
  to, and the pointer to it second.  Lose power between them and the
  chain is exactly what it was.  The other order puts a live pointer
  on the disk to a record that has not been written yet, which is a
  chain that walks into somebody's data.

ONE SECTOR FOR A DELETE, TWO FOR A CREATE, AND THE MASTER BOOT RECORD
IS NEVER TOUCHED BY EITHER.  The container does not change size or
position when something inside it comes or goes, and a program that
adjusted it anyway would be answering a question nobody asked with a
write to the one sector on the disk that has to be right.

THE WALK NOW INSISTS THE CHAIN RUNS FORWARD, which merely counting
links did not.  Every tool that has ever written one of these wrote
it in ascending order, because the list is laid out in the space it
describes; a pointer that goes backwards, or outside the container,
is a table something has damaged.  Refusing to walk it is the point:
this program EDITS the chain now, and surgery on a structure whose
shape could not be established is how a disk with one broken link
comes back with all of them broken.

THE NUMBER TYPED AT /C IS NOT WHERE IT GOES, and the help says so.  A
primary partition is put in the slot it was named for, because the
four slots are four fixed places in one sector.  A logical drive has
no such thing - its place in the chain is decided by where the free
space is - so 5 and 9 both mean "make one", and what it turns out to
be numbered is printed rather than demanded.


/P, /M AND /S ON A LOGICAL DRIVE COST FIFTEEN LINES, and that is the
entry worth reading.  The engine was already right; it was being
handed its argument in only one of the two ways a partition table can
express it.  fd_entptr resolves the named partition to

    pl_ent    -> its sixteen bytes, in mbr_buf or in ebr_buf
    pl_base   what its start field is measured from: 0 for a primary,
              the record's own sector for a logical drive
    pl_sec    the sector that has to be written back afterwards
    pl_lo/hi  the region it may not leave - the disk, or the container

and ONE POINTER AND ONE BASE is the whole difference.  Everything
else the planner and the executor do - reading the BPB, scanning the
FAT for the highest cluster in use, moving three regions in an order
chosen by the direction, laying down a new boot record - is about a
VOLUME AT A SECTOR, and a volume has no idea which kind of table
entry describes it.

TWO THINGS GENUINELY ARE DIFFERENT, and both are walls.

  ITS OWN BOOT RECORD IS A WALL, and it is the one a first attempt
  leaves out.  The record stays where it is, so the volume may move
  anywhere inside the container EXCEPT onto the one sector that
  describes it.  Without that line a /M down to the start of its own
  link writes the volume's boot sector over the record naming it, and
  the chain ends there.

  THE POINTER IN FRONT OF IT CARRIES THE LINK'S LENGTH, so a resize
  has to put that right as well - rx_fixprev.  NOTHING WALKS THE
  CHAIN BY THAT FIELD, which is exactly why it is the field that
  rots quietly: a table can be wrong there for years and every tool
  that reads it will still find every drive.  It is written because
  the next program to read it may not be one of those tools.

The walls are a little table now rather than a scan of the four
primary slots, which is what made rl_room and the overlap check the
same code for both kinds.


FAT32 COST LESS THAN ANY OF IT, and the reason is the one the earlier
entries had backwards.  "FAT32 has no root-directory region to
relocate and is therefore a different executor" - no: a region of no
sectors is a region that does not move, and the relocator handled it
already.  The same-layout argument is about CLUSTER NUMBERS
surviving, and FAT32 keeps its root in the data area as an ordinary
cluster chain, so BPB_ROOTCLUS is a cluster number and a cluster
number that survives needs no adjusting at all.

What actually had to be written was four small things:

  - THE SECTORS-PER-FAT COUNT IS ZERO AT 16h AND REAL AT 24h, and
    BOTH fields have to be written, not just the one that changed.
    An operating system reads the sixteen-bit one first and believes
    it, so a stale value there outranks the correct one at 24h
  - FOUR BYTES TO A FAT ENTRY, of which the TOP FOUR BITS ARE
    RESERVED.  A scan that did not mask them would read a free
    cluster as used on any volume whose driver had ever set one -
    and that scan is the floor on how far a shrink may go
  - THERE IS A BACKUP BOOT SECTOR, six sectors in.  A resize that
    wrote one of the two would leave a spare copy of the volume's OLD
    size: a backup that is worse than none, because it is the one
    that gets believed when the first is damaged
  - AND A CACHED FREE-CLUSTER COUNT in the FSInfo sector, which is a
    lie the moment the volume changes size.  It is a HINT and not a
    record - the specification says so - and the value meaning "I do
    not know, go and count" is all ones.  Writing that costs one pass
    over the FAT at the next mount; leaving the old number costs a
    free-space figure that is wrong until something notices


/MBR WRITES 440 BYTES AND NOT 446, which is the one place it differs
from the FDISK it is named after.  The boot code proper ends at 1B7h;
the six bytes after it are where every system since Windows NT writes
the disk's own identity, and the partition table starts at 1BEh.  DOS
knew nothing about those six bytes and its FDISK wrote straight over
them, which on a modern machine means every drive letter reassigned
at the next boot.  This leaves them alone - our loader is 229 bytes,
so there was never an argument about the room.

IT INSISTS ON A SIGNATURE, which looks like the wrong way round -
surely a damaged record is the case this is for.  But what makes the
operation safe is that the partition table SURVIVES it, and a sector
with no AA55 in it is a sector this program cannot say that about.
Writing a loader in front of sixty-four bytes of unknown is building
a disk that looks bootable and is not.  It prints the table it is
about to preserve before it asks, and says so when the code in there
is already this one.

The 512 bytes come from BIN\MBRBOOT.BIN through BIN2INC, the same way
SYS16.COM carries its boot sectors and for the same reason - wasm has
no INCBIN.  It is CARRIED and not read off the running system for the
obvious reason: the disk /MBR is there to repair may be the one it
would have read it from.


THE MENU IS A SHELL AND NOT A SECOND IMPLEMENTATION, and it was
written LAST on purpose.  A menu is a way of ASKING, and everything
it can ask for had to exist as something that could be TOLD first:
the command line is what a test harness drives, and driving it is how
every number this program prints was proved.  A menu written first
would have been a menu over an engine nothing had tested.

Each choice gathers the arguments the command line already takes,
writes them into the same fd_args, and jumps to the same verb - and
ECHOES THE LINE IT JUST BUILT before running it, because what is
worth knowing is what to type the second time, and the second time is
usually in a batch file where there is no menu at all.

IT DOES NOT CLEAR THE SCREEN and does not draw a box.  What a verb
printed stays above the menu that comes back, which is what makes the
transcript of a session readable afterwards - and it means the whole
program still works down a serial console.

HOW A VERB COMES BACK.  Every verb in this program ends by jumping to
fd_done or fd_fail, and both of those end the process - which is
right for a command line and no use at all in a loop.  So fd_menugo
remembers its own ESP and fd_done, in menu mode, puts it back and
jumps to the top.  THE STACK IS DISCARDED, NOT UNWOUND: what sits
above the loop's frame is saved registers belonging to frames that
