will never return, and there is nothing in any of them that has to be
put back - this program owns no handles, holds no locks and allocates
nothing.  It is a longjmp written out in the two instructions it
actually is.

AND IT CAN BE TYPED AT BY A FILE, which is how it is tested.  INT 21h
AH=0Ah reads a redirected stdin a line at a time, and the menu treats
an empty line as "leave" - so a file that runs out ends the session
instead of spinning forever, which is what a menu that re-prompted on
blank would do the moment anybody drove it from one.

WRITES ARE STILL ARMED SEPARATELY.  Being interactive is not consent:
W toggles the arming, the menu says which way it is set, and until it
is pressed every key in there is safe.


TWO BUGS IN CODE THAT WAS ALREADY HERE, and the first is the better
entry of the two.

A MOVE WHOSE RANGES OVERLAP WROTE A BOOT SECTOR MADE OF FILE DATA.
rl_wrboot read its template from pl_ostart - where the volume was -
and patched and wrote it at the destination.  But a MOVE copies the
whole volume, boot sector and all, so by the time rl_wrboot runs the
sector to patch is already at the destination, and reading the old
address back is wrong twice over: harmlessly when the ranges do not
overlap, and fatally when they do, because the copy has by then
written something else into that very sector.  What came back was a
BPB made of somebody's file, and the volume it was written over
stopped being a volume.

It had been there since the move was written, and the reason it went
unseen is worth as much as the fix: a move UP is copied back-to-front
so the first sector is read LAST and is still intact when the writer
asks for it.  Every move anyone had tried happened to go up.  The
test that found it moves a logical drive up and then back down again,
which is the shape of a test worth having - do it, undo it, and
compare - and the second half is the half that failed.

THE SHRINK AND GROW LIMITS IGNORED THE WIDTH'S OWN FLOOR.  The type
of a FAT volume is its CLUSTER COUNT and nothing else, so a volume
shrunk past the bottom of its band stops being the kind of volume it
was - which rl_plan refuses.  But "can shrink to" was computed from
what is stored and nothing else, so it printed a number the next
screen would turn down.  It showed up on FAT32, where the floor is
65525 clusters and the old answer was out by an order of magnitude,
and it was just as wrong on FAT16 all along: a 16MB FAT16 volume
offered to shrink to 36 sectors and now says 4150.  rl_maxsize had
the matching hole at the top - its ceiling was a two-way choice
between FAT12 and FAT16, so every FAT32 volume was told it could grow
to 66580 sectors whatever the disk said.

AND ONE ABOUT THE SHELL, found the expensive way: THIS COMMAND.COM
DOES NOT CARRY A REDIRECTION INTO A BATCH FILE.  "FDLTEST > C:\OUT" -
and "CALL FDLTEST > C:\OUT" - both create the file, leave it EMPTY,
and print the whole run to the screen.  Real MS-DOS keeps the
redirection for the life of the batch; this one puts the handles back
after the first command.  Two four-minute test runs finished with
nothing to read before that was established.  TOOLS\MKCAP.PL now
rewrites a test batch with the redirection on every line, which is
what a capture run needs; the test batches themselves stay readable,
which is the point of generating it rather than writing it.


THE ALIGNMENT COLUMN, which was the smallest thing on the list and is
the one that pays every time the report is read.  A star after the
size means the partition does not begin and end on a cylinder
boundary, with the two exceptions that are not anybody's choice: a
primary may begin one track in, where the master boot record left
off, and the head of an extended chain must begin exactly where the
container does.  NOTHING CORRECTS IT - moving somebody else's
partition to tidy the arithmetic is exactly the kind of unasked-for
write this program does not do - it is reported and that is all.

It is discriminating, which is the test of it: HD16.IMG comes out
clean because MKDISK aligns properly, and every row of MULTI.IMG is
starred because MKMULTI lays its partitions out on TRACK boundaries
from LBA 63, so their ends land one track short of a cylinder every
time.  Both of those are true and neither was visible before.


WHAT THE TESTS SAY.  Four new batches beside FDTEST.BAT, all verified
2026-09-21 in DOSBox 0.74 with the output captured off the image by
FATGET.PL rather than read off a photograph of the screen:

  FDLTEST.BAT   the chain.  Delete the LAST link and the other two do
                not move; create in the space it frees and the record
                lands on a cylinder boundary at 157248 with the
                volume one track behind it at 157311 + 6993; delete
                the HEAD and the record at 91791 stays and takes over
                the second volume, with the container's own entry
                untouched; empty the chain and the container can then
                be deleted; create into an empty container and the
                record goes exactly at 91791 because the table names
                that sector.  Every number predicted before the run
                and every number matched
  FDRTEST.BAT   /P, /M and /S on a logical drive, each change
                followed by the change that undoes it - which is what
                caught the boot-sector bug above.  Three refusals a
                primary does not have: onto its own boot record,
                outside the container, and into the neighbour
  FD32TEST.BAT  FAT32, on HD32.IMG as the second disk.  81585 sectors
                down to 70000 and back: 628 sectors/FAT to 539 and
                back, 80297 clusters to 68890 and back, the backup
                boot sector byte-identical to the primary afterwards
                and the FSInfo free count set to all ones.  A shrink
                to 60000 is refused because the width would change
  FDMTEST.BAT   the menu, typed at by a file it writes itself with
                ECHO.  A report, a /P on a LOGICAL drive, a choice
                that is not one of the choices, a refusal from inside
                a verb - both of which have to come back to the menu
                rather than end the program - then W and a real
                delete

ONE THING DOES NOT COME BACK FROM A RESIZE AND IT IS NOT A BUG: THE
TYPE BYTE.  A 06h volume taken down to 20000 sectors and back is
described by 04h, because rl_typebyte works the byte out from the
shape the volume HAS rather than remembering the shape it used to
have, and 04h and 06h are the same filesystem spelled for two
different sizes.  Worth knowing before reading the report and
thinking something was lost.

STILL NOT DONE, and now it is a short list: a resize that needs the
CLUSTER SIZE to change, which renumbers every cluster on the volume
and would have to rebuild every chain and rewrite every directory
entry recursively - rl_plan still answers RL_REMAP and says what it
would take.  That is the one regime SAFEPART has code for and refuses
to run, and this port still does not carry it.

EVERY COMMAND ANSWERS /? NOW, INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL (2026-09-20).

Charlie asked for it after the rest of v0.60 was done, and it turned
out to be two questions rather than one: WHERE the check goes, and
WHEN a "/?" in the argument is a question rather than text.

THE CHECK GOES IN THE DISPATCHER AND NOWHERE ELSE.  cmd_table used to
be two columns - verb, handler - and is four now: verb, handler, the
help, and flags.  exec_line tests for /? at tbl_hit, once, in front of
every handler, so a command cannot be added without help and cannot be
written in a way that forgets to look.  MS-DOS 6 puts the same check
in the same place (cmd/command/tmisc1.asm), which is where the rest of
this section comes from too - S:\DOS6SRC settles what real DOS does in
a way that black-box testing on an emulator never quite does.

THE SECOND QUESTION IS THE INTERESTING ONE.  Most commands should
answer /? wherever it appears among their arguments: "DIR *.SYS /?" is
a question about DIR and there is nothing else it could be.  But

    ECHO Run SETUP /? for help

must print its sentence, and

    REM the /? switch is documented below

must stay silent, and "SET V=/?" must set the variable.  A single rule
gets one of those two groups wrong whichever rule you pick.  DOS 6
carries a per-command flag for it, spelled fLimitHelp in tdata.asm,
and flags exactly REM, PAUSE, SET, PROMPT, ECHO, GOTO, IF and FOR -
the commands whose argument is text.  CF_HELPALONE here is that flag
and that list, plus CALL, LH and LOADHIGH, which DOS does not flag:
the argument they are handed is a whole command line, and a /? in it
belongs to the command at the front of it, not to the verb that ran
it.  "LH FOO /?" should tell you about FOO.

"DIR/?" WITHOUT THE SPACE.  The verb scanner read that as a command
named "DIR/?" and answered Bad command or file name.  The obvious fix
is to make '/' a delimiter and it is the wrong one: a verb is a path
as often as it is a name, and a shell that splits
"C:/TESTS/APITEST.COM" has broken something nobody asked it to look at
in order to fix a help switch.  '/' ends the verb only when a '?'
follows it.

AND THE BUG WORTH THE ENTRY: A TERMINATOR THAT CAN APPEAR IN THE TEXT
IS NOT A TERMINATOR.  The help strings were '$'-terminated like every
other message in COMMAND.COM, printed through 21h/09h.  PROMPT's help
has to print $P, $N, $G, $L, $B, $Q, $D, $T, $V, $E, $H, $_ and $$ to
be of any use at all - so the screen stopped dead after

    PROMPT [text]

and the entire content of that help, the list of codes, was never
printed.  Every other help screen was perfect, which is what made it
easy to miss: the failure was invisible in twenty-nine of thirty
cases and total in the thirtieth.  The help strings are NUL-terminated
now and go out through print_asciiz.  It was caught by reading the
captured run rather than by a check that could fail, and the general
form is worth keeping: a message format that reserves a character
cannot be used for text that is ABOUT that character.

WHAT EACH HELP SAYS IS THIS SHELL AND NOT MS-DOS.  Copying DOS 6's
wording was tempting - it is better written than anything here - and
it would have documented switches PM-DOS does not have: DIR takes
/P /W /S /O and not /A or /B, COPY has no /Y because nothing here asks
before overwriting, FOR has no /F.  A help screen that lists a switch
the command will ignore is worse than no help screen, because the
reader stops looking for the real reason nothing happened.  Two claims
were written wrong on the first pass and caught by reading the code
rather than the comments: PROMPT's default is $P$G and not $N$G, and
REN takes no wildcards but DOES move an entry between directories,
because the kernel's 56h always could.

THE EXTERNALS EACH PARSE THEIR OWN TAIL, so each was a separate chance
to have forgotten: CHOICE, MORE, SORT, SYS, FORMAT and DRIVES had no
/? at all, and MEM and FDISK printed their usage but exited with code
1 - so a batch file that asked for help was told it had made a mistake.
/? exits 0 everywhere now and an argument mistake still exits 1.  MORE
needed the check in front of the filename, because everything that is
not a switch to MORE is a file to page and "/?" came back as "File not
found": a true sentence and a useless answer.  FORMAT and SYS needed
it in front of the DRIVE for the same reason.  TOOLS\SYS16.COM, which
runs on real DOS, got the same treatment.  MOUNT already had it.

DISK\HELPTEST.BAT is the test and it is meant to be READ: every verb's
help, then the rules section, where ECHO and REM and SET have to print
their text and DIR has to print its help.  Verified 2026-09-20 in
DOSBox with the output captured to a file - 606 lines, all thirty-five
table rows, eleven external commands, nothing formatted, no boot
sector written, no partition table touched and CHOICE not waiting for
a key.

MOVE.COM, AND THE KERNEL BUG IT WAS THE FIRST THING TO REACH.

CMD\MOVE.ASM.  "MOVE [/Y | /-Y] source[,source...] destination" - move
files, rename a file, rename a directory.

WITHIN ONE VOLUME NOTHING IS COPIED, and that is the whole reason the
command is worth having beside COPY.  21h/56h is a rename that moves:
it writes the directory entry into the new parent and tombstones the
old one, so the file's clusters are never read.  A 600MB file changes
directory in the time it takes to write two sectors.  Between volumes
the bytes have to travel and 56h says so exactly - ERR_NOTSAME, 11h -
and MOVE copies and deletes.  THE ORDER IS THE SAFETY ARGUMENT: the
source goes only after the copy is written, stamped, closed and given
its attributes, and every failure before that removes the PARTIAL
DESTINATION and leaves the source alone.  A half-moved file is worse
than an unmoved one, because the next thing to read it will not know.

AND THE BUG.  The cross-volume test moved a file from D: to E: and
reported success - and the source was still there, and the destination
was the right SIZE and full of ZEROES.  Three impossible things at
once, which is usually one cause.

21h/56h's "same volume" check read fat_drive, and FAT.INC says what
fat_drive is on the line it is declared: "BIOS drive of this volume".
THE PHYSICAL DRIVE.  D: and E: are two partitions of MULTI.IMG, so
they are both 81h, so they compared EQUAL and the rename went ahead -
copying the entry into the target volume's directory carrying the
SOURCE's start cluster, which is a cluster number in the source's FAT
and means something else entirely in the target's, and then
tombstoning "the original" after a ctx_restore that puts the DIRECTORY
back but not the VOLUME.  So the erase landed on the target volume at
the source's slot index.  Every symptom follows: the destination reads
as whatever is at that cluster number on the other volume, the source
was never erased, and a slot on a volume nobody had touched was.  The
fix is one word twice - cur_vol, "logical drive held in vol_state".

NOTHING HAD EVER ASKED.  COPY does not call 56h; COMMAND.COM's REN
takes its second argument through two_args and a new name carries no
drive; the CMD tests rename within a directory.  A cross-volume 56h
was unreachable from the shell, and the first program to build both
paths itself found it in its first run.  THE GENERAL FORM IS THE ONE
TO KEEP: a field whose name says "drive" has to be read as the kind of
drive it IS, and this kernel has three of them - a logical letter, a
BIOS number, and a pseudo-unit for images and ATAPI.  fat_drive is the
second; cur_vol is the first.

WHAT FOUND IT WAS "BUILD move", which is IMG_DEBUG's trick one level
up: MOVE prints the count 3Fh returned, the address it asked to be
filled and the bytes that are actually there.  The first run said the
buffer was fine and full of "travelle" - and the second said nothing
at all, because the trace never printed, because the copy path was
never entered, because 56h had returned SUCCESS.  A trace that does
not appear is evidence too.

THE REST OF THE DESIGN, briefly, since each piece is a decision:

  THE NAMES ARE COLLECTED BEFORE ANYTHING MOVES.  A find walks a
  directory by slot index and moving a file rewrites that directory
  underneath the walk, so enumerating and moving in one loop skips
  files.  Collect, close the search, then move.  A pattern matching
  more names than the pool holds is done in passes - everything moved
  has left the directory, so the next pass finds the next batch - and
  a pass that moves NOTHING ends it, or a directory where every move
  failed would be enumerated for ever.

  LONG NAMES SURVIVE.  714Eh returns a file's real name and 56h is
  LFN-transparent, so "MOVE *.TXT \DOCS" keeps "Quarterly Report.txt"
  spelt that way.  With LFN=OFF the 71h family is absent by design and
  MOVE falls back to 4Eh/4Fh, which is the right answer on a machine
  that has declared it has no long names.

  AN EXPLICIT NAME MEANS WHAT IT SAYS; A WILDCARD MEANS THE ORDINARY
  FILES.  "MOVE SUB NEWSUB" moves a directory because the user named
  one; "MOVE *.* \DOCS" does not sweep up subdirectories, hidden files
  and system files.  One rule, one place, in the attribute mask.

  A DIRECTORY CAN BE RENAMED AND NOT MOVED, which is the kernel's rule
  and not a shortcut: its ".." points at its parent.  MOVE says that
  in a sentence rather than passing on "access denied", which would
  send the reader looking for a permission that does not exist.

  THE PROMPT IS THE DEFAULT AND /Y IS THE OVERRIDE - the other way
  round from COPY here, deliberately.  A COPY that overwrites destroys
  one file; a MOVE that overwrites destroys one file AND takes away
  the only other copy of the one replacing it.

  60h ANSWERS "IS THIS THE SAME FILE".  "A.TXT", ".\A.TXT" and
  "C:\WORK\A.TXT" are one file spelt three ways and comparing what was
  typed would say they are three - which matters because the overwrite
  path DELETES the destination first, so a move onto itself would
  delete the file in order to move it.

DISK\MVTEST.BAT is the test and it runs on MULTI.IMG's volumes, never
on the disk PM-DOS booted from.  It finds them BY MARKER and not by
letter: MKMULTI prints "expected letters: C: PRIMARY-ONE", which is
true when MULTI.IMG is the only disk and wrong by one when it is the
second, so the test looks for PRIM1.TXT and LOG1.TXT wherever they
landed.  Its guard names a FILE for the same reason IF EXIST always
has - it tests plain files only, so "IF EXIST D:\" is false on a
machine with a perfectly good D:, and the test skipped itself silently
the first time it ran.

Verified 2026-09-20 in DOSBox: rename, move-into-directory with the
file still readable afterwards, a wildcard moving three at once with
none left behind, the four refusals, /Y replacing with the new
contents, a directory renamed with its contents intact, and a
cross-volume move whose source is gone and whose destination reads
back correctly.

TWO SMALL THINGS THE WORK PASSED THROUGH, both in COMMAND.COM:

  A VERB IS A PATH, NOT A NAME.  verb_buf was sixteen bytes and the
  copy capped at twelve - "FILENAME.EXT" - so

      C:\TESTS\APITEST.COM

  arrived as "C:\TESTS\API" and came back "Bad command or file name"
  about a program that runs perfectly well when PATH finds it, because
  PATH builds the same string in path_buf and never goes through that
  copy.  A QUOTED verb already had the room, so the shell could run
  what it could not be told plainly.  The cap is QVERB_MAX now.  No
  internal command is twelve characters long, so the table match is
  unaffected.

  DEL SAID "FILE NOT FOUND" FOR EVERY FAILURE, including the ones
  where its own find had just matched the name - a statement the
  program had disproved a moment earlier.  It keeps the last error and
  says "Access denied" when that is what it was, which is what real
  DOS says for a read-only file and what v0.60 needs for the two new
  reasons: a file that is a mounted drive letter, and one open by
  somebody.

AND ONE IN A TEST, found by running the regressions: ALLOCTST EXECs
itself from a path it no longer lives at.  The v0.59 BIN split moved
it to \TESTS and the literal still said the root, so "could not run
the child" had been the answer since, and the second half of that test
had not run.  It reported a FAILURE rather than going quiet, which is
the only reason it was ever noticed.


CMD\ IS ONE DIRECTORY PER EXTERNAL COMMAND, AND CHKDSK AND LABEL RUN
ON PM-DOS (2026-09-25).

Asked for in that order: give each external a directory of its own,
as CMD\CHKDSK and CMD\LABEL already had, and then find out whether
those two - C programs, written against DOS 7's FAT32 calls for "a
32-bit DOS" in general - would run here.  They would not, for four
reasons, and none of them was in the code that checks a disk.

THE LAYOUT.  CMD\<name>\<name>.ASM for all twelve assembly externals;
CMD\ itself keeps only the shell.  The rebuild after the move was
byte-identical for every binary.  BUILD.CMD's stale-object sweep names
each directory, because wasm exits 0 on an error and a directory
missing from that list is one whose failed assembly links yesterday's
object.

WHY THEY DID NOT RUN:

  1  THE FORMAT.  They linked as an MZ stub plus an LE image, and
     exec_kind decides by the D32 magic alone, so the file went to the
     DOS box and the stub said "This program requires a 32-bit DOS".
  2  48h IN PARAGRAPHS.  PM-DOS's native 48h takes BYTES, so every
     block would have been a sixteenth of what was asked for - and
     CHKDSK /F writes a FAT it has built in those blocks.
  3  7302h GIVEN A DRIVE NUMBER.  PM-DOS names the drive for the whole
     73h family with a PATH at EDX, as 7303h does, so drive+1 went
     through the ring-3 bridge as a pointer: slot offset 1 to 26, which
     is the guard page.  r3_flat refuses only 0, so it was the KERNEL
     that took the page fault.  The block that comes back is PM-DOS's
     own layout as well, not the DOS 7.1 extended DPB.
  4  THE FAT32 FAT HELD WHOLE.  Four bytes a cluster, plus the one-byte
     cluster map: HD32.IMG, at 80,297 clusters, needed about 400K of
     heap out of a 512K slot that also holds the program and its stack.

THE FIXES ARE IN THE PROGRAMS; THE KERNEL IS UNCHANGED.  SYS_D32.C is
the one file in each that knows what system it is on, and it now
states PM-DOS's ABI at its top: 48h in bytes, the top of memory as the
dword at PSP+4, 7302h given "X:\" and PM-DOS's block turned into a
BPB, and no INT 25h/26h fallback - PM-DOS always has 7305h, and its
25h/26h have no packet form.  4409h never reports a drive as remote
here, so F101h is asked what the filesystem is: 0 means ISO9660 or
UDF, a CD-ROM or a MOUNTed .ISO, and that gets the answer DOS gave a
CD-ROM, "Cannot CHKDSK a network drive".

A FAT32 FAT IS READ THROUGH A WINDOW NOW - sixteen 4K blocks, least
recently used - and FAT12 and FAT16 are still held whole.  A CHANGED
block is never evicted: without /F the corrected FAT is what the rest
of the check is worked out from and is never written, so until
fat_write() a changed block is the only copy of the change.  Checked
three ways against one damaged FAT32 volume on the Windows harness
(SYS_NT.C): the window, a one-block window that evicts on nearly every
access, and the whole FAT.  Identical reports, and byte-identical FATs
after /F.

THE LINK WAS THE SUBTLE PART, and it is worth knowing before the next
C program: wlink's "form raw bin" does two things that a one-segment
assembly program never meets.
  - IT WRITES ONE GROUP STRAIGHT AFTER ANOTHER.  With the code in a
    group of its own, the three bytes of alignment between the end of
    _TEXT and the start of DGROUP were simply not written, and every
    string and table sat three bytes short of the address the code
    used for it.  DOSINT.ASM puts _TEXT in DGROUP.
  - IT STOPS AT THE LAST INITIALISED BYTE, so the BSS was not in the
    file, and a header saying BSS=0 would have had the kernel build
    its heap on top of the program's globals.  DOSINT.ASM ends the
    image with a D32END segment, and "order ... clname BSS clname
    D32END" makes wlink write the BSS out as zeroes to reach it.
  The map file gave the right addresses both times.  Only the bytes
  in the file said otherwise.

Verified 2026-09-25 in DOSBox-X, headless (C:\DOSBox-X, portable; SDL's
dummy video driver, -silent and -time-limit, so no window ever opens
and the run ends itself - the log is read back off the floppy image).
CHKDSK on FAT12, FAT16 and FAT32 at 80,297 clusters; /F on a damaged
FAT32 volume recovering 21 chains, leaving a FAT byte-identical to the
harness's and a corrected FSInfo; /F on a damaged FAT16; a MOUNTed FAT
image; the default drive.  LABEL setting, prompting for and deleting
labels on FAT16 and FAT32, with VOL and DIR seeing each change at once.
The refusals: no such drive, a bad switch, an invalid label, and a
MOUNTed .ISO for both programs.  THE FIRST THING CHKDSK FOUND ON EVERY
STOCK IMAGE WAS A CROSS-LINK, and it is right: MKDISK gives the
long-named test files one cluster between them, on purpose.

SYS_DPMI.C and SYS_NT.C are still there - the same programs for
DOS/32A and for a disk image on Windows - but nothing in the tree
builds them, and STUB.ASM is no longer used by anything: the D32
header carries its own 16-bit stub.

STILL OPEN, and all three are the kernel's:
  - r3_flat accepts offsets inside the guard page, so a program that
    passes a small number where a pointer goes faults the kernel
    rather than getting an error back.  Refusing below SLOT_PSP would
    do it.
  - 7302h and 7304h take a path where DOS 7 takes DL, and that holds
    for a 16-bit guest too, which is quietly told about the default
    drive instead of the one it named.
  - 7305h fails with 0Bh or 08h, never with the 13h-1Fh extended
    errors, so LABEL on a write-protected disk says "General failure".
  [ALL THREE FIXED the same day - see the next entry.]


THE KERNEL'S OPEN LIST, AND THE SHELL DOS HAD: DIR /A /B /L, COPY /Y,
REN WITH WILDCARDS, FOR /F, COMMAND /C AND DOSKEY (2026-09-25)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Asked for together: everything left on the kernel's list of bugs and
limits, and the internal commands brought up to what DOS has - DIR's
switches, COPY /Y, FOR /F, DOSKEY built in, directories renamed by REN
and MOVE.  MD, RD, REN, BREAK, CALL, ECHO, DEL, GOTO, IF, PATH, PAUSE,
PROMPT, REM, SET, SHIFT and TYPE were on the list too and were already
here; BATTEST, HELPTEST and SWTEST go over them again below.

THE KERNEL.

  r3_flat REFUSES THE WHOLE GUARD PAGE, not just zero.  Offset 1 used to
  become a flat address in the slot's first page - the one that is not
  present - so the program's mistake was the KERNEL'S page fault.  And
  cbuf_ok now holds a native program's buffer inside its own slot
  (r3_inslot), because r3_flat only looks at where a pointer STARTS.

  EVERY FIXED-SIZE ANSWER IS MEASURED BEFORE IT IS WRITTEN.  buf_ok
  closed the pointer-plus-length hole for 3Fh, 40h, 0Ah, 60h and the
  finds in v0.37; the calls that write an answer of a KNOWN size into a
  caller's buffer were never asked: 47h (64), 5Ah (the nine bytes on
  the end of the path), 7147h and 7160h (260), 714Eh/714Fh (318),
  71A0h, 7303h, 38h, 65h, F1h AL=3/6/8, the FCB family's FCB and the
  DTA 11h/12h fill, and INT 25h/26h's buffer.  An FCB call refused
  says so the FCB way, AL = FFh.

  4Eh AND 714Eh SAY "PATH NOT FOUND" (3) when the directory is what is
  missing.  Every failure came through f4E_none, which wrote
  ERR_NOFILE over whatever resolve_parent had said.

  32 LONG-NAME FIND HANDLES, OUT OF THE ARENA, WITH OWNERS.  Four, in
  the image, owned by nobody, was a countdown: a program killed in a
  directory walk kept its handle until the reboot.  The image has 13K
  left under DOS_LIMIT, so the table is bought at boot with cur_own
  zeroed (cache_addchunk's trick), and 4Ch and the DOS box's exit both
  sweep it by owner.

  7302h AND 7304h ARE DOS 7.1'S.  7302h takes DL and returns DOS 7.1's
  61-byte extended DPB - word fields for FAT12/16, dword ones from 21h,
  and the word sectors-per-FAT zero on FAT32, which is how a reader
  tells them apart - and refuses a short buffer with 18h.  7304h takes
  the FAT32 API's seven-dword request; its layout is from memory of
  that document and not from a source, and says so.  CHKDSK and LABEL
  went back to DOS 7.1's convention and to FAT.C's bpb_from_dpb, as
  their DOS/32A builds always were.  THE BUG THIS TURNED UP: f73_drv is
  the byte after the 7302h block, and the block was cleared with
  rounded-up STOSDs, so every block ever returned said drive A:.  It
  was true of the old 47-byte block too; nothing had looked.

  7305h, 25h AND 26h REPORT THE DRIVER'S STATUS.  7305h answers 13h-1Fh
  (the INT 24h code plus 13h), and 25h/26h DOS's own word, AH the
  status and AL the code - they both used to say 0Bh for everything.
  DOSBox-X's BIOS answers a write to a read-only image with 20h,
  "controller failure", not 03h, so LABEL there still says General
  failure; the write-protect path wants 86Box or iron.

  LOGICAL SECTORS OF 1024, 2048 AND 4096 BYTES MOUNT.  fat_mount turns
  the BPB into 512-byte units once - cluster, reserved area, FAT, total,
  and the root rounded up to a LOGICAL sector - and nothing above it
  knows; 36h, 1Bh/1Ch, 7302h, 7303h, 25h/26h and 7305h divide back out
  through fat_lshift.  A PHYSICAL sector that is not 512 is still not
  reachable, because nothing in the block layer asks a device.
  TOOLS\MKLSEC.PL writes such a volume, TOOLS\FLOPGET.PL reads one back,
  and on a 2048- and a 4096-byte-sector image MOUNTed from a floppy
  DIR, TYPE, COPY in both directions, MD, F32TEST and CHKDSK all agree.

AND THE BUG THAT WAS NOT ON THE LIST: A PARENT CAME BACK FROM ITS
FIRST CHILD WITH THE CHILD'S HEAP.  r3h_lo and r3h_hi are one pair of
globals and exec_load sets them for every program it loads, so after
any external command the shell's 48h walked the SHELL'S slot with
ATTRIB's heap bounds, found no block headers in its own code, and said
"no memory".  DIR /O answers that by listing unsorted, which looks like
nothing at all.  DOSKEY's pool made it loud: the shell's first
allocation became a permanent one, and REN *.TXT said "Insufficient
memory".  The bounds are in the EXEC nesting record now (XN_HLO,
XN_HHI) and 4Ch and a failed 4Bh put them back.

THE SHELL.

  DIR: /A[[:]HSDAR, "-" for not], /B (and /B /S with whole paths), /L,
  /C and /CH (taken; nothing is compressed), /OC, and /4 (DOS 7's; the
  years were already four digits), with /-x and DIRCMD for all of
  them.  The find can only be told which attributes may be PRESENT, so
  /A asks as wide as it needs and dir_want keeps or drops each entry.
  VOL and DIR's first line name the drive now: " Volume in drive C is".

  COPY /Y, /-Y and COPYCMD, with DOS 6.2's default: ask at the prompt,
  not in a batch file.  "Overwrite X (Yes/No/All)?" reads its key from
  standard input, so a batch file can answer it with "< N.ANS".

  REN takes wildcards in both names and keeps the new name in the old
  one's directory; a drive or path in it is "Invalid parameter", as in
  DOS.  The matches are collected first, for MOVE's reason.  A
  directory renames by name; MOVE renamed one already.

  FOR /F - NT's, over files, a "string" or a 'command', with eol= skip=
  delims= tokens= and usebackq.  The command runs through COMSPEC /C,
  which is NT's way and means a batch file or a pipe works there.

  COMMAND /C - which the startup comment had claimed for a long time and
  nothing implemented.  Everything after /C is the command's, switches
  included; the shell exits with its errorlevel once any batch file it
  started has run out.

  DOSKEY, BUILT IN AND ALWAYS ON: CMD\DOSKEY.INC, written against
  S:\DOS6SRC\cmd\doskey - the template model, every key in
  template.asm's table, the history and macros sharing one /BUFSIZE
  pool, macros packed and listed as trans.asm packs and lists them.
  The DOSKEY command is internal.  The editor runs only when stdin and
  stdout are both the console, and places the cursor with 21h/F0h
  rather than INT 10h; after every redraw the line's start row is
  worked out again from where the console says the cursor stopped,
  which is how a line that scrolled the screen keeps its place.  No
  insert-mode cursor shape and no bell: INT 21h has neither.

HOW THE EDITOR WAS TESTED, and it is worth keeping.  DOSBox-X's
AUTOTYPE crashes DOSBox-X (0xC0000409) typing "echo x" into its OWN
shell, and after grey keys it hung the run outright.  But 21h/07h reads
a redirected stdin a byte at a time and a zero then a scan code IS an
extended key, so KYTEST=1 lets the editor take its input from a file,
TOOLS\MKKEYS.PL writes DISK\KEYTEST.KEY, and "COMMAND < KEYTEST.KEY"
types thirty lines - every editing key, F1-F9, Alt+F7/F10, macros,
$T and Ctrl+T - each of which writes a file KEYTEST.BAT reads back.

TESTS: FNDTEST.EXE (new), F32TEST.COM (rewritten for DOS 7.1, and the
guard-page pointer), DIRTEST, RENTEST, FORFTEST and KEYTEST.BAT, all on
the images.  Regressions from a scratch HD16 with MULTI.IMG, every
batch test captured through COMMAND /C: API, BUF, FCB, LOL, MCB, ALLOC,
R3, F32, FND, CACHE, XMS, EMS, DPMI, UMB, CTRY and CFG green; BATTEST,
GOTO, RED, LFN, CMD, NEST, DEEP, IMG, NUL, SW, HELP, MV, ATTR and DISK
as expected.  Not green and not new: VFYTEST (DEVICE=TESTBLK.SYS is
commented out), HNDTEST (opens C:\WINDOWS\SYSTEM.INI, which only the
Windows graft provides), CURTEST inside VDMTEST (it measures the
screen, and the harness sends it to a file), and EXECTST, which EXECs
ARGS.COM from the current directory - the v0.59 split moved it to
\TESTS, exactly as it did ALLOCTST's.

STILL OPEN: DIR /V (DOS 7's verbose listing); a physical sector that
is not 512 bytes; a third hard disk (MAX_PHYS is 2); EXECTST's path.


CMD.EXE, AND A 16-BIT COMMAND.COM FOR THE PROGRAMS THAT ASK FOR ONE
(2026-09-26)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie's question: should the shell become CMD.EXE with a 16-bit
COMMAND.COM beside it, or keep its name and grow a 16-bit stub that
does what the 32-bit one does?  The first.  A stub that does what the
shell does IS a second shell, only sharing a file with the first; and
the program that needs it is not the user at the prompt but a DOS
program shelling out.  That program EXECs whatever COMSPEC names, in
its own DOS box, as real-mode code.  A D32 program there prints "This
program requires 32-bit DOS mode." and stops, and under Windows 3.1
standard mode the kernel is parked and nothing 32-bit runs at all.
Two programs under two names is what NT did, for the same reason.

THE NAMES.

  CMD.EXE is the native shell, formerly COMMAND.COM, now CMD\CMD.ASM.
  The kernel starts A:\CMD.EXE (the drive patched as before), and
  falls back to A:\COMMAND.COM so an older disk - IMAGES\HD16.IMG's
  Windows graft, for one - still boots.
  COMSPEC is set by CMD.EXE to COMMAND.COM IN CMD.EXE'S OWN DIRECTORY
  (F103h's path with the name swapped), unless one was inherited.
  FOR /F's 'command' goes through CMD.EXE itself, found the same way,
  because it is CMD.EXE's syntax that is in the quotes.
  SYS copies CMD.EXE (required) and COMMAND.COM (optional); SYS16 says
  "skipped" when it is missing.
  INC\PMVER.INC holds the version: the kernel, both shells and
  BUILD.CMD's FIND all read the one file.

COMMAND.COM, CMD\COMMAND\: wasm, a raw .COM of 33K whose resident part
is 23K - the help texts and INIT come after resident_end and the
stack overlays them, and /? reads its help back out of the file.  It
is written against the DOS API and nothing else, and its command set
is DOS 6.22's: no long names, no FOR /F, and no line editor of its own
(a loaded DOSKEY is asked with INT 2Fh AX=4810h, as DOS's shell asked
it, and 0Ah edits otherwise).  It runs on real DOS, and that is how it
was checked: DOSBox-X with its own DOS set to ver=6.22, MS-DOS 6.22's
COMMAND.COM (from S:\User backups\Charlie\DOS\MSDOS622) and ours
running the same batch files, and the output diffed.  S:\DOS6SRC was
read for what DOS does; nothing was copied out of it.

The 6.22 behaviours that are not obvious until something diffs them:
  - Every error message goes to STDERR, which is why "> NUL" never
    hides one.
  - ECHO skips exactly ONE character after its name: "ECHO   x" keeps
    two blanks.  ECHO., CD.. and CD\ are prefix forms: the name ends
    at a "." or a "\" for the commands that allow it.
  - DIR /W pads its columns with tabs; DIR /S's headings have no
    leading blank; a batch file with ECHO OFF gets no CRLF before the
    prompt.
  - Inside an INT 24h handler only 21h functions 01h-0Ch are allowed,
    and the Abort/Retry/Fail prompt must reach the screen even when
    stdout is a file: the handler points the current PSP's JFT[0] and
    [1] at the shell's own and puts them back (6.22's SavHand and
    RestHand).
  - 6.22's COMMAND.COM reads a batch line up to CR.  An LF-only file
    is one long line to it - "@ECHO OFF<LF>REM ..." echoes "OFF" and
    the next three lines.  Ours takes CR, CRLF or LF; C16TEST.BAT and
    C16SUB.BAT are CRLF so the real one can run them.
Where ours differs on purpose: the default prompt is $P$G (6.22's is
drive and ">" unless it built the environment itself), because a box
opened from CMD.EXE should look like CMD.EXE; COMMAND /C returns the
command's errorlevel, where 6.22's does not; and VER names PM-DOS.

WHAT MS-DOS 6.22'S COMMAND.COM FOUND IN THE KERNEL, which is the
reason to run the real one and not only our own.

  THERE WAS ONE LEVEL OF HANDLES.  In DOS a handle indexes the
  program's own table in its PSP, and the table points into the shared
  SFT; here a handle WAS a kernel slot, for everybody.  After every
  command 6.22's shell closes handles 5-19 (its HeadFix), which DOS
  keeps empty - and here that closed CMD.EXE's saved standard output,
  so CMD.EXE could not put its redirection back and wrote a file size
  that lost everything the box had appended.  DOS\JFT.INC gives a DOS
  program - V86 code, or a DPMI client, which is the same process - the
  table its PSP always had room for.  jft_pre and jft_post wrap every
  guest INT 21h (F_EIP=1 in k21, and the DPMI entry): a handle in BX
  becomes its slot and is put back; a new slot becomes the program's
  LOWEST FREE HANDLE; 3Eh, 45h, 46h and 67h are done there outright,
  because they are the table.  jft_ref counts the entries pointing at
  each slot and a slot closes when its count reaches zero - never slots
  0-2.  A child inherits its parent's entries less the no-inherit ones
  (80h); a box's first program gets CMD.EXE's three and AUX and PRN on
  3 and 4, as DOS gave, so its first file is handle 5 as it was in DOS
  (and CFGTEST's "handles opened at once" is 21h where it was 23h).
  The per-call state lives in the frame's F_ESP slot, not a global,
  because a critical-error handler makes DOS calls while the failing
  call is still open.  The first cut counted FIVE standard handles, as
  DOS does, where PM-DOS has three - so a file on handle 3 or 4 never
  closed.  PSP:34h was given a flat address instead of a segment and
  offset.  And the Windows park check counted the new AUX and PRN
  entries as open files; it skips devices now.  67h with no memory for
  a bigger table succeeds without growing it: the count is a ceiling,
  and a refusal made programs give up for no reason.

  65h's TABLES WERE REFUSED: 02h and 04h (uppercase), 05h (filename
  terminators), 06h (collating) and 07h (DBCS).  MS FIND matched
  nothing and MS SORT hung.  They are real tables now at GNLS_OFF in
  DOSDATA - identity above 80h for uppercase, DOS's terminator list,
  a collating table that folds a-z and the accented letters onto their
  base letters, an empty DBCS table - and the answer is five bytes at
  ES:DI, CX=5, as DOS gives it.  6507h had been pointing at GLOL_DBCS,
  which is followed by CON's device header: a DBCS table that did not
  end where it should.

  THE BRIDGE GAVE BACK DX AND BX CHANGED.  vdm_result copies EAX-EDX
  back to the guest, and when DS:DX or ES:BX went in as a pointer the
  kernel's EDX or EBX was the FLAT ADDRESS.  SORT reads with ADD DX,AX
  in a loop, so every read after the first landed somewhere else.  Now
  the guest's own DX or BX goes back when it carried a pointer and the
  kernel left that register as it found it.

  THE CHARACTER FUNCTIONS IGNORED THE PROGRAM'S TABLE.  01h-0Ch read
  and wrote kernel slots 0 and 1 whatever the program's handles 0 and
  1 were.  std_set points them at the guest's JFT[0] and [1] for the
  length of the call (std_inp and std_outp, which fn06, 09h, 0Ah, 0Bh,
  0Ch, std_in, std_out and std_write now go through).

  DOSDATA grew to 1200h for the tables, so V86_TPA moved up by 20h
  paragraphs: the first MCB is 0520 and MEM says 618K.  CFGTEST's check
  2 asked 67h for more handles than it had memory for; it shrinks
  itself first now, which is what a DOS program has to do.

THE HANG THAT WAS A CLOCK.  SYS B: with two floppies stopped with
CMD.EXE at 0 bytes, and a plain COPY of PMDOS.SYS to B: stopped after
it.  The build from before this work stopped in exactly the same
place, and with 150 seconds instead of 40 both finish - DOSBox-X is
slow writing a floppy, and a time limit only tests itself.  When the
old build fails the same way, look at the clock before the code.

TESTS: DISK\C16TEST.BAT and C16SUB.BAT, run by "COMMAND /C" in the
regression.  C16TEST's output is 6.22's line for line except VER, the
prompt, the environment's segment and REN's order: 6.22's REN goes
through FCB 17h, which renames in place, and the kernel's 56h writes a
new entry.  HELPTEST runs both shells' /?.  The rest of the regression
is as before, apart from the MCB move, 618K, CMD.EXE in the listings
and the handle count above.

STILL OPEN:
  - ^C in a box ends the whole box, and 6.22's COMMAND.COM, which makes
    itself its own parent and expects ^C and Abort to come back to it,
    ends its box the same way.
  - A guest's own hooks of INT 21h and 2Fh are never called (V86C_TRAP
    takes 20h-2Fh), so a TSR that chains them, or a DOSKEY loaded in a
    box, is not seen.
  - A box cannot run a D32 program: CMD.EXE typed at COMMAND.COM prints
    the stub's message.  That is the native bridge, not started.
  - The MS-DOS Prompt under Windows 3.1 standard mode has not been
    tried with the new COMMAND.COM.
  - IMAGES\HD16.IMG still has the old D32 COMMAND.COM and no CMD.EXE;
    it boots through the fallback.  It needs the files grafted in, not
    MKHD, which would take the Windows install with it.
  - 56h should rename in place when the new name needs no more
    directory entries than the old one.
  [ALL BUT THE WINDOWS ONE FIXED - see the next entry.]


A BOX'S OWN VECTORS, ^C THE DOS WAY, 32-BIT PROGRAMS FROM A BOX, AND
WHAT A WINDOWS DOS SESSION FOUND IN RMDOS (2026-09-26)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

THE GUEST'S HOOKS ARE CALLED.  The monitor used to trap INT 20h-2Fh
before they reached the guest's vector table, so a TSR that hooked 21h
or 2Fh - which is what a TSR is - never ran, and DOSKEY loaded in a
box was never asked.  The real-mode IVT's DOS vectors now point at
stubs (VDM.INC, vdm_stubs) that trap into the kernel, and the monitor
reflects the vector like any other: a program that hooks one is called
first and chains to the stub, as it would chain to DOS.  INT 29h, an
IRET that lost the character, writes to the screen.

^C GOES TO THE PROGRAM, AS DOS SENDS IT.  It used to end the whole box.
Now the program's INT 23h is called: an IRET, a RETF 2 or a RETF with
the carry clear makes the call again (with a changed AH, that function
instead); a RETF with the carry set, or no handler at all, ends that
program - only it - and 4Dh says ^C.  A program that is its own parent
(6.22's COMMAND.COM) is sent to its terminate address.  A child's
INT 24h is put back when the child ends.  COMMAND.COM's "Terminate
batch job" and FOR behave as 6.22's do (ContCTerm clears ForFlag for
the level it is in - a FOR that CALLs a file whose child was ended
runs on).

A BOX RUNS 32-BIT PROGRAMS.  CMD.EXE, SORT or MEM typed at COMMAND.COM
ran into the D32 stub's "requires 32-bit DOS mode".  vdm_d32 builds a
native INT 21h frame and uses the ordinary 4Bh; the DOS program's
handles 0-2 become slots 0-2 for the run and what the 32-bit program
did to them is copied back, so COMMAND.COM's redirection works, an
errorlevel comes back, and a DOS program that one starts runs on top
of the box that started it.

56h RENAMES IN PLACE when source and destination share a directory,
as DOS's SIMPLE_RENAME does, long name included (lfn_storeat puts the
new run where the old one was).  A renamed file no longer jumps to the
first hole in the directory.

TESTS, all headless in DOSBox-X and all in the regression:
  HOOKTEST.COM  hooks 21h/2Fh and chains; INT 25h/26h both forms; ^C
                through every handler shape, typed with INT 16h AH=05h
                so no key is ever pressed; its own children for the
                cases that end a program.  Exit code = failures.
  BOXTEST.BAT   a DPMI client ending and an unhandled ^C, both under
                COMMAND /C, and the shell carries on after each.
  D32TEST.BAT   32-bit programs started by COMMAND.COM: redirection,
                errorlevel, a DOS grandchild.
  CCALIVE/CCFOR/CCONE.BAT   ^C at an interactive COMMAND.COM, checked
                against 6.22's.

IMAGES\HD16.IMG IS REFRESHED WITHOUT MKHD.  TOOLS\FATREPL.PL puts new
copies of named files onto a FAT16 image in place: a file that is
there has its chain freed and its entry rewritten, a new one takes a
free entry, and nothing else on the image is touched.  It will not
free a cluster another entry also points into (claimed()), which is
the only reason it survived MKDISK's cross-linked test files (below).
Both HD16.IMGs (IMAGES\ and the 86Box VM's) now carry CMD.EXE and this
release's binaries, checked file by file against BIN\ and with every
chain walked.  HNDTEST gives memory back with 4Ah before it asks 67h
for sixty handles - from a .COM that owns every free paragraph, 67h
had nowhere to put a bigger table and the test measured nothing.  It
now shows the table moved to 60 entries and the opens stopping at
FILES=40, which is DOS's answer.

WINDOWS 3.1 NOW RUNS WITH NOBODY AT THE MACHINE.  DOSBox-X headless
(SDL dummy driver) boots PM-DOS and Windows standard mode, and three
things make it usable:
  - "config -avistart" in [autoexec] records the screen from before
    the boot; TOOLS\ZMBVSHOT.PL decodes the ZMBV capture into BMPs, so
    a Windows screen can be looked at without a window.
  - [dos] int33=false.  DOSBox-X's own mouse driver's vector survives
    "boot" and points into memory the booted system reuses; Windows'
    MOUSE.DRV calls it and runs into FF FF.
  - The "rme9" build (BUILD rme9, DOS\RME9.INC): RMDOS writes one line
    per INT 21h to port E9h, which DOSBox-X logs with "bochs debug port
    e9=true".  One OUT per character, nothing buffered, so the line a
    hung machine never finished is the answer.  It also catches INT 6
    and prints where the invalid opcode was and the stack above it.
TOOLS\WINDRV.C (WINDRV.EXE, Win16) goes in WIN.INI's run=: it starts a
DOS program - DISK\WINDOS.BAT by default, which runs COMMAND.COM
tests into C:\WINDOS.TXT - waits for it, logs to C:\WINDRV.TXT and
exits Windows.

WHAT THE DOS SESSION FOUND IN RMDOS.  Starting a DOS program from
Windows means WINOLDAP writing a swap-information file, the first
thing to WRITE through RMDOS in any quantity, and RMDOS had never
been asked:
  - FAT16's end-of-chain was compared as FFF8h against a value widened
    to 32 bits, so the second cluster of a FAT16 file was never found
    and every write past the first failed with error 9.
  - Deleting a file wrote E5h into the FIRST entry of its directory
    sector as well as its own (CONFIG.SYS, in the run that found it).
  - Creating one lost BX in rd_stamp and wrote the time, date and ten
    zeroes into the SECOND entry of the sector (AUTOEXEC.BAT), and the
    century MUL wrote DX, so every date was month 0, day 0.
  - fat_freechain tested the wrong value for the end of the chain;
    dir_zero wrote a growing directory's zeroes through BX, which was
    also the buffer, so every sector past the first went to the wrong
    LBA.
  - "CD .." never worked, and CD did not change what 47h reports.
  - The List of Lists gave the SFT chain as FFFF:FFFF - which is what
    held Windows on its splash screen once the rest worked.
RMDOS gained MD, RD, REN (in place, or a file moved to another
directory), TRUENAME, 29h, 1Bh/1Ch, 66h, 69h, 6501h and 6523h; paths
go through one canonicaliser (rd_canon) that resolves "." and "..".
The kernel's own were checked against DOS 6 while there: TRUENAME of
a device is "C:/CON", RD of any drive's current directory is error
16, and 66h and 69h are answered.

RMFSTEST.COM makes all of those calls, writes exactly as WINOLDAP
writes, and runs on both DOSes - from the prompt for PM-DOS, through
PARKTEST for RMDOS.  What it cannot see from inside (the entries it
never looks at, lost clusters) was checked by walking the image before
and after.

FOUR MORE, FOUND WHILE BANKING ALL OF THAT.  The refreshed HD16.IMG
booted to "Bad or missing command interpreter" after one run of the
new tests - its root directory's second sector was a boot sector.
  - THE KERNEL'S 69h read the boot sector into sec_buf, which is the
    DIRECTORY cache, and left sec_lba naming the directory sector it
    had held.  The next entry update - closing the file RMFSTEST's
    output was redirected to - wrote the boot sector back over that
    sector.  69h forgets sec_lba before its read now, and fat_mount,
    which borrows the same buffer and forgot it only on success, does
    so on entry.  RMFSTEST now closes a file after 69h and looks for
    it; the old kernel fails that and wrecks the disk doing so.
  - RMDOS's 69h failed with error 5, and RMFSTEST called it a pass
    because its failure jump was a JC into an expect-ZF check.  The
    read was for sector 33,554,495 - 63 with 02h in the top byte -
    and the cause was sub_fromdir restoring SI: sub_create went on to
    use the VOLUME RECORD as the new file's SFT.  Every RMDOS create
    set SFF_WRITTEN in the top byte of VOL_START (breaking 69h, INT
    25h/26h and every floppy remount), and a create that truncated
    zeroed VOL_FATLBA, had file_trunc free a chain on the wrong drive,
    and never truncated the file.  sub_fromdir returns the SFT in SI.
    RMFSTEST checks a truncating create and a 69h after it.
  - MKDISK pointed its long-named test files at the last file's chain
    to save the space, so every disk it built had cross-links CHKDSK
    reports, and deleting a fixture would free a real file.  They get
    copies in clusters of their own now (FAT12, 16 and 32), and every
    existing image was repaired in place.
  - Unparking remounted EVERY drive letter through vol_select, which
    mounts what is not mounted: an empty floppy drive was read twice
    on each unpark, with the BIOS's retries - ten failed reads in
    DOSBox-X's log, and a grinding drive on a real machine each time
    Windows exits.  park_remount now reaches each letter with
    vol_swap and remounts only what was mounted.
And one for the drive: the flush after an ATA write was FLUSH CACHE
EXT (EAh) on a 48-bit drive.  DOSBox-X advertises the 48-bit feature
set, refuses EAh and aborts, so there the flush never happened.
FLUSH CACHE (E7h) empties the whole cache on any drive; it is used on
all of them.

STILL OPEN - both Windows, both set aside (Charlie, 2026-09-26):
  - A DOS program started from Windows 3.1 does not run.  WINOLDAP now
    writes its swap file whole and correct, and then the machine runs
    into FF FF.  One cause was found and fixed: RMDOS left a HLT in
    the DOS vector stubs of vectors a program had hooked before the
    park, and Windows restores that pre-park table - rd_vecs now puts
    a JMP FAR in every stub.  The run after that still hung, and its
    log has not been read.
  - Exiting Windows resets the machine.  Not looked at in this entry.


XCOPY.EXE, AND A ^C THAT NEVER ARRIVED TWO LEVELS DOWN (2026-09-26)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

CMD\XCOPY\, a native D32 program in C built the way CHKDSK and LABEL
are (Open Watcom, no C library, DOSINT.ASM first on the link line):
MAIN.C the command line and what the source and destination are,
COPY.C the walk and the copying, PATH.C names, MSG.C the words,
SYS_D32.C every system call.  18K.

THE MODEL IS WINDOWS 98'S XCOPY32, the one that keeps long names -
not the real-mode XCOPY in front of it, which shows 8.3 names and
says "Reading source file(s)..." first.  Both were read out of the
Win98 SE disk (C:\86Box\VMs\Win9x\Win9x.vhd, a dynamic VHD) as test
oracles and run under DOSBox-X's own DOS at ver=7.10 with lfn=true:
the real-mode half ran, and its Win32 half gave its message table.
So: every switch it has - /A /M /D[:date] /P /S /E /V /W /C /I /Q /F
/L /H /R /T /U /K /N /Y /-Y, COPYCMD - its messages word for word
("File not found - X", the count right-aligned in nine columns, the
three questions), and DOS's errorlevels: 0 copied, 1 nothing found,
2 ^C, 4 could not start or out of space, 5 a read or write failed.
The /? screen is this program's own description of those switches.

HOW IT DECIDES WHAT THE DESTINATION IS, before anything is copied: a
directory if it is one, ends in a backslash, or /I says so for a copy
of more than one file; a file if a file of that name exists; a
TEMPLATE if its last element has wildcards (each copy renamed through
it, name and extension halves separately, as COPY renames); otherwise
DOS's question, "file or directory?".  A file name is a template with
no wildcards in it, which is why one code path does both.  Cyclic
copies and copies onto themselves are caught on FULL paths: 7160h's
long form of the longest part that exists, with the rest added as
typed, so a short name on one side and a long one on the other are
still the same directory.

EACH DIRECTORY IS READ WHOLE BEFORE ANYTHING IS DONE WITH IT - the
files listed into memory and the search closed, then the same for the
subdirectories.  A search held open while copies are made can meet
its own copies ("XCOPY * *.BAK" in one directory), and one held open
at every level of a deep tree runs out of the kernel's thirty-two
find handles.  Destination directories are made when something needs
them, so /S without /E leaves no empty ones behind.  The long-name
calls are used first and the classic ones when the kernel answers
7100h (LFN=OFF), which was run and works.

^C RAISES A FLAG, and the copy stops between blocks, deletes its
half-written file and ends with errorlevel 2 - except at a question,
where the handler ends the program there and then.  A handler that is
not going back must call 21h/F105h first, as CMD.EXE does; without it
the 4Ch after it hung, with the kernel still holding the interrupted
call and the handler as running.

TESTS: DISK\XCTEST.CMD (a .CMD, so quotes group long names) with
DISK\XCEL.BAT to show each errorlevel - thirty-one cases, from every
switch to the questions answered from files, the errors, a ^C typed by
HOOKTEST's new /C mode, and PMDOS.SYS copied and compared byte for
byte from outside.  In the regression, run by CMD /C.

THE BUG IT FOUND IN THE KERNEL.  That ^C test hung under CMD /C and
worked from AUTOEXEC, and E9h markers in a scratch kernel said why:
r3_thunk took the "ignore" branch.  4Bh loaded every transient program
with r3_useslot(1) - "the transient slot, whatever the depth" - so
r3_depth said 1 for a program at depth 2, while r3_hook had recorded
its handler at exec_depth, 2.  r3_thunk runs a handler only when those
agree, so EVERY PROGRAM TWO OR MORE LEVELS DOWN - anything a batch
file ran under CMD /C - had its INT 23h and INT 24h handlers ignored:
the ^C was echoed and lost, and a critical error answered Fail without
the program being asked.  4Bh now names the child's depth; the slot
is the same one.  And a handler whose owner is PARKED - a shell two
levels up whose vector the child inherited - cannot be run; for INT 24h
Fail is still the answer, but for INT 23h "nobody answered" swallowed
the ^C, so it now does what int23_default does and ends the program.
LABEL, waiting for a label two levels down with no handler of its
own, used to hang on ^C and is ended by it (XCTEST case 30).

AND TWO IN CMD.EXE, both seen in XCTEST's listings.  DIR /B /S showed
"C:\XT\D2\LONGDI~1\DEEPER\Deep File.dat": the walk goes by 8.3 names
to keep its memory small, and printed the path it walked.  It still
walks by them, and shows the path as 7160h renders it (dir_showpath,
once per directory).  And with LFN=OFF, DIR /S listed one directory
and DEL /S deleted in one, silently: dir_resolve asked only 7160h,
and a failure dropped both to their flat forms.  It falls back to the
classic TRUENAME now.

NOT DONE, ON PURPOSE: a name valid as 8.3 but written in lower case
("mid.txt") is stored upper case with no long-name entry, where
Windows 95 keeps the case in one.  That is rule (1) of the long-name
design - classic calls leave directories byte-identical to real DOS -
and XCOPY copies what is there.


EDIT.EXE, AND A CONSOLE FOR PROGRAMS THAT OWN THE SCREEN (2026-09-26)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

CMD\EDIT\, native D32 C built like XCOPY: MAIN.C the command line, the
windows and the commands; DOC.C the text; VIEW.C an edit window, its
keys and its drawing; UI.C menus and the dialog framework; DLGS.C the
dialogs; HELP.C the help; SCR.C the screen and the keyboard; SYS_D32.C
every system call.  54K.

THE MODEL IS DOS 7'S EDIT - the stand-alone editor, not QBasic's -
with what it has: the File, Edit, Search, View, Options and Help menus,
up to nine files open at once in one or two windows, a shared
clipboard, Find and Change with "verify", the WordStar ^Q/^K keys and
bookmarks, binary mode (/nnn, a width, with every byte shown as itself
and a line end as no more than another byte), /B /H /R /S, wildcards on
the command line, Settings (tab stops, printer port), Colors, Print,
and a warning when a line is too long for it.  The menu names and
shortcut keys are DOS's, because they are what hands remember; the
help and every longer sentence are this program's own.

A NATIVE PROGRAM CANNOT DO WHAT A FULL-SCREEN DOS PROGRAM IS MADE OF -
write B800:0, read 40:17 for the shift keys, call INT 16h - so the
kernel does those three things for it, as 21h/F0h AL = 4 to 0Ah (the
contract is at fF0_put and fF0_lines in DOS\INT21.INC):

    AL = 4/5   cells onto / off the screen: ESI or EDI, ECX cells, EBX
               the first.  PMIO's con_putcells/con_getcells clip to the
               screen; both pointers are in vdm_subptr so a box's
               program is translated like any other
    AL = 6     the cursor shape, in scan lines, straight to the CRTC -
               NOT into 40:60, which is the box's business
    AL = 7     a key, with the shift state beside it
    AL = 8     wait for a key OR a change in the shift keys - the only
               way to see Alt pressed and let go on its own, which is
               how EDIT's user reaches the menu bar
    AL = 9     the shift state
    AL = 0Ah   25 lines or the most the adapter has (EDIT /H): INT 10h
               through the real-mode thunk, mode 3 and then 1112h
    AL = 3     (older) now gives CL = character height as well, which is
               what a cursor shape is measured in

EDIT paints the whole screen into memory on every pass and hands the
kernel only the runs of cells that changed, so nothing remembers what
was under a dialog and a full repaint costs what it changed.  The
screen it started on is read with AL = 5 and put back when it ends.
^C is a key to an editor: its INT 23h handler returns, and ^C reaches
it as a character.

THE TEXT is one record per line - pointer, length, capacity - and a
file is loaded in two passes, lines counted and then copied into 32K
pools, so a loaded line costs its own bytes and nothing else; a line
leaves the pool for its own block the first time it is edited.  In the
512K slot that makes about 390K of text: a 339K file loads and saves
back byte-identical, and a 477K one gets DOS's "not enough memory"
and nothing is lost.  [Since 2026-10-01 48h grows the slot, so the
ceiling is the machine's rather than 390K.  Not measured again.]  Memory that runs out while typing is said, not
fatal - only what EDIT cannot start without ends it.

TWO NATIVE REGISTER CONTRACTS that cost time, because both look right
and are half-right:  42h in a native program takes the offset in ECX
and returns the new position in EAX - NOT CX:DX in and DX:AX out, so
a file-size routine that reads DX:AX gets a large number from nowhere
(it was taken as "this file needs all the memory there is").  And 48h,
when it fails, gives the largest block in EBX, as DOS does, not EAX.

TESTS: DISK\EDTEST.BAT, thirteen sessions and EDIT /?.  With EDTEST
naming a log file and standard input a key file, the keys come from
the file - the bytes 21h/07h would give, 0 and a scan code for an
extended key, FFh and a byte for the shift state, FFh FFh to write the
screen, the cursor and the memory left into the log - and end of input
leaves EDIT (EDHOLD keeps it on the screen instead, for a picture).
TOOLS\MKEDKEYS.PL writes DISK\ED1.KEY to ED13.KEY; DISK\EDBIN.DAT,
EDTABS.DAT and EDLF.DAT are the binary, tab and LF-only fixtures, and
every saved file is TYPEd or compared.  Screenshots under DOSBox-X
(DBXRUN -Cap) settled the look: menus, dialogs, help, /B, and the DOS
screen back as it was.

NOT DONE: THE MOUSE - done the same day, see the next entry.  Settings
are not written anywhere, so tabs, colours and the printer port last
for one run.

THE MOUSE: INT 33h IN THE KERNEL, FOR BOTH KINDS OF PROGRAM (2026-09-26)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------

IO\MOUSE.INC, in PMIO beside the keyboard: it is hardware and an IRQ,
and PMDOS has 7K left before DOS_LIMIT.  PMIO grew from 16.7K to 26K;
PMDOS by 200 bytes of hooks.  One driver, one state, answering INT 33h
as Microsoft's 8.20 does, reached two ways.

THE HARDWARE.  A PS/2 mouse on the 8042's aux port first: A9h must
answer 00h, then A8h, the command byte with IRQ 12 on and the mouse's
clock running, FFh (FAh, AAh, the ID), F4h.  Failing that a Microsoft
serial mouse on COM1 or COM2: 1200 baud 7N1, DTR and RTS dropped and
raised, and an 'M' within a third of a second ('3' after it: Logitech's
third button, a fourth byte).  Bus and InPort mice are not looked for.
Two things had to change for IRQ 12 to stay on at all: pic_to_pm put
the masks back to "timer and keyboard" on every return from the BIOS,
so they are a global now (GV_PICMASK) that ms_init adds to; and the
timer tick, which has drained stray mouse bytes since v0.36, now feeds
them to the driver instead - a byte that arrives during a BIOS call has
had its interrupt masked and would otherwise sit there blocking IRQ 1.
While the driver itself talks to the mouse (ms_probing) both leave the
bytes alone.

THE 8042's MOUSE IS THE KERNEL'S, as its keyboard already was.  From a
box, D4h is swallowed with its data byte and never answered, A7h, A8h
and D3h are dropped, a written command byte keeps IRQ 12 and the aux
clock on, and a mouse byte is neither offered by 64h nor given by 60h.
INT 15h C2h (the BIOS's pointing-device calls, which would reset the
mouse) answers CF and AH=86h, "not here", so a program falls back on
INT 33h - which is there.  A mouse driver loaded in a box therefore
finds no PS/2 mouse, and does not need to.

A BOX'S INT 33h goes through its own IVT to a stub below 1MB (8
paragraphs, owner 8, set once at boot like the DOS vectors, so a TSR's
hook survives): HLT, which vdm_halt hands to IOS_MSHLT.  The frame the
INT pushed comes off first, as vdm_dvs does.  An EVENT HANDLER (0Ch,
14h, 18h) is called at the three places IRQ 1 is delivered into a box
(v86_run's entry, v86_resume, v86_irqexit - all through ms_boxwant): a
frame pushed and the guest sent to the stub's second entry, which
saves every register, HLTs for the kernel to load AX..DI and the far
pointer, CALLs the handler with DS the driver's segment, HLTs again,
and IRETs.  Never re-entered: one handler call at a time, whichever
kind.

A NATIVE PROGRAM'S INT 33h is a DPL 3 gate PMIO owns (it was the DPMI
host's reflector; ms_int33 jumps there for a client, so dst_33 left
dpmi_veclist).  The registers are Microsoft's, WIDENED - a negative
position is a negative 32-bit number - and a pointer is an offset in
EDX measured against the slot descriptor.  Its EVENT HANDLER is called
like a signal: on the way out of an INT 21h (IOS_MSR3, in i21_r3native)
or of any IRQ that stopped the program at ring 3 (irq_common), the
context is kept, the frame is pointed at the handler with the event's
registers, and a far return to PSP+56h lands on an INT 33h that puts
everything back.  Not while an INT 23h/24h handler of the kernel's is
running, and not while the program is blocked INSIDE a DOS call - the
handler runs as that call returns.

THE CURSOR is drawn from the interrupt: the software text cursor (the
AND/XOR masks, 77FFh/7700h by default), the hardware one (the CRTC's,
moved and put back), and the 16x16 graphics cursor in 04h/05h (masks
two bits to a pixel, as Microsoft's are), 06h, 0Dh-12h (four planes,
the VGA's sequencer and graphics registers read and put back, indexes
and all) and 13h.  A cell a program wrote over while the cursor was on
it is left as the program wrote it.  The mode is read from 40:49 at
every draw and a cursor from an old mode is dropped, not "restored".
THE KERNEL'S OWN CONSOLE takes the cursor off around every write
(ms_conhide/ms_conshow in con_out, con_cls, con_putcells and
con_getcells), so EDIT never draws over it or reads it back.

WHOSE IT IS.  An owner token per call - a box program 10000h plus its
PSP, a native one its depth plus one - and IOS_MSEXIT when a program
ends (vdm_cleanup for a box, not for a TSR; fn4C): its handlers go, and
if it was the last to reset the driver, its cursor is hidden.  DOS
leaves a dead program's handler to be called; this does not.

PARKED FOR RMDOS: the mouse is told to stop sending (F5h) and INT 33h
points at the stub's IRET; after, it is reset and started again and
the cursor drawn afresh.

21h/F0h: AL = 8's DH is now bits - 1 not to wait, 2 to wake for the
mouse (AL = 2) - where any non-zero DH used to mean "don't wait".  AL =
0Bh is for the tests: buttons and mickeys as if the mouse had sent them,
or raw PS/2 or serial bytes through the decoders, or (BH = 3) a PS/2
packet put into the 8042 with D3h so that it arrives through IRQ 12 and
the cascade like a real one.  SIXTEEN-BIT ARGUMENTS, because a box's
INT 21h reaches the kernel with the high halves of its registers gone:
-24 in ECX arrived as FFE8h, which the speed test then doubled.

NOT DONE: 11h, 12h, 28h/29h (setting video modes), 2Bh-2Eh (the
acceleration profiles), 30h, 33h-35h; SVGA modes and EGA (whose
registers cannot be read back); the BIOS pointing-device interface for
box programs (refused, not emulated - which is also why Windows 3.1's
MOUSE.DRV will not find a PS/2 mouse; set aside with Windows).

BUGS THIS FOUND: mh_event wrote the handler's registers through ESI
after ms_pick had used it, which put them at address 0 - in the IVT -
and hung the box.  Movement added to ms_x as a word wrapped round;
ms_step clamps in 32 bits first.  DOSBox-X delivers a D3h byte a
moment after the command, so the injection waits on a count of bytes
received rather than on the status register.

TESTS.  TOOLS\MSTEST.ASM (39 lines, a box: the functions, the
arithmetic, the decoders, IRQ 12, the text and graphics cursors checked
cell by cell and pixel by pixel, VGA registers kept, handlers with their
registers, the 8042 and INT 15h refusals) and TOOLS\MS32TEST.ASM (13, a
native program: widened registers, pointers, the handler on the way out
of INT 21h and from a clock tick, F0h AL=8).  DISK\MSTEST.BAT runs both
and the H/C pairs (a handler and a cursor left behind, and gone after).
DPMITEST has an INT 33h line.  The regression runs MSTEST.BAT, and
MSTEST again after the RMDOS park.  Run as well on a DOSBox-X with no
PS/2 port and a serial mouse on COM1: found, type 2 on IRQ 4, the three
PS/2-only lines skipped.  The 8042 refusal was checked the other way
too: with the D4h swallow taken out, its line fails.  NOT exercised
headless: a physically moved mouse (DOSBox-X's own packets), the serial
IRQ path (detection and decoding were), and an event delivered by the
IRQ that interrupts a running box (the same routine as the tested
resume path).

EDIT HAS THE MOUSE: SCR.C polls INT 33h (05h/06h for presses and
releases since the last look, 03h for where) whenever F0h AL = 8 wakes
for it and queues events - press, release, drag, double click (a second
press on the same cell inside 0.4s) - behind the keys as K_MOUSE.
Click places the cursor; drag, and click then Shift+click, select; a
double click selects a word; the scroll bars' arrows and track repeat
while held and the boxes drag; a click in the other window activates
it and the lower title bar drags the line between; menus open on a
press and choose on a release, or click then click; dialog buttons
press on release, check boxes, options, fields and lists take a click,
and a double click in a list is Enter; help links, the status bar's F1,
F10 and F6, Size Window and the F4 screen all take a click.  A help
topic says so.  Key files have FEh, buttons, row, column: the pointer
is put there with 04h and the buttons set with F0h AL=0Bh, and EDIT
reads the result through INT 33h like the mouse's ({CLICK r,c} etc. in
MKEDKEYS.PL).  ED14-ED17 are the mouse sessions.  EDIT is 61.6K.

ULTRA DMA 66, 100 AND 133, AND THE CABLE THEY NEED (2026-09-26)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

v0.43 stopped at Ultra DMA 2 for two reasons it wrote down: PM-DOS
could not write a host adapter's timing, and mode 3 and up need a
cable it had no way to ask about.  Both are answered now.  New:
IO\IDEHOST.INC, IDECABLE= in CONFIG.SYS, UDMA3 to UDMA6 as names for
IDEDMA=, and BUILD nohost.

THE HOST'S HALF IS IO\IDEHOST.INC, for two families.  Intel: PIIX3,
PIIX4 and the ICH line to ICH7 - an enable bit and two bits of cycle
time a drive (48h, 4Ah), and from the ICH a 33/66/100MHz clock a drive
(54h).  VIA: VT82C586A to VT8237A - a byte a drive at 50h-53h, whose
meaning depends on the south bridge, which is identified by its ISA
bridge and revision because the IDE function is 1106:0571 in all of
them.  Each has a fastest mode: none for PIIX3, 2 for PIIX4, 4 for the
ICH, 596B and 686A, 5 for ICH2 on and 686B, 6 for the VT8233A on.  ANY
OTHER CHIPSET IS A STRANGER and its timing is never written.

THE CABLE IS ata_cables, a verdict a channel, from four witnesses in
the order they are believed:
  - IDECABLE=40 or 80, the user
  - the BIOS having left a drive on the channel in a mode past 2
  - the host's register (Intel 54h bits 4-7; VIA bit 4 of the drive's
    byte on the 100 and 133 bridges; the 66 ones have none)
  - IDENTIFY word 93 bit 13 from either drive
and nobody speaking means forty conductors.  A host that says 40 is
believed over a drive that says 80: the drive's test needs a capacitor
on the board's detect pin and says 80 to everything where it is
missing.

THE CHOICE IS TWO PASSES NOW.  ata_identify used to choose the mode
while the IDENTIFY block was still in ata_idbuf.  A cable is a
channel's, so the master cannot be decided before the slave has
answered: ata_keepid writes what the choice needs into the device
entry (ATD_LEN 20 -> 24), and ata_init chooses for everyone after the
probe.  The mode the BIOS left is kept from the FIRST probe only, in
ata_bios outside the table - ata_config probes again for every
CONFIG.SYS line, and by then "selected" may mean selected by PM-DOS.

ata_limit IS THE RULE.  The mode wanted, brought down to the host's
fastest, then to 2 if the channel has not got eighty conductors, then
to the fastest the drive offers under that.
  - AUTO wants what is selected and skips the host's limit: the BIOS
    chose it for this board.
  - ON wants the drive's best.  On a stranger it stops at the mode the
    BIOS was seen to use, or 2.
  - IDEDMA=UDMAn is a ceiling, where v0.43 had "that mode or nothing":
    UDMA6 on a drive that stops at 5 is 5.  MWDMAn is still exact.  On
    a stranger a named mode is taken at the user's word, cable apart.
When the mode changes the drive is told first and then the host
(ideh_udma), or the host's Ultra DMA is turned off for a multiword
mode (ideh_noudma).

THE ONE REFUSAL (ata_newmode): a drive is not brought down to mode 2
or under on a stranger whose BIOS timed it for a mode past 2.  The
host would go on writing at the old speed down the cable just judged
unable to carry it.  That device goes to PIO.

A CRC ERROR BRINGS THE MODE DOWN (ata_slower, from ata_rw).  The drive
reports a burst that failed its CRC in bit 7 of the error register and
has stored nothing.  From a mode past 2 the device comes down to 2,
host and all; from 2 or under, or on a stranger, it comes off DMA; the
chunk is done again.  This is what a wrong cable verdict costs.  Disks
only: a packet device reports the same thing as a sense key and is
left as it was.

WHAT v0.43 WOULD HAVE DONE WRONG AND NEVER MET: IDEDMA=ON on a PIIX3,
which has no Ultra DMA, selected UDMA 2 on any drive that offered it.
It is multiword mode 2 now.

21h/F1h AL=0Ah SAYS MORE.  A device: AH the ATI_* byte (does DMA, saw
80 conductors, mode is PM-DOS's, host registers agree), bits 16-23
its channel's ATC_* cable byte, bits 24-31 the Ultra DMA modes
offered, CH the mode the BIOS left.  The controller: EDX bits 8-11 the
host family, 12-15 its fastest mode, 18-19 the IDECABLE= policy.  AL
and CL are what they were.

TESTS.  IDETEST prints the host, and under each device what it offers,
what the BIOS left, the cable and who said so, and whether PM-DOS set
the mode and the host matches.  Check 3 fails a mode the drive does
not offer, a mode past 2 without the cable, and - for a mode PM-DOS
chose on a host it knows - a mode past the host's fastest or a host
whose registers, read back, say something else.  BUILD nohost makes
every host a stranger, for the stranger's rules on a board whose BIOS
selects a fast mode.  TOOLS\IDE86.PS1 is the rig: a scratch 86Box VM
for a named board, a fresh 32MB disk for each CONFIG.SYS given, and
IDETEST's report read out of the image while the machine is up.

VERIFIED on 86Box, IDETEST 9 of 9 and checksum 98461D56 in every run,
the same as a fresh copy of that disk gives in DOSBox-X by PIO:
  - ASUS CUV4X-LS (VIA 686B): AUTO keeps the BIOS's UDMA 5; ON is 5;
    ON or UDMA5 with IDECABLE=40 is 2; AUTO with IDECABLE=40 is 2;
    UDMA4 and UDMA3 are themselves; UDMA6 is 5; MWDMA2.  Host matches
    wherever PM-DOS set the mode.  Disk and CD-ROM alike.
  - ASUS P3B-F (PIIX4E): ON and UDMA5 are 2; UDMA1 with host matching.
  - Intel VS440FX (PIIX3): AUTO is PIO (the BIOS selects nothing), ON
    and UDMA5 are multiword 2.
  - ASUS P5A (ALi, a stranger): ON is the BIOS's 2, UDMA5 is 5, UDMA5
    with IDECABLE=40 is 2.
  - CUV4X-LS under BUILD nohost: AUTO and ON 5, UDMA4 is 4, IDECABLE=40
    and UDMA2 are PIO.

NOT VERIFIED.  86Box keeps a timing register and ignores what is in
it, so "host matches" proves the right bits were written and not that
a real chipset runs at them.  Nothing here has been on real hardware.
The Intel ICH clock register (54h) and its cable bits, the VIA cable
bit, and the 33, 66 and 133 rows of the VIA table have not run at all
- 86Box has no ICH, and the 686B's BIOS selects a fast mode before the
host is ever asked.  So the cable's witness was the BIOS on the 686B
and word 93 on the other three boards, and never the host's register.
ata_slower has not run: nothing emulated produces a CRC error.

PCI AND PLUG AND PLAY: A CARD'S INTERRUPT, ITS MEMORY, AND WHERE A
BUFFER REALLY IS (2026-09-27)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The question was what PM-DOS needed to support PCI and Plug and Play,
and the answer was five things, none of which is PCI resource
assignment and only one of which has PCI in its name.  New:
IO\IRQ.INC, IO\VPIC.INC, IO\VDS.INC, IO\BUS.INC, pg_mapphys in
IO\PAGING.INC, most of IO\PCI.INC, 21h/F1h AL=12h, INT 31h 0800h and
0801h, BUILD irqtest, six test programs, DISK\BUSTEST.BAT and
TOOLS\BUS86.PS1.  Still v0.60.

WHAT WAS ALREADY TRUE, and is now tested rather than supposed: a DOS
box reaches configuration space, because CF8h and CFCh are not ports
the monitor keeps, and the PCI BIOS answers INT 1Ah from one, because
nothing here ever claimed the vector.  NICIRQ finds its card that way.

1.  A CARD'S INTERRUPT, IN A DOS BOX (IO\VPIC.INC).  A driver hooks a
vector, clears its line's bit at port 21h or A1h, and ends every
interrupt with an EOI.  All of that went to the machine's own 8259s,
whose vectors are at IRQ_BASE: the interrupt arrived at irq_none and
was thrown away, the mask the driver wrote lasted until the next trip
into the BIOS, and a box that masked line 0 had stopped the kernel's
clock.  VPICTEST run on the kernel as it was says exactly that - the
mask reads back, the clock stops, the interrupt never comes.

The four ports are the monitor's now, claimed in the TSS bitmap like
the three of the A20 gate, and behind them is a pair of controllers
that exist only in VPIC.INC.  The mask is the box's own; clearing a
bit for a line a box may have (VP_GUEST: 3, 4, 5, 7 and 8 to 11) opens
the real line.  An interrupt on it is owed to the box and THE REAL
LINE IS SHUT UNTIL THE BOX'S OWN EOI.  That sentence is the whole of
level-triggered support.  A PCI line stays asserted until the card has
been dealt with, the kernel's EOI is sent before the driver has run an
instruction, and an open line would deliver the same interrupt again
for ever.  It is delivered where a keystroke is - the IRQ that
interrupted the guest, a resume out of the monitor, an entry to
v86_run - at 08h or 70h and up, when the guest's interrupt flag is set
and nothing more urgent is in service.  The order is the 8259's, the
cascade included: a line behind it stays blocked until the handler has
sent the FIRST controller its EOI as well.

The keyboard goes through the same registers, which it has to: its
handler's EOI is a non-specific one, and the only way to know it is
not some other line's is to have the keyboard in service when it
arrives.  A box that masks line 1 is not sent INT 09h.  Nothing is in
service, and the keyboard is unmasked, when a program starts
(vpc_boxreset, from kb_boxreset).

A DPMI CLIENT IS A BOX THAT IS SOMEWHERE ELSE.  An interrupt it has a
protected-mode handler for (0205h) goes to that handler when the
client is in protected mode with its interrupt flag set: the frame is
built on the client's own stack, in the width its code segment says an
IRET will pop (vpc_pmchk, from irq_common and from pm3_done, which is
where an STI is emulated).  0400h reports the controllers' bases as
08h and 70h now.  It reported IRQ_BASE, the wrong way round, and a
client that believed it would have hooked vectors nothing is delivered
to.

2.  A LINE HAS A CHAIN (IO\IRQ.INC).  IOS_IRQHOOK puts a handler on a
line, IRQ_CHAIN of them to a line; every one is called for every
interrupt and answers CF clear if its device was asking.  All of
them, not the first to claim it: two devices on a line can both be
asking.  The timer's, the keyboard's and the mouse's lines keep one
owner and refuse.  A DOS box is the last thing on every chain -
vpc_raise is what an interrupt nobody claimed is offered to.

irq_sync IS THE ONE PLACE THE MASK REGISTERS ARE WRITTEN.  What the
8259s are told is worked out from what the kernel wants, what a box
has open and what a box still owes an EOI on, and it is written to
GV_PICMASK as well, because pic_to_pm puts that back after every BIOS
call.  ms_irqon is one call to it.

Two things an ISA kernel never needed.  Lines 7 and 15 are where an
8259 reports an interrupt that went away before it was acknowledged,
and the in-service register tells those from the real thing; they are
handed to nobody.  And an interrupt nobody claims on a level-triggered
line comes straight back, so a run of 256 of them inside a second
shuts the line (IRQF_DEAD) - the alternative is a machine that does
