LRGDISK.386: 32-BIT DISK ACCESS PAST 504MB, BY LBA, TO 128GB (2026-10-07)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie asked for a driver of our own to take the place of WfW's
built-in one for 32-bit disk and file access, which stops at 504MB -
first to 2GB, then, since PM-DOS reads FAT32, to everything 28-bit LBA
reaches.  CMD\LRGDISK\LRGDISK.ASM is it: a BlockDev disk driver - a
"FastDisk", as WDCTRL is - built as an LE VxD by wlink.  In SYSTEM.INI's
[386Enh]:

  device=lrgdisk.386        in place of device=*wdctrl
  32BitDiskAccess=on        as for WDCTRL
  LRGDiskReport=on          optional: LRGDISK.TXT in the boot root

device=*int13 and device=*blockdev stay.  32-bit file access needs
nothing more: VFAT reaches a disk through BlockDev and finds LRGDISK
there as it would have found WDCTRL.  On p3bf's 2047MB disk WfW runs
its whole sweep list with 32-bit disk and file access on LRGDISK, and
on a 128GB one a DOS box writes and reads the last sectors 28-bit LBA
has through INT 13h's extensions - and the host finds the bytes at
those sectors of the image.

WHY WDCTRL STOPS AT 504MB.  The Windows 3.1 DDK on S:\win16ddk has
WDCTRL's source (386\WDCTRL), and WfW 3.11's built-in copy fills its
descriptor the same way (WIN386.EXE 250B5h: BlockDev 3.0Ah, flags
13h, its own fields from 64h).  It drives the controller with the
geometry in the BIOS's fixed disk table - INT 13h's geometry - and its
start-up proves that geometry is the drive's by reading sectors through
the BIOS and looking at the controller's registers afterwards.  Past
1024 x 16 x 63 a BIOS makes up a geometry of its own for INT 13h's
ten-bit cylinder - p3bf turns a 2047MB disk into 519 x 128 x 63 - and
talks to the drive by LBA, and WDCTRL finds head numbers that do not
fit in four bits and refuses.  (p3bf refuses it even at 504MB: its
tables put the cylinders at AH=08h's highest plus 1, and WDCTRL allows
only plus 2 or plus 3.)

WHAT LRGDISK DOES INSTEAD.  It keeps the BIOS's geometry for everything
Windows sees - INT13.386 turns a DOS box's CHS into a sector number
with it, and answers AH=08h from it - and talks to the drive by LBA,
which reaches every sector the drive has, wherever that addresses the
same sectors as the BIOS: when the BIOS itself uses LBA, and when the
BIOS's CHS is the drive's own geometry (a BIOS that does not translate,
or one that translates by CHS and sends the drive's real 16 heads).
CHS, the BIOS's, only for a drive with no LBA.  None of that is
guessed.  The real-mode start-up reads four sectors through the ROM's
INT 13h (2Fh AH=13h's ES:BX) - the first; cylinder 1, head 1, sector 3;
seven-eighths in; the last - with the registers poisoned first (sector
0, cylinder FFFFh) so that a read through another cable or drive
leaves them so, and narrows, read by read, what the registers the BIOS
left are consistent with: an LBA equal to the sector number, the CHS of
the BIOS's geometry, the CHS of the geometry the drive is set to
(IDENTIFY's words 55-56).  Then it reads each sector again through the
BIOS and itself, the chosen way, and compares; by LBA it also reads the
drive's LAST sector through the BIOS's extensions, if the BIOS has
them, and compares that.  The table INT 41h or 46h names must agree
with AH=08h on heads and sectors, its cylinders 1 to 3 past the
highest; the protected-mode side reads it again, so only four bits a
drive cross over in the reference data - taken, LBA, and the cylinder
difference.  It refuses, with a reason on the screen, a drive it cannot
account for, a DOS that does not answer 2Fh AH=13h, a program between
DOS and a ROM entry below A000h that does not answer BlockDev's chain
check, IRQ 14 masked, and anything on the first cable it does not drive
- a CD-ROM as the slave - because it takes the cable's ports from the
DOS boxes as WDCTRL does.

THE PROTECTED-MODE SIDE is WDCTRL's design, written again: a command at
a time for both drives, one sector an interrupt, 127 a controller
command, scatter/gather, three retries, a message if a command takes 20
seconds or a DOS box touches the ports.  By LBA, BlockDev is given the
drive's own last sector (IDENTIFY, polled with nIEN, before BlockDev
has the IRQ), not the BIOS geometry's, so all of a big drive is
there - and a partition laid out for 16 heads that runs past the BIOS's
last whole cylinder (every MKDISK image) is all in reach.

INT 13h's EXTENSIONS, WHICH INT13.386 NEVER HAD.  INT13.386 turns every
INT 13h for a drive with a 32-bit driver into BlockDev commands from a
table that stops at AH=1Ah, so with WDCTRL - or LRGDISK - loaded,
AH=42h fails: and RMDOS reaches every sector past cylinder 1023 with
it.  A FAT32 volume over 8GB, or one that starts there, could not be
read from Windows at all.  LRGDISK hooks INT13.386's
Int13_Translate_VM_Int (Hook_Device_Service) and answers AH=41h, 42h,
43h, 44h, 47h and 48h for its own drives through BlockDev - pages
locked as INT13.386 locks them, a semaphore per request in the command
block's client field (BlockDev calls a completion with ESI -> the
block) - and hands everything else on.  Hooked there, below DOS, rather
than on V86 INT 13h, so that a disk cache hooked on INT 13h is not
gone round.  A BIOS without the extensions (the vli486sv2g's, 1994)
gets them from LRGDISK while Windows runs.

BUILT BY wlink, which makes the same LE layout as LINK386: locked code
and data, discardable start-up code, and a 16-bit real-mode object as
the module's entry (a near RET ends it, as the DDK's do), the DDB
exported as ordinal 1.  One difference: LINK386 resolves the 16-bit
object's own offsets and leaves it no fixups, and wlink leaves them for
a loader that may not apply them in real mode.  So no address in the
real-mode code is named directly - every one is "label-rbase" - and the
object has none (wdump).  It assembles with MASM 6.13 as well (.model
flat).  wasm -dLRG_TRACE builds a version that writes a character a
command and a line for anything unusual to LPT1.

LRGTEST.COM (TOOLS, new; not in RUNTESTS - it needs a real controller)
runs LRGDISK.386's own real-mode object under plain DOS, with a
stand-in for WIN386's loader, and prints the report.  Under real MS-DOS
5 (a copy of the DOS VM's disk, scratch lrg\lrgprobe86.ps1):

  vli486sv2g, 504MB    1023/16/63, the table 1024; LBA, the BIOS's CHS
                       being the drive's own; no BIOS extensions to
                       check the end with
  p3bf, 504MB          1024/16/63, the table 1024 (plus 1: WDCTRL's
                       refusal); LBA, the end checked through AH=42h
  p3bf, 2047MB         519/128/63, the table 519; LBA as the BIOS reads
  p3bf, 128GB slave    1024/255/63, the table 1024, 268,435,440 sectors;
                       LBA, and sector 268,435,439 read through AH=42h -
                       which left the LBA bit clear (A0h) with the LBA in
                       the three registers below: so the end check asks
                       only for the low 24 bits

An absent slave reads status 01h on 86Box, not the 00h ATA-2 gives, so
only DRDY counts as "a drive is there"; anything else is given IDENTIFY
DEVICE, and an ATAPI drive's refusal leaves its signature.

MKDISK COULD NOT BUILD A 2GB DISK.  It held the whole image in memory,
and a 32-bit process cannot have 2047MB; its size check allowed it and
calloc said no.  It now holds the front - up to the data area and the
clusters the file list fills, counted as the build loop uses them - and
writes the rest as zeros; sec() refuses anything past what it holds.  A
32MB FAT16 disk, a fragmented 600MB FAT32 one and a floppy come out
byte-identical to the old tool's.

THE SWEEPS (86Box; IFSBOX runs I13X - scratch lrg\I13X.ASM, INT 13h
CHS or extensions, counts 1 to 129 so that a request takes more than
one controller command, 3,500 calls - and copies compared with CMPF):

  vli486sv2g, 504MB, by CHS and then by LBA: every I13X call right;
  LRGDISK answers AH=41h and 48h on a BIOS that has no extensions, and
  the pattern AH=43h left in the drive's last 512 sectors is in the
  image (lrg\chk7.pl).  CACHEBOX stops there, at the same byte of its
  output every time, with LRGDISK's LPT1 trace showing every command it
  was given finished - when WINSWEEP looks in on the box while it is
  still running (its 60 seconds are up at 63, and under LRGDISK the
  box takes a few seconds longer than under WDCTRL).  Given 150
  seconds it finishes, the list runs to the end and Windows exits.
  That is the open DOS-box stall, and now one that happens on demand:
  vli486sv2g, LRGDISK, CACHEBOX at 60 seconds (scratch wsweep\
  run_lrg.ps1 -Box vli -List lrg3.lst).
  p3bf, 2047MB: the whole list, Windows out - booted from it, with the
  boot sector told 128 heads (MKDISK writes 16; wsweep -BpbHeads).
  p3bf, 504MB and a 128GB slave, both LRGDISK's at once: the whole
  list; I13X at the top of LBA28, and the host finds its pattern at
  sectors 268,434,928-268,435,439.
  p3bf, 2047MB with 32-bit file access: the entry above.

WINSWEEP WAITS A MINIMIZED BOX'S WHOLE ALLOWANCE, in guest time, and
p3bf runs slower than real time: an IFSBOX given 900 seconds ran two
sweeps into the 1500-second limit, and they looked hung.  lrg3.lst
gives it 240.

OPEN: past 128GB, only the first 128GB (no LBA48); a device LRGDISK
does not drive on the first cable keeps it out altogether; the second
cable is not looked at; Control Panel's 32-bit disk access box was not
tried with it (LRGDISK reads 32BitDiskAccess itself); nothing here has
run on real hardware.

Files: CMD\LRGDISK\LRGDISK.ASM (new), TOOLS\LRGTEST.ASM (new),
TOOLS\MKDISK.C, BUILD.CMD, MKHD.CMD (LRGDISK.386 in HD16's root,
LRGTEST in TESTS).  LRGDISK.386 is 15,557 bytes.  BIN\LRGDISK.386,
BIN\TESTS\LRGTEST.COM, and HD16.IMG's root and TESTS (the VM's copy
too) carry them.  To use it: LRGDISK.386 into WINDOWS\SYSTEM, and
SYSTEM.INI as at the top of this entry.


A WRITE PAST THE END LANDED IN THE WRONG CLUSTER, AND THE WRITE OF
NOTHING MADE A FILE LONG WITH NOTHING BEHIND IT (2026-10-07)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Found while chasing a stall in LRGDISK's sweeps on the vli486sv2g
(16MB): the disk a stopped run left behind had \WINDOWS\WIN386.SWP,
Windows' temporary swap file, 3MB long in its directory entry and one
cluster long in the FAT (scratch lrg\fatchk.pl, a CHKDSK-like walker).

Two RMDOS bugs, the second making the first matter:

  40h with CX=0 - the write of nothing, which makes a file exactly as
  long as its position - set the length and nothing else (RMFILE2.INC,
  file_trunc).  MS-DOS's WRTEOF (DOS6SRC dos\disk3.asm) makes the chain
  cover the new length: ALLOCATE to reach it, RELBLKS to give back what
  is past it.  So a file made longer had no clusters behind its end,
  and a file made shorter kept all of its clusters, lost once closed.

  A write past the end of the chain (file_io) added ONE cluster and
  wrote into it wherever the position was.  A write two clusters past
  the end landed in the first cluster past it, and a read at the
  position found no cluster at all.

Windows makes its swap file with the first and pages into it with the
second: created, seeked to 3MB, written nothing, then written in pages
wherever they fall.  Fixing them did NOT end the stall (the LRGDISK
entry has it); they are bugs on their own, which SEEKWR shows without
Windows.

Both now as MS-DOS has them.  file_trunc grows the chain to the
cluster of the last byte (sft_grow until sft_clus finds it) or ends it
there and gives the rest back (fat_freechain), then sets the length,
and drops the SFT's place in the chain since it may be gone; a full
volume leaves the length as it was.  file_io grows the chain a cluster
at a time until it reaches the position.

THE KERNEL had half of it: its write past the end grows the chain
properly (file_wchunk, zeroing what it adds) and its truncate gives
clusters back, but a write of nothing that makes a file longer set the
length alone - so the free count did not drop and a disk with less
free than the new length said yes.  INT21.INC's file_trunc now grows
the chain as file_wchunk does (f40_extend).

SEEKWR.COM (TOOLS, new; RUNTESTS, after NETTEST) makes the checks on
the kernel and, parked, on RMDOS: 4 bytes at 100000 in an empty file,
read back from there; nothing written at 300000, and the clusters for
300000 gone from the free count; 4 bytes at 250000 read back and the
ones at 100000 still there; nothing written at 50000 and the clusters
past it back; the length after a close and an open; every cluster back
after the delete.  Before: RMDOS failed five of them (the read back
from 100000 among them - the bytes had gone into the wrong cluster)
and the kernel one; now none.

Files: DOS\RMFILE2.INC, DOS\INT21.INC, TOOLS\SEEKWR.ASM (new),
TOOLS\RUNTESTS.PS1, BUILD.CMD, BASELINE\.  SEEKWR.COM is in BIN\TESTS
and HD16.IMG's TESTS; RMDOS.SYS and PMDOS.SYS went out with the
entries above.


LRGDISK 1.1: LBA48, AND A CD-ROM ON THE SAME CABLE (2026-10-08)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie asked for 48-bit LBA in LRGDISK.386, and for the slave problem
the entry above left open: anything on the first IDE cable that
LRGDISK did not drive - a CD-ROM as the slave, the usual place for
one - kept it from loading at all.

LBA48.  A drive with the 48-bit feature set, supported and on
(IDENTIFY words 83 and 86, bit 10), gives its size in words 100-103;
past 2TB LRGDISK takes the first 2TB, a sector number in DOS and in a
partition table being 32 bits.  A transfer that reaches sector
0FFFFFFFh or past it goes as READ or WRITE SECTORS EXT (24h, 34h),
each register written twice, the high-order byte first; everything
below that is the 28-bit command it always was.  The start-up still
reads the drive's last sector through the BIOS's AH=42h, and past 28
bits it now looks at the high-order bytes too (device control's HOB
bit) - poisoned with FFh first, so that a BIOS that drops the top bits
and reads sector n mod 2^28 shows.  A BIOS that cannot read that far,
or reads the wrong sector, has the last sector 28 bits reach checked
instead, and LRGDISK goes on past where the BIOS stops, as it already
went past the BIOS's last cylinder.

SHARING THE CABLE.  WDCTRL takes the cable's ports from the virtual
machines and keeps them, and so did LRGDISK.  Now, with something on
the cable it does not drive, it lends them (ld_vmio, behind the port
trap).  The VMs' I/O reaches the controller whenever LRGDISK has no
command on it.  A command they write makes the cable theirs until a
read of the status shows it over - and LRGDISK's next command is HELD
till then (ld_held), with a look every 50ms in case nobody reads the
status, and the cable taken back anyway after 30 seconds.  A command
they write while LRGDISK's is on it waits (ld_vmwait) and goes out the
moment LRGDISK's is done, ahead of LRGDISK's next.  What they wrote is
kept two deep (a 48-bit command writes every register twice) and what
they last read is kept, and both go back into the controller
(ld_restore) before they touch it again after LRGDISK has used it;
while LRGDISK has it, their reads find what they last saw, and the
status BSY if their command is waiting.  Their interrupts are not
LRGDISK's to claim: BlockDev ends an interrupt no driver claims as the
BIOS's own handler would - 40:8Eh set and the waiting VM woken, or,
with VirtualHDIrq=off, passed to the VM (BLOCKDEV.386 disassembled,
WfW 3.11's).  LRGDISK's own drives stay out of their reach as before:
with one of its units selected a read finds FFh, a write goes no
further, and a command is refused with the message.  A device with no
foreign neighbour gets the old behaviour exactly.

WHICH UNIT.  BIOS disk 80h was taken to be the master and 81h the
slave; now each one's unit is read off where the BIOS's own read of
its first sector went (step 5 of the start-up), so a disk alone as
the slave, or a CD-ROM as the master, is fine.  The check that refused
anything but a ready master is gone.  The reference data is a byte a
unit: taken, LBA, LBA48, BIOS disk 81h, the cylinder difference, and
"something else is here".  The report says what the something is:

  Unit 1 of the first IDE cable is a CD-ROM drive or other ATAPI
  device (14EB4100).  DOS drivers share the cable with LRGDISK.

THE SECTOR AFTER.  QEMU's IDE leaves the address of the sector AFTER
the one read in the registers; WDCTRL and LRGDISK 1.0 both wanted the
one read, and refused the disk.  ATA-4 and later leave the registers
undefined after a read that worked, so a newer drive may do the same.
Either is taken now, as the same numbering - which still catches a
read that went to the other cable or another drive, or was addressed
another way.

QEMU.  86Box's IDE has no LBA48 (no EXT commands, no high-order bytes,
disks to 128GB), and DOSBox-X does not run RMDOS in enhanced mode.
QEMU 11.1 (scratch qemu\, unpacked from the weilnetz Windows build
with 7-Zip, not installed) runs PM-DOS, RMDOS and WfW 3.11 in
enhanced mode with NO WINDOW: -display none, LPT1 and port E9h to
files, screendumps and the CPU's state through its monitor on a local
port.  rig\runqemu.ps1 (-Catch pauses a reset and saves the registers)
and wsweep\run_lrgq.ps1, the run_lrg.ps1 sweep on it; a copy of
WINSWEEP takes -1 seconds as "start it and go on" (build2), so that a
DOS box can run beside the ones after it.

RESULTS (QEMU unless said):

  504MB master + 200GB slave (sparse): the slave is "419430400
  sectors, LBA and LBA48", its last sector checked through SeaBIOS's
  AH=42h and the high-order bytes; I13X's extended reads and writes
  at sectors 419,429,888-419,430,399 all right, one past the end AH
  04h, and the host finds pattern 7 in exactly those sectors of the
  image (lrg\chk7.pl) - and nothing at 150,994,432, where a 28-bit
  wrap would have put it.  Windows out.
  504MB master + a CD-ROM as the slave (16MB of seeded random data):
  LRGDISK takes the master and says the slave is "a CD-ROM drive or
  other ATAPI device (14EB4100)".  A box left running reads the disc
  through the ports twelve times (ATAPIRD) while IFSBOX (I13X through
  LRGDISK, copies compared) and CACHEBOX use the disk, and Windows
  starts programs: every pass's checksum is BADF658F, which is the
  image's, with no errors - passes 2 to 5, the ones beside the disk
  work, taking three to four times as long.  LRGDISK's trace: 6,146 of
  the box's commands (twelve passes of 512 READ(10)s, IDENTIFY and
  READ CAPACITY), 1,508 of them waiting for LRGDISK's, 1,514 of
  LRGDISK's held for theirs, no errors, no time-outs, nothing taken
  back by force.  Windows out.

  86Box, tree6: the vli486sv2g's 504MB disk (a BIOS without the
  extensions; LRGDISK gives them), lrg3 with CACHEBOX at 60 seconds -
  the stall's own list - the whole list and Windows out; p3bf's 2047MB
  disk (519/128/63) with VFAT - 32-bit file access holding C: - the
  whole list and Windows out; p3bf's 504MB master and the 128GB slave,
  both LRGDISK's (the slave found as unit 1), I13X at sectors
  268,434,928-268,435,439 and the host finding them in the image.  The
  QEMU runs are of the final build.

ATAPIRD.COM (TOOLS, new; BIN\TESTS and HD16's TESTS; not in RUNTESTS,
it needs the drive) reads a CD-ROM on the first cable as a DOS
CD-ROM driver does - ATAPI packets, PIO, polled with the interrupt
left on - and gives a checksum a pass, which the host can work out
from the image.

OPEN: the second cable is still the BIOS's; PIO only (no bus-master
DMA, so no Ultra DMA); a DOS CD-ROM driver that hooks IRQ 14 itself
needs VirtualHDIrq=off; a VM that resets the cable (SRST) resets
LRGDISK's drives too, and a CHS-only drive is not told its geometry
again; nothing here has run on real hardware.

Files: CMD\LRGDISK\LRGDISK.ASM, TOOLS\ATAPIRD.ASM (new), BUILD.CMD,
MKHD.CMD.  LRGDISK.386 is 21,316 bytes.


THE DOS-BOX STALL: TWO MACHINES IN ONE DOS CALL (2026-10-08)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The stall three entries have left open - a DOS box's output stopping
part way, WINSWEEP never logging another line, Windows not exiting -
was RMDOS letting a second virtual machine into a call the first had
not finished.

FOUND UNDER QEMU.  The LRGDISK entry above brought QEMU into the rig,
and the first sweep on it stalled exactly as the vli486sv2g did, with
LRGDISK not even loaded: CACHEBOX's output ending after "the
directory, twice", and on the screen a dialog nobody could answer -
"WINOLDAP caused Segment Load Failure in module USER.EXE".  Windows
had gone to read a discarded segment of USER.EXE through the handle
KERNEL keeps on it, and the handle was no longer KERNEL's.  QEMU, with
no window, sends port E9h to a file, so the rme9 build of RMDOS could
watch every call of the run.  Just before the end: the box's
COMMAND.COM writing "EXEC failure" to handle 2 and being told it was
not a handle, opening CACHEBOX.TXT and being given handle 0, writing
to handle 1 - not a handle either; and the System VM's close of
WINSWEEP's picture file refused the same way.  Then the call that
showed why: the box ending (4Ch, inside IFSHLP's 2Fh/1122h), and the
next line a call from the System VM with InDOS and the depth both
ZERO inside it.

WHAT HAPPENED.  RMDOS keeps the process state a call works with - the
current PSP, the DTA, the drive, the error, InDOS - in variables of
its own, pulled out of the published SDA as a call comes in (DOSMGR
gives every machine its own copy of those bytes) and put back as it
leaves (RMINFO.INC, sda_pull and sda_sync).  Those variables, the depth
counter and the stack slots are one of each for all the machines, and
the DOSMGR critical section (INT 2Ah 8001h, crit_in) is what makes
them one machine's at a time.  But i21 took the section AFTER pulling
the state in, raising InDOS and the depth, and writing the caller's
PSP - so a machine whose call was under way, holding the section,
could be switched out and the next machine to call would pull ITS
state over the working copies before waiting for the section.  Here
the box was ending: its terminate then wrote the System VM's state
into the box's own SDA, set InDOS and the depth to zero, let the
section go, and the System VM's call went on with the box's parent as
its process.  From then on each machine had the other's PSP: the box's
handles were looked up in Windows' task and Windows' in the box.

THE FIX is the order: crit_in first, before anything that is shared
is read or written (RMDOS.ASM, i21).  A machine that calls while
another is inside DOS now waits before it touches anything.  The
console's wait (RMCON.INC), the one place a call lets the section go
on purpose, already took it back before pulling the state.

PROVED with the lrg3 list (CACHEBOX looked in on at 60 seconds), WfW
3.11, under QEMU unless said:

  rme9, old order    CACHEBOX ends after "the directory, twice";
                     MOVEPROB's EXEC refused (0Bh) and "EXEC failure"
                     to a handle that is not one; 335 calls run with
                     InDOS and the depth at zero; Windows does not
                     exit
  rme9, new order    the whole list: CACHEBOX looked in on at 70.8
                     seconds, still running, then ending by itself
                     with all of its output; not one call with InDOS
                     and the depth at zero; Windows out (545 s)
  release, new order the same, with LRGDISK 1.1 under it (looked in
                     on at 69 seconds; Windows out, 547 s)
  86Box vli486sv2g   release, new order, LRGDISK 1.1 - the machine and
                     list that stalled every time: CACHEBOX looked in
                     on at 62.7 seconds and ending by itself four
                     seconds later, all of its output there; the whole
                     list, Windows out

A DOS box reading a CD-ROM beside two others using the disk (the
LRGDISK entry above) showed it the other way round before the fix:
IFSBOX's six-file copy came out 0 bytes ("Insufficient disk space"),
the CD box's redirected output went to its window, and Windows fell
over into real mode.

Regression: RUNTESTS 83 tests on all seven rows - SFTSCAN, RMFIND
and RMTEST re-recorded: where "CON " lies moves up a byte with RMDOS,
and TESTS has ATAPIRD.COM in it now (a file more, three clusters
less).  The 86Box sweeps of the LRGDISK entry above ran on this fix
too.  MASM 6.13 assembles RMDOS.ASM plain and with RMDOS_E9.

Files: DOS\RMDOS.ASM.  RMDOS.SYS is 59,912 bytes (62,187 with the E9
trace).


LRGDISK 1.2: BOTH CABLES, BUS-MASTER DMA, TWO BUGGY CHIPS (2026-10-08)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie asked for the second IDE cable, bus-master DMA, something
for a DOS CD-ROM driver that hooks IRQ 14 itself, and something for
a DOS program's reset of the cable; then, with DMA in, for the CMD640
and the RZ1000 to be found and their data corruption bugs kept out
of the way.

TWO CABLES.  LRGDISK drives the BIOS's disks 80h to 83h wherever
they are: either unit of the first cable (1F0h, IRQ 14) or of the
second (170h, IRQ 15).  Each cable has a state of its own (CBL_*,
EBP -> it in every routine that works a cable): the command on it,
and the DOS programs' view of it, so that one cable waits for
nothing on the other.  Which cable and unit a BIOS disk is comes
from where the BIOS's own read of its first sector went: both
cables' registers are poisoned first, both units of each, and the
cable whose selected drive is ready and shows cylinder 0 afterwards
is the one.  BlockDev owns IRQ 14 and calls LRGDISK for it; IRQ 15
LRGDISK takes from VPICD itself (VPICD_Virtualize_IRQ, with an EOI
procedure that ends an interrupt it sent on to a VM).  Before a
cable is taken its interrupt is TRIED: the vector pointed at a stub,
the IRQ unmasked, and the drive given a read with its interrupt on -
SeaBIOS polls and leaves IRQ 15 masked, and a mask is no proof the
line is wired.  INT13.386 knows disks 80h and 81h only (it tests
DL against 01111110b), so for 82h and 83h LRGDISK's hook on its
translation answers the whole of INT 13h - 02h, 03h, 08h, 15h, the
extensions, and the calls INT13.386 says yes to - the same way.

BUS-MASTER DMA.  A PCI IDE controller's engine (BAR4: eight ports a
cable) moves the data itself from a table of physical addresses (the
PRDs): one interrupt a controller command instead of one a sector.
LRGDISK uses it for a drive that has a DMA mode SELECTED - IDENTIFY
words 88 (Ultra) and 63 (multiword), the high bytes - by whoever set
the drive and the controller's timing up before Windows: the BIOS,
or the kernel (IDEDMA=).  It sets no mode of its own; the kernel's
IDEHOST.INC is the measure of what that would take.  The table lives
in a page from _PageAllocate (two tables, a cable each; a page never
crosses a 64K boundary, which a PRD table may not); the buffers'
physical addresses come from _CopyPageTable, a page at a time, runs
within one 64K merged into one entry.  A transfer the engine cannot
be pointed at - an odd address, a page not present, more pieces than
the table holds - goes by PIO, and a drive whose engine gets a
transfer wrong once (the engine's error bit, or a table it had not
finished when the drive stopped) is PIO from then on.  LRGDiskDMA=off
in [386Enh] keeps the engine out of it; the engine's sixteen ports
are taken from the VMs.  The engine is found by the real-mode
start-up through the PCI BIOS (the report says where) and again by
the protected-mode side through configuration mechanism 1, and told
it may master the bus.

WHAT WIN386'S LOADER LEAVES A REAL-MODE START-UP, which cost most of
the night: nothing.  A record a unit was to be handed over in a block
of DOS memory (AH=48h: no memory - the loader's MAXALLOC is FFFFh and
it never shrinks), then in extended memory (XMS 09h: nothing left -
the loader has taken it all for the VxDs' pages), then by a pointer
into the start-up's own segment (gone by Sys_Critical_Init: the next
device's start-up is loaded over it - "DOST" was found there), and
loader service 7, Copy_Extended_Memory in later DDKs, comes back with
CF set.  So EDX is all there is: a byte a unit (RF_*: taken, LBA,
LBA48, something else there, DMA, bits 5-6 the BIOS disk less 80h;
bit 7 of unit 0's byte "one cable at a time", of unit 1's "DMA
allowed"), and the protected-mode side measures again what it needs:
IDENTIFY for the sector count and the mode, the BIOS's AH=08h for
the geometry.

AND WHEN.  The geometry needs a VM to run the BIOS in, which
Sys_Critical_Init has not got; but registering at Device_Init
instead (first try) left the disk to the BIOS: BlockDev decides at
ITS Device_Init, from the drives registered by then, whether to hook
the VMs' INT 13h at all - and with none it does not, so every INT 13h
went to the BIOS, whose first port write LRGDISK refused.  So the
drives are registered at Sys_Critical_Init as WDCTRL registers them,
with a stand-in geometry, and told the BIOS's at Device_Init - with
an init order of 0D000000h, right after VPICD, because PageFile
(18000000h) reads the disk in its Device_Init and a stand-in
geometry would have sent its reads anywhere.  The AH=08h is run in
the System VM with Exec_Int, and LRGDISK's own hook lets it past
INT13.386 (ld_rawbios), which would otherwise answer it from the
descriptor - the stand-in.  (A far call to the IVT's INT 13h, as
INT13.386's comments suggest, reaches INT13.386 all the same: the
IVT's entry is BlockDev's.)  And a shell message - the refusal, the
20-second one - wants EBP -> the VM's registers: the VMM runs the VM
for it, and with EBP left pointing at the cable's state it wrote a
VM's registers over it, which looked like a command that never
finished.

THE AWARD BIOS AT THE PORTS.  With QEMU passing everything, 86Box's
P3B-F would not start Windows at all - with DMA, with LRGDiskDMA=off,
with the trace build, and with no trace on its printer (86Box's text
printer writes the control characters and drops the letters; the trace
build now writes to COM1 as well, and run_lrg -Com reads it off
86Box's serial-passthrough named pipe, as the kernel's trace was
read).  1.1 on the same rig started.  The difference is LRGDISK's own
AH=08h at Device_Init: by then the cable's ports are trapped, and the
Award BIOS's INT 13h touches them on its way to the table - SeaBIOS
reads the table and touches nothing - so the trap refused the BIOS and
put up the message, with nobody to press a key.  Now the trap lets the
BIOS through while LRGDISK's question is running (ld_rawbios): nothing
of LRGDISK's is on the cable then, and the real-mode start-up let the
BIOS at the ports in the same way.  With that, the P3B-F runs the
sweep with DMA (the BIOS's Ultra DMA mode 2).

THE EMULATOR'S TRANSLATED CODE.  With everything above right, Windows
still ended ten seconds in: KRNL386.EXE, loaded by the engine into
memory at 8D000h-9E000h that had run the loader's programs, ran a
few calls and quit.  The data was right - every sector read by the
engine was read again by PIO and compared, and matched - and the
same bytes by PIO worked.  QEMU's TCG keeps the code it has
translated for a page until the PROCESSOR writes the page; a device's
write does not throw it away, and the old code ran.  So ld_prdbuild
reads a byte of every page and puts it back on its way through: a
few hundred nanoseconds a page, nothing on hardware (a bus master's
write reaches the memory the processor reads), and QEMU is a rig
that is here to stay.

THE DOS CD-ROM DRIVER THAT HOOKS IRQ 14.  A DOS program's device on a
shared cable interrupts; with VirtualHDIrq on, BlockDev used to end
it as the BIOS's handler would and nobody in the box saw it.  Now
LRGDISK, knowing whose command is on the cable (CBL_VMBUSY), sends
it on to that VM (VPICD_Set_Int_Request): the VM's own handler runs
- the BIOS's INT 76h or 77h, or a driver's that hooked it - and
BlockDev's EOI procedure (or LRGDISK's, on IRQ 15) ends it at the
PIC when the VM has, which is what the VM would get with no 32-bit
disk access at all.  VirtualHDIrq need not be set.

A DOS PROGRAM'S RESET.  SRST written to a cable's control register
resets LRGDISK's drives too.  Now it marks the cable (CBL_RESET) and
before LRGDISK's next command on it each of its drives there is
given its parameters again, polled with its interrupt off: a drive
used by CHS its geometry (INITIALIZE DEVICE PARAMETERS), a drive
used by DMA its transfer mode (SET FEATURES 03h).  A reset written
while LRGDISK's command is on the cable is kept and done for the
program when the command is over (CBL_VMSRST), and the program's
status reads say BSY meanwhile.  TOOLS\SRSTTEST.COM (new, in
BIN\TESTS) does the reset as a DOS driver would, for a DOS box.

THE CMD640 AND THE RZ1000.  Both are PCI IDE controllers without an
engine, so LRGDISK would be PIO on them, and both bugs are the kind
Windows hits: the PC-Tech RZ1000 (1042h:1000h, and the RZ1001)
corrupts a PIO read when its read-ahead is on and the processor is
interrupted between sectors; the CMD640 (1095h:0640h) corrupts data
when both its cables transfer at once, and with read-ahead on.  The
real-mode start-up finds either through the PCI BIOS and does what
Linux does: read-ahead off (RZ1000: register 40h bit 13; CMD640:
CNTRL 51h bits 6 and 7, ARTTIM23 57h bits 2 and 3), and on a CMD640
the cables are used ONE AT A TIME (ld_serial): a command, LRGDISK's
or a DOS program's, waits while the other cable has one (CBL_XHELD;
ld_xrelease lets it go when the other cable is idle).  LRGDiskSerial
=on asks for that on any controller.  Neither chip is in 86Box or
QEMU, so the detection ran against nothing; the serial mode ran
under LRGDiskSerial=on.  The VLB CMD640 is not looked for.

RESULTS (the final build, LRGDISK.386 23,798 bytes).  QEMU 11.1
(PIIX3, SeaBIOS; the drives at Ultra DMA mode 5), the lrg3 sweep each
time - IFSBOX (I13X's 24 checks of a disk's last sectors through
INT 13h and the extensions, WIN386.EXE copied and compared, six copies
end to end twice), CACHEBOX, DOSBOX1 and nine programs, 12 in all -
Windows out at the end:
  - the first cable alone, DMA: 0 wrong, copies the same (491 s);
    LRGDiskDMA=off the same by PIO
  - a 200GB LBA48 slave as 81h, DMA: I13X on its last 512 sectors,
    the host's chk7 of the image 0 wrong
  - THREE disks - a 20GB slave 81h, a 128GB secondary master 82h -
    with I13X on 82h, which INT13.386 never sees: 0 wrong, the host's
    chk7 of the 128GB image 0 wrong (the sectors zeroed first)
  - a disk on each cable with LRGDiskSerial=on: I13X on the second
    cable's disk 0 wrong, chk7 0 wrong
  - a CD-ROM beside a 20GB disk on the SECOND cable, CDBOX in the
    background: SRSTTEST's reset, ATAPIRD's 12 passes (BADF658F every
    one, 0 errors), SRSTTEST again, while IFSBOX and CACHEBOX used the
    disks; the trace build shows the two resets marked and the drives
    given their parameters again.  The same on the first cable.
86Box 4.x:
  - P3B-F (PIIX4, the Award BIOS, Ultra DMA mode 2): the lrg3 sweep
    with DMA, all 12, I13X 0 wrong, copies the same, Windows out
  - P3B-F, a 504MB disk and a 128GB slave as 81h, DMA: all 12, I13X on
    the slave 0 wrong, the host's chk7 of the image 0 wrong
  - VL/I-486SV2G (ISA, no engine: PIO): all 12, I13X 0 wrong, copies
    the same
LRGTEST (TOOLS\LRGTEST.ASM, prints the answer's bytes) under real
MS-DOS 5 on QEMU and 86Box: 80h, 81h and 82h found with their cables,
units and modes; every real-mode message seen.  RUNTESTS 83 x 7 after
re-recording RMFIND and RMTEST (SRSTTEST.COM in TESTS; ATAPIRD.COM and
LRGTEST.COM changed size) and CACHETST on six of the seven rows (its
file starts somewhere else now: one more cache element owed a write).
MASM 6.13 clean: LRGDISK plain and trace, LRGTEST, ATAPIRD, SRSTTEST.
Neither the CMD640 nor the RZ1000 could be run against: 86Box and QEMU
have neither chip.

THE FLOPPY BOOT ON HARDWARE: EMS, AND THE CHECK'S MEMORY (2026-10-08)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie's second run from the floppy: WIN said an expanded-memory
driver was in the way; after a reboot the kernel wanted C: checked
and CHKDSK C: /F stopped with "Insufficient memory"; with EMS off,
Windows got nearly to the desktop and the machine hung with a
blinking cursor and the floppy light on; WIN /D:C hung the same way.

THE EXPANDED-MEMORY DRIVER.  Reproduced under QEMU in one run: a
floppy boot with the shipped DISK\CONFIG.SYS, which says EMS=AUTO,
and "ERROR: Unsupported expanded-memory driver already installed"
on the screen.  Every sweep had run Windows with no EMS line.  With
EMS on, INT 67h points at an IRET in a paragraph of conventional
memory that carries EMMXXXX0 at offset 0Ah - the detection the LIM
specification recommends - and the calls themselves are answered by
the monitor, which traps INT 67h before the IRET is reached.  Parked
there is no monitor: WIN386's loader reads the vector, finds the
name, calls a manager that is nothing but an IRET, and refuses.  So
park_savevecs blanks the eight bytes for the trip and park_restvecs
puts them back (PARK.INC); a program under Windows finds no manager
of ours, which is right - Windows brings its own.  The same floppy
boot now runs the sweep with EMS=AUTO.

THE CHECK'S MEMORY.  The boot-time CHKDSK ran "in the shell's place:
same slot" - the interpreter's slot at SHELL_SLOT, SHELL_SIZE (256K)
and fixed, because slot_grow refuses depth zero.  CHKDSK keeps a byte
a cluster and reads each directory whole, so the check of a FAT32
volume of any size said "Insufficient memory" and never finished;
run from the prompt the same CHKDSK has a slot out of the arena that
grows, and nobody had left a big volume dirty at boot before.  Now
shell_restart takes an arena slot at depth zero before ack_next loads
CHKDSK into it, gives it back when there is nothing to check, and
frees the last round's at the top (slot_sweep stops at depth 1); the
row for depth zero goes back to the interpreter's values each time,
and cur_psp is taken from the PSP build_psp made rather than assumed
(DOSMAIN.ASM).  Proven with a 2000MB FAT32 image (4,032,401 clusters
of one sector, MKDISK's choice) left dirty by a file held open when
DOSBox-X's time limit stopped the machine: the old kernel stops at
"Insufficient memory", this one checks it to the end and the volume
is marked clean (RESULTS).

THE HANG WITH EMS OFF is not reproduced here.  The same floppy boot
with EMS=NO in the shipped CONFIG.SYS runs the sweep under QEMU
(Windows up, WRITE run, Windows out).  The floppy light staying on
says only that the kernel's own read of RMDOS.SYS from A: left the
motor running when the park took the machine - nothing on the far
side counts the BIOS's motor timer down until the BIOS's INT 08h is
running again - so it is not evidence of a floppy access at the
crash.  What differs from the rig is the machine and the CONFIG.SYS
on the floppy: whether it has DEVICE=C:\WINDOWS\IFSHLP.SYS (the
shipped one does not; without it WfW 3.11 cannot start enhanced mode
with 32-bit file access), and whether WINCACHE= is set.  Left open
until the hardware says more - the memory size, the disk, and the
floppy's CONFIG.SYS as booted.

RESULTS.  QEMU, a floppy boot with the shipped DISK\CONFIG.SYS plus
DEVICE=C:\WINDOWS\IFSHLP.SYS and WINCACHE=2048, Windows from the hard
disk: EMS=AUTO, the old kernel - "Unsupported expanded-memory driver
already installed", no Windows; EMS=AUTO, this kernel - the sweep
runs (WRITE, Windows out); EMS=NO, the old kernel - the sweep runs.
DOSBox-X, the 2000MB FAT32 volume left dirty: the old kernel - "Drive
D: was not shut down properly. Running CHKDSK D: /F." then
"Insufficient memory" and the shell; this kernel - the check runs to
its report (3 files, 4,032,401 allocation units, CHKDSK's own slot
grown to 4,587,520 bytes) and the volume is clean when the shell
comes up.  RUNTESTS 83 x 7, no baseline changed.  MASM 6.13 clean on
DOSMAIN.  Rig: rig\runqemu.ps1 -Floppy, hw\flopwin.ps1 (-ConfigFrom,
-ShotEvery), hw\chktest.ps1 (dirty, check) with hw\HOLDOPEN.COM,
which holds a file open until the time limit.

Files: DOS\PARK.INC, DOS\DOSMAIN.ASM.  PMDOS.SYS is 152,151 bytes.

AUTOEXEC.TXT, A BOX FROM THE DISKETTE, MSD, AND THE NETWORK (2026-10-09)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie's third run from the floppy: the boot-time CHKDSK C: /F now
finished, but the machine came up with 361KB of conventional memory
free, and Windows got as far as its start-up sound before the hang.
He also asked for AUTOEXEC.BAT to be the commands and nothing else.
Then, in the morning: WIN /N and Windows is fine, so the hang is the
network start; Quarterdeck's Manifest for Windows crashes the machine;
MSD crashes the DOS box; and a question about the dirty bit.

AUTOEXEC.TXT.  DISK\AUTOEXEC.BAT had grown 469 REM lines - where
everything is, the two shells, the tests, Windows, the CD-ROM, DOSKEY,
what a boot says - around three commands.  The text is DISK\
AUTOEXEC.TXT now, the REM prefixes gone and a short header first, as
CONFIG.TXT is to CONFIG.SYS; the batch file is @ECHO OFF, PROMPT,
PATH and one REM naming the text.  BUILD.CMD puts the text on the
boot disk and MKHD.CMD on the hard disks, whose AUTOEXEC.BAT (BIN\HD\,
made by MKHD from the diskette's with its own PATH) is four lines
now.  Charlie's note for later: all of that text belongs in an online
help system when there is one.

THE CONVENTIONAL MEMORY is not lost on the rig.  The same kernel,
booted with the 2000MB FAT32 volume dirty (the check runs CHKDSK D:
/F to the end) and again with it clean (no check), and MEM run from
AUTOEXEC each time: 617K of 618K free both times.  What the check
does leave behind is in the XMS pool: 4,340K used against 1,372K,
sixty-two blocks against thirteen - the disk cache holding what
CHKDSK read, which it gives back when a program asks for memory it
has not got (slot_grow, arena_alloc).  So the 361KB on the hardware
is something the rig does not do, and the number itself - 618K less
361K is 257K, which is SHELL_SIZE and a kilobyte - points at
something sized like a slot.  Charlie's next boot after a check
had the proper 617K, so the machine does not do it every time
either; not reproduced, open.

A DOS BOX WHOSE COMSPEC IS ON A: COULD NOT START.  Not the hang, but
found looking for it: a floppy boot puts COMSPEC on A:, and under
QEMU every DOS box then said "Cannot start application", while a
box with COMSPEC=C:\COMMAND.COM ran, and a box already running could
DIR, TYPE and COPY from A: and even run A:\COMMAND.COM /C VER.  The
RMDOS trace (RME9.INC, which now prints the buffer with every BIOS
transfer and the registers with every failed one) showed WIN386's
EXEC of A:\COMMAND.COM reading its sectors one a call straight into
the box's memory from 191B:0000 up, and the fifty-sixth, at
191B:6E00 - linear 1FFB0h, which crosses the 64K boundary at 20000h -
refused by the BIOS: a diskette is read by DMA, the DMA controller
cannot carry one transfer across a 64K page, and the BIOS checks
first.  rd_raw cut runs at the boundary but let THE SECTOR THAT
ITSELF STRADDLES ONE go alone, as if alone were enough; RMDOS reads
whole sectors straight into the caller's memory, so where a sector
lands is wherever the file happens to fall in the program's image,
and the first program ever to have one straddle was COMMAND.COM
loaded at WIN386's box address.  A sector that straddles now goes
through rd_bounce, two sectors long so that one half of it is within
a page wherever RMDOS was loaded (rd_bncsel picks the half), read
there and copied out, or copied in and written from there.  The
first build of that clobbered EAX - the sector - with the flat
address, so the BIOS was asked for cylinder 1023 of a diskette and
the straddler still failed, with a different error, until the trace
printed the registers.  With it right: a floppy boot, Windows from
C:, COMSPEC on A:, and WINSWEEP's two DOS boxes run (hwbox11).

TWO SECONDS, AS MS-DOS HAS IT.  The same trace showed every sector of
that file costing three BIOS transfers: rd_getvol re-mounted a
diskette on every call - geometry, boot sector - because "an
excursion is short and one boot sector costs nothing".  Fifty-six
sectors were a hundred and seventy transfers, two thirds of them of
the boot sector on track 0 with the head travelling there and back,
and a DOS box under a floppy boot loads COMMAND.COM from A: every
time it opens.  So a diskette asked for again within two seconds of
the last time is the same diskette (VOL_TICK, VOL_SAME_TICKS, the
BIOS tick count read by rd_ticks) - MS-DOS's own rule for a drive
with no change line, and nobody has swapped one faster.  The stamp
is refreshed on every access; the count wraps at midnight and the
subtraction comes out huge, which is one spare mount a day.

MSD CRASHED THE BOX ON THE RIG TOO: "VDM: the guest faulted, vector
0D at 0111:001D", linear 112Dh, the LIDT in the real-mode stub's road
back to protected mode (IORM.ASM), reached in V86 mode by a transfer
to 0111:0000.  Three instruments found the road there.  vdm_fault
now prints a second line - SS:SP, twelve words of the stack, six
bytes of code - and a third with the registers, so that a fault on
real hardware can be read off a photograph; MSD's said SP was ODD
(4786:35D3), which no compiled program does to itself.  The fault
ring of a BUILD lptlow kernel (DBGSINK.INC, read back off the disk
with scratch hw\dbgring.pl) gave the last five hundred faults: MSD
selected drive A (0E00h), the kernel raised INT 24h through the
callback paragraph, MSD's handler ran, and MSD went on; then four
INT 2Fh questions and the fault, with no trap in between - MSD had
got there on its own.  And QEMU's monitor disassembled MSD at the
last question: the end of a C function, pops and a RETF, whose
return address was whatever lay thirty bytes up the stack.

THE CAUSE IS A FRAME DOS LEAVES AND THIS KERNEL DID NOT.  MS-DOS
raises INT 24h on the caller's own stack with the caller's INT 21h
return on top and, under it, the caller's registers as the
dispatcher pushed them - AX, BX, CX, DX, SI, DI, BP, DS, ES - and
the C library's _hardretn RELIES ON THE SHAPE: it drops its own
frame and those nine words and IRETs through the caller's, straight
back into the program with the error in AX and carry set.  MSD does
that for every drive it probes.  The monitor had popped the caller's
frame before serving the call (vdm_ciret) and kept the registers in
vdm_ctx, so a handler doing the arithmetic landed thirty bytes above
where it meant to and popped a local variable as its return.  Now
crit_guest builds the frame below the caller's SP - the return, the
nine words - and raises the interrupt beneath it; a handler that
IRETs onto the landing pad leaves it as dead stack, and one that
goes home the other way leaves SP at the caller's, which vdm_loop
watches for (vdm_cgchk) and takes as the answer: the simulated
interrupt is over without its HLT, the DOS call is over without its
answer, and the kernel stack above the box loop's anchor is all of
it, so crit_direct unwinds there and the box goes on from where the
handler put it - as MS-DOS does.  MSD /P writes its whole report on
the rig now.  Noted on the way: 0Eh (select drive) reads the medium
here and raises a critical error for an empty A:, where MS-DOS only
sets the letter; left as it is.

THE HANG AFTER THE START-UP SOUND IS THE NETWORK, by Charlie's own
test: WIN /N and Windows is fine.  The sound plays when PROGMAN
starts; what runs after it is WFWNET.DRV's start of the network.  The
QEMU rig had no network, so one was given it: the NDIS 3 drivers off
the WfW disks (VNETSUP, VREDIR, VSERVER, NDIS, NE2000, NETBEUI,
WFWNET.DRV, NETAPI.DLL; expanded under DOSBox-X, since Windows'
EXPAND copies the KWAJ files unexpanded), SYSTEM.INI and
PROTOCOL.INI written as Setup writes them for an NE2000 at 300h, IRQ
9, and QEMU's ne2k_isa on its user-mode network (runqemu -Nic,
flopwin -WinSrc/-Nic/-SysIniDrop; scratchpad wfwnet\).  Two things
came of it before the rig ran out of likeness to the machine:

  * VNETSUP.386 SETS THE MACHINE NAME as the network starts - INT 21h
    5E01h - and RMDOS refused it with error 1, as it refused every
    5Eh and 5Fh.  MS-DOS keeps the name itself ($UserOper, DOS6SRC
    dos/macro.asm): fn5E (RMINFO.INC) now takes it (5E01h) and gives
    it back (5E00h, CH = 1 once set, CL = the NetBIOS number); 5E02h
    to 5E05h and 5Fh - redirected printers, the redirection list -
    are the redirector's business through INT 2Fh 111Eh in MS-DOS and
    stay refused.
  * On QEMU Windows went no further than its logo and came back to
    the prompt without a word: KRNL386 had loaded WFWNET.DRV and
    NETAPI.DLL and then WIN386 unwound (XMS handles freed, vectors
    restored, WIN386.SWP deleted, 4CFFh).  A hand-made network
    install is not Charlie's; and the BOOTLOG.TXT he sent, which
    was read here as a WIN /N run because it reached PROGMAN, was
    the lockup's - the next entry has what that meant.  WDCTRL
    must be dropped from SYSTEM.INI for the QEMU run (its validation
    fails at phase 07 with the card in the machine); LRGDISK is the
    answer there as everywhere.

THE DIRTY BIT at the prompt: the prompt is a commit point, so a
machine turned off there has every volume marked clean (VOLFLAG.INC,
vfl_cleanall from dos_commit); only a program with a file half
written when the power goes leaves its volume dirty, which is the
truth.  While Windows runs, the park marks the hard disks dirty
(vfl_parkmark) and the unpark cleans them, so power off inside
Windows is a check at the next boot - as Windows 95 does it.

Files: DOS\CRITERR.INC (crit_guest's frame), DOS\VDM.INC (vdm_cgchk,
crit_direct, the fault report), DOS\RMDISK.INC (VOL_TICK, rd_ticks,
rd_getvol, rd_raw and rd_bounce), DOS\RMINFO.INC (fn5E), DOS\RMDOS.ASM
(the table), DOS\RME9.INC (the buffer and the registers in the disk
trace), DISK\AUTOEXEC.BAT, DISK\AUTOEXEC.TXT (new), BUILD.CMD,
MKHD.CMD, BIN\HD\AUTOEXEC.BAT (regenerated).  RUNTESTS: RMTEST and

THE NETWORK START CALLED ZERO (2026-10-09)
------------------------------------------

Charlie, in the morning: the BOOTLOG.TXT he sent was the lockup's -
the try after it was the one he gave WIN /N - and the card in the
486 is a 3Com EtherLink III, a 3C509 on the ISA bus.  So the log
ends where the hang is, at INITDONE=Installable Drivers with nothing
after it; and on this kernel's rig, the same WfW tree with an NE2000,
WIN /3 /B stops at the same line and Windows is back at the prompt
with 4CFFh and not a word.  The same point, a different ending.

WHAT ENDS THERE.  The kernel's LoadStart lines stop at Installable
Drivers because USER tells the kernel the boot is over then; what
runs next in Windows for Workgroups is the network driver, WFWNET.DRV
and NETAPI.DLL, loaded after MMSYSTEM in the RMDOS trace.  It starts
by asking DOS three things - the version, the collating table (6506h,
then a selector set on the table's address), the extended country
information (6501h, 36 bytes) - and then it CALLS THE CASE-MAP
ROUTINE in that block, a far call into real mode through DPMI 0301h,
to upper-case a name.  RMDOS's block had zero there ("the case-map
call, which is none"), so the call went to 0000:0000 and the system
VM ran the interrupt table as code.  On QEMU the fourth byte is an
invalid opcode: the VMM takes a fault in the system VM as fatal and
leaves for DOS with code FFh and no message, which is the quiet exit
the earlier entry could not explain.  On the 486 the table's bytes
are the BIOS's and the kernel's own vectors, and what they decode to
runs until the machine stops: the blinking cursor.  WIN /N never
loads the network driver, so it never asks.

QEMU'S OWN LOG FOUND IT.  Nothing on the DOS side showed where
Windows went after 6501h, and the kernel's fault ring is parked with
the kernel.  runqemu -DLog int has the emulated CPU write every
exception it takes - vector, privilege, CS:EIP, CR2, the registers -
and hw\intlog.pl and hw\intwin.pl read the log: WIN386's ring 0 had
no fault at all (fifteen page faults from the pager, the first-time
VxD calls), and the ring-3 window before the exit read, in order,
5100h, two DPMI 0303h callbacks, 3000h, 6506h, a selector on the
table, 3000h, 6501h, then INT 31h 0301h from the same code segment -
and the next exception was an invalid opcode in V86 mode at
0000:0003.  Eighty megabytes of log for three minutes of boot; the
digest is forty lines.  The screendumps of such a run show the boot
text whatever Windows is doing, so the log is the witness.

THE FIX IS THE KERNEL'S OWN.  PMDOS's 38h and 6501h point the
case-map call at the far return in the guest block (GLOL_RETF; "zero
there would be a call into the interrupt table", INT21.INC): a
character comes back as it went, which is the whole of codepage
437's case mapping beyond ASCII that this DOS does.  The same byte
sits at the same offset in the low block RMDOS adopts (RL_DEVRET),
so rd_lowsave writes rd_lowseg:RL_DEVRET into rd_country's case-map
field each time it takes the block, and 38h and 6501h copy it out as
before.  Nine bytes.  The two DOSes' country tables are checked
against each other at assembly time (PARK.INC); the block's contents
were not, and this is the field that differed.

WITH IT, THE SAME RUN GOES ON.  The bootlog carries past Installable
Drivers to INIT=TSRQuery and INITDONE=TSRQuery, which is where a WfW
3.11 boot ends.  The network driver then put up "Networking
functionality will not be available" - the same box, word for word,
that the same tree gives on real MS-DOS 5 (hw\dos5net.ps1, the
control), and the cause was the install, not the DOS: SYSTEM.INI
had no "netmisc=ndis.386", so the NDIS 3 wrapper the card and
protocol drivers bind through never loaded (the trace opens
NE2000.386 and NETBEUI.386 and never NDIS.386; netini.pl writes the
line now).  With it THE NETWORK STARTS UNDER PM-DOS on the rig:
PROGMAN with its Network group, WINSWEEP runs its program and
leaves, Windows exits with 4C00h and the floppy-boot AUTOEXEC runs
to its end - with and without LRGDISK.386 loaded (hwnet8, hwnet9),
and on real MS-DOS 5 the same (dos5net6).  runqemu -Keys sends the
monitor's sendkey to the guest, which answered the box while it was
there.  The screendumps of a -DLog run show the boot text whatever
Windows is doing, so the log is the witness there.

THE CRASH ON EXIT Charlie then reported from the 486 is therefore
not what this stack does on the rig: the exit after a bound network
session is clean here.  What the screen says at his, and whether
WIN /N's exit does it too, is what the next round starts from.

"THE NETWORK DRIVER WAS UNABLE TO LOAD".  Charlie's next boot from
the floppy, with the new RMDOS: no lockup, but a box at startup -
"The Windows for Workgroups network was not started ... The Windows
for Workgroups network driver was unable to load" - and nothing
about it in BOOTLOG.TXT.  The rig had never shown it because every
rig floppy loaded C:\WINDOWS\IFSHLP.SYS from its CONFIG.SYS and the
shipped DISK\CONFIG.SYS did not: booted from the shipped file, the
rig puts up the same box word for word (hwnet10).  IFSHLP.SYS is
the real-mode helper Workgroups' redirector and its 32-bit file
access run through, and WIN.COM and WIN386 both open IFS$HLP$
before the network driver comes to it.  So the shipped CONFIG.SYS
loads it now, with a REM saying why; a machine with no Workgroups
at C:\WINDOWS gets the line echoed with "Bad or missing device
driver" and boots on, which is what cfg_device has always done and
what MS-DOS does with the same line.  CONFIG.TXT says so under
DEVICE=.  Booted from the new file, the rig loads the driver and
leaves Windows clean (hwnet11).  Whether QEMU's NE2000 then binds
is a coin toss there - byte-identical images pass and fail (hwb4
against hwb9), and real MS-DOS 5 tosses the same coin (dos5net6
bound, dos5net7 and 8 did not) - so that part is the emulator's
and not the DOS's; eleven runs say so.  The crash on exit is still
his word only; nothing here has shown one.

THE 3C509.  Neither emulator here has one - 86Box has the 3C503 and
the 3C501, QEMU the NE2000 - and the WfW disks carry ELNK3.386.
Nothing on the road to the crash touches the card: the call comes
before the card is bound.  What the 486 does after it is Charlie's to
see.

Files: DOS\RMDOS.ASM (rd_lowsave), DOS\RMINFO.INC (rd_country).  The
rig: rig\runqemu.ps1 (-DLog, -Keys), hw\flopwin.ps1 (-WinArgs,
-DLog, -Keys, BOOTLOG.TXT fetched), hw\dos5net.ps1 (the control on
real DOS 5), hw\intlog.pl, hw\intwin.pl.  RUNTESTS: SFTSCAN
re-recorded on every row (RMDOS.SYS is nine bytes longer and the
"CON " addresses moved by nine), 83 x 7.  MASM 6.13: RMDOS.


THE LETTERS UNDER WINDOWS, AND THE CD-ROM (2026-10-09)
------------------------------------------------------

Charlie, after IFSHLP.SYS went into the shipped CONFIG.SYS: the
network starts, but the logon script that maps his network drives
maps none; File Manager shows C: to H: on a machine with a C: and a
CD-ROM; D: is the CD-ROM and shows nothing; and the prompt never
comes back when Windows exits - that one is his next round, with
LRGDISK.386.  The first three are here.

THE PHANTOM LETTERS.  WINSWEEP now writes a line a letter as it
starts - GetDriveType, 4409h, 4408h, MSCDEX's 150Bh - and on the rig
it said what File Manager draws: D: to H: fixed disks, while every
DOS question about them said "invalid drive".  Windows 3.1 tests a
letter by SELECTING it (0Eh) and seeing whether 19h moved, and RMDOS
let any letter below eight be selected.  MS-DOS selects only a letter
whose current directory structure is in use ($SET_DEFAULT_DRIVE,
GetVisDrv), and now so does RMDOS (cds_inuse, which 29h and 47h ask
as well): a redirector's drive is in use, so a mapped network letter
can still be made current.  The real MS-DOS 5, same Windows, same
list, gave A:, C: and nothing else; PM-DOS now gives the same.

B: went too.  The kernel gives B: a slot of its own on every machine
(FAT.INC, disk_scan) and RMDOS answered 440Eh with "no other letter",
so Windows drew a second diskette drive; MS-DOS answers 1 for both A:
and B: when there is one drive, A: having it, and Windows takes a B:
that is not its own owner for nothing.  RMDOS reads the BIOS's
equipment word for it, as MS-DOS learns the count.  440Eh and 4408h
on a redirector's drive are "invalid function", as DOS has them.

LASTDRIVE.  RMDOS had eight letters, A: to H:, fixed, for its volumes
AND for the current directory structures - and a network drive is a
structure Windows for Workgroups writes into.  With eight, there was
no I: to Z: to map, and D: to H: looked taken (they passed the test
above).  The structures go to twenty-six now (RL_NCDS) while the
volumes stay at eight; how many are in use is LASTDRIVE= as written -
the kernel caps its own at P: and now hands the line over uncapped
(RMH_LASTDRV) - never fewer than the volumes, and all twenty-six with
no line, as the kernel takes all of its own with none.  The shipped
CONFIG.SYS says LASTDRIVE=Z; CONFIG.TXT says why.

THE KERNEL KEEPS ITS OWN BYTES NOW.  Twenty-six structures made the
low block RMDOS builds in 4K, and RMDOS kept a copy of the kernel's
bytes there in its own 64K to put back - and the traced build no
longer fitted the segment.  The kernel keeps them instead, above the
megabyte (park_lowkeep, saved in park_fillhdr, put back first thing
in park_recover), and RMDOS keeps only what it reads before building:
its volumes' current directories and NUL's link (RD_KEEPLEN).
RMDOS.SYS came out smaller than before (61,148), the traced build
fits (63,544), and PMDOS.SYS is 4K bigger.

5FH AND 5E02H-5E05H go to the redirector now, as INT 2Fh 111Eh and
111Fh with the caller's own registers, as MS-DOS's $AssignOper and
$UserOper send them; 5F07h and 5F08h are DOS's own and are done here.
A redirector answers those calls by writing the caller's register
frame through the SDA's user_SP and user_SS - in MS-DOS's order,
which RMDOS's frame is not in - so one in that order is built for the
call and copied back (net_user).  5E00h/5E01h now keep fifteen bytes
and a NUL and give CX back as it was set, as UserGet does.  Path
roots: rd_canon and 47h take a redirector's root from its structure's
curdir_end, so a drive whose root is \\SERVER\SHARE is spelled the
way MS-DOS hands it to a redirector.

WHAT THE RIG COULD SHOW OF THE NETWORK.  NET USE in a box on the rig,
with NET.MSG and NETH.MSG expanded from the disks and a [Password
Lists] section so that NET can log on, never reaches DOS at all: the
trace has no 5F03h and no redirector call - Windows' own redirector
answers it above DOS - and NET, having logged on, raised "General
failure" for a server that does not exist, there being no server on
the rig.  So the mapping itself is Charlie's to see.  What stopped it
on the 486 is most likely what is fixed above: a letter past H: had
no structure to be mapped into, and D: to H: looked taken.

THE CD-ROM UNDER WINDOWS: RMCD.SYS (DOS\RMCD.ASM, new).  The kernel
reads a CD itself - ISO9660.INC, UDF.INC, ATAPI.INC, all 32-bit - and
none of it runs while it is parked, so under Windows the CD's letter
was simply not there (on the 486 it was there only as a phantom).
RMCD is that letter's other half the way MS-DOS had it: a redirector,
as MSCDEX is.  The park loads it when the kernel has a CD-ROM on an
IDE channel (park_cdfind, park_loadcd) into 8K after RMDOS's 64K in
the same block - the block vl_winres reserves when WIN386.EXE loads
is that much bigger then, so RMCD is below WIN386 with RMDOS and
global to every virtual machine, as MSCDEX loaded before Windows was
- and fills in its header: the letter, the command and control ports
(IOS_CDUNIT gives the control port now, in EBX's high word) and
master or slave.  RMDOS marks the letter's structure C080h - in use,
redirected, and bit 7, which keeps it out of the network's list of
connections - and calls cd_init, which hooks INT 2Fh on top of
RMDOS's vectors.  The park restores a vector that points into RMCD's
room as it restores RMDOS's.

What it does: the 11xxh calls RMDOS makes for the letter - CHDIR,
the attributes, open, read, seek from the end, close, find first and
next, the drive's size - out of the primary ISO 9660 tree of the
first session, names as 8.3 by the kernel's rule (";1" gone, the last
dot the extension); everything that would write is "access denied",
as MSCDEX has it; and MSCDEX 2.23's 1500h, 150Bh, 150Ch, 150Dh,
1502h-1505h and 1508h.  The drive is driven by PIO, its interrupt off
for each command and on again after, for a BIOS disk on the cable;
LRGDISK lends the cable to it.  A disc spinning up is waited for, a
changed disc is mounted again and a file opened on the old one says
"invalid disk change".  The Office CD on the rig, D:: DIR of the root
and of POWERPNT\DISK1, CD into WORD_NT\I386 and back, three files
copied - 106,497, 39,856 and 2,778 bytes - IDENTICAL to tar's copies,
writing refused; WINSWEEP's line for D: says remote, 4409h 1000h,
150Bh FFFFh/ADADh; File Manager draws d with the CD-ROM icon and
opens it - "D: CD-ROM", the tree, "0 bytes free, 116MB total".  The
names are the ISO tree's: that disc's EXCEL.NT is EXCEL_NT there,
which is what MSCDEX showed DOS too; the dotted name is Joliet's.

Two bugs of RMCD's own on the way: open wrote the file table entry
through ES:DI after the path walk had used DI - the entry stayed
blank, RMDOS took the file for a local one and read nothing, and the
fields went into RMDOS's own segment - and the walk borrowed FS,
which RMDOS keeps no copy of for its caller.

Not done: Joliet's long names, UDF-only discs and the later sessions
of a multisession disc (the kernel's, outside Windows), a second
CD-ROM drive, a SCSI CD-ROM (it would need an ASPI manager under
Windows), and 1501h/1510h, which hand the caller a device driver.

The rig: WINSWEEP's drive report; flopwin -List/-Root with RMCD.SYS
on its floppy, -Cd2 for an ISO, -Keys for the guest; runqemu -Nic
model:irq:iobase; the NE2000 binds on QEMU about half the time under
load, on PM-DOS and on MS-DOS 5 alike (nineteen runs) - the network
box it puts up is the emulator's.

Files: INC\RMDOS.INC (RL_NCDS, RMH_LASTDRV, RMH_CDSEG, RCH_*,
PARK_CDPARAS, RD_KEEPLEN), INC\RMSDA.INC (new: the SDA offsets, out
of RMINFO.INC, for RMCD too), DOS\RMDOS.ASM, DOS\RMINFO.INC,
DOS\RMDISK.INC, DOS\RMFILE.INC, DOS\RMFILE2.INC, DOS\RMNAME.INC,
DOS\RMNET.INC, DOS\RMCD.ASM (new), DOS\PARK.INC, DOS\VDM.INC,
DOS\CONFIG.INC, DOS\INT21.INC, IO\CDUNIT.INC, INC\PMDOS.INC,
BUILD.CMD and MKHD.CMD (RMCD.SYS built and on the disks),
DISK\CONFIG.SYS (LASTDRIVE=Z), DISK\CONFIG.TXT.  RUNTESTS 83 x 7
with four re-recorded on every row: RMTEST (four clusters less free:
PMDOS.SYS is bigger and RMCD.SYS is new), SFTSCAN (the "CON " scan
moved), CDSTEST (LASTDRIVE in the list of lists is 26 with no line)
and NETTEST (the highest letter with no drive is Z: now, and its
test file's device word carries Z:).  MASM 6.13: RMDOS plain and
traced, RMCD.  On the rig, besides the CD: Windows with the NE2000
network and LRGDISK and an EMPTY CD-ROM drive starts and exits clean,
D: there as a CD-ROM with no disc in it.


MSD'S AARD CHECK, THE DPB CHAIN, AND THE WAY BACK (2026-10-09)
--------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie, with LRGDISK.386: the network works; the domain's logon
script still maps nothing and goes by too fast to read, though NET USE
and File Manager map the same drives by hand; Windows still hangs on
exit at a blinking cursor; and MSD crashed the box - "VDM: the guest
faulted, vector 0D at 4702:0744", ES:DI = FFFF:FFFF, code 26 03 05.

MSD'S CRASH IS MICROSOFT'S AARD CODE.  The bytes are not in MSD.EXE,
which is packed; a memory dump of MSD running under QEMU has them, in
MSD's own stack segment - the check copies itself there, decrypts the
next twenty words and runs, which is why CS, DS and SS were all 4702.
Its stack matched the photograph word for word: the list of lists
copied in, and at [BP+2] the first field, the first drive parameter
block, which this kernel answered FFFF:FFFF ("PM-DOS has no DPBs").
The check adds up the block's first twenty words without testing the
pointer - ADD AX,ES:[DI] at FFFF:FFFF - and a word read at offset
FFFFh is a general protection fault on a real processor, in V86 mode
as in real mode.  QEMU does not check a real-mode segment's limit and
reads on, which is why the rig ran MSD; DOSBox-X checks some forms of
the access and not ES:[DI].  LOLDPB.COM (scratch segtest) does what
the check does, and says "READ OK" now.

THE DPB CHAIN (GDPB_, PMDOS.INC; vdm_dpbfresh, VDM.INC).  MS-DOS 4's
21h-byte block for every drive letter with a FAT volume, in a slot of
its own at 17C0h of the DOS data segment, chained in drive order from
the list of lists' first field, the last one's next pointer FFFF:FFFF.
Written from each volume's state on every 52h - nothing is selected
and nothing read; a drive not mounted yet says so with FFh in the
access byte, as DOS's does - and each current directory structure's
45h points at its drive's slot.  A CD-ROM has none, as under MSCDEX.
The segment is 210h bytes longer for it and the arena starts at 059Dh
instead of 057Ch: 528 bytes of conventional memory, which MS-DOS spends
on its blocks too.  1Fh and 32h answer now (they were "invalid
function", AL=1, which a caller testing AL for FFh took for success):
the volume is selected - mounted, as DOS's 32h reads the disk - its
slot written, and DS:BX points at it.

MSD /P STILL STOPPED AT "DISK DRIVES" - on the rig too, with "Error
Writing" and "Invalid argument", and two causes, found with a trace of
every DOS call a box makes written to port E9h (a scratch patch to
vdm_result, never in the source):

  * 440Dh CX=0860h, Get Device Parameters, was refused - all of 0Dh
    was.  f44_genblk answers it now (DVP_, PMDOS.INC): a fixed disk's
    type, the BIOS's cylinders, heads and sectors (IOS_DRVGEO) and the
    volume's BPB; a diskette drive's type from the BIOS (FDF_TYPE) and
    the BPB of its own format, or, with bit 0 of the first byte, of
    the disk in it.  The rest of 0Dh is still refused.
  * 0Eh read the disk.  MSD walks every letter with 0Eh and 19h, and
    mounting an empty B: was a critical error; MSD's own handler
    noted it in a flag and answered it, and its report writer turns
    that flag into "Error Writing", with whatever errno says.  A DOS
    box's 0Eh now selects any letter that names a drive without
    touching it (vdm_seldrv), as MS-DOS's $SET_DEFAULT_DRIVE does; the
    disk is read when something reads it.  CMD.EXE keeps the kernel's
    own 0Eh, which mounts or leaves the drive alone, because its "A:"
    is built on that; 16-bit COMMAND.COM's prompt asks 47h, as MS-DOS's
    does, and an empty drive's critical error comes from there.

And MSD listed the CD-ROM as a 1.44M diskette drive of 265 cylinders:
under MSCDEX a CD letter is a redirector's, so 4409h says remote (bit
12) and 4408h says "invalid function", and MSD tells a CD-ROM drive by
exactly that.  The kernel's 4408h and 4409h give those two answers for
a CD-ROM now, as RMDOS has under Windows, and its current directory
structure is C080h, as MSCDEX and RMDOS mark one.  MSD /P writes its
whole report on QEMU (CD-ROM in D:) and DOSBox-X: A: and B: floppies,
C: "31 Cylinders, 16 Heads ... 63 Sectors/Track", D: "CD-ROM Drive".

THE HANG ON EXIT: NOT REPRODUCED, AND NOW INSTRUMENTED.  What MSD showed
is a class: a real 486 faults where both emulators here carry on, and in
REAL mode the fault goes through vector 0Dh, which is IRQ 5's - whose
handler returns to the instruction that faulted, for ever, at a blinking
cursor.  BUILD exittrace (INC\XTRACE.INC) writes a letter on the top
row, white on red, for each step home: W for Windows' exit broadcast, X
for the end of the program that parked, G and J for rd_goback, a b c for
PMIO's unpark and A20 (! for an A20 that would not open), K L M V C for
park_go and park_recover, the letter of each drive park_remount mounts
and a "-" after the last, R E U for the rest, Z when WIN.COM's box runs
again, T when that box is over, and Q when the kernel waits for a key,
which is the prompt.  And RMDOS takes 06h, 0Ch and 0Dh while it is the
DOS: a fault in real mode that is not IRQ 4 or 5 (the PIC's in-service
register) and not Windows' (SMSW's PE bit) writes F, the vector, CS:IP,
four code bytes and the registers across the second row and
stops.  BAD0D.COM (MOV AX,[FFFFh]) run by PARKTEST under DOSBox-X -
which does check that form - shows "F000D 15D4 0100 A1FFFFB8 ...";
HELLO.COM run the same way shows "XGJabcKLMVC-REU" and Q.  WIN.COM sets
the screen's mode again as it leaves, so a good exit from Windows - the
QEMU rig, network, LRGDISK, a disc in D: - leaves only T and Q beside
the prompt, and a hang before WIN.COM runs again leaves the row as far
as it got.  IMAGES\EXITTRC.IMG is that build's boot floppy; a photograph
of the top two rows at the hang says where it stopped.

THE LOGON SCRIPT.  NETAPI.DLL maps the domain controller's NETLOGON
share to the highest free letter, Z: down, and runs LMSCRIPT.EXE in a
box through LMSCRIPT.PIF: "LMSCRIPT.EXE <COMSPEC> /e:1024 /C Z:\<the
script>", taking the drive away again afterwards.  LMSCRIPT.EXE
(expanded from the disks into wfwnet\lms) EXECs that COMSPEC with
that tail and 0000:0000 for both FCBs; COMMAND.COM takes /e:1024 /C.
The PIF has "Close window on exit" set, which is why it goes by.  The
rig has no domain controller, so what it says is Charlie's to read:
PIF Editor, LMSCRIPT.PIF, that box cleared.

Files: INC\PMDOS.INC (DOSDATA_SIZE 19D0h, V86_TPA 59D0h, GDPB_, DVP_,
DVT_, GCDSF_CDROM, GVP_XT), DOS\VDM.INC (vdm_dpbfresh, vdm_dpbstate,
vdm_dpbone, vdm_seldrv; 1Fh/32h to vdm_dsptr; 44h/0Dh's DS:DX),
DOS\INT21.INC (fn1F, fn32, f44_genblk, 4408h/4409h for a CD-ROM).
INC\XTRACE.INC (new), DOS\PARK.INC, DOS\RMDOS.ASM, DOS\RMINFO.INC,
DOS\RMMEM.INC, IO\IORM.ASM (and a check that rm_unpark has not grown
into the GDT) and BUILD.CMD (exittrace) are EXIT_TRACE only, as are a
few lines in the first three; PMIO.SYS and RMDOS.SYS build byte for
byte as before.  RUNTESTS 83 x 7, after re-recording fifteen tests on
every row - MEM, ARGS, DPMITEST, EXECTST, HELLO, HELLOX, HNDTEST,
LOLTEST, MCBTEST, PROBE13, RMTEST, SFTSCAN, WINTEST, XMSREPT, XMSTEST
- every difference the arena starting 21h paragraphs higher, the 1K
less conventional memory that is, and RMTEST's two clusters less free
(PMDOS.SYS is 158,756 bytes).  MASM 6.13: DOSMAIN, IOPM, IORM, RMDOS
and RMCD, plain and with EXIT_TRACE.


THE WAY BACK FROM WINDOWS, AND A 7 AT EVERY PROMPT (2026-10-09)
---------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie booted IMAGES\EXITTRC.IMG on the 486 and started WfW: the
logon script still mapped nothing, and on the way out of Windows the
top row said W X G J and nothing more, at the blinking cursor.  And
every boot - the ordinary floppy too - ended at "A:\>7".

THE HANG WAS A JUMP PATCHED INTO THE CODE IN FRONT OF ITSELF.  After J
(rd_goback, RMDOS.ASM) there was nothing left but six instructions and a
far jump to PMIO's rm_unpark, whose first act is the a that never
came.  Two of those instructions stored the target into the jump's own
operand - JMP FAR <patched>:<patched>, 0000:0000 in the file - the last
of them immediately in front of it.  A 386 or 486 fetches and decodes
ahead of the instruction it is running; a store into those bytes changes
memory and not what the processor already has, and Intel's rule is a
jump between the store and the code it changed.  So the 486 took JMP FAR
0000:0000, into the vector table, with interrupts off.  QEMU, 86Box and
DOSBox-X all see the store.  DOSBox-X has CPU types that model the queue
(486_prefetch, 386_prefetch, core=normal), and a scratch test, SMCQ.COM,
shows them running stale bytes - 486_prefetch up to 12 bytes ahead of a
store, 386_prefetch up to 4 - but PARKTEST came home on all of them, by
the look of it because they refill the queue a block at a time and a
refill fell between the stores and the jump.  A real 486 keeps fetching
up to 32 bytes ahead.

Three of these were in the real-mode code, and all three are now jumps
through a pointer, which is data: rd_back (rd_backvec, the way home, the
stores 0 and 6 bytes ahead), rd_go in RMDOS (rd_govec, PARKTEST's
program, 22 bytes ahead) and park_go in IORM.ASM (park_vec, where the
kernel hands over to RMDOS, 30 bytes ahead - inside a 486's 32, and
working on Charlie's machine only by where the fetches fell).  The RMDOS
header and GV_PARK keep the segment before the offset, so each pointer
is copied the right way round for the jump.  pm2rm's INT number, patched
60 bytes ahead of the INT, is left as it is; every BIOS call the kernel
makes goes through it, the 486's included.  No far jump with a zero
target is left in PMIO.SYS or RMDOS.SYS (scratch hw\farjmps.pl).

THE 7 WAS THE CONTROLLER'S COMMAND BYTE.  The mouse probe (ms_kbcaux,
MOUSE.INC) asks the 8042 for its command byte three times, with
interrupts off, and reads the answers itself.  But the controller raises
IRQ 1 for an answer as it does for a key, and the PIC holds the request
until interrupts are on again; irq_keyboard then read port 60h without
asking whether there was anything in it, and got the last answer
again.  On Charlie's 486 it can only have been 47h - both ports'
interrupts on, as a BIOS that drives a PS/2 mouse leaves them - which is
the keypad's 7, and with no Num Lock tracking the keypad's keys are
digits.  A QEMU run with the handler logging to port E9h (scratch
hw\kbe9.pl, hw\e9kb.pl) shows exactly one IRQ 1 inside the probe, status
1Ch - nothing in the buffer - and the old handler reading 41h, QEMU's
command byte: F7, which a prompt ignores, which is why no rig ever
showed it.  irq_keyboard now reads the status first and returns when bit
0 is clear, as Linux's i8042 driver does; the same run shows the IRQ
skipped.  Only bit 0: on an AT controller with no mouse port, bit 5 is a
time-out flag and not "the mouse's byte", and a keyboard byte left
unread in the buffer stops the keyboard.

NET.EXE AND "PROGRAM TOO BIG TO FIT IN MEMORY" (2026-10-09)
-----------------------------------------------------------

Charlie, on the build above: the way back from Windows works and the 7
is gone.  He mapped Z: to the domain controller's NETLOGON share by hand
and ran its LOGON.BAT, which is nothing but NET USE lines, and every one
of them said "Program too big to fit in memory".

That is COMMAND.COM's answer to an EXEC that failed with error 8, and
NET.EXE is a program that loads high: MINALLOC and MAXALLOC both zero, a
142,672-byte image and overlays after it.  RMDOS gives it the largest
block with the image at the top (f4B_got), as DOS does, and its first
instructions then move house: 51h for the PSP; the PSP's 256 bytes
copied to the paragraphs just under the image, with its handle table
pointer and its environment's owner made the new PSP's; 50h to make the
new PSP current; 4Ah to shrink the block it was loaded in so that it
ends where the new PSP begins - which leaves a free header exactly
there; that header given the old block's owner; and the old block given
back.

MS-DOS'S 4AH SETS THE OWNER.  $SETBLOCK finishes in $ALLOC's
alloc_set_owner, which writes CurrentPDB into the block on every resize
that works (DOS6SRC dos/alloc.asm), so the owner NET copies is its new
PSP, and 4Ch - which frees what CurrentPDB owns - frees the
image.  RMDOS's 4Ah left the owner alone.  NET copied its OLD PSP into
the image's header, the process that ended was the new one, and the
image stayed: 22E5h paragraphs, 142,928 bytes, after every NET command.
In a DOS box under Windows, after the NET USE Z:, the NET USEs that
followed had no room left.

Measured with a scratch tool, MCBWALK.COM (every MCB, and the largest
block 48h will give), around two NET HELPs:
  * RMDOS (PARKTEST running scratch RUNT.COM, which runs COMMAND /C on
    a batch file, on DOSBox-X): the largest block 7E67h before, 5B81h
    after the first, with 22E5h paragraphs at 7D19h owned by NET's old
    PSP.  The second run looked clean only because MCBWALK's next PSP
    landed on that same segment, 2097h, and its own exit freed the
    leftover by owner - a coincidence worth knowing about before
    trusting a second sample.
  * Real MS-DOS 5 (the DOS5K rig): 9A41h before, between and after.
  * A DOS box on PM-DOS itself: 9016h throughout - the kernel's box
    gives back the block it was given (vdm_setpsp), whoever 50h says
    owns it.

fn4A (RMMEM.INC) now writes the current PSP into the block's owner on
every resize that succeeds - the same size, smaller, or larger into the
free space after it - as MS-DOS does, and RMDOS shows 7E67h before,
between and after.  Not reproduced under Windows here: the rig's network
never starts (the NE2000 does not bind), so NET sits at its logon
prompt.

Files: DOS\RMMEM.INC (fn4A).  RMDOS.SYS 61,163 bytes (7 more); nothing
else changed.  RUNTESTS 83 x 7, after re-recording SFTSCAN on every row:
two of its addresses moved by those 7 bytes and nothing else (scratch
hw\sftshift.pl).  MASM 6.13: RMDOS, plain and with EXIT_TRACE.  WfW on
QEMU (network, LRGDISK, a CD) runs the LMSCRIPT test and exits to the
end of AUTOEXEC.
