RMDOS.SYS AND RMCD.SYS ARE SYSTEM FILES (2026-10-09)
----------------------------------------------------

Charlie: "if RMDOS.SYS and RMCD.SYS are required OS components that
need to be in the root, shouldn't they have the System, Hidden, and
Read-Only attributes along with PMDOS.SYS and PMIO.SYS?"

They should, and for PMIO.SYS's reasons.  The kernel opens both by name
in the root of the boot drive (park_loadrm, park_loadcd), RMDOS.SYS is
the DOS for as long as Windows runs, and a DEL *.* in the root took
Windows with it.  Their names also read as drivers somebody might put on
a DEVICE= line.  MS-DOS 6 has the same case and answers it the same way:
DBLSPACE.BIN is not needed to boot, IO.SYS loads it from the root if it
is there (DOS6SRC bios\syspre.asm), Setup marks it system, hidden and
read-only (install\oem\addfiles.c) and SYS carries it (cmd\sys\sys1.asm).

NOTHING HAD TO CHANGE TO FIND THEM.  A lookup by name sees every entry -
only a directory search leaves hidden and system files out (FAT.INC) -
and 3D00h asks for nothing a read-only file refuses.  RUNTESTS says so
on every run now: its disk's RMDOS.SYS is hidden, and DRVTEST, BLKTEST,
NETTEST and SEEKWR park on it.

WHAT MARKS THEM.  MKDISK gives the three attributes to the first two
files in the root, by position.  RMDOS.SYS and RMCD.SYS come late in
every list, so they are known by name (rm_sysfile), on a floppy and on a
bootable hard disk; the first-two rule is as it was.  FATREPL.PL, which
refreshes an image MKHD cannot rebuild, kept whatever attribute an entry
had and gave a new file the archive bit; the two names in the root now
get 07h there too, new or replaced, and that is what brought HD16.IMG's
copies into line.

SYS DID NOT COPY THEM AT ALL, which was the real hole, and the reason
the attributes could not be changed on their own: a hidden file is what
a wildcard leaves behind, so once the two are hidden SYS is the only
thing that takes them to another disk.  Until now SYS C: after a floppy
boot made a disk that started everything but Windows - "RMDOS.SYS is not
in the root of the boot drive or of the current one" - unless somebody
copied the two files afterwards.  SYS.COM and SYS16.COM now copy
PMIO.SYS, PMDOS.SYS, RMDOS.SYS and RMCD.SYS with the three attributes,
then CMD.EXE and COMMAND.COM; FORMAT /S runs SYS.COM and gets it for
nothing.  The two are optional, as COMMAND.COM is: a source without them
still transfers, and the target keeps whatever it had.

AN OPTIONAL FILE THAT WILL NOT COPY IS AN ERROR NOW.  SYS.COM made
COMMAND.COM optional by ignoring sy_copy's carry, so a COMMAND.COM cut
short by a full disk would have been followed by "System transferred".
sy_copyopt forgives only a source that is not there (src_absent).
SYS16 already told the two apart.

AN OLD DISK is brought up to date by SYS from the new floppy, which
takes the attributes off a file before it replaces it, or by ATTRIB +R
+S +H on the two files.  And a new RMDOS.SYS no longer goes onto a disk
with COPY: SYS, or ATTRIB -R -S -H first.

SYS.COM is 1,633 bytes (1,541) and SYS16.COM 8,553 (8,490); the other
136 files the build makes, and TESTS.IMG, are byte for byte what they
were.  RUNTESTS is 83 x 7 with no baseline changed.  With no window:

  * SYS D: on DOSBox-X, from a hard disk with both files onto one whose
    root had a stale RMDOS.SYS as an ordinary file.  Both arrive
    hidden, system and read-only, and the six files are the build's
    byte for byte.  SYS D: a second time, over its own copies, works.
    The target, booted, says 0.63 to VER, and PARKTEST runs HELLO on
    its RMDOS and comes back.
  * A source with neither file: "System transferred", and the target
    has neither.
  * A target with room for PMIO.SYS, PMDOS.SYS and 27K more: "Cannot
    copy the system files", exit code 1.
  * SYS16 A: on real MS-DOS 5 (the C:\DOSBoxRoot\RIG disk, with a
    diskette in A:): the same six files, a stale RMDOS.SYS that was
    itself read-only, hidden and system replaced, and the diskette
    boots and parks.
  * QEMU, booted from a floppy with the two files hidden and no
    RMDOS.SYS on the hard disk, Windows for Workgroups started from C:
    in enhanced mode with the network, LRGDISK and the Office CD:
    WINSWEEP has "DRIVE D: type 4, 4409 1000, 4408 e1, 150B ax=FFFF
    bx=ADAD", File Manager runs, and Windows exits to the end of
    AUTOEXEC.

SYS16 ONTO A HARD DISK WAS TRIED FIRST AND DID NOT GET AS FAR AS A
FILE, which is not this change's doing and is left as found.  With a
MKDISK hard disk as D: under MS-DOS 5, SYS16 stopped after "System
files taken from" (the rest went to the screen, which nobody saw), and
DIR D:\ showed an unlabelled, empty root.  The likely reason is in
DOS6SRC bios\msinit.asm: for a hard disk MS-DOS reads bytes 8 to 10 of
the boot sector as the version in the OEM name and does not trust a BPB
older than "3.1" (no_os2).  Ours are "S  ", the end of 'PM-DOS  ', so
DOS works out a BPB of its own and looks for the root where that one
puts it - the case sy_agree is there to refuse.  A disk MS-DOS formatted
itself has one reserved sector and no room for stage 2.  If that is
right, SYS16 makes diskettes and nothing else, and MS-DOS cannot read a
hard disk that carries our boot sector; an OEM name ending in a version
would be the cure.  Not chased.

Files: TOOLS\MKDISK.C, TOOLS\FATREPL.PL, CMD\SYS\SYS.ASM,
TOOLS\SYS16.ASM, DISK\CONFIG.TXT (CDROM=: the two are hidden system
files and SYS copies them).  S:\BIN (SYS.COM, SYS16.COM),
TOOLS\MKDISK.EXE, IMAGES\PMDOS.IMG, IMAGES\EXITTRC.IMG, IMAGES\HD16.IMG
(FATREPL: SYS.COM, CONFIG.TXT, and RMDOS.SYS and RMCD.SYS for their
attributes) and the 86Box VM's two copies carry it; copies of the
delivered floppy and HD16 boot, and on HD16 ATTRIB shows SHR on all
four and PARKTEST comes back.  NOT RUN: FORMAT /S, which EXECs SYS.COM,
and the 486.  HD32, HDBIG, PMDOSATA and PMDOSFDD were not rebuilt.
Still v0.63.

IMAGES\EXITTRC.IMG WAS DELETED the same evening, at Charlie's word: it
has done what it was for.  BUILD exittrace still makes that floppy, as
the IMAGES\PMDOS.IMG of the tree it is run in.


PMD.EXE: MSD FOR PM-DOS, AND A PROCESSOR ASKED WHAT IT IS (2026-10-09)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie: "Let's port the Microsoft Diagnostics (MSD) to PM-DOS as PMD
(PM Diagnostics), and update the CPU detection piece to using CPUID
instruction if supported."

MSD itself runs in a DOS box - the entry before last was about getting
it there - and says what a box can see: "Processor: Unknown" on anything
later than a 486, and nothing of the kernel underneath.  PMD is the same
program for the system itself: native, 32-bit, CMD\PMD, built by
BUILD.CMD like EDIT and on every disk.  The thirteen pages are MSD's
and so are the main screen, the menus, the report and the switches;
MSD 2.00a's source (DOS6SRC c6ers\msd200a) and 6.22's MSD.EXE were what
it was checked against, page by page.  None of that source is in it: a
real-mode program that reads the machine through far pointers and COW's
windows has nothing a ring-3 program here can use, and the words on the
help screen are ours.

  PMD [/I]               the screen; nothing looked at until a page
                         is opened
  PMD /F file            asks who the report is from, then all of it
  PMD /P file            all of it
  PMD /S [file]          the summary, to the screen with no file

WHERE THE FACTS COME FROM.  A native program's segment is its slot, so
it can read no vector, no byte of the BIOS data area, no ROM and no
memory block of the conventional arena.  Every fact is one of four
things, and two of them are new:

  21h/F1h as it was     the kernel's own accounts: memory (4, 8, 9,
                        1Ah), drives and disks (1, 6, 0Ch, 14h, 17h),
                        the buses (12h), the coprocessor (13h), VBE
                        (1Fh)
  21h/F1h AL=20h, NEW   the first megabyte.  LMF_READ copies bytes from
                        below 1MB into the program's buffer; LMF_RAM
                        says whether an address from A0000h up keeps a
                        byte written to it - the byte's complement
                        stored, read back and put right, interrupts off
                        for the three.  That is the test MSD makes of
                        the adapter area, and reading cannot make it:
                        shadowed ROM reads as ROM does
  21h/F1h AL=21h, NEW   a BIOS call that only asks.  DL = the interrupt,
                        ESI -> a BQ_LEN record of registers in and out.
                        It goes through the real-mode thunk IF the
                        interrupt and AH (and for two rows AL or BL) are
                        in bq_table: 10h/0Fh, 12h BL=10h and 1A00h; 11h;
                        12h; 14h/03h; 15h/84h, 88h, C0h, C1h and D800h;
                        17h/02h.  Anything else is ERR_ACCESS - INT 15h
                        is also where a BIOS moves extended memory and
                        leaves real mode, and neither may be asked for
                        from ring 3
  IN and OUT            which fault at ring 3 and are carried out by the
                        kernel (pm3_fault), a byte at a time

Both new calls are for native programs only (a box has the first
megabyte and the BIOS itself) and neither changes anything.  Everything
below 1MB is what a DOS box can already read.  r3_pflags answers AL=20h
by hand - EBX is an address in the machine for both functions and must
not have the slot's base added - and AL=21h has a row in vdm_subptr.

THE PROCESSOR (CPU.C).  MSD's test is what the flags register will
hold: an 8088, a 286, a 386, and by the AC flag a 486, where it stops.
PMD asks the processor.  If the ID flag holds there is a CPUID: leaf 0
is the maker, leaf 1 the family, model and stepping and what it can do,
and leaves 80000002h-4h, where they exist, the processor's own name for
itself, which is believed over any table.  The tables behind it know
Intel from the 486DX to the Pentium 4, AMD from the Am486 to the Athlon,
Cyrix, IDT and VIA, UMC, NexGen, Rise, Transmeta, SiS and National.
With only the AC flag it is a 486 from before CPUID - "486DX" or
"486SX" by the coprocessor, as MSD says it - unless a divide leaves the
flags alone, which is a Cyrix, and then DIR0 behind ports 22h and 23h
says which.  With neither it is an 80386; PM-DOS runs on nothing older,
so MSD's tests for the 8088, the V20 and the 286 are gone.  The Computer
page has two lines MSD has not: the CPUID identity, and the features.
The coprocessor is the kernel's to say (F1h AL=13h) - an x87 instruction
on a machine without one would be a fault - and only on a 386 is it then
asked whether it is an 80287 (infinity compared with minus infinity).

WHAT IS DIFFERENT FROM MSD, page by page, because the machine is:

  Memory          "PM-DOS Program Memory" - the kernel's arena, which is
                  what native programs and XMS are given out of - beside
                  conventional, upper, EMS and DPMI.  The map is MSD's:
                  option ROMs by their 55 AA, length and checksum, RAM
                  by LMF_RAM, FFh throughout as nothing, the rest
                  "possibly available", and the EMS frame and the upper
                  memory blocks drawn over it
  IRQ Status      "Handled By" is PM-DOS Kernel for the lines the kernel
                  keeps (BUS_IRQSTAT) and otherwise whoever owns the
                  address a DOS box's vector has; "PCI Device" for a
                  line a card was routed to
  Other Adapters  the game port (INT 15h/84h), and then what MSD never
                  had: every function on the PCI bus with what it is
                  and its line, and how many Plug and Play cards
  Disk Drives     from the volume table.  A drive whose disk comes out
                  is described and not read; B: is left out when the
                  equipment word says one diskette drive, as MSD leaves
                  it out.  SHARE is found by trying it: the program's
                  own file opened deny-all will not open again
  Network         PM-DOS has none of its own: a packet driver on 60h to
                  80h, PROTMAN$, IFSHLP, and the PCI network cards
  OS Version      PM-DOS's version beside the DOS version it reports,
                  and "DOS Located in: Extended Memory", which is true
                  and which 3306h has no flag for
  Mouse           the kernel's INT 33h, version 8.20
  COM Ports       a port the mouse is on is read and not touched: its
                  speed is behind the divisor latch, and a byte the
                  mouse sent while that was switched in would be lost
  TSR Programs, Device Drivers
                  the conventional arena and the driver chain a DOS box
                  is given, read through AL=20h.  Run PMD from
                  COMMAND.COM and the shell is in the list

THE SCREEN is EDIT's - SCR.C and the dialog half of UI.C, copied, with
MSD's colours - so it has EDIT's mouse and EDIT's test mode: PMDTEST
names a log, the keys come from a redirected file, and FFh FFh writes
the screen into the log.  TOOLS\MKPMDKEYS.PL writes DISK\PMD1.KEY to
PMD5.KEY and DISK\PMDTEST.BAT runs them: every page, the menus, the
mouse on a button, Memory Block Display, Memory Browser, Find File,
Print Report to a file, and Insert Command replacing one line of a
file and adding another.  RUNTESTS has PMD /S on every row, so a
kernel that stops answering AL=20h or AL=21h changes a baseline.

Insert Command's list is PM-DOS's CONFIG.SYS, not Windows 3.1's
SYSTEM.INI.  A line that sets the same thing is replaced if that is
wanted and the rest of the file is written back byte for byte.

A THING FOUND ON THE WAY.  7303h's record here begins with a word and
then the sectors per cluster (F73_SPC = 02h).  DOS 7's begins with two
words - the size and the level - so its sectors per cluster are at 04h,
and a program written for DOS 7 reads this one two bytes out.  PMD and
CMD's DIR use the F73_ offsets and are right for this kernel; a DOS 7
program in a box is not.  Not changed here.

VERIFIED, with no window anywhere.  DOSBox-X: /?, /S, /S and /P to a
file and the two refusals; PMDTEST.BAT's five key files and the /B /I
run, 56 screens read back out of the logs - every page, every menu and
every dialog - and four of them looked at as pictures.  The processor
on six of its machines: 80386 with an 80387, 486DX with no CPUID
(486old), 486DX with one, Pentium, Pentium MMX and Pentium Pro.  QEMU
(pentium2, a PCI NE2000, a CD-ROM): Intel Pentium II where MSD 2.11
says Unknown, A: C: D: as MSD lists them, the CD-ROM and MSCDEX, the
card and its line; run from COMMAND.COM the shell is in the TSR list.
RUNTESTS 84 x 7, recorded and run again: PMD /S is new on every row,
and RMTEST was re-recorded on every row - its count of free clusters
fell by the ninety PMD.EXE takes on the test disk.  MASM 6.13
assembles DOSMAIN and PMD's DOSINT.ASM.  PMDOS.SYS 159,249 (493 more),
PMD.EXE 90,688.

Files: CMD\PMD\ (new: MAIN, SCR, UI, TEXT, CPU, PGSYS, PGMEM, PGPORT,

DOSSHELL.EXE: THE MS-DOS SHELL FOR PM-DOS, TEXT AND GRAPHICS (2026-10-10)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie: "Let's port DOSSHELL to PM-DOS as a native 32bit application.
It should keep the text mode and graphics mode capabilities for both
EGA and VGA, but also include a check for VBE 2.0+ and offer a 256
color VGA 640x480 graphics mode too."

NONE OF THE ORIGINAL IS IN IT, and none could have been.  The MS-DOS
Shell (DOS6SRC dosshell) is C on top of COW, of which that tree has
only 16-bit libraries; its graphics are loadable .VID and .GRB drivers
and its swapper is real-mode assembler.  Nothing of that links into a
flat ring-3 program, and the real DOSSHELL.EXE already runs in a DOS
box.  So this is the same program made again for the system itself, as
EDIT and PMD were: native, CMD\DOSSHELL, built by BUILD.CMD and on
every disk.  The screen, the menus, the keys, the views and the shape
of DOSSHELL.INI are the MS-DOS Shell's; the code is new and the words
on the screen are ours.

  DOSSHELL                     as it was last left (DOSSHELL.INI)
  DOSSHELL /T[:L|H]            text: 25 lines, or 50 (43 on an EGA)
  DOSSHELL /G[:L|M1|M2|H1|H2]  graphics: 25, 30, 34, 43 or 60 lines
  DOSSHELL /G:M1 /256          ...640x480 in 256 colours

WHAT IS THERE.  A title, the menu bar, and under them a file window -
the path, the drives, the directory tree and the files of the selected
directory - and the program list, with a status bar at the foot.  View
has the five arrangements: one file window, two, All Files with the
file, selection, directory and disk summed up beside the list, files
with programs, and programs alone.  File among files: Open, Run,
Print, Associate, Search, View File Contents (text and hexadecimal),
Move, Copy, Delete, Rename, Change Attributes, Create Directory, Select
All, Deselect All.  File among programs: New, Open, Copy, Delete,
Properties, Reorder, Run.  Options: Confirmation, File Display Options,
Select Across Directories, Show Information, Display, Colors.  Tree:
expand a level, a branch, everything; collapse.  Help: eleven subjects
in EDIT's viewer.  The mouse does what it did: a click selects, Shift
and Ctrl extend, a double click opens, the scroll bars scroll, and
files dragged onto a directory or a drive are moved or copied there.
Names are long ones where the volume has them, and sizes and dates are
the country's (21h/38h).

ONE SCREEN OF CELLS, SHOWN TWO WAYS.  Everything is drawn into memory
first and only what changed is sent, as in EDIT - but a cell here is
32 bits: the character and its colours, and for a graphics screen a
slice of an icon in place of the character and lines along the cell's
edges (CF_*).  On a text screen a run of changed cells goes to 21h/F0h.
On a graphics screen GFX.C paints each changed cell into a picture, 640
pixels across and a byte a pixel whatever the hardware, and copies the
scan lines that changed to the screen in the form the mode wants:

  EGA 640x350 and VGA 640x480, 16 colours (BIOS modes 10h and 12h).
  Four bit planes behind one window.  The changed lines are made into
  planes in memory and then written a plane at a time, so a whole
  screen is four writes to the sequencer's map mask and not one for
  every byte.  That matters here: a port write at ring 3 is a fault
  the kernel answers.

  640x480 in 256 colours (VBE mode 101h, or whichever mode the BIOS
  lists for that).  A linear frame buffer, copied a line at a time.
  The first sixteen colours are the VGA's and the rest are shades that
  the title bars fade through.  It is offered when 4F00h says VBE 2.0
  or later AND 4F01h says the mode is there, is a byte a pixel and has
  a linear frame buffer - the kernel sets no banked mode.

The pointer and the cursor are not in the picture: they are laid over
each scan line as it is copied out, so moving the pointer is two small
rectangles copied again.  The kernel's mouse driver could draw a
pointer in modes 10h and 12h but not in a VBE mode, so the shell draws
its own in all three, leaves the driver's hidden, and tells the driver
how big the screen is (33h/07h and 08h) since it cannot know.

NOTHING IN THE KERNEL CHANGED.  VBF_SET (21h/F1h AL=1Fh) already took a
BIOS mode and answered with the selector for the window at A0000h; that
was written for mode 13h and serves 10h and 12h as well.  What was
missing was a font, and no call hands one over: INT 10h/1130h answers
in ES:BP, and the list of BIOS calls a native program may make (AL=21h)
carries no pointers back.  But a mode set leaves the font of that mode
in vector 43h and the height of its characters at 0040:0085, because
the BIOS's own text in a graphics mode needs them there - and AL=20h,
which PMD brought, reads the first megabyte.  So mode 12h is how the
8x16 font is found and mode 10h the 8x14; the 8x8 font's first half is
at F000:FA6E in every BIOS since the PC's and vector 1Fh has its second
half.  A font is read once.  A mode that uses another mode's font - 34
lines on a VGA is the 8x14 font in mode 12h, and every 256-colour
screen borrows - costs one extra mode set, the first time.  On a kernel
without AL=20h the shell offers text and nothing else.

PROGRAMS ARE RUN BY THE INTERPRETER, "/C" and the command (the one
F1h/03h names), because PATH, batch files and redirection are its.
The screen goes back to text and is cleared first and is taken again
afterwards, and the drives that are showing are read again.  The
program gets a slot of its own from the kernel, so the shell stays in
memory and nothing is swapped to disk - which is all the MS-DOS Shell's
loader and swapper were for.  A program in the list is a title, its
commands with semicolons between, a directory to start in, a password,
help text (F1 on the entry), whether to wait for a key afterwards, and
for each of %1 to %3 the box it is asked with.

DOSSHELL.INI is beside DOSSHELL.EXE and is written when the shell is
left: [savestate], [associations] and [programstarter], the last one
"key = value" lines with braces round a group or a program, laid out
as the MS-DOS Shell laid its own.  With no file the list is Main -
Command Prompt, Editor - and a Disk Utilities group of DISKCOPY, FORMAT
(and /Q), CHKDSK, UNDELETE and FDISK.

WHAT IS NOT THERE, AND WHY.
  - The Task Swapper, the Active Task List, and with them a program's
    shortcut key and its Advanced properties.  The swapper was one DOS
    program frozen so that another could run; PM-DOS runs one program
    at a time.
  - /B.  PMD lost its black and white yesterday for a reason that holds
    here.  Monochrome is still one of the eight colour schemes.
  - Copying or moving a directory.  Delete (when empty), Rename and
    Create Directory are what the tree has.
  - A clock that ticks.  The time in the status bar is the time of the
    last key or mouse movement: the kernel's wait for a key (F0h/08h)
    has no time limit, and waiting by asking again and again would keep
    the processor busy for the sake of a minute hand.

TEST MODE is EDIT's: DSTEST names a log, the keys come from a
redirected file (TOOLS\MKDSKEYS.PL), {DUMP} writes the cells to the log
as text whatever kind of screen they are on, and {SHOT} writes the
picture as a .BMP file beside it.  A test run reads and writes no
DOSSHELL.INI unless DSINI names one, so the tests start from the same
screen every time and leave the settings of whoever runs them alone.
DISK\DSTEST.BAT is nine sessions, DS1.KEY to DS9.KEY.

VERIFIED.  DOSBox-X (an S3 with VBE 2.0): text at 25 and 50 lines, and
six graphics screens - EGA at 25 and 43 lines, VGA at 30 and 60, 256
colours at 30 and 34 - in which the picture the shell wrote of itself
and the emulator's recorded frame of the same screen, held still, are
the same in every pixel but the clock.  That is the planar path and the
frame buffer both, all three fonts, and a font borrowed from another
mode.  VGA at 34 lines and 256 colours at 60 were looked at as
pictures.  Eight key scripts and DSTEST.BAT's 62 screens: every menu
and dialog, copy, move over a file, rename, attributes, delete, a new
directory, Search, selection kept across directories, Print (to the
captured printer), the viewer, a program run and the shell back in its
mode afterwards, the program list's New, Copy, Reorder, Delete, a
question for %1, a password; settings written and read back; and the
mouse, drag and drop included.  QEMU, whose ROM is a different one
(SeaBIOS, SeaVGABIOS): the fonts found where its BIOS keeps them
(C000:7260 and C000:8260), modes 10h and 12h and the 256-colour mode
at 30 and 60 lines, the PS/2 mouse moving the pointer, the keyboard in
the menus, Shift+F9 to the prompt, VER, EXIT and back.  RUNTESTS
84 x 7 after two answers were re-recorded for where files now lie on
the test disk: RMTEST's free clusters (126 fewer, which is
DOSSHELL.EXE) on every row, and CACHETST's count of owed writes (0005
for 0004) on the six that cache.  MASM 6.13 assembles DOSINT.ASM.
DOSSHELL.EXE is 128,980 bytes.

A RECORDED FRAME TAKEN AS THE MODE CHANGES IS NOT A PICTURE OF
ANYTHING.  The last frame of a recording that ends when the shell does
showed a box of red and cyan stripes over the lists, and 28,000 pixels
"wrong".  It is the decoder's residue (ZMBVSHOT.PL says as much), not
the screen: the same screen held still for a minute is the one that
matched.

THE FIRST SCREEN CHARLIE SAW OF IT WAS UNREADABLE (the same day):
DOSSHELL /G on the 86Box machine - VS440FX, Cirrus Logic GD5436 - with
every icon, bar and line where it belonged and every character a
fragment.  THE CIRRUS BIOS HAS NO 8x14 FONT.  Its ROM holds the 8x8
table and the 8x16 one and nothing between; in mode 10h it says 14
lines at 0040:0085 and leaves vector 43h pointing at the 8x16 table
(C000:6E91).  Read 14 bytes to a character, that table gives '*' for
'0' and character 1Ch for a space, whose foot is the dashes that ran
across the whole screen.  The check that was there asked only that the
capital A not be empty.  Now a table is believed when its space is
empty and its A and its block (DBh) are not (FONT_SANE in GFX.C), which
a table read at the wrong height does not pass; and a VGA whose BIOS
has no 8x14 font gets one made from the 8x16 by dropping the top and
the bottom line of every character - the 8x16 taken from that same
vector while mode 10h is set, so here the made font costs no mode set
at all.  The BIOS is asked for each font once (ROM14, ROM16), and
FONT_LOAD can no longer call itself in a circle when neither is there.

It is not only Cirrus.  A scan of the 151 video ROMs that 86Box ships
for a table with an empty space and a full block finds the 8x16 one
and no 8x14 one in 19: eleven of Cirrus Logic's (the GD5434, GD5436,
GD5440, GD5446 and GD5480 among them), three of Matrox's, the ViRGE/DX
and /GX, a Trio64V2/DX, a Trio3D/2X and a Mach64 VT2.  The S3 ROM in
DOSBox-X and SeaVGABIOS in QEMU have all three fonts, which is why
nothing here had shown it.

REPRODUCED, THEN VERIFIED.  QEMU with no window will run a real card's
ROM as its video BIOS: a folder holding the ROM under the name
vgabios-cirrus.bin, given with -L ahead of QEMU's own, and -vga cirrus
(the GD5446's ROM, whose PCI ID is the card's) or -device
isa-cirrus-vga (the GD5436's - the VM's own).  Both drew Charlie's
screen exactly, and both draw /G, /G:M1, /G:M2, /G:H1 and /G:H2
readable now.  86Box itself, the VM's machine and card on a scratch
disk, started minimized and closed by a message: the shell's own
pictures of those five screens came off the disk readable.  The same
machine with the two cards whose BIOSes have VBE 2.0 and no 8x14 font
either, the S3 Trio64V2/DX and the Cirrus GD5480: /G, and 256 colours
at 30, 34 and 60 lines, the title bars shaded - the first time the
256-colour mode has been set by a card's own ROM in 86Box.  (A scratch
boot with either of those cards was not done in 110 seconds, where the
GD5436 takes under a minute; 150 were enough.  Cut off early it looks
like a hang: nothing on the disk.)  DOSBox-X:
the pictures of six screens are the same in every pixel as the ones the
build before drew, so a BIOS that has an 8x14 font still has its own
used; DSTEST's 62 screens differ in nothing but the size of
DOSSHELL.EXE, now 129,184 bytes.  RUNTESTS 84 x 7 with three answers
re-recorded - ACROREAD.EXE (the next entry) arrived in BIN the same
hour and moves two of them by itself: RMFIND's third root entry is
ACROREAD.EXE where it was ATTRIB.EXE (seven rows), RMTEST's free
clusters are 73EB for 748A (seven) and CACHETST's owed writes 0004 for
0005 (six).

NOT RUN: real hardware, a real EGA, a printer that is not ready, a
diskette changed under the tree.  A BIOS with VBE 1.2 only: the probe
finds no 256-colour mode on the GD5436 and GD5446 ROMs (the trace under
QEMU says so), and what /256 then does was not looked at.  On 86Box
the pictures are the shell's own, read back from the disk - they show
the mode was set and the fonts are right, not what the frame buffer
put on the glass: nobody has looked at that screen since the change.

Files: CMD\DOSSHELL\ (new: MAIN, SCR, GFX, ICONS, UI, TREE, FILES, OPS,
VIEW, PROGS, DLGS, HELP, RT and SYS_D32 .C, SHELL.H, RT.H, SYS.H,
TYPES.H and DOSINT.ASM), BUILD.CMD, MKHD.CMD, TOOLS\MKDSKEYS.PL (new),
DISK\DSTEST.BAT and DS1.KEY to DS9.KEY (new), DISK\HELPTEST.BAT,
DISK\AUTOEXEC.TXT, and BASELINE (RMTEST.OUT on seven rows, CACHETST.OUT
on six).  S:\BIN (DOSSHELL.EXE), IMAGES\PMDOS.IMG, IMAGES\TESTS.IMG,
IMAGES\HD16.IMG (FATREPL: DOSSHELL.EXE and AUTOEXEC.TXT, and the test
files in \TESTS) and the 86Box VM's three copies carry it; a copy of
the delivered HD16 boots and runs DOSSHELL from DS1.KEY in text and
DS7.KEY in 640x480.  HD32, HDBIG, MULTI, PMDOSATA and PMDOSFDD were
not rebuilt.  Still v0.63.

The font fix: CMD\DOSSHELL\GFX.C and nothing else.  BIN\DOSSHELL.EXE,
IMAGES\PMDOS.IMG (whole, ACROREAD.EXE on it as BUILD.CMD now makes it),
DOSSHELL.EXE by FATREPL into IMAGES\HD16.IMG and into the VM's own
HD16.IMG as it stood (the VM had been used since, so its disk is no

ACROREAD.EXE: A PDF READER FOR PM-DOS (2026-10-10)
--------------------------------------------------

Charlie: "let's write a PDF reader for PM-DOS that supports all
versions of PDF document formats.  The executable should be named
ACROREAD.EXE to match the Acrobat PDF reader name.  It should support
text mode viewing, graphics mode, and a VBE 2.0+ check to support up
to full color VGA at 640x480."  And, while it was being written:
"Let's write the application in C or C++."

IT IS C, native, CMD\ACROREAD, built by BUILD.CMD and on every disk,
as EDIT, PMD and DOSSHELL are: no C library, DOSINT.ASM for a start,
SYS_D32.C the only file that knows it is on PM-DOS.  161,572 bytes.
Nothing of anybody else's is in it - every decoder, every font reader
and the rasteriser were written here - and there is no floating point
in it anywhere, so it runs on a 386 with no coprocessor.

  ACROREAD file            the first page, as a picture
  ACROREAD file /T         ...as its text, on the text screen
  ACROREAD file /G         a picture in 16 grays in the VGA's own mode,
                           whatever the video BIOS has
  ACROREAD file /P:n       starting at page n
  ACROREAD file /X         the document's text to standard output, a
                           form feed between pages (... /X > PRN)

THREE SCREENS, which is what was asked for.  (1) VBE 2.0 or later:
the 640x480 mode with a linear frame buffer and the most colours - 32
or 24 bits, else 16 or 15, else 256 with a palette of its own and a
dither - through 21h/F1h AL=1Fh and SEL_VBE.  (2) No VBE 2.0, or /G:
mode 12h with the palette set to sixteen GREYS.  Sixteen colours
cannot show a page in colour; sixteen greys and a dither show one in
grey very well, and text drawn with coverage needs the greys.  (3) The
text screen: the page's characters put back into lines (TEXT.C), with
Find.  Tab goes between picture and text on the same page.  F1 lists
the keys; PgUp/PgDn run on from page to page; + - W F zoom; R L turn;
G goes to a page.

WHAT "ALL VERSIONS" CAME TO (XREF.C, CRYPT.C, FILTER.C say more):
  1.0  a cross-reference table            1.1  ...and /Prev tables
  1.2  Flate                              1.4  RC4 to 128 bits
  1.5  cross-reference STREAMS, object streams, hybrid files
  1.5  crypt filters, AES-128             1.7+ AES-256 (R5)
  2.0  AES-256 with the SHA-256/384/512 hash (R6)
and a file whose table is wrong or gone is read end to end for its
objects.  Filters: Flate, LZW, ASCII85, ASCIIHex, RunLength, the PNG
and TIFF predictors, DCT (sequential JPEG), CCITT Group 3 and 4.
Fonts: TrueType, Type 1, CFF, Type 3, simple and composite, with
ToUnicode for the text; a font the file does not carry is drawn by a
face built into the program (SFONT.C: a pen's path for each
character, drawn to the widths the file gives).  GFX.H lists what is
drawn and - in a table - what is not: tiling patterns, mesh shadings,
soft masks, JBIG2, JPEG 2000 and progressive JPEG are the ones that
will be met.

HOW A PAGE GETS TO THE SCREEN.  It is drawn into a canvas in memory -
three bytes a pixel for VBE, one for the greys - by a rasteriser that
samples four times a pixel down and exactly across, and the canvas is
then put on the screen a line at a time (through SEL_VBE; mode 12h a
band of 48 lines and four plane writes at a time, because a port is a
trap at ring 3).  The canvas is the whole page if 48h will grow the
slot that far, else a piece the width of the screen; 700K is left for
the drawing itself, and where a colour screenful would not leave that
(a 4MB machine) the canvas is grey and the bar says so once.  A page
that cannot be finished - damaged, or out of memory - is left by
JMP.ASM's longjmp; everything it had is in pools and goes with them.
Numbers from the file are a 30-bit mantissa and an exponent (FX.C)
where matrices are multiplied, 16.16 where points are transformed.

PROVEN, all headless.  On Windows, as ACROHOST.EXE (the same sources;
CMD\ACROREAD\MKHOST.CMD): every page of eight Open Watcom manuals,
3,885 pages, drawn with no failure and no growth of the heap; a page
printed by Edge (TrueType, composite fonts, gradients, alpha) drawn
and read; and TOOLS\MKPDF.PL's nineteen documents, one for each way a
file can be put together - 1.0, saved twice, bad table, streams plain
and deflated, bad stream table, a hybrid, R2 R3 R4 R5 R6, a user
password, LZW, RunLength, ASCII85, a JPEG, a Group 4 fax, an inline
image, a Type 3 font, and a Type 1 font program written by the script
itself (a subroutine, a division, the enciphering) - all opened, read
and drawn.  On PM-DOS in DOSBox-X: the same nineteen through /X on a
386 with 4MB; the picture at 32, 16, 15 and 8 bits (SET ACROBITS=n
picks a depth, for trying a card) and in mode 12h; the text screen
and Find; zoom and scroll; the grey canvas on 4MB.
NOT RUN: any real machine, 86Box, a VBE 1.2 card (which should get
mode 12h), a mouse (it has none); and no Type 1 font out of a real
document - the test's is the format as TYPE1.C understands it, made
by the same understanding.  NOT DONE: RUNTESTS and HELPTEST do not
know it - a test for it wants documents on TESTS.IMG, which is nearly
full.  One more file in BIN does move three baselines (RMFIND's third
root entry, RMTEST's free clusters, CACHETST): the DOSSHELL session
re-recorded those with its own delivery of the same night.

Files: CMD\ACROREAD\ (new: 29 .C, PDF.H, GFX.H, VIEW.H, RT.H, SYS.H,
TYPES.H, DOSINT.ASM, JMP.ASM; and for Windows only HOST.C, SYS_NT.C,
MKHOST.CMD), BUILD.CMD (its section, the object list, the boot disk),
MKHD.CMD, DISK\AUTOEXEC.TXT, TOOLS\MKPDF.PL (new).  BIN\ACROREAD.EXE,
IMAGES\PMDOS.IMG (made again by BUILD.CMD's own line), IMAGES\HD16.IMG
and the 86Box VM's HD16.IMG (FATREPL, each in place: ACROREAD.EXE,
AUTOEXEC.TXT, and ACROTEST.PDF - a page to try it on) and the VM's
PMDOS.IMG carry it; a copy of each hard disk boots and runs it.
TESTS.IMG, HD32, HDBIG, MULTI, PMDOSATA and PMDOSFDD were not
rebuilt.  The whole BUILD.CMD was not run: ACROREAD's section was,
word for word, in a mirror.  Still v0.63.


LRGDISK 1.3: PIO BY THE BLOCK, A LOOK BEFORE THE INTERRUPT (2026-10-10)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie asked what else would make the disk faster, was given a list,
and asked for its first three in order - block mode, staying in the
interrupt handler while the drive keeps up, and 32-bit PIO - tested
on the emulators first; the real hardware is his.  All three are
about PIO, which was still WDCTRL's: one sector an interrupt, a word
at a time.  Under Windows the interrupt costs more than the sector
does - VPICD, BlockDev and back for every 512 bytes.

AND PIO IS NOT ONLY FOR MACHINES WITHOUT AN ENGINE.  The trace build
counts now, and on QEMU's sweep with the drive at Ultra DMA mode 5,
5,410 of 25,829 commands went by PIO all the same - the ones whose
buffers the engine cannot be pointed at - and all but two of them
were more than one sector long: 23,408 sectors, which were 23,408
interrupts and are 5,408.  So this is for a DMA drive too.

BLOCK MODE (LRGDiskBlockMode=off to be without it).  READ and WRITE
MULTIPLE (C4h, C5h; 29h and 39h past 28 bits) move a block of sectors
for one interrupt.  WHOSE SIZE: the one the drive is set to, IDENTIFY
word 59.  A BIOS with block mode on set it and reads with it at the
DOS prompt, so it is never changed (and one set to blocks of one
sector is left at that).  A drive set to none is set to the highest
power of two it takes (word 47), 16 at most - a BIOS that reads a
sector at a time never notices, READ SECTORS being what it always
was.  The real-mode start-up works the size out and gives the drive
the command, for the report; the protected-mode side works it out
again and gives the command again (ld_setmult), whichever size it
is.  THE DRIVE'S TAKING THE COMMAND IS WHAT COUNTS, not what IDENTIFY
says afterwards: nothing changes in a drive told the size it had, and
QEMU's drive goes on saying what it said the first time it was asked,
whatever SET MULTIPLE MODE has done since (a scratch SETMULT.COM
showed it; the first cut asked the drive again, was told "none" by a
QEMU CompactFlash card that had just taken 16, and went without).  A
command of one sector is still READ or WRITE SECTORS.  A DOS
program's reset of the cable loses the size, and ld_reinit gives it
back with the geometry and the transfer mode.  A block-mode command
that ends in an error is tried again a sector at a time, and that
drive stays so until Windows is started again.

THE SIZE IS NOT TAKEN ON TRUST WHILE THE DATA MOVES EITHER.  Inside a
block each sector after the first is moved only if the drive still
has DRQ up for it, looked at 400ns after the one before (ld_xfer).  A
drive whose blocks were shorter than the size it gave would otherwise
be read past what it had, and what a data port gives then is not on
the disk.  The block ends where the drive ends it and the rest comes
as the drive offers it.  It costs five reads of a port a sector.

STAYING IN THE HANDLER (LRGDiskPoll=off).  A drive with the next
block in its buffer has it ready microseconds after the last one was
taken, and so has one just given a block to write.  After a block
the handler waits the 400ns a drive may take to raise BSY, then looks
at the alternate status LD_POLLN (128) times - about what one
interrupt costs, which is the point past which waiting for the
interrupt is cheaper - and if BSY has gone it reads the status, with
interrupts off, and moves the next block there and then.  The read of
the status drops the drive's request before the processor has seen
it.  LD_BURST (32) sectors at most for one interrupt; a write's last
block is looked for the same way, so a short write may end without
its interrupt.  The kernel's own driver polls like this, with the
same four reads for the 400ns (IO\ATA.INC).

THE HANDLER HAD TO BE WRITTEN AGAIN FOR IT, because it believed its
interrupts.  1.2 took any interrupt with a command in hand and the
drive not busy to be the next sector, and read 256 words.  A block
taken by looking leaves its request behind in an interrupt controller
that latches the edge - QEMU's does; an 8259A forgets a request that
is withdrawn before it is acknowledged, and 86Box's does the same -
and that interrupt arrives later with nothing behind it.  Now the
handler goes by the drive's status and by nothing else: busy is not
this interrupt's; DRQ is a block wanted, if one is owed; neither is
the end of a write whose blocks have all gone, or else nothing.
CBL_GO says a controller command is out and, for a write, its first
block sent: until then the status is not the command's and the
handler leaves the drive alone.  1.2 had the hole without any of
this, by reading and not by a run: an interrupt from before, arriving
while ld_start waited for BSY with a DMA command made ready but not
yet written, would have been taken for that command's end, and the
command reported done.  The engine's own interrupt bit is asked for
now before a DMA command is ended.

NOTHING WAITS LONGER FOR THE DISK THAN IT DID.  Sixteen sectors with
interrupts off would be sixteen times what a serial port had to put
up with.  Between the sectors of a block, and after one, the handler
lets other interrupts in (ld_window: a moment with interrupts on).
One of the cable's own that comes in then is ended and no more
(CBL_INXFER; ldh_within) - the code that let it in goes by the status
next.  The look for the next block is made with interrupts off after
such a moment, so a request raised during the look is still there
when the handler returns, and one that came during the moment finds
the drive ready at the first look: no block is left waiting for an
interrupt that has been and gone.

AND IF ONE EVER IS: ld_tick runs every two seconds now (LD_LOSTMS),
from the start, and a command the controller has had that long is
looked at as the handler would look (ld_kick).  The drive busy:
nothing, the command is slow.  Not busy: the interrupt was lost, and
the command goes on from there.  The 20-second message is as it was.
On a loaded host the emulators' commands do take two seconds now and
then, and the trace shows the look finding the drive busy and leaving
it.

32-BIT DATA (LRGDisk32BitIO=off).  REP INSD and REP OUTSD: half the
bus cycles.  It is the kernel's IDE32=AUTO over again (IO\ATA.INC,
ata_pick32 and ata_prove32): offered where the drive says so
(IDENTIFY word 48, of ATA-1 and ATA-2) or the controller is a PCI
one, and then proved - the IDENTIFY block read a word at a time and
a doubleword at a time must be the same 512 bytes, with nothing left
in the drive.  An ISA card reads a doubleword of 1F0h as a word from
1F0h and a word from 1F2h and reports nothing; the proof finds half
the block still in the drive, takes it and says no.  A write cannot
be proved without writing one and goes on the read's word, as in the
kernel.  Never on a CMD640: its 32-bit path is the read-ahead LRGDISK
switches off (Linux says the same of it).

WHAT THE START-UP HANDS OVER.  The reference data had two bits left,
bit 7 of the second cable's two bytes: "the controller is a PCI one"
and "a CMD640" took them.  The three switches the protected-mode side
reads for itself (Get_Profile_Boolean, VMM service B1h, which WDCTRL's
own Sys_Critical_Init shows is there to be called).  The 32-bit proof
is made twice, once in real mode for the report and once in protected
mode for use.

THE REPORT says how PIO will go, for every drive, DMA or not:

  BIOS disk 80h: 1023/16/63, the table says 1024
    the drive, unit 0 of the first cable: 1032192 sectors, LBA
    read by LBA, as the BIOS reads it; the last sector too, ...
    PIO: LRGDiskDMA=off
    PIO in blocks of 16 sectors, as the drive was set
    PIO data 32 bits at a time

"set by LRGDISK" when the start-up set the size; "a sector at a time"
and "16 bits at a time" with the reason after a colon.

A RESET THAT WAS SWALLOWED, found on the way.  A DOS program's write
to a shared cable's control port, made when LRGDISK had used the cable
since the program last did, went through ld_restore - which puts the
program's registers back and never gives a reset - and no further.
So SRST from a DOS box did nothing on a cable in use: SRSTTEST on the
first cable said "status 41, reset, after it 41", in 1.2 as well.  The
control port's byte goes out itself now, and the reset is marked: the
same test says "after it 00", and the trace shows the drives given
their parameters again each time, the block's size with them.

THE TRACE BUILD COUNTS (ld_st; a line starting '#' when a count has
moved): interrupts taken, with nothing to do, and let in by a window;
sectors and blocks moved by PIO; blocks found by looking and not;
sectors moved 32 bits at a time; block-mode commands; looks from the
time-out; blocks the drive ended early.  Three more things wasm -d
sets, for a rig: LD_POLLN, the number of looks - QEMU's drive answers
through the host's own disk and 86Box's by a timer, and 128 looks
find the next block about half the time on QEMU and never on 86Box;
LD_TESTLONG and LD_TESTSHORT, which make LRGDISK take the block for
twice and for half what the drive has, to see the nets hold; and
LD_LOSTMS.

RESULTS.  The final build, LRGDISK.386 25,795 bytes (1.2: 23,798).
Every run below is the lrg3 sweep unless it says otherwise - a DOS
box with I13X's 24 checks of a disk's last sectors through INT 13h
and its extensions and WIN386.EXE copied and compared, CACHEBOX,
DOSBOX1 and nine programs - and every one ended with every I13X line
"0 errors, 0 sectors wrong", the copies the same, the host finding
I13X's pattern in the image where I13X put it, and Windows out.

QEMU 11.1 (PIIX3, SeaBIOS; its drive comes set to 16), on PM-DOS:
  - PIO (LRGDiskDMA=off), the release build and both trace builds:
    86,718 sectors for 26,132 interrupts.  With all three switches
    off, which is 1.2's way: 86,285 for 86,285.  Block mode alone
    (LRGDiskPoll=off): 25,730.  Block mode off and the look on:
    50,810 at 128 looks, 26,211 with the look made long.
    LRGDisk32BitIO=off: the same counts, 16 bits.
  - DMA (Ultra DMA mode 5): the PIO share said at the top.
  - a 200GB slave past 28 bits, by PIO and by DMA: READ and WRITE
    MULTIPLE EXT, and the host finds the pattern at sectors
    419,429,888 to 419,430,399.
  - a disk on the second cable as 81h, by PIO and by DMA; with a
    slave on the first as well, as 82h (LRGDISK's own INT 13h); and
    the two cables one at a time (LRGDiskSerial=on).
  - a CD-ROM as the first cable's slave and as the second's, read
    twelve times through the ports by ATAPIRD in a box (every pass
    BADF658F) between two SRSTTEST resets, beside the disk work: the
    resets happen, the drives are given their parameters again, and
    the block-mode commands after them are right.
  - the boot disk as a CompactFlash card (QEMU's ide-cf: no size
    set, multiword DMA): "PIO in blocks of 16 sectors, set by
    LRGDISK", by DMA and by PIO, and with block mode off.
  - LD_TESTLONG: 391 blocks ended by the drive at half what LRGDISK
    took them for, and every byte right.  LD_TESTSHORT with
    LRGDiskPoll=off and LD_LOSTMS=20: 2,515 commands taken up by the
    time-out, and every byte right.
QEMU, real MS-DOS 5.00 (HIMEM and IFSHLP, the WfW tree as C:\WFW): a
DOS box with I13X and the compared copies, and three programs, by PIO
and by DMA.  LRGDISK had not run a sweep on MS-DOS before.
86Box 4.x:
  - VL/I-486SV2G (ISA, no engine; its BIOS sets the drive to 16): the
    sweep in blocks of 16, 16 bits at a time ("no PCI controller, no
    32-bit I/O in the drive").  With the look made long, on a build
    of earlier in the night: 256 blocks found by looking and not one
    interrupt left over.
  - P3B-F (PIIX4; the Award BIOS sets 16 too): by DMA (Ultra DMA mode
    2) and by PIO, 32 bits at a time.
  - LRGTEST under real MS-DOS 5: a drive set to 8 beforehand, "blocks
    of 8 sectors, as the drive was set"; and with LD_TESTSET and
    LD_BLOCKMAX=8, the BIOS's 16 taken for none, "blocks of 8
    sectors, set by LRGDISK".  (86Box's drive refuses a size of 0 or
    of 1, so "none" cannot be had from it any other way.)

ONE RUN IN NINETY-SIX FELL OVER, AND NOT AGAIN.  It was the CD-ROM
run on the first cable, the long-look build.  Ten seconds after the
second reset, as the box that had read the disc was ending, Windows
was in real mode and the processor was going round an invalid opcode
in RMDOS's memory at 07BC:DA43 with AX 4310h - WIN386 on its way out,
asking for the XMS driver.  The sweep's log stops in CACHEBOX with no
word of why.  LRGDISK's own trace is clean to the end: both resets
marked and answered, no error, no time-out, no interrupt lost, 611
commands done after the last reset.  The scenario was then run 84
more times with this driver - 68 with the resets, 48 of those with
QEMU logging every exception, and 16 without them - and 16 times with
LRGDISK 1.2, and every one ended.  Not explained, and not laid at
anything; what is known is where it stopped, and that the driver was
saying nothing odd.

WHAT THE EMULATORS CANNOT SAY is how much faster any of it is: their
drives take no time and their interrupts cost nothing.  They say the
bytes are right and the interrupts fewer.  The speed is the 486's to
show.

NOT RUN: real hardware.  The CMD640 and the RZ1000, which no emulator
has.  A VLB controller, and a 32-bit proof that says no (no emulated
controller halves a doubleword read; the kernel's proof, which this
one copies, was written because a real machine did).  A drive that
ends a command in an error.
OPEN: the look is a count of port reads, not a time, so it is shorter
on a fast bus; a drive that loses its block size by itself, with no
reset, costs one failed command and then goes a sector at a time.

To use it: nothing new - the three are on unless SYSTEM.INI says off.
On the 486, LRGDiskReport=on and C:\LRGDISK.TXT say what was chosen.
If a disk misbehaves, the switches come off one at a time, in the
order LRGDisk32BitIO, LRGDiskPoll, LRGDiskBlockMode; with all three
off the data moves as 1.2 moved it.

Files: CMD\LRGDISK\LRGDISK.ASM, BUILD.CMD (the description says 1.3).
BIN\LRGDISK.386; IMAGES\PMDOS.IMG (made again by BUILD.CMD's own
line), IMAGES\HD16.IMG and the 86Box VM's HD16.IMG (FATREPL, in
place) and the VM's PMDOS.IMG carry it.  MASM 6.13 assembles it plain
and with LRG_TRACE.  RUNTESTS was not run: nothing it boots has
LRGDISK.386 on it, and no other file changed.  Still v0.63.


'CD', AND AN MS-DOS PROGRAM IN FRONT OF EVERY COMMAND (2026-10-10)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Charlie asked whether the D32 format could carry his initials the way
the DOS .EXE carries Mark Zbikowski's, and then for the rest of what
'MZ' has: a standard MS-DOS program in front of every D32 command that
says "This application requires 32-bit DOS mode", an image with
nothing in front of it still loading, and room for a program that is
BOTH - the SETUP yet to be written, which is to upgrade a disk when it
is started from MS-DOS and lay one out from nothing when the machine
is booted from the install diskette.

WHAT A D32 FILE IS NOW.  The image begins 'CD' where it began with a
jump and, at +4, 'D32',1Ah.  A file is the image and nothing else,
which is what wlink writes; or it is an MS-DOS .EXE with the image
behind it and the image's offset in the dword at 3Ch of the MZ header
- the place 'NE' and 'PE' are found from.  Real MS-DOS runs what is in
front.  PM-DOS looks behind it and never does.

    +0   'C','D'    the signature (D32_SIG, 4443h as a word)
    +2   CDh,20h    INT 20h
    +4   version    D32_VER, 1
    +5   type       D32T_PROG, 0; then a spare word
    +8   base, entry, bss, stack - what they were, where they were

The header is still 32 bytes and code still starts at base + 32, so no
program's source changed: D32_HEAD in PMDOS.INC is the one place the
layout is written down.

THE TWO BYTES AFTER THE SIGNATURE are for an image with nothing in
front of it, on real MS-DOS.  It is loaded as a .COM; 'C' and 'D' are
INC BX and INC SP there, and INT 20h ends it.  Without a word, but it
ends.

THE OLD STUB DID NOT WORK FOR A LARGE PROGRAM, which nobody had seen
because nobody had run one on MS-DOS.  It was reached the .COM way,
and DOS reads at most FF00h bytes of a .COM and refuses a file that
has more (DOS6SRC, dos\msproc.asm, at OkRead).  MS-DOS 5 says "Cannot
execute" of 0.63's PMD.EXE (90,340 bytes) and ACROREAD.EXE (161,572),
and DOSSHELL.EXE is between them.  An MZ header says how much of the
file is the program, so the stub is loaded and run whatever is behind
it.

THE STUB IS TOOLS\D32STUB.ASM, 128 bytes: an MZ header written out as
data, fourteen bytes of code, the sentence, errorlevel 1.  It is
linked as a flat binary so that the header is the one PMDOS.INC
describes - no fixups, the fixup table's offset at 40h, the image's
offset at 3Ch - and not what a linker's "system dos" emits, which has
the table at 20h.

TOOLS\D32BIND.C PUTS A STUB IN FRONT OF AN IMAGE, in place.  It is
given the program and the stub: TOOLS\D32STUB.EXE, or any 16-bit .EXE.
Two things are made true there because the kernel counts on them.
The stub's fixup table starts at 40h or later, which is what says an
MZ header has a 3Ch at all; a table that is lower is moved, inside the
header when there is room and into a longer header when there is not
(HELLOX.EXE's seven fixups at 20h: its header goes from 40h to 60h,
and it runs).  And the image starts on a paragraph with its header
inside one 512-byte sector, so the header is whole in one cluster on
any disk.  It refuses a program that is not an image, a stub that is
not an .EXE, and a stub whose 3Ch is already somebody's - a Windows
program, or a command that has been bound.  Binding twice gives the
same file.

THE KERNEL.  d32_find (INT21.INC) is given an open handle and says
where the image is: 0, what 3Ch says, or nowhere.  exec_kind is that
between an open and a close, where it was a read of eight bytes; it
costs an MZ program a seek and a two-byte read.  4Bh AL=3 asks it too,
so that an image behind a stub is refused as an overlay as a bare one
always was.  exec_load reads the file its own way - it is how the
interpreter is loaded, with nobody's handle table to open a file in -
and now starts where the image does: the clusters in front of it are
stepped over by following the chain, not read, and the part of a
cluster by exec_skip, which the first pass of the copy uses up.  It
refuses a header of another version, a type that is not a program, an
offset that is not on a paragraph and one that would put the header
across a sector.  CMD says "Bad command or file name" of all four, as
of any file 4Bh will not have.

BUILD.CMD BINDS THE 27 THAT SHIP, by name, in one FOR line after the
last of them is linked: CMD.EXE and every 32-bit command on the boot
disk, the seven called .COM among them.  The name decides nothing, on
either system.  COMMAND.COM and SYS16.COM are 16-bit programs and not
images.  THE 32-BIT PROGRAMS IN BIN\TESTS ARE LEFT BARE, on purpose:
twenty of them, seventeen in RUNTESTS, and they are the proof that an
image with nothing in front of it still loads.

A PROGRAM FOR BOTH SYSTEMS is one D32BIND line: the image, and the
program's own 16-bit .EXE where the stub would go.  Tried with
HELLOX.EXE in front of DRIVES.EXE: DRIVES at the prompt, from a DOS
box and from a diskette; HELLOX on real MS-DOS 5 and on RMDOS with the
kernel parked.  And with a 32K program in front, which puts the image
63 clusters into the file on a diskette.

WHAT A MIXED DISK DOES.  A program built before today is not an image
to this kernel, so it goes to a DOS box as the .COM its first bytes
say it is - and its own old stub prints "This program requires 32-bit
DOS mode", on PM-DOS, which is how to know one.  An older kernel takes
a bound command for a DOS program and prints the new sentence, and
ends a bare image without a word.  Neither runs the wrong thing; both
mean that a disk is brought up to date whole, the commands with the
system.  (The interpreter is the exception to the first: exec_load
takes nothing to a box, so this kernel with an older CMD.EXE has no
shell.  Read, not run.)

FOR A DRIVER, LATER.  Nothing loads a native driver and nothing here
decides how one would be loaded.  The type byte is so that the same
header can say "driver" when that is settled, and 4Bh already refuses
every type but a program.

RUN, headless.  RUNTESTS 84 x 7, with one baseline moved: RMTEST on
every row, 73EBh free clusters to 73E8h - PMDOS.SYS is 424 bytes
longer and each command about 71, and between them they take three
more clusters of the test disk.  On PM-DOS in DOSBox-X, from a hard
disk and from a diskette: the bound interpreter and commands, bare
images, the two-program files above, the four refusals, D32TEST.BAT
(SORT and CMD.EXE started by COMMAND.COM, three shells deep), and five
16-bit programs whose headers are of every kind - fixups at 1Eh, 20h
and 40h, 3Ch pointing at 'NE', at 'PE' and at nothing - whose output
is byte for byte what 0.63's kernel gave.  On RMDOS, by PARKTEST: the
sentence from MEM.EXE, HELLOX from the two-program file, and a bare
image ending with nothing said.  On real MS-DOS 5 (a copy of the 86Box
machine's disk, in DOSBox-X): the sentence and errorlevel 1 from
CMD.EXE, from ACROREAD.EXE at 161,640 bytes and from SYS.COM, and a
bare image under either extension ending with errorlevel 0.  MASM 6.13
assembles DOSMAIN, D32STUB, CMD and two programs that use D32_HEAD.

NOT RUN: real hardware; 86Box; a DOS box under Windows itself (RMDOS
was reached by PARKTEST); FORMAT /S, which starts SYS.COM; a program
started from a CD-ROM.

Files: INC\PMDOS.INC (D32_HEAD, D32_*, EXE_LFANEW), DOS\INT21.INC
(d32_find, exec_kind, exec_load), DOS\VDM.INC (vc_overlay),
CMD\CMD.ASM (a comment), TOOLS\D32STUB.ASM and TOOLS\D32BIND.C (new),
BUILD.CMD, BASELINE\*\RMTEST.OUT.  PMDOS.SYS is 159,673 bytes.  BIN
has the 48 files that changed - the kernel, the 27 and the twenty
tests - and IMAGES\PMDOS.IMG and TESTS.IMG are BUILD.CMD's own;
IMAGES\HD16.IMG and the 86Box VM's HD16.IMG had the 48 put in by
FATREPL, in place, and no program in the old format is left on
either; the VM's PMDOS.IMG and TESTS.IMG are copies.  HD32, HDBIG,
MULTI, PMDOSATA and PMDOSFDD were not rebuilt, and what is on them is
from before.  Still v0.63.


A COUNTRY AND A KEYBOARD: COUNTRY=, COUNTRY.SYS, KEYB AND KEYBOARD.SYS (2026-10-10)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Asked for as "country and keyboard support in the same fashion MS-DOS
did", with a COUNTRY.SYS if that keeps the kernel smaller and a
KEYB.COM if one is needed.  Both are.

THE COUNTRY IS A FILE.  The kernel still has one country built in, the
United States in code page 437, and that is what a machine with no
COUNTRY= line has - every answer it gave before, byte for byte, but
for one pointer (below).  Every other country is a row of
COUNTRY.SYS: 38h's 34 bytes, the capitals of 80h-FFh, the collating
weights, and the letters for yes and no.  COUNTRY=code[,[page][,file]]
in CONFIG.SYS reads it as MS-DOS's sysinit did (DOS\NLS.INC,
cfg_country and nls_load): \COUNTRY.SYS on the boot drive unless a
file is named, and with no page the FIRST entry the file has for the
country.  It left the list of statements that do nothing, where it had
waited with a note saying a second country was a data problem.

THE FILE IS IN MS-DOS'S FORMAT - FFh,'COUNTRY', a list of country and
code page pairs, and for each a list of tables by number - so either
DOS's file loads on the other.  PM-DOS's own is written by
TOOLS\MKNLS.PS1 from NLS\COUNTRY.DEF, one line a country, into
NLS\COUNTRY.ASM, which BUILD.CMD assembles.  The script is not part of
the build - BUILD.CMD needs Open Watcom and nothing else - so the .ASM
it wrote is kept in the tree.  Forty countries, 82 pairs, 17,407 bytes.
A country's first pair is 437 wherever 437 has its letters and the
national page where it has not (865 for Denmark and Norway, 860, 863,
852, 866, 857, 861, 737), because the screen is the video card's font
and nothing here changes it.

THE TABLES ARE MADE BY RULE AND ARE NOT MICROSOFT'S BYTE FOR BYTE.  A
small letter's capital is its capital where the code page has one and
the unaccented capital where it has not; a letter weighs what its
unaccented capital does, a currency sign what '$' does, and Denmark,
Norway, Sweden and Finland have their three letters after Z.  Checked
against MS-DOS 6.22's COUNTRY.SYS with a dumper that reads both: the
rule gives 6.22's collating table for 437 and for 850 exactly, and its
852 capitals; 6.22's capitals for US/437 differ in one byte (e-acute
to E, where the rule says E-acute, as 6.22's own table for Belgium
does), and its 850 tables fold every accented letter to ASCII.

NO NLSFUNC.  MS-DOS needed it resident to answer 38h for a country
that is not the current one, 6501h for another pair, and CHCP,
because DOS could not open a file from inside a DOS call.  This kernel
can: fn38, fn65 and fn66 call nls_load, which reads the file COUNTRY=
named into a staging area and commits it only if it was asked to and
the pair was whole.

WHAT THE THREE CALLS ANSWER NOW (DOS\INT21.INC).  38h: the country in
use, another one out of the file (AL or BX names it), or error 2; with
DX = FFFFh it sets one.  6501h follows dos\getset.asm: BX and DX name
the pair, FFFFh each for the one in use; five bytes is the least it
writes into; the length word is cut to the room; CX comes back as what
was written and AX as the code page the system started in.  The table
calls refuse a pair that is not the one in use, as MS-DOS does with no
NLSFUNC.  6520h-6522h go through the table 6502h hands out, and so do
A0h-A2h, DOS 7's names for the same three.  6523h takes the country's
two letters.  6601h is the page in use and the page at startup; 6602h
loads the same country's tables for another page.

THE CASE-MAP CALL IS CODE NOW.  The far pointer in the country block
pointed at a RETF, which was right while the table was the identity.
It points at twelve bytes in the DOS data segment (GNLS_CASEMAP) that
look AL up in the table - so CTRYDMP's and CTRYTEST's answers moved
from 0400:00D0 to 0400:02D0 on every row, and nothing else of theirs.

THE DOS BOX'S BRIDGE PASSED 65h WITHOUT BX (vdm_ctryext): it was
scratch for ES times sixteen, and came back to the guest that way.
Nothing read it while there was one pair.  And LOLTEST called 6501h
with DX never set; MS-DOS refuses that too, so the test sets it.

RMDOS answers for the country the kernel parked with: the handoff
header carries the block, the code, both pages and yes and no
(RMH_CTRY, contract 1.05), and the tables are in the low block, which
RMDOS leaves as it finds (RL_NLS, sixteen bytes longer for the case
map and the stub below).  RMDOS reads no file: another country asked
of 38h is refused, and 6501h answers for the pair in use whichever
pair is named, as it always did.

CMD.EXE writes a date in the country's order and with its separators
- DIR, DATE, TIME and the prompt - and DATE takes one in that order.
The clock stays 24-hour whatever the country says, as it was.  CHCP is
in CMD.EXE as well as COMMAND.COM.

THE KEYBOARD IS THE KERNEL'S, SO KEYB DOES NOT STAY.  MS-DOS's KEYB
was a resident program on INT 09h.  IRQ 1 here never reaches an INT
09h unless a DOS box has hooked it, so the layout is a table the
kernel's decoder is handed: KEYB.COM, a native program, finds the
record for the layout and the code page in KEYBOARD.SYS and passes it
down (21h/F1h AL=22h, IOS_KBLAYOUT), the kernel checks every count in
it once and keeps the one copy, and KEYB ends.  The record (KBL_ in
PMDOS.INC) is six bytes a key - scan code, flags, and the character
alone, with Shift, with AltGr and with both - and the dead keys, each
its own character and a list of letter and result.

WHAT THE DECODER DOES WITH IT (IO\KEYBD.INC, kb_nat).  The right-hand
Alt is AltGr, and so is Ctrl with Alt, as it was for KEYB; a key with
nothing at that level is Alt and the key.  A dead key waits for the
next character; with a letter it has no result for, the accent goes in
first and the letter after it; the space bar gives the accent alone.
Caps Lock shifts the keys the layout says it shifts - the letters, and
on the French and German boards the digit row too.  Ctrl and a letter
is by the letter on the key.  Alt and a letter is reported as the US
key with that letter, so Alt+Z is the key marked Z.  The keypad's
decimal key types the layout's.  Ctrl+Alt+F1 is the US keyboard and
Ctrl+Alt+F2 the layout again, and neither reaches a program.

A DOS BOX THAT HOOKS INT 09h AND PASSES THE KEY ON reached the ROM's
handler, which types US keys.  Once KEYB has loaded a layout, INT 09h
in the vector table is a HLT in the DOS data segment (GNLS_KBSTUB) and
kb_hlt answers it: the latched code through the same decoder, the
shift state to 40:17, the EOI, the IRET.  The box's codes are decoded
with a shift state of their own (kb_boxfl) - the same codes as the
wire's, later - which kbq_put makes agree with the wire's whenever the
box has caught up.  Only if nothing had hooked INT 09h before KEYB
ran: a resident program in front keeps the ROM's address.  For a park
the stub becomes a far jump to the ROM's handler and comes back a HLT
(kb_park).

KEYBOARD.SYS IS PM-DOS'S OWN FORMAT, not MS-DOS's: a list of layout,
keyboard ID and code page, and the records.  MKNLS.PS1 writes it from
NLS\KEYBOARD.DEF - the four rows of keys as they are on the board, a
line a level - into NLS\KEYBOARD.ASM.  Thirty layouts, 65 records,
25,174 bytes.  A layout is written once, in characters; the script
makes a record for each code page it is given, and a character the
page has not got is a key that types nothing there.  The sections were
drafted by TOOLS\KBDDUMP.PS1 from the layout files Windows has for the
same national keyboards (read as bytes; nothing is loaded).

WHAT IS NOT DONE.
  - The screen.  MS-DOS changed the font with DISPLAY.SYS, EGA.CPI and
    MODE CON CP; none of that is here, so a code page is tables and a
    layout, and the characters shown are the video card's.
  - File names.  A name is upper-cased in ASCII and a byte from 80h up
    is stored as typed, as before; table 4 and table 5 of the file are
    read past.
  - Windows.  Its own programs have its own layout; a DOS box inside
    Windows has the US keyboard, since the layout is the kernel's and
    Windows runs on RMDOS.
  - A key pressed while the BIOS has the machine for a call of the
    kernel's is the ROM's to decode, and is a US key.
  - Num Lock and Scroll Lock are still not tracked, and Ctrl+Break is
    still not a key.  KEYB's INT 2Fh calls (AD80h) are not answered.
  - Double-byte pages, and the pages 6.22 has for Hebrew and Arabic.

THE TESTS.  21h/F1h AL=23h is a key as if the keyboard had sent it,
for a test with nobody typing, as F0h AL=0Bh is for the mouse.
KBLTEST.COM presses keys with it, thirty-nine rows of them, and prints
what INT 16h reads, once with INT 09h alone and once with its own
handler passing each key on; NLSTEST.COM prints what 38h, 65h and 66h
say.  Neither judges: the answers are baselines, the US ones in
RUNTESTS's rows and one row for each country in TOOLS\NLSTESTS.PS1,
which boots a CONFIG.SYS with a COUNTRY= line and runs KEYB first.
RUNTESTS.PS1's disk has the two .SYS files now.

RUN, headless, on DOSBox-X.  RUNTESTS 86 x 7 - the 84 and the two new
ones - against a build of the sources as they were: 79 answers the
same, CTRYDMP and CTRYTEST moved by the case-map pointer, SFTSCAN by
RMDOS.SYS being 56 bytes longer, and RMFIND and RMTEST by the files
added to the test disk (those two differed from the baselines in the
tree before this work as well; all are re-recorded).  NLSTESTS, eight
rows: the United States (every way KEYB is refused, the second Italian
keyboard by ID, CHCP), Germany (also a park and back with the layout
loaded, and CHCP 850), France in 850, the United Kingdom, Denmark in
865, Spain, Poland in 852 and Russia in 866 - each layout's keys
the same through a hooked INT 09h as without one.  A CONFIG.SYS of bad
COUNTRY= lines boots and says which was wrong with each.  DIR, DATE
and TIME under Germany and Sweden.  On RMDOS, by PARKTEST under
COUNTRY=049 with KEYB GR loaded: NLSTEST's answers are Germany's, the
case-map call in real mode among them, and the layout is the
keyboard's again after the park.  MASM 6.13 assembles DOSMAIN, RMDOS,
IOPM, CMD, KEYB, the two tests and the two data files.

NOT RUN: real hardware; 86Box; Windows; a real keyboard - every key
here was pressed by the test call.

Files: DOS\NLS.INC, CMD\KEYB\KEYB.ASM, NLS\*, TOOLS\MKNLS.PS1,
KBDDUMP.PS1, NLSTESTS.PS1, NLSTEST.ASM and KBLTEST.ASM (new);
INC\PMDOS.INC, INC\RMDOS.INC, DOS\INT21.INC, CONFIG.INC, VDM.INC,
RING3.INC, PARK.INC, RMDOS.ASM, RMINFO.INC, DOSMAIN.ASM, IO\KEYBD.INC,
BUS.INC, IOPM.ASM, CMD\CMD.ASM, TOOLS\LOLTEST.ASM, RUNTESTS.PS1,
BUILD.CMD, MKHD.CMD, DISK\CONFIG.TXT, AUTOEXEC.TXT, HELPTEST.BAT.
PMDOS.SYS is 162,122 bytes (+2,449), PMIO.SYS 58,447 (+1,084),
CMD.EXE 60,207 (+703), RMDOS.SYS 61,219 (+56), KEYB.COM 3,681.
Still v0.63.


NOT EVERYTHING IN THE ROOT: THE INTERPRETER'S DIRECTORY, AND RMCD.SYS
AN ORDINARY FILE (2026-10-10)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Asked for after the entry above: "let's not require everything to be
in the root.  Eventually the SETUP program is going to place
everything in a folder with the default being DOS", and RMCD.SYS as "a
non-required non-system file".

ONE RULE, AND THE KERNEL HAD IT ALREADY.  The system's files are where
the interpreter was loaded from: shell_name up to its last '\'.  With
no SHELL= line that is the root of the boot drive, and a diskette with
everything in its root works as it did; SHELL=C:\DOS\CMD.EXE /P makes
it C:\DOS, and that one line is all an installed system has to write.
The check at startup has found CHKDSK that way since VOLFLAG.INC was
written, CMD.EXE makes COMSPEC out of it, and FORMAT /S and KEYB find
SYS and KEYBOARD.SYS through COMSPEC.  What still named the boot
drive's root outright was COUNTRY.SYS, RMDOS.SYS and RMCD.SYS.  Those
go through sys_open now (DOS\DOSMAIN.ASM, with sys_beside and
sys_inroot): the name beside the interpreter, then in the root of the
boot drive, so a file is missing only when it is in neither.

WHAT STILL HAS TO BE IN THE ROOT: PMIO.SYS and PMDOS.SYS, because the
boot code reads nothing else, and CONFIG.SYS and AUTOEXEC.BAT, which
are read from there as MS-DOS read them.

SHELL= IS READ ON THE FIRST WALK OVER CONFIG.SYS, with DOS= and EMS=
(cfg_phaseof).  COUNTRY= is on the main walk and may stand above the
SHELL= line, and it has to find COUNTRY.SYS in the directory that line
names.  SHELL= only stores a name and a tail, so nothing else changes
by moving it.

COUNTRY.SYS WITH NO FILE NAMED IS LOOKED FOR EACH TIME (nls_load) and
the place is not remembered: ctry_path keeps its '?' until a COUNTRY=
line names a file, and 38h, 6501h and CHCP look where the interpreter
is at that moment.  The messages name what was tried: "COUNTRY=: cannot
open COUNTRY.SYS" when it is in neither place, and the whole path of
the file sys_open found when that file is not one or has not got the
country.

RMDOS.SYS IS LOOKED FOR IN THE ROOT FIRST, the other way round from
everything else (park_loadrm): it is the kernel's other half, SYS puts
it in the root beside the kernel and replaces no other copy, and an
older one in the system's directory must not be the one that loads.
Then beside the interpreter, then in the current drive's root as
before.  It stays read-only, hidden and system.

RMCD.SYS IS AN ORDINARY FILE.  Nothing needs it but the CD-ROM's letter
under Windows, so it is no more a system file than MSCDEX was: it is
kept with the system's other files, looked for beside the interpreter
and then in the root (park_loadcd), and COPY carries it.  SYS.COM and
SYS16.COM do not copy it, MKDISK does not mark it, and FATREPL.PL
writes one as an ordinary file wherever it replaces one.  A copy an
earlier SYS left on a disk - read-only, hidden, system - is found as
before; SYS makes such a copy on its target ordinary and leaves what
is in it alone, so that COPY can replace it afterwards.

BECAUSE SYS NO LONGER KEEPS IT IN STEP WITH RMDOS, the park reads its
version word: RC_VER in INC\RMDOS.INC, which is the header and what
RMCD takes from RMDOS's data (RMSDA.INC).  An RMCD.SYS with another
number is not loaded, and Windows starts without the CD-ROM's letter.
RC_VER IS TO BE RAISED WHENEVER THAT HEADER OR RMSDA.INC CHANGES: the
check is only as good as that.

SYS FINDS ITS SOURCE THE SAME WAY (CMD\SYS\SYS.ASM, sy_beside).
PMIO.SYS and PMDOS.SYS come from the source drive's root.  RMDOS.SYS,
CMD.EXE and COMMAND.COM are looked for there and then beside the
interpreter (21h/F1h AL=3), when the interpreter is on the source
drive - an interpreter loaded from another disk says nothing about
this one, and the rule also keeps the file found from being the file
about to be written.  Everything lands in the target's root, where a
disk with no CONFIG.SYS boots.  Before, SYS from a system kept in a
directory stopped at "Cannot copy the system files".

THE IMAGES ARE AS THEY WERE: everything in the root, RMCD.SYS among
it, now without the three attributes.  The directory is SETUP's to
make.

TESTED on DOSBox-X.  RUNTESTS.PS1 has -SysDir: the disk an installed
system has - PMIO.SYS, PMDOS.SYS and RMDOS.SYS in the root, the rest
in C:\DOS, SHELL= as the last line of CONFIG.SYS.  The whole list of
86 runs to the end there; 77 answer as they do from the root, and the
nine that differ print the layout: COMSPEC and PATH (ARGS, DPMITEST,
EXECTST), a PSP one paragraph up for the longer environment (HELLO,
HELLOX, SFTSCAN), and what is on the disk (RMFIND, RMTEST).  CACHETST
counts one write owed fewer, which is put down to the disk and was
not looked into.
NLSTESTS.PS1 has a row for it, nls-dir: COUNTRY=049 with no file
named and above the SHELL= line, KEYB GR, CHCP 850, and two parks -
NLSTEST's and KBLTEST's answers are nls-gr's, byte for byte.
RUNTESTS is 86 x 7 with no answer changed; the eight NLSTESTS rows
from before match.  DBXRUN.PS1 has -Cd, an .iso in an ATAPI drive,
and with one the park was run on seven disks: RMCD.SYS beside the
interpreter, RMDOS.SYS there too and not in the root, RMCD.SYS in the
root with the interpreter in C:\DOS, everything in the root, no
RMCD.SYS, one with version 2, and no RMDOS.SYS.  On the first four the
DOS under Windows gives the CD-ROM's label, lists its root and reads a
file; on the next two it has no CD-ROM and is otherwise whole; on the
last the park is refused with "file not found" and the kernel carries
on.  SYS from a diskette with its system in A:\DOS, with RMDOS.SYS in
either place, and from one with everything in the root: the five
files on the target are the build's, byte for byte, an old RMCD.SYS
there comes out ordinary with its contents untouched, and the disk
boots.  COUNTRY= with the file in neither place, in the root only,
not a country file, without the country, and named but missing: the
right message or the right country each time.  MASM 6.13 assembles
DOSMAIN, RMCD, SYS and SYS16.

NOT RUN: real hardware; 86Box; Windows itself - the CD-ROM was read
through the DOS Windows runs on, by a test program, not by File
Manager.

Files: DOS\DOSMAIN.ASM, NLS.INC, CONFIG.INC, PARK.INC, WINDOWS.INC,
RMCD.ASM, INC\RMDOS.INC, CMD\SYS\SYS.ASM, TOOLS\SYS16.ASM, MKDISK.C,
FATREPL.PL, RUNTESTS.PS1, NLSTESTS.PS1, DBXRUN.PS1, DISK\CONFIG.TXT,
AUTOEXEC.TXT.  PMDOS.SYS is 162,318 bytes (+196), SYS.COM 1,983
(+279), SYS16.COM 8,574 (+21); RMDOS.SYS, RMCD.SYS, PMIO.SYS and
CMD.EXE are the same bytes as before.  Still v0.63.
