FC, FIND, DISKCOPY AND DISKCOMP: MS-DOS 6.22'S, AND A DISKETTE IN ONE PASS
(2026-09-30)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The user asked for FC.EXE and FIND.EXE "from MS-DOS", and DISKCOMP.COM
and DISKCOPY.COM "with single pass compare or copy", in C or
assembler.  FIND, DISKCOPY and DISKCOMP are assembler: CMD\FIND\
FIND.ASM, CMD\DISKCOPY\DISKCOPY.ASM, CMD\DISKCOMP\DISKCOMP.ASM, the
last two sharing INC\DISKIMG.INC.  FC is C, CMD\FC\FC.C with a
DOSINT.ASM startup like LABEL's, because 6.22's line resync is easier
to keep exact in C.  All four are native D32 programs and are on the
floppy and both hard disks.  v0.61 (the entry above).

THE ORACLE IS 6.22 ITSELF.  The real FIND.EXE, FC.EXE, DISKCOPY.COM
and DISKCOMP.COM (S:\User backups\Charlie\DOS\MSDOS622) were run under
DOSBox-X's own DOS with [dos] ver=6.22: 45 FIND cases, 59 FC cases,
and DISKCOPY/DISKCOMP between two floppy images, with one drive and
two, captured to a file - standard error too, through a scratch
wrapper that dups handle 1 onto 2 and EXECs.  The same cases on
PM-DOS give the same bytes everywhere except the /? screens, which
are in my own words, and the lines DOSBox-X's DOS prints in place of
the texts a real COMMAND.COM supplies: "Extended Error 2" for
"File not found - NAME", "Parse Error 9" for "Parameter format not
correct", each with an extra blank line the real retriever does not
add (S:\DOS6SRC\inc\msgserv.asm, $M_ADD_CRLF and the " - " for
substitution 0).

FIND.  Switches anywhere and one letter each (/N/I is two, /VCN is an
invalid switch); the string in double quotes with "" for a quote; each
file searched as the parser reaches it, so a missing one is reported
between its neighbours' output, and no wildcards (6.22 opened the name
as typed).  A heading per file - blank line, ten dashes, the name in
capitals, ": n" on it under /C - and none for standard input, where
/C prints the bare number.  A line ends at LF, is matched without its
CR LF and written out as it came, terminator and all; ^Z ends the
file; an empty line contains nothing, so "" matches no line and /V ""
prints them all.  Errorlevel 0 if any line held the string (/V too), 1
if none, 2 for an error - and a match after an error puts it back to
0, as 6.22's did.  /? leaves 1.  Errors go to standard error with
"FIND: " in front only until a file has been named.  /I folds through
the country's table, made by one 21h/6521h over the 256 byte values.
-dERR_TO_OUT builds a copy that puts the errors on standard output,
for a test run: CMD.EXE has no 2>.

FC.  6.22's LineCompare, BinaryCompare and wildcard expansion (the
first name searched for, the second's * and ? filled from each file
found) reimplemented, not copied: lines read 127 characters at a time
with every CR dropped and tabs to every 8th column, /T keeping both,
/W, /C, /A, /N, /LBn, /nnnn, the .EXE .COM .SYS .OBJ .LIB .BIN rule,
"Resync failed.  Files are too different".  Errorlevel 0 whatever the
files hold, 1 only for an unusable command line, and an unknown switch
is reported and the comparison goes on - all 6.22's.  Two of its slips
are kept because the output depends on them (a resync search whose
second file runs out carries on with the FIRST file's length; under /W
a blank line still takes a buffer place) and one is not: under /T 6.22
chopped the last character off a line with no LF after it.

DISKCOPY AND DISKCOMP: 6.22's prompts, messages, flow and errorlevels
(0 / 1 read-write error or, for DISKCOMP, different / 2 ^C / 3 a disk
that could not be read / 4 command line, drives, memory or mismatched
disks), each disk done in ONE PASS: the whole of it is read into
memory first.  With one drive that is one swap where DOS 6.0 asked for
several, and DISKCOPY then offers "Do you wish to write another
duplicate of this disk (Y/N)?" as 6.22 did when it could hold a disk
in a file on C:.  Where the image does not fit it is done in passes,
as DOS did; DISKCOPY /M forces that by keeping the image in the slot.
The sectors go by F1h AL=0Dh/0Eh, which name the DRIVE; FDF_SETGEO is
told the source's shape before each pass, and both letters are
remounted at the end (F1h AL=2) because the kernel was not told the
disks changed.  INT 24h is answered Fail for that remount; the raw
calls raise none, so "Not ready" and "Write protect error" are asked
about by the programs ("Press CTRL+C to abort, or correct this problem
..."), as 6.22's did.

DISKCOPY's target: its boot sector is read first.  The same shape is
written as it is; no BPB, or another format of the same kind of disk,
is formatted first ("Formatting while copying", FDF_BEGIN/TRACK/END);
a disk of another density (a 1.44M disk formatted 1.44M under a 720K
source) is refused, as 6.0 refused it.  A write that fails on a disk
that looked formatted formats from that track on and tries again.  The
copy gets a serial number of its own, from the clock as FORMAT makes
one, when the source has an extended BPB - so DISKCOMP of a disk and
its copy reports track 0, which 6.22 did too.  DISKCOMP takes the
second disk's shape from its BPB if it has one and refuses a different
one; a second disk with no BPB is compared anyway, track by track, as
6.22 compared a blank one.

THE IMAGE NEEDS A KERNEL CALL: 21h/F1h AL=1Ah, XMF_* in bits 16-23 of
EAX (PMDOS.INC).  A native program's segment is its 512K slot, less
than one 1.44M disk.  [Since 2026-10-01 the slot grows, so 48h could
hold the disk too.  DISKCOPY and DISKCOMP still use the XMF calls
first; /M, which takes 48h, should now need one pass where it took
four.  Not run since.]  XMF_ALLOC/FREE/GET/PUT/AVAIL give it blocks of
the arena it cannot address and copy in and out of them - XMS 0Bh in
a flat program's shape.  The blocks ARE XMS handles (one pool, and MEM
counts them), stamped with cur_own, so fn4C's arena sweep frees what a
program leaves and fn4C now calls xms_relown for the table, as
vdm_cleanup already did.  Only the handle's owner may use it (a native
program could otherwise read a DOS box TSR's block), native callers
only, both ends measured before a byte moves.  r3_pflags answers it by
hand: P_DI for XMF_GET, P_SI for XMF_PUT, nothing for the rest.

FOUND AND FIXED ON THE WAY:
  - XMS: xms_handleno divided by shifting four, "XH_LEN is 16" - and
    XH_LEN has been 20 since XH_OWN.  The FIFTH handle open at once
    came back numbered 6, which xms_find takes as the sixth slot: a
    program sized, moved into, locked or freed a block that was not
    its own.  Now a DIV.  Reproduced on the old kernel with six blocks
    of 1K..6K asking 0Eh for their sizes: blocks 5 and 6 said 6K and
    7K.
  - F1h AL=0Dh/0Eh failed with 1Fh whatever the BIOS said.  Now the
    status goes through crit_map and comes back as DOS's extended
    error: 13h write protected, 15h not ready, 17h CRC, 1Bh sector not
    found, 1Fh the rest.  FORMAT and FDISK test only the carry.
  - 3Dh on a DIRECTORY said "file not found": the search leaves
    directories out.  DOS found the entry and refused it, and FIND
    says "Access denied - C:\DOS", FC "Permission denied".  open_core
    looks once more for a directory of that name (long name re-armed).
  - 21h/6521h wrote CX bytes having checked only where they started;
    it is measured with cbuf_ok now, like every other pointer call.

FOUND AND LEFT: a 16-bit program that runs a native one hands it its
handles 0-2 as COPIES of the SFT entries (VDM.INC, d32_swapin), not
the entries themselves.  If two of them were the same entry - a DOS
program that dupped stdout onto stderr - the native program gets two
independent file positions, and one's output lands on top of the
other's.  That is how the first FIND run here went wrong; the tests
were then run from CMD.EXE instead.

VERIFIED, DOSBox-X headless, on a copy of HD16 with floppy images as
A: and B: (scratch rig pmrun.sh): every FIND and FC case against 6.22
as above; DISKCOPY and DISKCOMP two drives (blank target formatted,
formatted target written as is, /V, /1, /8, /M in passes, "copy
another", a bad answer re-asked, end of the key file taken as ^C,
every command-line and drive error at errorlevel 4) and one drive
(A: A:, a second duplicate, /M A: A: in four passes with the swaps),
1.44M against 720K refused both ways, a read-only target (DOSBox-X
answers 20h, not 03h: formatting fails, "Unrecoverable write error
... track 0", "Target diskette unusable").  DISKCOMP of a disk and a
blank one, and the one-drive copy and duplicate flows, are byte for
byte 6.22's.  Every copy made is the source exactly, bar the four
serial bytes at 27h; no source was written.  A native test of
F1h/1Ah: round trip, both bounds, a bad handle, a double free, too
much, and a 64K block left at exit given back (free memory the same
on a second run).  Whole regression (reg2.ps1, old kernel against
new): identical bar PMDOS.SYS's size.  BUILD.CMD builds clean in a
mirror of the tree; floppy and HD32 boot to a prompt.

NOT VERIFIED: real hardware; real diskettes (an image reads as zeros
where a real blank disk fails to read, so the format paths were
reached through the BPB check and DOSBox-X's own failure); the "Write
protect error" and "Not ready" prompts (DOSBox-X can produce neither);
^C during a copy rather than at a question; 360K, 1.2M and 2.88M
disks; a machine short of extended memory (the pass logic was run
through /M only).

Sizes: PMDOS.SYS 134,741 (+516).  FC.EXE 12,384, FIND.EXE 3,106,
DISKCOPY.COM 5,887, DISKCOMP.COM 5,066.  FC.EXE built from S: is 8
bytes longer than the same source built on C: - the wcc386 -ox
difference already seen with XCOPY and EDIT; BIN has the S: one.

DELETE PROTECTION: UNDELETE=ON|OFF, \RECYCLED, AND UNDELETE.EXE
(2026-09-30)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The user asked for "built-in file delete protection": deleted files
saved to a hidden RECYCLED directory on each drive, no more than 10%
of the free space for them, UNDELETE=ON|OFF in CONFIG.SYS, *.TMP left
out, UNDELETE.EXE to recover them or clear them all out, and deletes
from 32-bit and 16-bit programs both covered.  DOS\RECYCLE.INC
(included after INT21.INC), CMD\UNDELETE\UNDELETE.ASM, the format in
PMDOS.INC under DELETE PROTECTION.  ON by default.  Still v0.60.

A KEPT FILE IS A MOVED DIRECTORY ENTRY.  Nothing is copied and no
cluster is freed: the entry goes into X:\RECYCLED (hidden + system,
made by the first delete the volume sees) the way 56h moves a file
between directories, under the name D + seven hex digits of a
sequence number + its own extension, and a 592-byte record goes into
X:\RECYCLED\UNDELETE.DAT (hidden + system) saying where it was: the
directory as canonical 8.3 components ("\DIR\SUB" - no drive letter,
that is wherever RECYCLED is), the 8.3 name, the long name if it had
one (the move would lose the chain; the record keeps the text), the
attributes, the size, the first cluster, and when.  Record 0 is a
header: 'PMUNDEL',1Ah, the record length, the next sequence number.
Getting a file back is a rename, which is all UNDELETE.EXE does.

ONE ROUTINE DOES EVERY DELETE, rcy_delete, and it has three callers:
41h (7141h is 41h here), the FCB API's 13h, and the new F1h AL=19h.
A 16-bit program in a DOS box reaches the same handlers a native one
does, so there was nothing else to hook.  rcy_plain is the delete
there always was, rebuilt from saved state (context, slot, long-name
chain start) so that any failure anywhere in the keeping can fall back
to it: the program asked for a delete, and a delete it gets.

THE INDEX IS WRITTEN WITH THE KERNEL'S OWN FILE ROUTINES - file_read,
file_write, sft_close - on a 64-byte table entry of its own (rcy_sft)
that is in no program's handle table.  sft_new is never called, so a
program with all its handles open can still delete, and share_release
finds nothing under it.  39h became mkdir_core (ESI path, [mk_attr]
the attribute byte) so that RECYCLED can be made without an INT 21h
frame.

THE ALLOWANCE: kept <= 10% of (free + kept), counting the file being
deleted as kept - so (100 - PCT) * kept <= PCT * free, in clusters,
which cannot overflow with FAT32's 2^28.  UNDEL_PCT = 10 in PMDOS.INC.
Counting free clusters walks the whole FAT, so fat_freeatleast stops
as soon as it has seen enough and the full count is made only when the
answer is no.  Then: a file that would not fit even with nothing else
kept is deleted outright, and otherwise the oldest records (smallest
sequence number) go for good, one at a time, until it fits - the
arithmetic redone on the numbers in hand, not by counting again.

NOT KEPT: UNDELETE=OFF; F1h AL=19h; *.TMP and *.$$$ - the shells make
and delete %PIPEn.$$$ for every pipe and CMD.EXE's FOR /F %FORF.$$$,
and keeping those would fill the allowance with plumbing; anything
deleted from inside \RECYCLED (how /PURGE works with plain 41h);
anything not on a FAT volume; a directory path too long for the
record; and a file that 5Ah made, which cannot be told from any other
- eight characters and no extension.

F1h AL=19h IS FOR PROGRAMS DELETING A COPY THEY HAVE JUST MADE SAFE.
MOVE's cross-volume source, and its half-written destination; XCOPY's
half-written file; COMMAND.COM's COPY when the disk filled (behind a
30h OEM check - F1h is ours alone).  Keeping those only wastes the
space.  MOVE's delete of a destination it is about to replace is NOT
changed: that one is real user data.  A kernel without the call says
"invalid function" and each falls back to 41h.  F1h AL=18h answers
UNDF_ON and the percentage.  vdm_subptr has F1h/19h as P_DX.

ONE QUESTION, NOT TWO.  On a write-protected floppy the first write
of the keeping raises INT 24h; answered Fail, the fallback would raise
it again.  crit_raise now counts Fail answers (crit_nfail), rcy_delete
notes the count on entry, and rcy_giveup returns "access denied"
without the plain delete if it moved.  NOT VERIFIED - DOSBox-X answers
a write to a read-only floppy with AH=20h, not 03h.

FOUND ON THE WAY: THE FCB DELETE NEVER HAD 41h's MOUNTED-IMAGE CHECK.
"DEL *.IMG" through 13h freed the chain of a file that was a drive
letter.  Same refusal now; the file is skipped like a read-only one.

UNDELETE.EXE (D32, 9.7K): UNDELETE [d:][path][name] [/LIST | /ALL]
[/S]; UNDELETE [d:] /PURGE; UNDELETE [d:] /STATUS.  The path is the
directory the files were deleted FROM - found canonical by going there
with 3Bh and asking 47h, and through 60h when it no longer exists -
and the name is matched against the 8.3 name and the long one.  The
default asks about each file from the current directory (Y, N, Esc).
Files come in deletion order.  A name taken since gets '#' (then % &
- 0-9 A-Z) for its first letter; a directory that has gone is made
again; the attributes go back on.  A record whose file has gone from
RECYCLED is let go on the way past.  /PURGE deletes everything in
RECYCLED and removes it.  Dates and times follow 38h.  Help text in
our own words.

VERIFIED, DOSBox-X headless (scratch rig udrun.ps1), DISK\UNDTEST.BAT
on FAT16 and FAT32, every check OK: CMD.EXE's DEL kept, .TMP and .$$$
not; /LIST, /ALL; the # rename; a long name back long; a removed
directory made again; /S; Y from a redirected file; COMMAND.COM's DEL
(16-bit 41h) and FCBTEST's 13h kept, FCBTEST still 22 of 22; LFNAPI's
7141h kept with its long name; the allowance - B5 too big, B2 and B3
let go for B4 on a 32MB disk (B3 stays on the 40MB FAT32 one, as the
arithmetic says); /PURGE; deletes inside RECYCLED not kept.  Also: a
FAT12 floppy as A: (fixed root, RECYCLED made and removed), MOVE
across volumes (source not kept, replaced destination kept, a move on
one volume deletes nothing), UNDELETE=OFF (no RECYCLED made), bad
command lines, N answered, UNDELETE run from COMMAND.COM.  Regression:
HNDTEST FNDTEST APITEST EXECTST DEVTEST SHARETST CACHETST FCBTEST
RENTEST ATTRTEST DIRTEST C16TEST, 429 lines on the old and the new
build - the only differences are "bytes free" (deletes are kept now)
and an environment segment two paragraphs up (COMMAND.COM grew).

NOT DONE: RMDOS.  Under Windows 3.1 in 386 enhanced mode every INT 21h
is RMDOS's, and its 41h deletes as before - keeping a file there would
mean the whole mechanism again in 16-bit real-mode code.  Documented
in CONFIG.SYS.  NOT VERIFIED: real hardware; INT 24h during keeping.

Sizes: PMDOS.SYS 134,225 (+3,661); UNDELETE.EXE 9,707.  BIN\EDIT.EXE
in the tree does NOT match what its sources build today (4,027 bytes
differ) and was left alone.  Images refreshed: floppy built and copied
to the VM; both HD16 copies by FATREPL (PMDOS.SYS, COMMAND.COM,
MOVE.EXE, XCOPY.EXE, UNDELETE.EXE, CONFIG.SYS, AUTOEXEC.BAT, TESTS\
HELPTEST.BAT, TESTS\UNDTEST.BAT); HD32 regenerated; MULTI unchanged.

SHARE IS IN THE KERNEL: SHARE.EXE'S RULES, AND SHARE= TO SIZE THEM
(2026-09-30)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The user asked to "build SHARE.EXE into the kernel with parameters
that can be specified in CONFIG.SYS like SHARE=10".  DOS\SHARE.INC,
included after JFT.INC; CONFIG.INC's cfg_share; SHARE=locks[,space]
| ON | OFF, on by default with SHARE.EXE's own twenty.  Still v0.60.

WHAT SHARE.EXE WAS, so that what this is makes sense.  DOS 3 gave
3Dh sharing bits - deny read, deny write, deny both, deny none - and
5Ch a lock call, and then put the code that made either mean
anything in a separate program, because the kernel was a program's
worth of memory away from having it.  Without SHARE.EXE every open
succeeded, every lock was granted, and INT 2Fh AX=1000h said so;
programs that cared - Word, dBASE, Windows' 32-bit file access,
most installers - asked, and some refused to run.  So the kernel
answered nothing on 1000h, 5Ch was a stub that succeeded (with an
honest comment: one program at a time, no second party to exclude),
and the sharing bits were masked off at the door of 3Dh and thrown
away.

THE RULES ARE SHARE.EXE'S, from S:\DOS6SRC\cmd\share\gshare.asm, and
they are three.  OPEN: the new open is judged against every existing
open OF THE SAME FILE by CUCA, a fifteen-row table indexed by
(sharing mode * 3 + access) with a bit per existing open's index,
bit 0 unused; two compatibility-mode opens never conflict (SHARE
compared user ids and a machine has one), compat against any deny
mode conflicts both ways, and a compat READ of a READ-ONLY file is
judged as deny-write read (GOM) so that two readers of one read-only
file do not fight.  LOCK: 5Ch refuses a range that overlaps ANY lock
on the file, its own included (SLE with Z clear), and an unlock must
name a lock exactly.  READ AND WRITE: a transfer that meets a lock is
refused unless the lock was taken on THIS handle by THIS program -
the "dcl" rule, so a child can lock on an inherited handle and use
it - and the same program through a second handle is refused.

THE SAME FILE is (SFT_DRIVE, SFT_DIRSTART, SFT_DIRENT, and whether
the directory is the root): the volume, the directory, the entry.
SHARE.EXE kept an MFT of file NAMES to say this, and its /F: sized
that; here no name is stored and no string compared, and the second
number on the SHARE= line is accepted so that a line carried over
from a real DOS is not an error, and means nothing.  A new field on
the SFT, SFT_SHARE, keeps the mode byte as the program gave it -
SFT_MODE has only ever held the access - and SFT_LEN went 60 to 64.
open_share is the byte in flight: 3Dh and 716C set it from the
caller (716C used to AND the sharing bits off before calling 3Dh,
which is the one place they were lost), and a create or an FCB open
is compat read/write, as SHARE judged those.

WHERE IT IS ASKED.  share_check runs in open_core and create_core
right after fat_search, when the entry and every open of it are
known and nothing has been committed - for the create that means
BEFORE the truncation, so a file open elsewhere in a deny mode is
not shortened on the way to being refused.  share_lock is 5Ch.
share_iochk runs in 3Fh and 40h before file_read and file_write.
share_release runs in sc_free (a real close, not sft_flush) and in
sft_new, so that nothing can name a slot that has been handed out
again; share_relown runs in 4Ch after the handle sweep, for the locks
a program took on handles it did not own.  share_int2F is in the 2Fh
chain after the cache's.

A REFUSAL IS A CRITICAL ERROR, as it was under DOS: 0Dh "Sharing
violation" for an open, 0Eh "Lock violation" for a read or a write,
Retry and Fail on offer, through crit_raise on the file's OWN volume
(SFT_DRIVE for the I/O case - cur_vol can be another drive there).
Retry judges again; Fail is error 20h or 21h.  5Ch itself does not
ask INT 24h: it returns 21h, or 24h "sharing buffer exceeded" when
SHARE= has no lock left.  CMD.EXE's handler table went to 0Eh
(COMMAND.COM's already reached 0Fh); CERR_MAXCODE is 0Eh.

THE LOCK TABLE IS 1024 ENTRIES OF 16 BYTES IN _KBSS, and _KBSS was
full: 31K of buffers and the 32K cluster buffer in 64K.  KBSS_LEN is
96K now and ARENA_BASE moved up 32K with it - every use was symbolic
(KBUF_HI3, the list of lists, arena_init) and only KBSS_BASE is on
the link line, so nothing else changed; MEM's "OS Reserved" is 32K
larger.  The table starts as zeros because the segment does, and
LK_SFT = 0 is a free slot.  share_held counts the locks so that
every read and write on a machine with none costs one compare.

WHAT WENT WRONG ON THE WAY: `lock` as a label is the LOCK prefix
under wasm ("invalid instruction operands" at every call), so
SHARETST's routine is lockr; shl_end was both a label and a variable;
SHARE_MAXLK was needed by CONFIG.INC before SHARE.INC defined it
(wasm cannot forward-reference an EQU), so both limits are in
PMDOS.INC; and the CONFIG.SYS variants for the rig did nothing until
I noticed MKDISK stores a host file under its own name - CFGOFF.SYS
on the disk is not CONFIG.SYS.

VERIFIED under DOSBox-X headless.  \TESTS\SHARETST.COM (16-bit, for
2Fh/1000h): sixteen checks, all SHARE.EXE's answers - compat twice;
deny-write beside compat refused 20h with INT 24h code 0Dh; deny-
write plus deny-none read allowed, plus deny-none write refused;
3Ch on a deny-all file refused and the file still 64 bytes; two
deny-none read/write handles, lock 0-9, lock 5-14 on the other 21h
with no INT 24h, the same range again 21h, read 0-3 on the other 21h
with code 0Eh, on the locker fine, at 10 fine, after the unlock fine,
a second unlock 21h, twenty locks then 24h, a close freeing them all.
SHARE=OFF: "not installed".  SHARE=5,2048: the sixth lock is 24h.
FCBTEST, FNDTEST, HNDTEST, APITEST, EXECTST, DEVTEST and CACHETST
unchanged beside it, with SFT_LEN 64.  Images refreshed.  NOT
VERIFIED: a program actually seeing "Sharing violation reading drive
C" at CMD.EXE's prompt (the string and the table row are there; the
16-bit test answers INT 24h itself); a DPMI client's 2Fh/1000h; FCB
reads and writes against a lock (not hooked - DOS's SHARE checked
them, and it is a five-line addition at FCB.INC's file_read call if
anything ever wants it); real hardware.

CDEX.EXE: WHICH LETTER IS WHICH CD-ROM DRIVE, AND WHAT THE DRIVE IS
(2026-09-30)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The user asked for "CDEX.EXE to show current optical drives and their
associated drive letters".  CMD\CDEX\CDEX.ASM, BIN\CDEX.EXE, 1,874
bytes, no switches but /?.  Still v0.60.

WHAT MSCDEX PRINTED WHEN IT LOADED - "Drive D: = Driver MSCD001 unit
0" - is the one thing a user still wants from a program this machine
deliberately does not have (MSCDEX.INC says why: the letter is a
volume, not a redirector).  CDEX prints that as a table, one row per
drive: the letter, the unit number MSCD001 and INT 2Fh AH=15h count
it by, where it sits on the IDE bus ("secondary master"), the label
of the disc in it or "no disc", and the name the drive gave
IDENTIFY.  A unit no letter reached - LASTDRIVE too small - is a row
with "--" for a letter.  A mounted .ISO is not a drive and is not
listed; MOUNT lists those.

THE KERNEL KEPT NO NAME FOR A DRIVE, and had no native call for a CD
unit either, so three small things were added:

  ATD_MODEL, forty bytes on the end of the ATA device record (ATD_LEN
  is 64 now), written by ata_keepid for disks and packet devices
  alike out of IDENTIFY words 27-46 with each word's two bytes swapped
  back into reading order - the standard hands over "eMTA" for "MATE".
  Nothing else in the record moved; every use of ATD_LEN was symbolic.

  IOS_ATAMODEL (E4h): AL = device index, EDI -> those forty bytes.
  IOS_CDUNIT (E0h): AL = ATAPI unit -> EDX = its device index, EBX =
  its channel's base port, ECX = units there are.  This one ASKS THE
  DRIVE NOTHING - IOS_CDINFO is TEST UNIT READY and a capacity read
  and fails with the tray open, which is right for a caller about to
  read the disc and wrong for one that wants to say which drive D: is.

  21h/F1h AL=17h: DL = unit, EDI -> a CDU_LEN record (unit, device
  index, ATDF flags, transfer mode, base port, model), ECX = units.
  The record is cleared first, for fF1_disk's reason.  And - the
  lesson of the morning applied the same afternoon - it has its row
  in vdm_flags.

The letter is not in that record on purpose: it comes from the volume
table, F1h AL=6, where a DRVF_CDROM entry's DRV_BIOS is the unit
number.  Whether there is a disc is asked by MOUNTING the letter,
F1h AL=1, under a critical-error handler that answers FAIL - the same
shape as DRIVES.EXE - and the label by 4Eh with the label attribute,
which the ISO9660 reader answers out of the volume id.

ONE WRONG NUMBER ON THE WAY: the base port came out 0000h because
ata_info's EBX is the bus-master ENGINE'S base, not the channel's.
IOS_CDUNIT hands back ATD_BASE itself now.  And DOSBox-X, asked for a
second disc with `imgmount e UDFTEST.ISO -t iso -ide 2s`, silently
mounted nothing: its own ISO reader cannot parse a UDF-only image and
the mount fails without a word.  An ISO9660 image on the same line
works, so the second disc in the rig is offnt42.iso.

VERIFIED under DOSBox-X headless with two ATAPI discs (secondary
master and primary slave): CDEX lists D: unit 0 primary slave OFFNT42
and E: unit 1 secondary master LFNTEST, both "DOSBox-X ATAPI CD-ROM";
DRIVES, CDXTEST (two drives, D: E:) and CACHE's table agree; /? and
a bad parameter.  A copy of HD16.IMG with PMIO.SYS replaced in place
by FATREPL boots to the prompt with the CD-ROM line.  NOT VERIFIED:
"no disc" (the emulator cannot present an empty drive - the path is
DRIVES' "(will not mount)"), a drive on a port other than the four
standard ones (printed as the port in hex), real hardware - where
the model column will finally say what the 486's drive is.

Images refreshed: floppy built and copied to the VM; both HD16 copies
by FATREPL (PMIO.SYS, PMDOS.SYS, CDEX.EXE, AUTOEXEC.BAT, TESTS\
HELPTEST.BAT); HD32 and MULTI regenerated round a backed-up HD16.

CACHE.EXE: SMARTDRV /S FOR A CACHE THAT IS PART OF THE KERNEL
(2026-09-30)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The user asked for "DISKCACHE.EXE which provides the same output as
SMARTDRV /S on MS-DOS, detailing the current status of the built-in
disk cache".  It is CMD\CACHE\CACHE.ASM and BIN\CACHE.EXE, and the
first thing to say is WHY IT IS NOT CALLED DISKCACHE: nine letters
do not fit 8.3.  MKDISK put the first build on the disk as
DISKCACH.EXE, which is what any FAT would have done, and the batch
that typed DISKCACHE got "Bad command or file name".  CACHE matches
the CACHE= line in CONFIG.SYS that sets the thing it reports on.
DISKCACH.EXE is the other honest name and is a three-line rename.
Still v0.60.

WHAT IT PRINTS is SMARTDRV 5.02's screen, line for line, taken from
the real binary under DOSBox-X's DOS (the oracle rig from the help
verification, with SMARTDRV copied in beside COMMAND.COM).  The
number formatter there - S:\DOS6SRC\dev\smartdrv\dec_out.asm -
prints NO padding, only the digits with the country's thousands
separator; the spacing that looks like right-alignment is in the
message strings, and so it is here.  The lines that differ are
deliberate: the banner is PM-DOS's and carries the KERNEL'S version
(F1h AL=0), because the cache is the kernel; and where SMARTDRV
shows two sizes, the DOS one and the Windows one, this shows THREE -
what the cache holds now, the floor a reclaim will not cross and the
ceiling a miss may grow to - because this cache is elastic and those
are what CACHE= sets.  "Cache size while running Windows" would be
zero here (cache_park frees every chunk before RMDOS takes the
machine) and a true zero on that line reads as a bug.  The table
keeps its buffering column, always "no": there is no double-buffer
driver and nothing to be honest about except that.  A drive turned
off with '-' leaves the table rather than showing a row of noes,
which is SMARTDRV's rule too.  The floppies say write cache "no",
which is what cache_mode says; SMARTDRV under DOSBox-X said "yes"
for A: and that is its business.

THE SWITCHES are the SMARTDRV ones that still mean something for a
cache that cannot be loaded, unloaded or sized from a command line:
/S adds the element count and the hit rate; /C commits; /R commits,
empties and ZEROES THE COUNTERS, because SMARTDRV /R unloaded and
reloaded and a restart that keeps counting is not one; /X turns
write-behind off on every letter; C, C+, C- are write off, both on,
all off; /Q prints nothing; /? is the help.  Nothing is changed
until the whole line has parsed, and a letter is checked against the
cache while parsing, so a line with a mistake in it does nothing.
The order of doing is SMARTDRV's: drives, /X, the commit or the
reset, then the report - read AFTER the changes.

THE KERNEL HAD NO WAY TO ASK.  The counters were there, the INT 2Fh
AX=4A10h interface handed them out, and a native program has no
INT 2Fh: that chain is the V86 monitor's, which is why CACHETST is
sixteen-bit.  So 21h/F1h AL=16h, the function in bits 16-23 of EAX
the way 12h and 14h carry theirs: CCF_STATUS fills a CST_LEN record
at EDI (flags, element size, blocks, used, dirty, the three sizes,
64-bit hits and misses); CCF_COMMIT is dos_commit; CCF_RESET is
cache_reset; CCF_DRIVE takes a letter in DL and a CCD_* request in
DH - SMARTDRV's own 0..4 for its subfunction 3 - and answers the
CCM_* bits the letter actually gets.  The equates are in PMDOS.INC
because a program reads them.  The body of 2Fh/3 became cache_drvctl
and both callers use it; the 2Fh side still speaks in SMARTDRV's
80h/40h/FFh.

TWO THINGS THAT WENT WRONG, one of them worth remembering:

  THE FIRST RUN SAID "THE DISK CACHE IS NOT RUNNING" while CACHETST,
  in the same batch, passed all ten checks.  The status call was
  being refused, and the refusal was cbuf_ok's: EDI had arrived as
  the program's own offset, not a flat address, because the pointer
  table vdm_flags - which the ring-3 bridge reads to know which
  registers to flatten - had no row for F1h/16h.  EVERY F1h CALL
  THAT TAKES A POINTER NEEDS A ROW THERE, and a new one is refused,
  not faulted, so the symptom is a clean "no".  And this call could
  not simply take a P_DI row: only CCF_STATUS carries a pointer, and
  CCF_DRIVE with a stray EDI outside the slot would have been refused
  as a bad pointer.  r3_pflags now answers F1h/16h by hand, as it
  does 38h and 65h and for the same reason - one flag byte keyed on
  the function is wrong for at least one of the functions - and the
  table row is there for the DOS box and DPMI bridges, which do not
  fail on a stray value.

  wasm's case folding, once more: a label cst_flags in cache_status
  against the equate CST_FLAGS, "unexpected colon" at the label.
  csta_ now.  And cdv_out was already CONFIG.INC's; cdrv_ now.

AND ONE THAT WAS ALREADY WRONG: 2Fh/3's "write caching on" set only
the write bit, and cache_mode tests the read bit first - so C- then
C+ left C: uncached.  SMARTDRV's own source says write caching
implies read caching; CCD_WRON sets both now.  CACHETST's ninth and
tenth checks did not catch it because they turn write OFF and on,
never read.

VERIFIED under DOSBox-X headless on a scratch FAT16 disk: /?; the
bare report; /S with the counters moving between runs (267 hits and
25 misses, then 579 and 40); C then C+ /S, A- (row gone) then A+
(row back), /X, C+ /C /S, /R /S with the count at 0 and 0; /Q silent;
five bad lines each answered "Invalid parameter - " and the token;
CACHETST 0 failed through the refactored 2Fh path; CACHE=OFF in
CONFIG.SYS giving "The disk cache is not running." and CACHETST's
"no cache installed".  The layout diffed against SMARTDRV's own
capture with the numbers masked: identical apart from the lines
above.  Images refreshed: PMDOS.IMG built and copied to the VM, both
HD16 copies by FATREPL (PMDOS.SYS, CACHE.EXE, AUTOEXEC, CONFIG,
HELPTEST), HD32 and MULTI regenerated with HD16 backed up and
restored round MKHD.  NOT VERIFIED: real hardware; a 64-bit hit
count, which is a machine up for a day; the DOS box and DPMI bridges
calling F1h/16h, which nothing does.

THE FLOPPY HAS 616K FREE and 34 of 224 root entries used.  What was
full last time was the TESTS directory's entry count, which MKDISK
now makes 384; there is room for programs, and the pressure the user
felt is entries and tidiness rather than bytes.

FDISK HAS A SCREEN: THE DISK AS A BAR, AND THE CHANGE BEFORE IT HAPPENS
(2026-09-30)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The user asked for FDISK to be "built with a TUI so that the user can
visually see the disk and how moving a partition will look on the
drive", with the command line kept for silent use - and for MOVE.COM
to become MOVE.EXE, which is what MS-DOS calls it.  Still v0.60.

MOVE.EXE FIRST, because it is the small one.  A D32 file is known by
its first bytes and not its name, so it is a rename: BUILD.CMD,
MKHD.CMD, MVTEST.BAT and the header of MOVE.ASM say .EXE now.  The
images had MOVE.COM in their roots and a .COM is found before a .EXE,
so TOOLS\FATREPL.PL grew "-del NAME" - the chain freed and the first
byte of the entry E5h, which is how DOS deletes - and both HD16
images had it taken off.

THE SCREEN IS CMD\FDISK\FDTUI.INC, included by FDISK.ASM where the
line-at-a-time menu of v0.60 was, and it keeps the one idea that menu
was built on: A SHELL OVER THE COMMAND LINE AND NOT A SECOND
IMPLEMENTATION.  Every key fills fd_args as the command line would,
jumps to the same verb, and reads the same fd_done or fd_fail at the
end - now recorded in fd_rc.  The verbs still print, because what
they print is what a person needs to read; while the screen is up,
puts and putc put the text into cap_buf instead of on the console
(they are the only two ways this program has ever written anything),
the panel under the table shows the end of it, and V shows all of it
a screen at a time.  tui_run remembers ESP and jumps to the verb;
fd_back lands on tui_after, which is a RET, so a verb "returns" to
whoever called tui_run - the same longjmp the menu used, one
instruction longer.

WHAT IT SHOWS.  A title bar with the disk number and whether the
writes are armed (in red when they are).  The disk's geometry.  Two
bars seventy cells wide: "Now", the disk as it is, each partition a
run of cells the length of its share of the disk, drawn with its own
number and colour, containers shaded under the logical drives that
live in them, free space dotted; and "Then", empty until something is
being considered.  The table: the four slots (empty ones too - a
create needs a row to stand on), the logical drives numbered on from
5 as /L prints them, and a "free" row after them where the next
logical drive would go.  The output panel.  The keys.  A status line.

THE SECOND BAR IS THE POINT, and it is drawn from what the VERB
worked out, not from what was typed.  M and S run /M or /S as a dry
run on every change - the writes held off whatever W said - and
pl_nstart and pl_nlen, which fd_change sets before it plans, are the
proposal, on the bar in green if the engine agreed and red if it
refused, with the refusal itself in the panel.  Left and Right slide
the start (or the length) a cylinder at a time, PgUp and PgDn ten,
Home and End to the ends of the disk, a digit opens a number line
that takes sectors or 40M, Enter asks, Esc leaves.  C on an empty
slot or the free row asks the two questions the menu asked (size and
type, blank meaning "you decide"), dry-runs the create, and draws
cr_start/cr_len - or lg_start/lg_len for a logical drive - as a run
of '+' before asking.  D draws the table without the partition.  A
and B (the boot code) ask and go.  P puts the plan in the viewer, and
before a move or a resize it is run first so its limits are in the
capture, above the dry runs that follow (cap_mark is where they
start).  Tab is the next disk.

WRITES ARE ARMED AS THEY ALWAYS WERE.  Nothing writes on one key: a
change is a dry run, then Enter, then a question, and if the writes
are not armed the question says so and asks again - a yes there arms
them for that one change and no longer.  W arms them for the session.

THE COMMAND LINE.  FDISK with nothing after it is the screen, as it
has been for every FDISK since 5.0; the report those used to print is
/STATUS, which is what MS-DOS calls it (told apart from /S the way
/MBR is from /M), and /L still prints it with the chain walked.  /I
still opens the screen.  FDTEST, FDLTEST and FD32TEST say /STATUS
where they said FDISK.

TESTABLE FROM A FILE, like the menu.  FDTEST=path in the environment
turns on the key file: standard input, in EDIT's format (a byte a
key, 0 and a scan code for a grey one, FFh FFh a picture of the
screen into the path), and an input that runs out is Esc from
everything and then Q.  TOOLS\MKFDKEYS.PL writes DISK\FDM1.KEY and
says what each key is for; DISK\FDMTEST.BAT runs it and TYPEs the
pictures.  The script: the table of disk 1, F1 in the viewer, the
plan of a logical drive, a move slid two cylinders and refused (it
would run into 6), a resize of the Linux slot refused (not FAT), a
key that is not one, B and D answered no, W, D answered yes and the
table read back with slot 3 empty, C abandoned at its first
question, and C again with both answers blank: '+++' on the second
bar, and slot 3 back at 84672 + 7056, WHICH ARE THE NUMBERS THE
CHAIN-SURGERY ENTRY SAID TO KEEP.

THE BSS IS A SEGMENT OF ITS OWN, as PMDOS.SYS's is.  The screen's
buffers - 8K of capture, 4000 bytes of cells, the row table, the
viewer's line index - were zeros in the file: FDISK.EXE went from
25K to 48K and the floppy, which was full to the entry, would not
build.  A dup(?) in the CODE segment is still written by wlink's raw
output (117K, tried); a dup(?) in a second segment of the group,
ordered after CODE on the link line, is not.  fd_entry carves its
buffers from bss_start now rather than img_end, the header's BSS
field is the two lengths plus sixteen for the alignment, and the end
of FDISK.ASM will not assemble if TUI_BSS_LEN stops matching what
_FDB holds.  31,677 bytes.  And the floppy's TESTS directory was at
its 256 entries: MKDISK's SUBDIR_ENTS is 384.

WHAT WENT WRONG ON THE WAY, for the next screen written here:

  mov esi,[SLOT_PSP + PSP_ENV] is an IMMEDIATE.  A bracketed constant
  in MASM syntax is the constant, so ESI was 102Ch and the environment
  was never read, and the first run sat waiting for a key that was in
  a file.  MEM.ASM loads the address into a register and dereferences
  that; so does this now.

  fd_isext answers CF CLEAR for an extended type.  Read the other

  Three names collided with equates under wasm's case folding:

  use, as always.

THE 486 HAD 763K FREE: A BIOS THAT HANDS BACK THE CALLER'S OWN CARRY
(2026-09-29)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The third report from the 486.  MEM showed a few hundred K free on a
machine with 18MB in it, and the first guess was that EMS had taken
the rest.  It had not: EMS.INC says "one pool, three doors" and means
it - a handle's pages leave the arena when the handle is opened and
not before, and EMS=AUTO costs the arena nothing at boot.  Still
v0.60.

REPRODUCED ON 86BOX FIRST GO: the ASUS VL/I-486SV2G with mem_size =
18432 printed "Extended memory reported by the BIOS: 0 KB", an XMS
pool of 1,023K and 763K of it free.  The pool is the slack under the
kernel's own reserve and nothing else, because get_extmem had sized
the machine at nought.

WHAT THE BIOS SAID, asked by a sixteen-bit program under real MS-DOS
5 on the same board (TOOLS\MEMPROBE.ASM, new, \TESTS\MEMPROBE.COM on
every disk - it prints E801h, 88h, the E820 map and the CMOS bytes,
each of the first two entered with CF clear and again with CF set,
and is worth running on the real machine under its own 6.22):

  E801h    CF=1, AH=86h.  Not supported.  Right.
  88h      AX=4400h (17,408K) and CF WHATEVER IT WAS ON ENTRY.  Called
           with CF clear it comes back clear; called with CF set it
           comes back set.  The BIOS sets CF for an error and does not
           touch it otherwise, which is what IRET does with the flags
           the caller pushed.
  E820h    five entries, the usable one at 1MB being 1100000h long.

get_extmem asked E801h, took the CF=1 refusal to ext_88, asked 88h
WITH THAT CARRY STILL SET, and read the answer back as "CF set: no
extended memory".  Two lines of assembler and a machine with 16MB
less than it had.

IO\IORM.ASM get_extmem now:

  CLC BEFORE EVERY INT 15h.  A BIOS is entitled to leave the flag
  alone.

  88h IS JUDGED BY ITS ANSWER.  CF set means an error only when AH is
  80h or 86h, the two codes the function has; anything else with CF
  set is the caller's own flag coming back, and AX is the count.

  E820 FIRST, WHEN THERE IS A MAP.  It was collected at MEMMAP since
  the early days and nothing ever read it.  The extended memory is
  the end of the usable region that 1MB falls in, less 1MB.  That is
  the one of the three that knows about a hole at 15MB: E801h reports
  the memory either side of one as two numbers this routine would
  have added together, and the arena is one block that cannot skip a
  megabyte.  A map with no usable region at 1MB is treated as no map.

  E801h that says CF clear and counts nothing falls through to 88h
  as well.

VERIFIED.  86Box VL/I-486SV2G, 18MB: 17,408K reported, 15,899K pool,
15,123K free - and the same numbers from a scratch kernel with the
E820 and E801h paths jumped over, so the 88h path is proven on the
BIOS that broke it.  DOSBox-X memsize=18 (no E820, E801h answers):
17,408K, as before.  PMIO.SYS is the same size - the real-mode stub
is padded to 4K.  NOT VERIFIED: the real 486; a BIOS with a memory
hole.

MEM'S REPORT, UNDER THE TABLE, HAD THREE RIGHT EDGES.  The extended-
memory lines were a label padded to column 38 with the number left-
aligned after it; the expanded-memory lines were right-aligned to a
column of their own, 52, with the unit glued to the number; the page
frame was somewhere else again.  On a real screen it was hard to
read, which the user said.  Now every line under the table is a label
LINE_W wide and a number NUM_W wide, so every figure on the screen

number somebody counted.  "XMS blocks: 12 in use, 1 free" became two
lines for the same reason.  MEM /? is worded the way 6.22's is.

THE HELP SCREENS, REWORDED TO MATCH MS-DOS 6.22 (the user's work,

  SYS'S NEW SCREEN WAS DANGEROUS: "SYS [drive1:][path] drive2:" is
  what 6.22 prints, but this SYS takes ONE argument, the target, and

  SWITCHES THE PROGRAMS TAKE HAD DROPPED OFF THEIR SCREENS: EDIT's
  /R and /nnn, XCOPY's /D with no date, DIR's /C[H] and /4, GOTO's

  Typos: Sortsinput, Coppies, grahics, "Uses use of", wether,
  eivnronment, batch-paremeters, [ddrive:], Specifie, "in a batch

  Usage lines were indented two spaces on eight screens and not on
  the rest; 6.22 indents none.  None now.

v0.59 - A DISK CACHE, AND THE REGISTER CONTRACT NOBODY HAD WRITTEN
        DOWN
---------------------------------------------------------------------

DOS\CACHE.INC, new, and it is the first thing in this kernel that sits
UNDERNEATH the filesystem rather than beside it.  Everything the
machine reads or writes goes through disk_read and disk_write; those
called dio_raw; and the cache is now what stands between the two.  A
block of eight sectors - four kilobytes - with a valid bit and a dirty
bit per sector, in a hash keyed by PHYSICAL DRIVE AND ABSOLUTE LBA,
with an LRU list over the top of it.

THE KEY IS THE ARGUMENT FOR WHERE IT WENT.  A drive letter is a
volume, and several volumes share a disk; a guest's INT 13h addresses
the DISK; INT 25h and 26h are handed a letter and immediately turn it
into one; FDISK's F1h AL=0Dh and 0Eh have no letter at all.  Only at
the drive-and-LBA level does "somebody has just written sector N of
disk 80h, what do we hold that is now wrong?" have an answer - and
vol_syncdrv, which already existed for exactly that question one layer
up, grew two calls and now answers it for the cache as well.

IT IS NOT THE SAME THING AS THE CACHES IN FAT.INC, and both stay.
Those are the filesystem's working set - the FAT, the directory sector
being walked, the cluster being read - one of each, per volume, and
they exist so the filesystem does not re-read what it is in the middle
of using.  This is a general store of SECTORS shared by every volume
on every disk, and it exists so the disk is not spoken to twice for
the same sector.  A FAT sector the filesystem drops still sits here
and comes back without a transfer.

WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CACHE is as much of the design as what
it does.  A transfer of seventeen sectors or more goes straight past:
that is file data, it is read once, it would evict every piece of
metadata in the cache to hold something nobody will ask for again, and
it is already one efficient transfer.  Seventeen is chosen so that a
FAT12 FAT - sixteen sectors, the largest single thing this kernel
moves - is still cached and a cluster is not.  A big READ flushes
anything dirty underneath it first; a big WRITE drops what we hold of
those sectors, or the cache would be describing a disk that had moved
on without it.

A MISS ON AN EMPTY BLOCK READS THE WHOLE BLOCK, which is the read-
ahead and is nearly free: one command instead of one, for eight
sectors instead of one, and the seventh sector of a directory is
usually wanted right after the first.  A block that is only PARTLY
present is filled a RUN at a time over the requested range only, and
that is not an optimisation - a sector already present may be DIRTY,
and reading over the top of it would put the disk's older copy back.

WRITE CACHING, AND THE PROMISE IT IS ALLOWED TO EXIST ON
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Lazy writing is on by default for FIXED DISKS ONLY, and the deal is
that every dirty sector is on the medium before the user can type the
next command.  dos_commit is what makes that true and there are four
ways in: INT 21h AH=0Dh, which is the function DOS has always had for
this and which COMMAND.COM's get_line now calls before it prints a
prompt; INT 21h AH=4Ch, a program ending - after its handles have been
closed, so the file's length and directory entry are in the cache
before the cache is told to empty; INT 2Fh AX=4A10h BX=1; and park_go,
which is where another DOS takes the disks over entirely.

So the window in which a write exists only in memory is ONE COMMAND
long.  Turning the machine off in the middle of a command can lose
that command's writes; turning it off at the prompt cannot.  That is
the whole of what was asked for, and it is why the commit is in
get_line rather than anywhere cleverer: the prompt is the thing a user
reads as "it is finished".

dos_commit DOES THE TWO LAYERS IN ORDER and the order is not
arbitrary.  The filesystem's own caches are flushed first, once per
DISK rather than once per letter, through vol_syncdrv; those flushes
turn into writes that land in the sector cache; and the sector cache
is committed second.  The other way round would leave the
filesystem's own writes sitting here unwritten, which is the same bug
one layer down.

FLOPPIES, CD-ROMS AND LOADED BLOCK DRIVERS ARE READ-CACHED ONLY, and
there is no switch for it.  One argument covers all three and it is
about what the kernel can SEE: a diskette can be swapped between two
commands with nothing to tell us, an ATAPI drive reports a disc change
only as a failure on the next command it is given, and a block driver
is somebody else's code and may be a RAM disk or a redirector keeping
state of its own.  Holding a write for any of them means holding data
for a medium that may not be there.  Their blocks are also dropped at
every commit, which bounds a stale READ to inside one command as well
- the same window, and the most that can be promised without a disk-
change line this kernel does not have.

THE OPTICAL SIDE IS THE SAME CACHE AND NOT A SECOND ONE.  iso_rdblk
calls cache_cdread instead of IOS_CDREAD; an ATAPI unit is given a
cache drive id of F0h upwards, a range no BIOS and no loaded driver
can collide with; and a CD block is four of our sectors, so a cache
block is exactly two CD blocks, aligned.  A miss therefore reads two
and keeps the one nobody asked for, which on a disc - where reading is
almost entirely sequential - is the right guess nearly every time.
iso_chkmedia and iso_rdblk's failure path both drop that unit's blocks
when the disc changes, which is v0.36's lesson arriving again: a cache
is exactly the thing that stops a change being noticed, and the more
blocks it holds the longer the old disc goes on answering.

VERIFY DEFEATS LAZY WRITING WHILE IT IS ON, because 21h/2Eh asks for a
write to be read back and there is nothing to read back until the
sector has been written.  One comparison in the write path, and it
keeps dio_verify honest.

THE MEMORY IS A RANGE AND NOT A SIZE
---------------------------------------------------------------------

CACHE=max[,min[,ON|OFF]] in CONFIG.SYS, sizes in kilobytes with an
optional K or M suffix, and CACHE=OFF to have none.  Absent, both
bounds come from the size of the arena - an eighth of it for the
ceiling, a quarter of that for the floor, clamped to [256K, 8M] and
[64K, 512K] - and there is NO CACHE AT ALL below two megabytes of
arena, because there the memory is wanted for programs.

THAT FLOOR IS EXACTLY THE MACHINE IN README.md.  The arena starts at
261000h, above the page tables, so a four-megabyte 386 - the stated
minimum for this project - has about 1.6MB of it and gets no cache and
loses no memory to one.  The rule was not chosen to produce that
answer, but it is the answer it produces, and it is the right one: a
cache on the smallest machine PM-DOS claims to run on would be taking
memory from the only programs that machine can still hold.

The cache buys memory in 64K chunks and it can hand chunks back.  It
grows on a miss while the arena is comfortable and - this is the part
that matters - ARENA_ALLOC ASKS IT FOR MEMORY BACK before it reports
that there is none.  So a program that wants sixteen megabytes gets
them: the cache shrinks to its floor, dirty blocks flushed on the way
out, and the allocation that would have failed succeeds because the
walk starts again from the bottom of the arena.  The floor is never
crossed, because a cache that can be reduced to nothing is one that
quietly stops existing on the machine that needed it most.

TWO SMALL THINGS IN ARENA.INC MAKE THAT WORK.  aa_asked bounds the
reclaim to once per request, so a failure cannot loop.  aa_probe is
the more interesting one: arena_avail asks for more memory than any
machine has, on purpose, so that the refusal comes back carrying the
largest block it found - and without a flag saying "this is a question
and not a need", every caller asking how much memory there is would
make the cache give some up to answer.  Including cache_addchunk,
which asks before it grows: the cache would have shrunk itself in
order to decide whether it could expand.

AND THE GROWTH TEST IS THE CHEAP ONE ON PURPOSE.  cache_addchunk has
to walk the whole arena to find out whether a chunk can be spared, so
asking on every miss would put a walk of the memory map in front of
every sector the machine reads.  A cache with an empty block in it
does not need another one, so cache_used is compared against
cache_nblk first and the expensive question is asked sixteen times per
chunk - once each time the cache genuinely fills up.

SMARTDRV'S INTERFACE, ANSWERED BY THE KERNEL
---------------------------------------------------------------------

INT 2Fh AX=4A10h, in the V86 monitor's own 2Fh chain beside XMS, DPMI
and MSCDEX, and the argument for it is MSCDEX.INC's word for word:
what programs need is the API, not the program.  SMARTDRV.EXE's own
start-up makes this call and exits if somebody answers, so answering
it stops a second cache being loaded on top of this one - two caches
holding two versions of one sector being exactly the failure the whole
file exists to avoid.

The numbers are not invented.  S:\DOS6SRC\dev\smartdrv\ is SMARTDRV
4.0 itself, and its int2f.asm carries the register conventions in a
header block: BX=0 statistics, with AX=BABEh, DX:BX hits, DI:SI
misses, CX dirty elements and BP the version in BCD; BX=1 commit; BX=2
commit and invalidate; BX=3 per-drive caching with the unit in BP and
the function in DL; BX=4 element size and count; BX=6 stop caching a
drive.  S:\DOS6SRC\c6ers\smartmon\int2f.asm is the same interface from
the CALLER'S side, and it settled the question that mattered most:
SMARTMON's commit_cache is INT 21h AH=0Dh and nothing else, which is
Microsoft agreeing that disk reset is where a cache commits.

BX=5 AND BX=7 ARE NOT ANSWERED and go down the chain.  Both hand the
caller something about a DEVICE DRIVER - the double-buffering driver,
and the original block device a cached drive was stacked on top of -
and there is neither here: this cache is not a driver stacked on a
driver, it is the block layer itself.  A synthetic answer would invite
a program to call a strategy routine that does not exist, which is the
reasoning that leaves MSCDEX 1501h chained.

BX=2's RESIZE HALF IS NOT HONOURED, and neither is it in SMARTDRV 4.0
- its source says so and says why.  Here the reason is different and
simpler: the size of this cache is the arena's business and CACHE='s,
and a program re-sizing it behind the user's back is undoing a
CONFIG.SYS line.

THE PER-DRIVE ANSWER IS THE EFFECTIVE ONE and not the permission.
cache_drvst is what the API has been TOLD about a unit; cache_mode is
what actually happens to it, which also depends on what kind of drive
it is and on whether lazy writing is on at all.  A program asking
whether A: is write-cached wants to hear no, and hearing yes because
nobody had explicitly disabled it would be a lie it acts on.

THE BUG, AND IT IS THE SAME BUG AS THE ONE ABOVE dio_verify
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The first boot with the cache in reached C:\> perfectly, printed the
first line of AUTOEXEC.BAT TO THE SCREEN although it was redirected to
a file, created that file with nothing in it, and then the batch
simply stopped.  Three symptoms, one cause, and the cause was in none
of them.

cache_io went into dio_try where dio_raw had been, and dio_raw
PRESERVES EVERY REGISTER: the block layer runs inside a pushad and the
service table is called through a pointer.  disk_read and disk_write
inherited that guarantee without ever stating it, and their callers
rely on it - fat_flush counts the FAT copies it still owes in ESI
ACROSS the call, and fat_secflush does the same.  A routine underneath
them that works in ESI turns that two-iteration loop into one that
never ends and writes the FAT across the whole disk.

Which is exactly what had happened.  The root directory and the FAT
were being rewritten underneath the batch file that was being read out
of them, so the file COMMAND.COM was reading line by line stopped
having a cluster chain.  Every symptom was downstream of that and not
one of them pointed at it.

IT IS THE IDENTICAL BUG TO THE ONE THIS FILE ALREADY DESCRIBES, one
level further down and arrived at from the other side.  v0.42's was a
PUSH somebody forgot to add around dio_verify; this one was a whole
new file that assumed the contract was "clobber what you like",
because nothing had ever written the contract down.  It is written
down now, in the header above cache_io, and cache_io is a six-push
wrapper round cache_iobody so that the body can stay readable.

The general form, for the next time: A ROUTINE THAT REPLACES ANOTHER
ROUTINE INHERITS ITS CALLERS' ASSUMPTIONS, INCLUDING THE ONES NOBODY
WROTE DOWN.  "What does the thing I am replacing promise?" is a
question with an answer, and the answer is not always in a comment.

THE OTHER THINGS THAT HAD TO BE THOUGHT ABOUT
---------------------------------------------------------------------

RE-ENTRANCY, and there are two write-back paths because of it.
cache_io is called FROM dio_try, which keeps the transfer it may have
to retry in the dio_ statics; anything this file did that ended up
back in disk_write would overwrite them and the outer retry would then
repeat the wrong transfer.  So cache_wbsilent, which runs from inside
cache_io, goes to dio_raw, raises nothing, and on a failure leaves the
block dirty and sets cache_error; cache_wbloud, which runs from
cache_commit at the top of a DOS call, goes through disk_wrsure and
raises the ordinary critical error.  A sector that will not write
stays dirty, is tried again, and the user is told about it at the
commit - which is where they are told about everything else that went
wrong during the command.

disk_wrsure IS NEW AND IS disk_write WITHOUT THE ISO GUARD.  That
guard asks whether the CURRENT volume is an ISO one, which is the
right question for everything coming down through fat_* and the wrong
one for a cache: a commit can perfectly well happen while the current
drive is the CD-ROM, and dirty blocks on the hard disk must not stop
being written because of where the user last typed a CD command.

DIRTY BLOCKS ARE NEVER EVICTED ON A MISS, which is what keeps
cache_get out of disk_write.  The watermark flush runs at the TOP of
cache_io, before any block of the transfer has been touched and while
nothing of ours is half finished; eviction then takes the oldest CLEAN
block, and a cache that has somehow become entirely dirty simply
refuses and the transfer goes to the disk uncached.

THE SWEEPS THAT DROP BLOCKS WALK THE CHUNKS AND NOT THE LRU LIST.
cache_unhook MOVES a block to the LRU end, so a walk that read the
next pointer afterwards would have had the list rewritten underneath
it - and, worse, would revisit blocks it had already moved.  Sweeps
that only WRITE blocks back leave the order alone and do walk the
list, oldest first, because the oldest dirty block is the one whose
coalescing is over.

A BLOCK CAN STRADDLE THE EDGE OF A RANGE and the two halves of it need
opposite treatment.  cache_droprange is the after-somebody-else's-
write call: sectors inside the range have been superseded and our
dirty copy of them is obsolete, but sectors OUTSIDE it are still the
only copy in the machine and dropping the block whole would lose a
write the filesystem believes it has made.  Eight sectors either side
of a boundary is not a rare case - a bulk write starts wherever the
caller's cluster starts.

A FAILED WRITE-THROUGH FORGETS WHAT IT WAS HOLDING.  Keeping it would
mean a later read of those sectors answering with bytes the disk has
never seen: the program is told its write failed and then shown the
new data anyway, which is worse than the failure.  The exception is
the sectors that were already DIRTY from an earlier lazy write, which
are left for the commit to argue with - dropping those would throw
away a write silently.

PARKING FLUSHES EVERYTHING NOW, and it did not before.  park_go called
fat_flush, which empties the LOADED volume's FAT cache and says
nothing about the other letters on the same disk; it calls dos_commit
instead.  On the way back park_recover drops the sector cache BEFORE
park_remount, because park_remount mounts, mounting reads, and a read
served out of blocks describing the disk as RMDOS found it would mount
the volume that used to be there.

AND THE CACHE GIVES ITS MEMORY AWAY FOR THE WHOLE EXCURSION, which is
the answer to "what happens to this under Windows" and was a
REGRESSION until it was written.  Parking hands the machine to
RMDOS.SYS: this kernel is not executing, the cache is not idle but
unreachable, and memory it goes on holding is memory nothing can use.
park_xmsgrab sizes the pool it hands over as "the largest free block
in the arena, less 128K" - so until cache_park existed, WINDOWS GOT
LESS EXTENDED MEMORY THAN IT DID BEFORE THERE WAS A CACHE AT ALL.

Worse than the cache's own size, too.  Chunks are bought 64K at a time
and land wherever first-fit puts them, so a cache holding half a
megabyte can cut the largest CONTIGUOUS run by several times that -
and arena_avail measures the run, not the total.  A cache that makes
Windows smaller is not paying for itself.

So cache_park commits both layers and frees every chunk, and it runs
BEFORE park_xmsreclaim so that the pool is measured against an arena
the cache has already left.  cache_unpark buys the floor back, and it
runs after park_release rather than inside park_recover, because
inside park_recover the pool is still allocated and the arena would
look full.  It is on the shared exit path so that a park which FAILED
gets its cache back too.

cache_on IS NOT TOUCHED BY EITHER, and that is deliberate: cache_on is
the USER'S setting out of CONFIG.SYS, and a park must not look like a
CACHE=OFF that nothing ever undoes.  What keeps the cache out of the
way meanwhile is that cache_get tests cache_nblk before it will
consider growing, so an emptied cache stays empty until somebody asks
it to buy chunks again.

WHICH SETTLES THE QUESTION FOR ALL THREE WINDOWS MODES.  Standard mode
parks, so the cache is suspended and Windows runs on an unbuffered
RMDOS exactly as it did before v0.59 - rd_rdsec and rd_wrsec go
straight to INT 13h and RMDOS has no cache of its own.  386 enhanced
mode is vetoed at 1605h and would have to be let in the same way
EMM386 does it, which is this same handover, so the same answer holds.
Real mode is not a thing Windows 3.1 still has.  The cache therefore
helps everything up to the moment WIN is typed and everything after
the moment Windows exits, and is absent in between - which is the
right trade while the machine underneath Windows is RMDOS.

AND CHECKING THAT FIX FOUND THE WORSE BUG UNDERNEATH IT, which is the
second time in this release that a number not adding up was worth more
than the thing it was printed for.

After a park, CACHETST said the cache had 0080h blocks - 512K, its
floor, bought back exactly as intended - and MEM said the arena had
138K allocated in it.  Both cannot be true.  138K is vol_slotp and
nothing else, so the cache was reporting memory it did not have.

arena_alloc STAMPS EVERY BLOCK WITH [cur_own], AND 4Ch SWEEPS THE
ARENA BY OWNER.  The cache grows on a MISS, and a miss happens inside
whatever program caused the I/O - so every chunk bought after boot
belonged to that program and was freed out from under the cache when
it exited.  The cache went on using it: descriptors, LRU links and
four kilobytes of payload per block, in memory the arena had already
handed to somebody else.

NOTHING HAD SHOWN IT because the floor was safe BY ACCIDENT.
cache_init runs before the shell exists, when cur_own is still zero,
and owner zero is the kernel's and is never swept - so on a machine
where the tests never filled 128 blocks, every chunk the cache owned
was a boot-time one and the bug had no way to appear.  The park test
was the first thing to make cache_addchunk run inside a program's
ownership, and even then it did not crash: it printed two numbers that
disagreed.

The fix is four lines - cur_own saved, zeroed, restored round the
allocation - and the lesson is about the test rather than the code: A
SELF-REPORT IS NOT EVIDENCE.  CACHETST asks the cache how many blocks
it has and the cache answers from its own counter, which is precisely
the thing that was wrong.  MEM asks the ARENA, which is a different
witness with no stake in the answer, and that is the only reason the
two could be compared at all.  Every check in this release that found
something was of that shape.

IF CACHING UNDER WINDOWS IS EVER WANTED it is a second implementation
and not a reuse, and the shape of it is worth writing down now.  It
would have to live in RMDOS.SYS - 16-bit real-mode code in the HMA
with a few kilobytes to spare - with its buffers in XMS reached
through the driver rather than as flat pointers into the arena.  And
it should be READ-ONLY: the disk Windows is writing its swap file
through is the last place to put a write-back cache, which is exactly
why SMARTDRV grew the smart_win_access structure - accessing_swap_
file, enhanced_mode_flags, delay_write_drive_unit - so that Windows
could tell it "this write is the pagefile, do not hold it".  Caching a
pagefile is caching memory in memory.  The same source also shows
SMARTDRV RESIZING itself on the 1605h/1606h broadcasts, for the reason
cache_park exists: Windows wants the memory more than the cache does.

WHAT IS VERIFIED
---------------------------------------------------------------------

DOSBox 0.74, 32MB of RAM, booting IMAGES\HD16.IMG with IMAGES\MULTI.
IMG as the second disk - seven volumes, FAT12 and FAT16, primaries and
logicals.  TOOLS\CACHETST.ASM is new and is SIXTEEN-BIT for CDXTEST's
reason: the interface lives in the V86 monitor's 2Fh chain and a
native program cannot reach it at all.  Ten checks, all passing:

  4A10/0000 installed?    OK        version 04.00
  4A10/0004 element size  1000 bytes x 0080
  does it really cache?   OK        hits AND misses both moved
  21h/0Dh commits         OK
  a write is owed         0005      dirty blocks after a closed file
  4A10/0001 commits       OK
  C: read+write cached    r+w+ OK
  A: read cached only     r+w- OK
  write caching off on C: r+w- OK
  ...and on again         r+w+ OK

The third of those is the one worth having: a cache that answers the
interface politely and does not actually cache passes every other
check in the program.  The fifth is the other one: five dirty blocks
after a file has been created, written AND CLOSED is the write cache
doing its job, and a zero there would have meant every write went
straight through.

WHAT IS NEXT
---------------------------------------------------------------------
  - flush coalescing stops at the block boundary.  Eight consecutive
    dirty sectors leave as one four-kilobyte transfer, which is eight
    times better than a sector at a time, but two adjacent blocks are
    still two commands.  Crossing that boundary needs the data staged
    into a contiguous buffer, because two cache blocks are not next to
    each other in memory
  - a floppy's cached blocks expire at each commit, which is a
    conservative guess rather than a fact.  INT 13h AH=16h is the disk
    change line and would turn the guess into an answer, on the
    machines whose BIOS implements it
  - MEM reports zero buffers, which is still the true answer about
    BUFFERS= - but there is now a cache above the megabyte with a size
    worth reporting, and nothing reports it


v0.58 - FILE MANAGER LISTS THE DISK, AND THE SEARCH THAT COULD NOT
        MATCH ANYTHING
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Windows 3.1's File Manager comes up on PM-DOS with a drive bar, a
tree pane holding C:\ and WINDOWS under it, and a file pane holding
the ninety-eight files that are in the root - "Total 98 file(s)
(723,868 bytes)", and 25,411KB free of 32,580KB, which is the image.
That is the second of the two things v0.57 left, and it turned out to
be TWO bugs stacked on top of each other, neither of which was in the
directory walk.

THE INSTRUMENT CAME FIRST, AND IT SHOULD HAVE THE RELEASE BEFORE THE
BUGS DO.  The v0.45 notes say in as many words that RMDOS's 4Eh and
4Fh went in "written and untested", and the first program ever to call
them was a graphical shell that draws an empty box when it does not
like the answer.  So: TOOLS\RMFIND.ASM, RMFIND.COM, the second program
in the tree that runs with no PM-DOS underneath it.  PARKTEST parks
the kernel and RMDOS answers it, exactly as for RMTEST, and it asks
the four questions File Manager asks:

  1. enumerate the root, count it, and keep the names
  2. a plain search must return no directories
  3. enumerate a subdirectory, which is a different path through
     dir_first and dir_next because a root is a fixed run of sectors
     and a subdirectory is a FAT chain
  4. TWO SEARCHES AT ONCE - start one, take two entries, run a whole
     second search to exhaustion in a different DTA, then point 1Ah
     back at the first and ask for the next entry

It found both bugs in one boot of forty seconds, and it prints its
answers, which a shell cannot.  Run it with PARKTEST \RMFIND.COM; the
line is in AUTOEXEC.BAT, commented out.

FIRST BUG: THE SEARCH TEMPLATE COULD NOT MATCH ANY FILE THAT EXISTS.
RMFIND's first check came back "the root holds 0002 - the search would
not start", which is not a resume problem or a walk problem: 4Eh
itself failed, on \*.*, in a root with ninety-eight files in it.

rd_name83 turns one path component into the eleven bytes everything
below it compares - "readme.txt" into "README  TXT" - and IT HAD NO
IDEA WHAT AN ASTERISK WAS.  It copied it.  "*.*" came out as an
asterisk, seven spaces, an asterisk, two spaces, and ff_match then
looked for a file with an asterisk in its name, of which there are
none, in any directory, ever.  Every search in RMDOS returned "no more
files" on its first call.  '?' was handled - ff_match has always had
the wildcard compare - so the machinery was all there and was being
fed a template that could never match.

An asterisk fills the rest of ITS OWN FIELD with question marks and
nothing else: "*.*" is "???????????" and "A*.T*" is "A???????T??".
Two four-line insertions, one in the base loop and one in the
extension loop, and the count went from 0002-and-fail to sixty-four
entries with COMMAND.COM first.

WHY IT SURVIVED THIRTEEN RELEASES: rd_name83's OTHER caller is
rd_path, resolving a path in order to OPEN it, and a path you are
opening has no wildcards in it.  Every test that had ever run through
that routine ran through the half of it that was right.  It is the
v0.48 lesson again - what nobody exercised was not a feature but a
shape of argument - and this time the untested shape was one
character.

SECOND BUG, AND IT IS THE ONE THE SYMPTOM WAS NAMED AFTER.  With the
template fixed, three of RMFIND's four checks passed and the fourth
said: "4Fh lost the first search, error 0002".

DOS KEEPS A SEARCH GOING IN THE CALLER'S DTA - the twenty-one bytes in
front of the result - and that is not an implementation detail
programs are unaware of.  It is the ONLY reason a program can have two
searches open at once.  File Manager's ReadDirLevel is built on it: it
enumerates a directory, recurses into every subdirectory it finds, and
then carries on with the outer FindNext.  RMDOS kept the search in one
set of globals, so the outer walk died the moment the inner one
started, and a tree read that way comes back with nothing in it.

The cruel part is that ff_fill had been WRITING those twenty-one bytes
since the day it was written, with a comment promising that "a program
that copies them about is entitled to expect 4Fh to carry on from
wherever it put them back".  fn4F read the globals.  The promise was
never kept and the bytes were decoration.  An instrument that says
something true and a routine that acts on something else is worse than
having neither, because the comment reads as a test that passed.

fn4F now calls ff_seek, which picks the search up out of the DTA.  The
layout is DOS's where DOS's is fixed - drive at 00h, the eleven-byte
template at 01h, the search attribute at 0Ch - and this kernel's where
it has to be, because RMDOS walks a directory by absolute sector and
wants a 32-bit cluster for FAT32:

  0Dh word   the entry's offset in its sector
  0Fh dword  the cluster the walk is standing in (0 = a fixed root)
  13h word   which sector of that cluster

EVERYTHING ELSE IS DERIVED RATHER THAN STORED.  The absolute LBA, the
sectors left in the cluster, whether this is a fixed root: ff_seek
gets them by calling dir_first on the stored cluster and then walking
forward the stored number of sectors, which is the same code that set
them in the first place.  There is no second copy to go stale, and it
is what makes the state fit: cluster-plus-index is six bytes where
LBA-plus-cluster-plus-count-plus-flag is thirteen, and DOS leaves
twenty-one.  ff_secidx is the other half, and it derives the index the
same way - dir_first sets the count for the whole unit and dir_next
counts it down, so what is LEFT says how far in we are, for a fixed
root and a cluster alike.

AND IT FIXED A THIRD THING NOBODY HAD NOTICED.  The old header wrote a
dword at 12h, which puts its top byte at 15h - where the found file's
ATTRIBUTE goes.  It got away with it for as long as it did because the
attribute was written immediately afterwards and overwrote the damage.
The new header ends exactly at 14h, which is where DOS's ends.

Also: 4Eh now records the drive the search is ON, from rd_path, rather
than the process's current drive.  Those are the same number for most
programs and are not for a program that enumerates D: while standing
on C:, which is a thing a file manager does with a drive bar.

MEASURED, on 86Box (Pentium II 450 / 440BX), release build:

  before  the root holds 0002 - the search would not start
  after   the root holds 0040 entries, first is COMMAND.COM       ok
          the attribute rule: 00 directories in a plain search     ok
          4Eh in a subdirectory \WINDOWS\*.* 002F entries          ok
          two searches at once: the third entry should be
            LFNAPI.COM and 4Fh gave LFNAPI.COM                     ok

0040 is RMFIND's own cap, not the directory's end.  002F is 47, and
that is the number to check rather than admire: \WINDOWS holds 43
files, SYSTEM, TEMP, '.' and '..'.  The subdirectory walk is right
down to the last entry, chain and all.

REGRESSIONS, all on the release build with both fixes in.  RMTEST's
nine checks pass, including the two that go through rd_name83 for a
name with no wildcard in it - PMIO.SYS opens and starts E9AB, CON
opens by name and answers 80D3 - and the kernel still opens a file
after the unpark.  PARKEXEC runs its three programs with "failures:
00" and unparks.  HNDTEST grants 003C handles and opens 0032 files
before the table runs out.  Nothing in the kernel's own file system
was touched: rd_name83 and ff_* are RMDOS's, and PM-DOS parses its own
paths in PATH.INC.

HOW THE WINDOWS RUN WAS DRIVEN, because it matters that this was not a
keystroke.  v0.57's harness lesson was that keybd_event is only valid
on an idle desktop and there is no way to tell from inside the run
that it was not - and on the first attempt here the Enter that should
have launched File Manager off Program Manager's first icon simply did
not arrive.  So the run was driven from Windows' own configuration
instead: `run=winfile.exe` in WIN.INI, which is the line that exists
for starting a program with the shell.  Stock shell (progman.exe),
stock binaries, one INI line, no keystrokes, and the result does not
depend on what else the host was doing.  An earlier run with
shell=winfile.exe in SYSTEM.INI gave the identical listing.  Nothing
in the Windows directory has been patched, on this release or any
other; S:\WIN31HD is untouched and the edited copy was made in a
scratch directory.

TOOLING.  TOOLS\FATPUT.PL is now IN THE TREE.  It is the script the
whole Windows workflow rests on - it is what puts \WINDOWS into
HD16.IMG, and MKHD.CMD rewrites that image every time, so it runs on
every single Windows test - and it has been living in a session
scratch directory since v0.51, one cleanup away from being gone.  The
order is still MKHD first, graft second, and the way to tell you got
it wrong is the "next free cluster" line: 7171 means one graft onto a
fresh image, 13432 means you have grafted onto an image that already
had a WINDOWS in it.

WHAT IS STILL WRONG.  EXITING Windows resets the machine.  Alt-F4 on
Program Manager, OK, and three seconds later the video BIOS banner is
back and an environment variable set before WIN is gone.  That is
v0.59's, and it is unchanged by this release: it is about handing a
machine back to a 32-bit kernel after the extender has had it.

AND THE NEXT THING IN THIS CORNER, written down because RMFIND is the
tool that would test it: RMDOS's 41h delete, 56h rename and 3Ch create
all resolve their path through rd_path, which uses dir_find, which
compares eleven bytes exactly.  A wildcard reaches them now as '?'
where it used to reach them as '*' - neither matches, so nothing
changed and nothing regressed - but "DEL *.TXT" from a DOS box under
Windows will fail rather than delete, and File Manager's own file
operations go the same way.  Real DOS refuses a wildcard on create and
EXPANDS one on delete.  Neither is done here.


v0.57 - A WINDOWS TASK CAN END NOW, AND THE FRAME IT ENDS ON IS NOT
        THE ONE DOS WOULD HAVE PICKED
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Escape on the Task List closes the Task List.  Clipboard Viewer starts
from Program Manager, runs, and exits back to it.  Both of those are
new, and both are the same one-word bug.

WHAT v0.56 LEFT.  Pressing Escape ended the Windows session: the first
task to call 4Ch got as far as its own reflector, made eight more DOS
calls, and then DOSX printed

  Standard Mode: Fault in MS-DOS Extender.
  EC=200C CS=0053 IP=4C18 AX=160C BX=0000 CX=4C00 DX=0D2F
  SI=0FEC DI=200F BP=2332 DS=004B ES=0000 SS=004B SP=2334

byte for byte the same on every run and on every build, and exited
4CFF.  The recorded next step was to MEASURE it rather than guess, and
that is what this release is.

THE INSTRUMENT FIRST, because the old one could not survive its own
subject.  The lptfz trace build stalls at the splash screen at DOS
call 113 - it writes the whole 8K buffer to the disk every 32 calls,
and Windows makes two and a half thousand - so nothing about a fault
at the END of a session was ever visible to it.  lptq is the same
trace with DBG_QUIET, which was written to answer a different question
and was left described as "its answer is a screenshot, not a trace".
That was wrong: rdbg_maybe returns early under DBG_QUIET but rdbg_mark
does not, and rd_goback sets RDBGM_BACK, so the ring is written ONCE,
at the unpark, after everything has happened.  That is a whole session
at release speed - 2547 INT 21h calls, Program Manager in a hundred
and seventy seconds - with the last 273 of them on the disk.  The
build that could not reach the desktop and the build that traces the
fault were the same build with one flush removed.

WHAT IT SHOWED.  The last calls before the extender faults are

  2522  AX=5500 BX=363F CX=0100 DX=41D2   build TASKMAN a PSP
  2531  AX=5027 BX=41D2                   make it current
  2532  AX=5100                           and check          (0DA5:02C0)
  2533  AX=4C00 BX=363F CX=0000 DX=41D2   terminate          (0DA5:0324)
  2534  AX=3E57 BX=0008                   close a handle
  2535  AX=1A2F                           set the DTA
  2536  AX=3D80 -> 0007                   open MMSOUND.DRV
  2537  AX=4200 / 2538 AX=3F00            seek and read it
  2539  AX=0953 / 2540 AX=0924            "Fault in MS-DOS Extender"
