Every one of them answered, none of them refused, nothing out of
memory and nothing out of handles.  The DOS side of that session is
clean.  So the fault is not in an ANSWER, it is in the HANDOVER, and
rdbg_term was extended to record it: the stack out of the parent's
PSP, the stack out of the child's, and the twenty-six bytes actually
lying at the parent's, copied before the terminate address is patched
into them.

  first terminate: PSP 41D2, parent 363F, terminate address 0DA5:0324
  resumed on the PARENT's stack 097A:2320; the 4Ch's own frame was
  097A:231E   <- A DIFFERENT FRAME
  frame there: ...0FEC 2332 363F 41D2 0000 4C00 0324 0DA5 3202...

TWO BYTES.  Read the same bytes one word lower and they are the 4Ch's
own frame exactly - AX=4C00, BX=363F, CX=0000, DX=41D2, and 0DA5:0324
where the return address goes.  Read them where RMDOS reads them and
every register is one slot out of step, and the extender's fault dump
says so: SI=0FEC, BP=2332 and CX=4C00 are in it because they are what
came off that frame.  Windows was handed back its own stack shifted by
a word and carried it for eight DOS calls before something noticed.

AND DOS'S RULE IS RIGHT FOR THE CASE DOS HAS.  reset_environment
(msctrlc.asm) resumes the parent on PDB_user_stack out of the PARENT's
PSP, and PDB_user_stack is stamped with the caller's SS:SP on every
INT 21h - msdisp.asm, three instructions after InDos goes up.  For a
child that was EXECed that is exactly the right frame: the parent is
standing inside a 4Bh that has never returned, and its stamp IS that
call.  The parent comes back as if the EXEC had returned, which is
what EXEC is documented to do.

WINDOWS DOES NOT EXEC ITS TASKS.  It builds a PSP with 55h, makes it
current with 50h, and calls 4Ch itself, on its own stack, in its own
code.  The parent it names has no outstanding call at all: its stamp
is whatever DOS call it last made on its own account - here the 50h
two instructions earlier, from a routine two bytes shallower - and
resuming there hands the task a frame that belongs to nothing.

So the question is not "the parent's stack or the child's".  It is
WHETHER THE PARENT IS WAITING IN A CALL, and RMDOS is the only thing
in the machine that knows.  It now records the PSP of every INT 21h it
is still inside, one per nesting level (rd_stkpsp, RMDOS.ASM), and
term_common asks whether the call enclosing this one was made by the
process named at PSP+16h.  If it was, the parent is waiting in it and
DOS's rule applies unchanged.  If it was not - and for a Windows task
the enclosing call is WIN.COM's EXEC of the extender, nothing to do
with this - the terminate is a PLAIN RETURN: the dying process's own
frame, its own registers, its own SP, with the terminate address in
place of the return address.

That is one comparison and it is the whole fix.  Escape on the Task
List closes the Task List and Program Manager is still there.  Ctrl-Esc
and Escape three times over, and it is still there.  Clipboard Viewer
starts, paints, and closes on Alt-F4, and Program Manager comes back
with the selection where it left it.  A Windows program has started and
exited on this DOS.

AND THE HANDLE TABLE, WHICH WAS WRONG TOO AND WAS NOT THIS.  The same
measurement counted what the clean-up did: EIGHTEEN handles closed at
TASKMAN's exit, every one of them the shell's.  DOS closes none of
them, and the reason is in CreateCopy's dup loop - SFFromHandle is
asked about every entry it has just copied and -1 is stored for
anything closed, marked sf_no_inherit, or a network FCB.  WINDOWS
OPENS EVERY FILE IT LOADS WITH MODE 80h, which is the no-inherit bit,
so on real DOS a task's PSP inherits the standard handles and nothing
else.  fn55 now asks the same question and stores FFh for the same
cases; the count went from eighteen to five, which is exactly the five
a task should have.  It did not change the fault by one register -
measured, same build, same run - so it is a correctness fix and not
the cause, and it is worth saying plainly that it was the lead this
project had written down as the likely one.

WHAT IS STILL WRONG.  EXITING Windows still resets the machine.  Alt-F4
on Program Manager, OK, and three seconds later the Voodoo3 BIOS banner
is on the screen and an environment variable set before WIN is gone -
so it is a reset, not an unpark, and that was checked rather than
assumed.  That is a different bug from this one: it is about handing a
machine back to a 32-bit kernel after the extender has had it, not
about a task ending inside a session.  File Manager still lists an
empty directory.  Those two are v0.58's.

REGRESSIONS, all on the release build with the fix in.  PARKTEST/RMTEST
nine checks pass, the excursion ends normally and PM-DOS still opens a
file afterwards.  PARKEXEC runs its three programs - HELLO.COM, a
relocated HELLOX.EXE with its own stack exiting through 4Ch, and a
NOSUCH.COM that must fail cleanly - with "failures: 00", and unparks;
that is the EXEC path through the new comparison twice over and it is
the test that would have caught it choosing the wrong frame.  HNDTEST
grants sixty handles.  Nothing in the Windows directory has been
patched, on this release or any other.

TOOLING.  RMTRACE.PL grew the handover report and lost two lines that
had been printing noise for three releases: "table:" read the INT 2Fh
ring and "open in the SFT:" read the string ring, neither of which is
what its label said.  Nobody was misled because nobody believed them,
which is the worst way for an instrument to be wrong.

v0.56 - THINGS IN WINDOWS RUN, AND TERMINATION BECOMES A PROPERTY OF
        THE PROCESS RATHER THAN OF RMDOS
---------------------------------------------------------------------

FILE MANAGER RUNS.  Select its icon in Main, press Enter, and thirty
seconds later WINFILE.EXE is on the screen with a drive bar from A to
H, C highlighted, and a status line that says "C: 25,415KB free,
32,580KB total" - which is the right answer for this image, so the
free-space call and the drive table come through the park correctly.
That is the first program other than the shell to run on this DOS
under Windows.

...AND ITS DIRECTORY LISTING IS EMPTY.  The tree pane shows c:\ and
nothing under it; the file pane says "No files found."; the status
line says "Total 1 file(s) (0 bytes)".  The root of that disk has a
hundred files and a WINDOWS directory in it.  So the enumeration
calls - 4Eh and 4Fh with a DTA - answer wrongly, or answer once and
then stop, and that is the next thing to find.  The trace shows a
4E17h during the EXEC of WINFILE that returned carry clear, so it is
not that 4Eh is missing.

DRIVING WINDOWS AT ALL.  scratchpad\keys86.ps1 is new and is what made
any of this possible: named keys rather than a typed line, so that
Ctrl+Esc, Ctrl+F6, the arrow keys and Escape can be sent.  Two traps
in it, both of which cost a run each:

  SCAN CODES, NOT VIRTUAL KEYS.  86Box reads the keyboard through raw
  input, and a raw input record carries the MakeCode - which for an
  injected event with wScan = 0 is ZERO.  keybd_event(vk, 0, ...) put
  the 86Box window in the foreground, and the window said it was in
  the foreground, and the guest never saw a key.  MapVirtualKey turns
  the VK back into the set-1 code the emulated 8042 is waiting for and
  everything works.

  AND POWERSHELL FOLDS CASE IN VARIABLE NAMES.  $KMAP for the table
  and $vk for the code out of it are ONE VARIABLE: the first lookup
  replaced the table with an integer and the second died in
  ContainsKey.  This is the same trap as wasm folding n_ini into
  N_INI, in a different language, in the same afternoon.

WHAT THE TASK LIST DID.  Ctrl+Esc runs TASKMAN.EXE - a whole DOS
process, EXECed nowhere, with a PSP that Windows builds itself - and
pressing Escape ends it.  On the release build that reset the machine,
three times out of three.  Under the trace build it did not reset; it
froze, which is what RMDOS_FREEZE does at rd_goback, and the trace
said why:

  2797  AX=5500 ... DX=4206     a PSP for TASKMAN, made with 55h
  2803  AX=502F BX=4206         ...made current
  2805  AX=4C00                 ...and terminated
  2806+ ...                     and then WIN.COM unwinding Windows

RMDOS ANSWERED THE FIRST TASK TO EXIT WITH WIN.COM'S EXEC RETURN.
Termination in RMDOS was five global words - rd_parpsp, rd_parseg,
rd_paroff, rd_parss, rd_parsp - written by 4Bh and read by 4Ch, plus
vec_save/vec_restore for interrupts 22h, 23h and 24h.  That is
indistinguishable from a DOS as long as every process is started by an
EXEC and processes end in the order they started, which was true of
everything that had ever run on it.  Windows does neither.  It builds
a PSP for each task with 55h and starts the task itself, so the words
still described WIN.COM's EXEC of DOSX, and closing the Task List took
Windows down with it.

WHERE A PROCESS GOES WHEN IT ENDS IS WRITTEN IN ITS OWN PSP, and
DOS6SRC says so in four places:

  msdisp.asm, three instructions after raising InDOS, writes SS:SP
  into PSP+2Eh - on EVERY call, for the process that is current.

  msproc.asm's EXEC pops the caller's CS:IP into the child's PSP+0Ah
  and into vector 22h, four instructions apart.

  SETMEM, at the bottom of $CREATE_PROCESS_DATA_BLOCK, copies the
  twelve bytes at 0000:0088 - vectors 22h, 23h and 24h - into PSP+0Ah
  of every PSP it builds, which is 26h and 55h as well as EXEC.

  msproc.asm's $Abort copies those twelve bytes back into the
  interrupt table, makes PSP+16h current, takes SS:SP out of the
  PARENT's PSP, restores the parent's registers off it, throws away
  the three words the parent's own INT 21h pushed, and IRETs to the
  terminate address with only the interrupt flag surviving.

All four are implemented now.  psp_stamp and psp_unstamp are the
twelve bytes in and out; exec_psp writes the parent's own CS:IP as the
terminate address; term_common reads the address, the parent and the
parent's stack out of PSPs and edits the parent's frame where it lies
rather than jumping anywhere.  f4B_back, the trampoline that used to
fix up the frame, is gone with the five words and with
vec_save/vec_restore.  The one thing that is NOT taken from the PSP
chain is the top of it: if the PSP that is ending is the one RMDOS was
handed at park time, the excursion is over and the machine goes back
to PM-DOS.  PM-DOS's own PSP chain, and the protected-mode terminate
address in it, are not RMDOS's to walk.

AND WHAT WINDOWS ASKS FOR IS NOW VISIBLE.  rdbg_term records the first
process to end - PSP, parent and terminate address - and it says:

  first terminate: PSP 4206, parent 363F, terminate address 0DA5:0324

0DA5:0324 is the return address of the very 4Ch that is terminating.
Windows is asking to be continued where it left off.  With the fix in
place that is what happens: the session no longer unwinds to WIN.COM,
the calls after the 4Ch come from Windows' own reflector at 0DA5:0257
rather than from WIN.COM at 0DA5:01C6 - and then DOSX faults:

  Standard Mode: Fault in MS-DOS Extender.
  EC=200C CS=0053 IP=4C18 AX=920C BX=0000 CX=4C00 DX=0D37
  SI=0FEC DI=200F BP=2332 DS=004B ES=0000 SS=004B SP=2334

which it reports through DOS calls of its own - AH=09h twice, at 2811
and 2812 - and then exits with 4CFF.  So the release build still ends
the same way, Windows dying and the unpark resetting the machine, but
it dies INSIDE WINDOWS now, four hundred instructions further on, and
for a reason Windows is willing to talk about.

THE LEAD THAT WAS NOT ONE, read again with the source open.  The first
guess was that DOS's 55h does not give the new process a handle table
of its own: $CREATE_PROCESS_DATA_BLOCK copies the whole PSP, which
copies the parent's PDB_JFN_Length and PDB_JFN_Pointer, then copies
twenty entries into the new PSP's own table at 18h "in case Set Handle
Count has been issued", and never repoints 32h/34h at them.  That is
true of the routine as far as Create_PDB_cont - and then the routine
FALLS THROUGH INTO SETMEM, which is not a separate call but an entry
point three instructions further down the same procedure, and SETMEM
finishes the job:

  MOV     WORD PTR DS:[PDB_JFN_Pointer],PDB_JFN_Table
  MOV     WORD PTR DS:[PDB_JFN_Pointer+2],DS
  MOV     WORD PTR DS:[PDB_JFN_Length],FilPerProc

with DS = DX = the new PSP and FilPerProc EQU 20.  So a 55h child DOES
get a table of its own, twenty entries at 18h, and RMDOS's fn55 - 32h
= 20, 34h = 18h, 36h = the new PSP - is byte for byte what DOS does.
There is no divergence here and nothing to fix.  The lesson is the
plain one about reading assembler with entry points in it: an `entry`
in the middle of a procedure is a label, not a boundary, and the code
after it runs for everybody who reaches it from above.

The one real difference left in the copy is small and in the other
direction: DOS's dup loop asks SFFromHandle about each inherited
handle and stores -1 for anything that is closed, marked no-inherit or
a network FCB, where RMDOS copies the twenty bytes wholesale and takes
a reference on every one of them that is not FFh.  A no-inherit handle
would be inherited by a 55h child on this DOS and not on that one.
Whether Windows has any is unmeasured.

So the extender fault has no explanation yet and needs measuring
rather than guessing at: EC=200C is an LDT selector error code, and
CX=4C00 in the dump is the AX of the 4Ch that started all this, which
says the fault happens with the terminate still on the stack.

AND THE OBSERVATION WITH NO EXPLANATION HAS ONE, AND IT IS NOT OURS.
Windows started every time and painted every time but only sometimes
took keyboard input - four runs took it and four did not, on both
builds, with the mouse captured and without.  It was the host.
keybd_event injects into whatever window has the foreground, and
Charlie was playing a game on the same machine while those runs were
being driven; the keys went to the game.  Re-run cleanly on 2026-09-07
with nothing else running: boot, WIN /S, and Program Manager takes
arrow keys immediately - two Rights walk the selection File Manager to
Control Panel to Print Manager - Ctrl+Esc opens the Task List, and
Escape closes it.  Nothing in RMDOS, nothing in the keyboard
controller, nothing in the emulator.  The harness lesson is worth
keeping anyway: a run driven with keybd_event is only valid if the
host desktop is otherwise idle, and there is no way to tell from
inside the run that it was not.

That run also confirms the release build's end state cleanly.  Escape
on the Task List still resets the machine, within four seconds, which
is the DOSX fault above running to its 4CFF and the unpark taking the
machine down with it.  The fix moved where Windows dies; it has not
stopped it dying.

REGRESSIONS.  PARKTEST/RMTEST nine checks all pass and the kernel
still opens a file afterwards.  PARKEXEC runs its three programs -
including a relocated .EXE that exits through 4Ch and a NOSUCH.COM
that must fail cleanly - with "failures: 00", and unparks.  Both of
those go through the rewritten terminate path twice over, which is the
point of running them.  HNDTEST grants sixty handles.  Both Windows
masters are byte-identical to the pristine copies afterwards; nothing
in the Windows directory has ever been patched.


v0.55 - WINDOWS 3.1 STANDARD MODE FINISHES STARTING
---------------------------------------------------

Program Manager comes up with its groups in it.  Main is open with
File Manager, Control Panel, Print Manager, Clipboard Viewer, MS-DOS
Prompt, Windows Setup, PIF Editor and Mouse Notes in it, and
Accessories and StartUp are minimised below.  Stock DOSX.EXE, stock
KRNL386.EXE, nothing in the Windows directory patched.  It gets there
in about a minute of emulated time after the handover, which is a
hundred and fifty seconds from power on.

THE BUG WAS INT 21h AH=55h, AND IT WAS NOT IMPLEMENTED.

55h is undocumented - it is not in any of the interrupt lists this
project has been working from - and it is how Windows creates a
process.  Not 4Bh: 4Bh is what RMDOS runs KRNL386 with, and after that
KRNL386 makes a PSP for every task it starts, with 55h, and Program
Manager is one of them.  DX is where the new PSP goes and SI is the
top of its memory; DOS copies the whole of the current PSP over it,
copies the parent's handle table into the new PSP's own twenty bytes,
takes a reference to every handle inherited, sets the parent, sets
PSP:32h to twenty and PSP:34h to 0018h:<the new PSP>, and makes the
new PSP current.  See $Dup_PDB and $CREATE_PROCESS_DATA_BLOCK in the
MS-DOS 6 source, DOS/misc.asm, which is what fn55 in RMMEM.INC now
follows.

RMDOS answered "unsupported".  So the PSP Windows built for the shell
was never initialised, PSP:32h - the number of handles the process is
allowed - was whatever was in that memory, which was zero, and every
file Program Manager tried to open was refused with error 4, too many
open files.  Twenty-four refusals of PROGMAN.INI in a row.  The shell
could not read the file that names its groups, so it had none, and it
sat there with a live mouse and an empty window looking exactly like
something that had hung.

AND 26h COPIED HALF A PSP.  DOS copies 80h WORDS.  This copied 80h
BYTES, which stops four bytes short of PSP:34h - the pointer that says
where the handle table is.  Nothing had noticed because nothing had
ever read PSP:34h.

WHICH IS THE SECOND HALF OF IT.  DOS finds a process's handles through
PSP:32h and PSP:34h - pJFNFromHandle in the MS-DOS 6 source,
DOS/util.asm, is six instructions and both of them are in it - and
this DOS filled those two words in correctly from its first release
and then never read them.  Twelve places indexed es:[bx+18h] against a
fixed limit of twenty instead.  That is wrong twice over: 67h moves
the table into a block of its own when a program asks for more, and
WINDOWS MOVES IT WITHOUT ASKING.  The trace says so: KRNL386's own PSP
has thirty-two entries at 44C6:0000, and it never once called 67h to
get them.  RMDOS was reading and writing twenty stale bytes in the PSP
while Windows used a table somewhere else.

So there is now jft_ptr in RMFILE2.INC, every access goes through it,
and 67h does what DOS does: allocate a block, stamp it as the
process's own so termination frees it, copy the old table in, and
point PSP:32h/34h at it.  HNDTEST.COM is the unit test - sixty
handles asked for, sixty granted, fifty files open at once - and it
runs on both DOSes so the two can be compared.  SFT_COUNT went from
forty to eighty at the same time: Windows keeps seventeen files open
before the shell has even started.

THE INSTRUMENT WAS BROKEN, AND THAT COST MOST OF THE RELEASE.

None of the above could be seen, because the trace build stalled at
the splash screen at about DOS call 100 while the release build
reached the desktop every time.  v0.54 recorded that as a layout
sensitivity - "the only difference between the two runs that changed
it was forty-eight more bytes of RMDOS" - and it was not.  It was a
fall-through.  rr_strfull in RMDBG.INC popped its five registers and
then ran on, past a comment block, into rr_exec, whose last
instruction is "jmp rr_str".  So the moment the string ring filled,
the twenty-fourth name sent the recorder round and round, five words
deeper on the stack each time, and the machine stopped.  The
forty-eight bytes were rdbg_env: one more string, which took the count
from twenty-three to twenty-four and over the edge.

Three things were built to find that, and all three are worth keeping:

  - park_loadrm takes a FIXED 64K block now, whatever the image
    weighs, so that park_seg - and therefore every address Windows
    will ever see - is the same in the release build and in the build
    with sixteen kilobytes of trace buffer in it.  It costs about
    forty kilobytes of a machine that has six hundred.  The reason it
    was written was wrong; it is still the right thing to have.
  - the trace buffer lives at the top of that block instead of being
    allocated out of the arena, for the same reason: an instrument
    that moves the machine it is measuring is not an instrument.
  - the flush is rate-limited to one in thirty-two calls, and the
    footprints WRAP.  They used to be the first sixteen, which
    answers "did the channel ever work" and not "is it still
    working", and those are different questions with the same
    silence.

RMSPEED.COM says the file system was never the problem.  On RMDOS a
DOS call that touches no disk costs under three microseconds, a BIOS
sector read costs twenty-seven, an open and close costs two hundred
and seventy-five, and the whole of a profile read - open, seek to the
end, seek back, read it, close - costs about half a millisecond.  A
release of theory about one-sector-per-BIOS-call being too slow died
on those four numbers in one boot, before any of it was written.

AND THE PRINTER PORT WORKS AFTER ALL, ALMOST.  DBGSINK.INC says the
printer was tried as a trace channel and never delivered a byte, and
that the cause was 86Box dropping lpt1_enabled out of its
configuration file every time it rewrites it on exit.  That is a line
in a file: armlpt.ps1 puts it back before every launch and the port is
there, the BIOS finds it at 0378h, the data register reads back what
is written to it and the strobe is seen.  What arrives on the host is
0Ch for every printable character, with CR and LF passing through
correctly, by all four strobe conventions and through the BIOS's own
INT 17h.  That is 86Box's Generic Text Printer and not this code.
LPTTEST.COM is the positive control and says so in one boot.

REGRESSION: PARKTEST/RMTEST nine checks all pass, PARKEXEC three
programs and no failures - including a relocated .EXE and a clean
"file not found" - HNDTEST sixty handles on RMDOS, and the masters at
S:\WIN31HD are byte-identical to the pristine copies with DOSXPOKE
reporting the 0007/0008 handlers untouched.

WHAT IS STILL WRONG.  Nothing that has been seen.  The obvious next
questions are whether anything in those groups RUNS - File Manager,
the MS-DOS Prompt, Write - and what happens on the way out, because
Windows exiting is a path nothing has exercised: RMDOS_FREEZE stops
the machine at rd_goback precisely because nothing ever got there.

v0.54 - WINDOWS 3.1 STANDARD MODE RUNS
--------------------------------------

It boots to Program Manager.  Stock DOSX.EXE, stock KRNL386.EXE,
nothing in the Windows directory patched, on a 128MB machine: the
handover, the extender's protected mode, KRNL386 loaded through
RMDOS's EXEC, its own protected mode, its global heap, its own
executable reopened, SYSTEM.DRV, KEYBOARD.DRV, MOUSE.DRV, VGA.DRV,
MMSOUND.DRV, COMM.DRV, the fonts, GDI.EXE, USER.EXE - and a desktop
with a working mouse.

TWO BUGS, both in RMDOS, both plain DOS behaviour that was missing.
Neither of them is in the XMS driver, which is where three releases of
notes were looking.

THE FIRST IS THE ENVIRONMENT, and it is the one that made the
difference between "a fault in the extender" and "a kernel".  A DOS
program is handed its environment as the strings back to back, an
empty string to end them, and then - since DOS 3.0 - the word 0001h
and THE FULL PATH OF THE PROGRAM ITSELF.  KRNL386 walks past the
strings, reads the count and OPENS THE PATH IT FINDS THERE, because
that is how the Windows kernel finds its own file to load its own
segments from.  RMDOS handed the child whatever segment the caller put
in the parameter block and nothing at all when that was zero - and
zero is exactly what the extender passes, because zero is how a
program says "give it a copy of mine".  So the kernel got no
environment, found no path, printed

    KERNEL: Unable to open KERNEL executable

and exited.  No open ever reached this DOS to say what it had wanted,
which is why the DOS-call trace could not show it: a trace cannot
record a call that was never made.  What showed it was recording the
ENVIRONMENT, at the moment the child was handed it - rdbg_env, tagged
FCh, printed with its NULs shown because the interesting half of that
string is all after a NUL.  It said "<none>".

MSDOS 6's EXEC is the specification and ep_envcopy now follows it to
the letter (msproc.asm, Exec_Check_Environ): the parameter block
first, the caller's PDB_environ if that is zero, nothing if that is
zero too - and then ALWAYS a fresh block of (length + 0Fh + 2 + name
length) >> 4 paragraphs, the strings copied, the word 0001h, the name.
DOS makes a copy even when it was handed a block outright, which is
why SET in a child never reaches its parent.  The block is stamped
with the CHILD's PSP so the child's termination frees it.

THE SECOND IS MAXALLOC ZERO, WHICH MEANS LOAD HIGH.  This is the one
that killed standard mode for four releases, and the path from the
symptom to it is long enough to be worth writing down.

The symptom was "Standard Mode: Fault in MS-DOS Extender EC=8DD8
CS=0053 IP=2B9A" - an IRET in DOSX popping a return address out of
memory nothing had ever written.  v0.53 established that much and got
the direction wrong: it concluded the question was on the Windows side
of the line.  It is not.

Reading KRNL386 rather than trapping it is what turned it round.  The
routine at seg1:BDF3 is the global heap being created: it asks DPMI
0500 how much memory there is, asks 0501 for a block, points a
selector at it with SetSelectorBase (seg1:2291, which writes the
descriptor through the kernel's own LDT alias at cs:[0032] - that is
why no DPMI 0007 for that selector is ever seen) and then asks DPMI
0008 for the matching limit.  It copies NOTHING into the block,
because there is nothing to copy: this is a scratch selector whose old
contents nobody wants.

The selector came back from DPMI 0002, Segment To Descriptor, at
seg1:C3F7, called on the first free paragraph above the kernel's
image.  AND DOSX SERVES 0002 BY SEARCHING THE LDT.  The search at DOSX
code 20E7 - reached from nothing else in the file - walks descriptors
downwards from 027F looking for one that already has the base asked
for, a limit of FFFF and access F2, ignoring the accessed bit, and
hands that one back rather than making a new one.  That is correct and
canonical behaviour.  The client's own stack fits the description
exactly.

So Windows asked for a descriptor onto its free memory, was given its
own stack, and threw the stack away.  A two-byte poke turning that
search into "stc / ret" was enough to prove it: the heap initialised
and the run moved on to the next failure.

WHAT PUT THE STACK THERE WAS RMDOS.  KRNL386.EXE's header says
MINALLOC 0 and MAXALLOC 0, and MAXALLOC zero has meant LOAD HIGH since
DOS 2: the program gets the largest block there is, the PSP at the
bottom of it, THE IMAGE AT THE TOP, and the free run in between
(msproc.asm, Exec_Load_High).  RMDOS asked for MAXALLOC and stopped,
so the kernel got a block exactly as big as itself with no free run at
all, and the paragraph it then asked 0002 about landed on top of a
descriptor it was already using.  fn4B now treats MAXALLOC zero as
"the largest run there is" and places the image at the top of it.

With both fixes in and DOSX PRISTINE - the poke reverted, the handlers
verified byte-for-byte against the master - Windows starts.

TOOLING.  RMDBG grew a second string ring: the old one keeps the FIRST
names, which is how a start-up got where it did, and the new one wraps
and keeps the LAST, which is what a program that will not stop is
doing.  A ring of firsts cannot name a file opened for the four
hundredth time.  BUILD.CMD gained lptfz, which is DBG_LPT and
RMDOS_FREEZE without the pool stamping - stamping 32 million dwords is
not free and is not wanted on every run.

REGRESSION: PARKTEST/RMTEST, nine checks, all pass, the excursion ends
normally and PM-DOS still opens a file afterwards.

WHAT IS STILL WRONG.  Program Manager comes up EMPTY - the window, the
menus and the mouse are all live, but no group windows and no icons,
after four hundred seconds.  The DOS-call trace at that point is a
tight repeating cycle - get attributes, open, get file time, read 40h
at 0, seek to 80h, read the NE header, read a name, seek, read a
resource, close, get current directory - which is the shell walking
program items for their icons, and it does not end.  MAIN.GRP,
ACCESSOR.GRP and STARTUP.GRP are all present and PROGMAN.INI names
them.  That is the next thing.

AND THE DEBUG BUILD IS NOT THE RELEASE BUILD.  The lptfz build stalls
at the splash screen at DOS call 113, deterministically, twice in a
row, where the release build reaches the desktop every time; the only
difference between the two runs that changed it was forty-eight more
bytes of RMDOS.  Windows is sensitive to where things sit to a degree
this project has now been bitten by twice.  Read a stall in a trace
build as a fact about that build until the release build agrees.

v0.53 - THE STACK THAT WAS NEVER BROUGHT ALONG
-----------------------------------------------

Two readings are withdrawn in this release and neither of them was a
small one.

THE LIMIT WAS NEVER THE CAUSE.  v0.52 had standard mode dying because
DOSX was asked to set a segment limit and the IRET afterwards did not
survive it.  That came from patching the 0008 handler and watching
what happened, and it does not survive the obvious control: DOSX's own
fault printer dumps EVERY register, not the three the earlier runs
quoted.  What it actually says is

  EC=0000 CS=0053 IP=2B9A AX=0008 BX=027F CX=0008 DX=807F
  SI=027F DI=9030 BP=01DC DS=0317 ES=0317 SS=027F SP=01A6

SS=027F.  The selector whose limit KRNL386 wants set is the client's
own stack, and the IRET at 2B9A pops its frame from it.  DOSX's exit
helper reloads SS from the descriptor table on the way out, so the
moment that base moves the stack is gone.  It is already gone before
DOSX writes anything: read the client's saved SP through a freshly
loaded 027F at the top of the handler and it reads zero.

AND THE POOL WAS NEVER THE PROBLEM EITHER.  The other candidate was
that the address this kernel reports for a locked XMS block is not the
memory it hands over.  It is.  rx_pooltest (XMSPOOLSTAMP) stamps every
dword of the pool with its own linear address and reads all of them
back, in real mode after the park with the page tables gone and A20
forced open - the machine Windows actually sees.  Thirty-two million
stamps across 128240K and every one answers correctly.  No aliasing,
nothing missing.

The stamps are the real gain, because they turn any read of extended
memory into an oracle: a dword either says its own address or says
somebody wrote it.  Zeros could have been anything.  With them in
place the fault report changes from EC=0000 to EC=8DD8, and 8DD8 is
the low word of the stamp at the exact address the IRET takes CS from.
The client's stack frame is not there and nothing ever wrote it.

rx_poolscan then names every page that lost its stamp, and over a
whole standard-mode start that is TWENTY-SEVEN PAGES out of 32060:
the extender's own 84K block in full, the last page of the 65535K
block, the first two pages of the 62620K one, the last page of the
544K block being sized, and the last page of the pool.  First page and
last page of each region is a SIZING PROBE.  128MB has been
allocated, locked, measured at both ends and then not used.

So the sequence that kills it is this.  KRNL386 runs from conventional
memory - selector 0317, base 00010320, exactly where RMDOS's EXEC put
segment 1 of KRNL386.EXE.  It takes a 544K block from the extender at
04299030 and points a second selector 0357 at the same base; 0357's
access byte still reads F2, accessed clear, so that alias has never
been loaded into a segment register.  It then writes 027F's base to
the same address with its own hands, through the LDT alias at
cs:[0032] - no DPMI involved, which is why no 0007 for 027F was ever
seen - and asks DPMI 0008 for the matching limit.  027F is its stack.
Nothing was copied.  The descriptor is otherwise perfect: all
thirty-two bits of base present (byte 7 reads 04, so the 24-bit
truncation this was once blamed on does not happen), access F3, and
027F is not part of a selector array either - 0287 has base 0 and
accessed clear, 0277 has an unrelated conventional base and is live.

Measured and NOT the cause: the XMS allocation granularity.  Rounding
a block's size up to a page leaves a hole - 65535K rounded up reserves
65536K, so the block ends a kilobyte before the next begins, where
HIMEM counts in kilobytes throughout and would have handed out two
blocks that touch.  One region against two is exactly the kind of
difference that makes a block move instead of growing in place.  With
RX_GRAN at 400h the blocks do touch and every address downstream
shifts by the missing kilobyte - the first allocation lands at
04298C30 rather than 04299030 - AND THE FAULT IS THE SAME FAULT.  The
page stays; the measurement is recorded in RMXMS.INC so it is not
repeated.

TOOLING, because two rounds were lost to it before anything was
learned.  RMDOS_FREEZE stops the machine at rd_goback instead of
unparking, so the screen keeps whatever the excursion left on it:
without it the fault report survives about half a second before the
unpark resets the machine, and a once-a-second screen poll caught it
once in twelve boot loops.  With it, one screenshot at any later
moment will do.  BUILD.CMD gained stamp, freeze, stampfrz and lptfrz.
TOOLS\DOSXPOKE.PL puts probes into HD16.IMG and never into the Windows
master, re-finding DOSX each time by a signature on the INT 31h
dispatcher - the one part of the file no experiment touches.
TOOLS\UNDIS.PL read both DOSX and KRNL386.  TOOLS\FASTWATCH.PS1 polls
the screen and saves only frames whose fingerprint it has not seen.

What is still not known is why the copy does not happen, and that is
on the Windows side of the line.  What is worth doing next is a LOG
rather than another trap - every probe here is a deliberate #GP and
shows one moment - and the two channels available inside the extender
are the LPT data port, which 86Box writes to a file, and DOSX's own
LDT, which RMDOS could dump at the freeze if it were told where the
alias points.

v0.52 - THE MACHINE WAS TALKING TO NOBODY
-----------------------------------------

Windows 3.1 standard mode is not failing where three releases of notes
have said it fails.  It does not die in DOSX's switch to protected
mode; it runs, loads and starts its own kernel through RMDOS's EXEC,
and then KRNL386 tries to open CON, is told ten times that there is no
such file, gives up and exits with code FFh.  RMDOS could not open a
character device by name.  It can now.

And the reset that has been read as Windows crashing happens AFTER
Windows has gone: the trace shows rd_goback reached, which is RMDOS
ending the excursion normally.  What resets is the unpark.

NONE OF THAT WAS READABLE UNTIL THE INSTRUMENT WORKED, so most of this
release is the instrument.

THE TRACE WROTE TO THE FLOPPY.

rdbg_flush ends:

        mov     ax,0300h + RDBG_SEC
        mov     cx,RDBG_CHS
        mov     dx,8100h                ; head 0, drive 81h
        int     13h

DH is the head and DL is the drive.  8100h asks for head 129 of drive
0, and drive 0 is the FLOPPY - there is one in the machine, so the
call did not even fail in an interesting way.  The comment on the line
said "head 0, drive 81h" the whole time and was read, every time, as
agreeing with the code beside it.

Three releases of theory rested on that write: the HMA (INT 13h writes
from up there move nothing), the bounce buffer, AH=43h against AH=03h.
Every one of them assumed the write was addressed to the disk it was
supposed to land on.

PROBE13.COM SETTLED IT IN ONE BOOT, which is the argument for building
the positive control the notes had been asking for since v0.50.  It
writes a signature into the gap either side of the park and reads it
back, and it separates three failures that had been sharing one
silence: the write erroring, the write landing somewhere else, and the
write never leaving the emulator.  Both writes landed, on the host
file, at the LBAs the arithmetic names - so the off-by-one this file
used to claim, the one the reader SCANS to work around, was invented
to explain a symptom that had a different cause and outlived it.

THEN THE FIRST BIOS DISK CALL AFTER EVERY PARK FAILS.

With the drive number right the trace appeared - and stopped after two
entries.  PROBE13 grew a loop, then a script, and measured it: after
the park the first read comes back AH=80h, "the drive did not become
ready", the second does too and the third hangs the machine.  The
drive is idle and ready the whole time - alternate status 50h, no
error - the tick is advancing, IF is set, INT 13h and 76h still point
at ROM, and the BIOS records status 00 for the call it just failed.

It is repaired by INT 13h AH=00h, and by nothing else that was tried.
This kernel's ATA driver addresses the disk by LBA and has
reprogrammed it since POST; AH=00h is how a BIOS is asked to establish
the drive's parameters again.  rm_park does it now, on both fixed
disks, in the same breath as putting the PICs back.

AND IT HAS ALWAYS FAILED, AND NEVER SHOWN, because RMDISK.INC retries
once through a reset on any error - with a comment about floppies
needing a second seek, which is true, and is why the retry was
written.  Every disk read RMDOS has ever done has been the second
attempt.  The trace had no retry behind it and no voice to say so.

Two more found on the way and fixed, neither of which turned out to be
the cause: IRQ 14 was masked in pic_to_rm, which unmasks timer,
keyboard, cascade, floppy and the RTC for the BIOS and was written for
rm_call - a short excursion where this kernel drives the disk itself
and has no use for the drive's interrupt.  A park is not an excursion.
And nIEN, which ATA.INC sets once at IDENTIFY and never clears, lives
IN THE DRIVE and survives the mode switch, the park and everything
after it; ata_toRM clears it going out and ata_toPM sets it coming
back.

THE BUILD EXITED ZERO WITH AN ERROR IN IT, and four experiments ran
against a kernel that contained neither of those fixes.  BUILD.CMD
printed "iorm.asm(337): Error! E551: Symbol ATA_DC_NIEN is not
defined" - the constant is in ATA.INC, which IOPM.ASM includes and
IORM.ASM does not - carried on to the end, and left the previous
PMIO.SYS in BIN.  Two fixes were tested that were never in the
machine and were written off as not working.  stage.sh greps the log
now: the exit code is not the answer.

WHAT THE TRACE THEN SAID, once it worked.

It records every INT 21h RMDOS serves with its arguments AND its
result, the first sixteen filenames opened or EXECed, and every string
printed through AH=09h.  Sixty-two calls, and the whole of Windows'
startup on the far side of the handover is legible in them:

  DOSX broadcasts 1605h with DX bit 0 set - standard mode, which is
  what PM-DOS parks for - and the frame it handed over says edx=1.
  Windows probes for SMARTDRV, reads SYSTEM.INI, asks for EMMXXXX0,
  EMMQXXX0, EMM and VCPIXXX0 and is correctly told there are none.
  It EXECs C:\WINDOWS\SYSTEM\krnl386.exe, which is the right kernel:
  the 286 and 386 kernels are chosen by processor, not by mode.
  The kernel gets the DOS version - 1606h, six point twenty-two,
  correct, twice.  Then it opens CON five times, gets
  ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND five times, tries again with another access
  mode, gets five more, closes ten handles it never got, prints
  "Incorrect MS-DOS version.  MS-DOS 3.1 or greater required." and
  exits FFh.  WIN.COM reads that code with 4Dh and exits with it too.

The message is about the DOS being unusable and not about its version,
and it sent this release looking at AH=30h, where the answer had been
right all along.

A DEVICE IS A NAME BEFORE IT IS A FILE.

sub_open went straight to rd_path and dir_find.  "CON" is not in any
directory, so 3Dh answered "file not found" - and so did NUL, PRN,
AUX, LPT1 and COM1.  Everything downstream of an open device has
worked since v0.45: dev_read, dev_write, the 44h that reports a
character device, and the five handles rd_sftinit gives every process.
The machine looked like it had devices.  It could not open one.

Nothing had ever asked.  A program that inherits its handles never
opens CON by name, and every test in this suite inherits them - which
is this project's oldest lesson arriving from the one direction it had
not come from yet: not a feature nobody exercises, but a feature every
test is standing on top of without touching.

dev_name takes the last path component, stops at the dot, upper cases
it and compares eight characters against a table.  DOS's rule is
strange and worth stating: a device name is recognised anywhere a
filename is, in any directory, with any extension - C:\DOES\NOT\EXIST\CON
is the console - so the path is not looked at, because DOS does not
look at it either.  sub_devopen then builds the entry exactly as
sfti_dev builds an inherited one, because everything downstream reads
SFF_DEVICE and SFT_DRIVE and nothing else.

RMTEST has a ninth check now, and it is the one that was missing.

WHERE IT STOPS.  Windows gets past the CON opens - handles 5 through E
now, and the closes release the right ones - and still ends the same
way, and the machine still resets when it goes.  Two questions are
left and they are separate:

  WHAT KRNL386 CHECKS BETWEEN CLOSING ITS TENTH HANDLE AND PRINTING.
  There is no DOS call between them, so whatever it rejects it already
  had in hand.

  WHY THE UNPARK DOES NOT SURVIVE.  rd_goback is marked, so RMDOS
  ended the excursion and jumped to rm_unpark; PARKEXEC and PARKTEST
  unpark cleanly in the same build, so the return path works when
  nothing has been in protected mode in between.  What is different is
  what DOSX left behind in the machine.  That is a PM-DOS bug and not
  a Windows one, and it is the first time it has been possible to say
  so.

VERIFIED, on the final release build:

  RMTEST on RMDOS         9/9, including a file off real FAT16 and
                          CON opened by name and reporting 80D3
  XMSTEST on PM-DOS       all OK, the 1MB wrap RUN and passed both ways
  UMBTEST                 11/11, failures 00
  WINTEST                 all checks passed
  PARKEXEC                3/3, failures 00
  PROBE13                 8 of 8 BIOS disk operations after the park,
                          where the first one used to fail
  and RMDOS's EXEC loads and runs KRNL386.EXE itself, in text mode,
  as far as "KERNEL: Unable to enter Protected Mode" - which is the
  right answer for a Windows kernel with no extender under it, and
  proves the loader on the largest real .EXE in the machine.

v0.51 - THE CHILD THAT COULD NOT SPEAK
--------------------------------------

RMDOS can load and run a program now.  A .COM with an exit code that
comes back through 4Dh, a real .EXE with a relocation table and a
stack of its own, and a name that is not on the disk failing cleanly -
all three, on the far side of the handover, with PM-DOS parked and no
kernel underneath.  4Bh returns to the program that called it and the
parent carries on.

Windows 3.1 standard mode uses that, gets its logo onto the screen,
and then resets the machine.  Where it stopped before, it now goes
wrong; that is the shape of the release.

TAKE WINDOWS OUT OF IT, WHICH IS THE WHOLE METHOD.

v0.50 ended with "the child starts and never calls DOS again", and the
only instrument pointed at that sentence was a bar painted into a
640x480 framebuffer by a DOS with no console, read off a screenshot,
one boot per reading, with Windows drawing over it.  Four releases of
notes say that reading an instrument has cost more than building it.

So PARKEXEC.COM.  It parks exactly as Windows does - INT 2Fh AX=1605h
with DX bit 0 set - and then does what Windows does next, which is to
EXEC a program.  The machine is in TEXT MODE, RMDOS's own console is
answering AH=09h, and every answer is a printed line.  It is
EXECTST.COM's run against the other DOS, deliberately: the two are
meant to agree, so a check that passes there and fails here names the
difference.

And PEKID.COM, the child, which writes '*K' STRAIGHT TO THE TEXT PAGE
before it asks DOS anything, then calls the BIOS, then calls DOS.
Three marks, three different claims: the far jump landed, the machine
is sane, the DOS answered.  Every other child announces itself with
INT 21h, which makes "the loader worked" and "the first DOS call was
served" the same observation - and when neither happens there is
nothing to tell them apart, and they are different faults in different
files.

That pair turned a sixty-second boot-and-squint into a sixty-second
boot-and-read, and everything below came out of it in one sitting.

WHAT WAS WRONG, IN THE ORDER IT CAME OUT.

  THE HEADER READ WENT TO OFFSET ZERO.  sft_get ends with MUL SI,
  which is a 16-bit multiply and therefore writes DX:AX - so a routine
  whose contract is "BX in, SI out" quietly destroyed DX as well, and
  the product never fills DX so what every caller saw was DX = 0.
  sub_read takes its buffer offset in DX and read it AFTER calling
  sft_get.  Every read EXEC has ever made went to offset zero of the
  destination segment.

  ...AND THE .COM LOAD WAS 256 BYTES TOO HIGH, which is what hid it.
  A .COM belongs at PSP:0100, which is execimg:0000 - the same address
  spelled two ways - and the code said execimg:0100.  The two bugs
  cancelled exactly, on the only branch anything ever took, for five
  releases.  Fixing sft_get alone would have broken every .COM in the
  machine.

  The .EXE branch had no such luck: with the header read landing in
  the wrong place, rd_exehdr held the zeroes it was assembled with, no
  file ever looked like 'MZ', and RMDOS could not load an .EXE at all.
  The twenty-eight bytes went to CS:0000 instead - which, with RMDOS
  in the HMA, is the top of the ROM and then RMDOS's own entry jump.

  THE COMMAND TAIL WAS COPIED OVER THE INTERRUPT VECTOR TABLE.  This
  is the one that mattered.  exec_psp ended:

        lds     si,dword ptr [ep_tail]
        mov     ax,[rd_execpsp]
        mov     es,ax

  LDS IS AN ASSIGNMENT TO DS.  rd_execpsp is a variable in RMDOS's
  segment and DS was no longer RMDOS's segment, so the destination
  came from whatever lay at that offset in the CALLER's.  It lay at
  zero.  A hundred and twenty-eight bytes of command tail went to
  0000:0080, which is the vector table from INT 20h to INT 3Fh, and
  INT 21h's vector became bytes 4 to 7 of the tail.

  The child was loaded correctly, jumped to correctly, and ran: it
  marked the screen, and the BIOS answered it, because INT 10h's
  vector is at 0000:0040 and the copy started at 0000:0080.  Its first
  DOS call went to the four bytes of its parent's own command line.
  The loader had already reported success.

  THE HANDLES WERE INHERITED THROUGH THE WRONG SEGMENT.  The same
  routine walks the parent's table with DS pointing at the parent's
  PSP, and calls sft_addref, which reaches RMDOS's handle table
  through DS.  So the reference count it incremented was a word in the
  parent's memory and the count that should have gone up did not.  The
  386 has two more segment registers than the code that has to be
  compatible with them; the parent goes through FS now.

  file_io HAD NEVER MOVED MORE THAN ONE SECTOR.  It clamps the
  transfer to the tail of the current sector - and it clamped ECX,
  which is not the size of the chunk, it is what is left of the whole
  call.  So the first pass cut the request down to 448 bytes, moved
  exactly that, subtracted it from itself, reached zero, and reported
  success.  Nothing had noticed in five releases because nothing had
  ever asked for a second sector: the boot-time reads are single
  sectors and the first program EXEC ever loaded was 178 bytes.  The
  first caller that wanted more was the .EXE loader, which got 448
  bytes of a 1184-byte program and jumped into the part that had not
  arrived.

  ...and sub_read ended with CLC, unconditionally, over the top of
  whatever file_io had returned.

  4Bh DID NOT RETURN TO ITS CALLER.  It ended the excursion instead -
  handed the machine back to PM-DOS - on the v0.45 reasoning that the
  frame the call was made through had been unwound with the stack.  It
  had not: term_toparent has just put SS:SP back to exactly where i21
  left the caller's own copy of it.  The frame is under our feet, and
  the call can be answered the ordinary way.  A parent whose child
  ends does not want the machine taken away from it; it wants its EXEC
  to return so it can ask 4Dh what happened and get on with the next
  one.  Windows EXECs a chain of them.

  THE CHILD'S MEMORY BELONGED TO ITS PARENT.  fn4B allocates the block
  before there is a PSP to own it, so mem_alloc stamped it with the
  parent's - and a block owned by the parent is a block the child's
  own termination does not free.  One EXEC emptied the arena for good;
  the second EXEC in the same program failed for want of memory the
  first had finished with.  exec_psp hands the block over now, which
  is the moment it becomes a process.

  MAXALLOC WAS NOT READ AT ALL.  An .EXE header carries two numbers:
  MINALLOC, what the program cannot run without, and MAXALLOC, what it
  would like - and a linker writes FFFF there to mean "all of it",
  which is what almost every .EXE says.  Asking for MINALLOC and
  stopping gave HELLOX.EXE 1.3K on a machine with half a megabyte
  free.  DOS's rule is: ask for MAXALLOC; if that will not fit take
  the largest run there is, provided it covers MINALLOC; only then is
  it out of memory.

  And PSP:2 was one paragraph too high, and the far jump into the
  child was built by writing its operands into the instruction eight
  instructions before executing it.  That is a DOS in the HMA being
  run by a recompiling emulator on a processor with a prefetch queue,
  which is the one case where all three get to disagree; the address
  goes in a variable and the jump reads it now.  It was not the fault
  - the fault was the vector table - but it costs nothing to not ask.

WHERE IT STOPS NOW.  Windows 3.1 standard mode takes the handover,
runs on RMDOS, loads and starts its next stage through EXEC, paints
its logo, and resets the machine.  A reset is a new failure and not
the old one: v0.50 stopped dead at the logo with the machine still
running.  What comes after the logo in standard mode is DOSX going
into protected mode on its own account, and the first thing to find
out is whether the reset is DOSX's own mode switch or something RMDOS
did to it.

AND THE INSTRUMENT IS STILL NOT FIXED.  RMDBG's disk channel went
silent in v0.50 because INT 13h WRITES from the HMA move nothing on
this BIOS; it now bounces the buffer through 4K of conventional
memory, which is demonstrably allocated - every PSP in the run moves
up by exactly its size - and the trace STILL does not reach the disk,
on either drive, at either sector.  Nor does PM-DOS's own DBGSINK in
the same build.  So there is no positive control: nothing has been
seen to write to that gap in this configuration, and a silence from
that channel is not yet evidence about anything.  Whoever picks this
up should make one deliberate write land before believing a word of
it.

ALSO IN THIS RELEASE.

  TOOLS\PARKEXEC.ASM, TOOLS\PEKID.ASM - the reproducer and its child.
  BUILD rmexec - RMDOS's EXEC traced through the BIOS teletype: the
  name asked for, the header, which branch, where it allocated, the
  bytes actually read, the CS:IP:SS:SP it is about to jump to with the
  four bytes that are there, the INT 21h vector as it stands at that
  moment, and every DOS call the child makes afterwards.  It needs a
  text-mode screen, which is exactly what PARKEXEC parks from and what
  Windows does not leave.

  XMSTEST's 1MB wrap test WROTE INTO RMDOS.  It proves the wrap by
  writing a byte to FFFF:0510, and since v0.50 that address is inside
  the HMA - so against a provider living up there the test scribbled
  into the code answering the very call it was making, and the DOS
  spent the rest of the run printing its own message table.  It asks
  the provider where its entry point is now: above the megabyte means
  the driver is in the HMA, and the check is skipped with a line
  saying so.  "The HMA is not on offer" would have been the wrong
  question - PM-DOS refuses it too, because it is keeping the HMA
  empty for RMDOS, and there the test is safe and worth running.

VERIFIED, on the final release build:

  RMTEST on RMDOS         8/8, including a file read off real FAT16
  XMSTEST on RMDOS        all OK, exit 0, wrap correctly skipped
  XMSTEST on PM-DOS       all OK, wrap RUN and passed, both directions
  UMBTEST                 11/11, failures 00
  WINTEST                 all checks passed
  PARKEXEC                3/3, failures 00 - and again with BUILD
                          rmlow, which is the control the low path
                          exists to be
  all eight build variants rc=0

v0.50 - SOMEWHERE TO STAND
--------------------------

Windows 3.1 in standard mode now takes the handover, runs on RMDOS,
reads its own files off the disk through RMDOS's own FAT code, counts
the conventional memory it has and is satisfied with it, and loads and
starts the next stage of itself through RMDOS's EXEC.  Then it stops.

That is four walls further than v0.49, which ended with the machine
resetting, and it is the first time anything in this project has been
stopped by Windows getting on with its work rather than by Windows
refusing to start.  What it is stopped on now is named at the bottom.

WHERE RMDOS LIVES, WHICH IS THE WHOLE RELEASE.

v0.49's blocker was arithmetic and there was no arguing with it.  The
handover has to load a 23K DOS into memory a real-mode segment can
reach; a .COM owns the whole transient program area until it shrinks
itself; and DOSX.EXE does its 4Ah AFTER broadcasting 1605h rather than
before.  At the instant it asks permission there is not one paragraph
free.  Park failed "not enough memory" on a machine with 620K of it.

So RMDOS goes in the HIGH MEMORY AREA - 100000h to 10FFEFh - which is
where a real DOS puts itself and for exactly the same reason.  It is
the only extended memory a 16-bit far pointer can address, it is real
memory the moment paging is off, PM-DOS has deliberately kept it empty
since v0.38, and it costs the DOS box nothing at all.  A DOS box still
has every byte it had before the handover, and RMDOS is not in it.

The price is sixteen bytes.  Segment FFFFh starts at FFFF0h, which is
in the ROM, so the image is assembled at ORG 10h and its first byte
lands on the megabyte.  RM_ORG is folded into every RMH_* offset, so
no field moved relative to the segment base and not one line of code
that reads the handoff block changed.  The same image still loads LOW
- at (seg+1)*16, so that offset 10h means what it says - and that is
the fallback for an image too big for 64K.  BUILD rmlow forces it,
because a path nothing exercises is a path nothing tests.

THE ONE RULE THE HMA CREATES: nothing running up there may ever close
the A20 gate.  With A20 off, segment FFFFh addresses zero, and the
instruction after the OUT that shut it is fetched from the interrupt
vector table - by a driver whose code, data, stack and caller have all
just stopped existing.  RMXMS's gate is chocked at rx_a20set, which is
the single point every route to the hardware passes through: the
detect probe, both disable functions, and the block move's habit of
putting the gate back as it found it.  The disables report success
anyway, because a gate wired permanently open is a real configuration
that every program has a path for, and because it is what a real DOS
does when it loads itself high.

AND THE MEMORY THAT STOPS EXISTING WHEN WE LEAVE.

PM-DOS's upper memory is ordinary RAM mapped into the holes between
A0000h and 100000h, and the MCB chain covers the whole span, because
a chain is contiguous and v0.38 had to make it so.  The park turns
paging off.  Every one of those addresses immediately goes back to
meaning what the hardware says it means - video memory and ROM - and
the chain is still there, describing them as blocks.

So a walk from the head runs off the top of conventional memory into
the frame buffer, reads whatever the VGA answers with as a block
header, and does not come back.  RMTEST could not walk it.  Windows
walks the same chain to find out how much conventional memory there
is, got an answer it did not like, and said so:

    Insufficient conventional memory to run Windows in standard mode.

park_chaincut ends the chain at the top of conventional memory for the
length of the excursion, and park_chainjoin puts it back.  This is not
a trick to get past a check - while parked, the machine genuinely has
no upper memory, and the chain is simply telling the truth for once.
RMH_MEMTOP, which has been declared by both sides of the contract
since v0.45 and written by neither, is filled in at the same time.

WHAT THE MOVE UNCOVERED, WHICH WAS ALWAYS THERE.

With the memory failure out of the way, Windows got far enough to
reset the machine, and the HMA was the obvious suspect - so the
question became whether RMDOS behaved differently high than low.  It
did not.  BUILD rmlow reproduced every failure exactly.  The HMA was
innocent and had been from the first boot; what the move had done was
carry the machine past the wall it used to stop at, into code nothing
had ever reached.  Underneath, none of it new:

  RMDOS COULD NOT MOUNT A VOLUME.  It read the boot sector, reported
  success, and rejected the BPB - because the buffer still held the
  zeroes it was assembled with.  INT 13h AH=42h, the extended packet
  read, returns carry clear and AH zero on this BIOS and moves no
  data.  RMDBG.INC found the identical thing about AH=43h in v0.48,
  wrote it down, and switched to CHS; RMDISK.INC never got the
  message.  CHS is the primary path now and the packet is the
  fallback for a cylinder past the tenth bit.

  RMTEST HAD BEEN SELECTING THE DRIVE IT THEN FAILED TO READ.  Its
  second check asks 0Eh how many drive letters there are, with DL=0.
  0Eh is SELECT DISK.  It spent the rest of its run on an empty A:.

  ...AND IT STOPPED AT THE FIRST FAILURE.  bad: printed the failure
  and RET'd - and it is JUMPED to, not called, so the RET unwound
  straight out of the run.  One broken check hid the state of every
  check behind it.  That is how a working file system came to look
  like a broken list of lists.  RMTEST is 8 for 8 now.

  ...and 52h was refused outright for answering FFFF:xxxx, because
  the check was "below A000h or it is garbage".  A DOS that has
  loaded itself high publishes its structures up there.

  EXEC HAD NEVER RUN.  v0.45 wrote it and said so.  Windows is the
  first thing that has ever called it, and it had two bugs waiting:
  the InDOS flag and the internal stack depth were raised on the way
  into the 4Bh and never lowered, because a 4Bh that starts a program
  does not return through i21_out - so the child began life looking
  at a DOS that was permanently mid-call.  And three of its reads
  passed the byte count in CX to a routine that reads all of ECX.

WHERE IT STOPS NOW.  Windows loads its next stage through RMDOS's
EXEC, the loader runs to completion - open, header, allocate, read,
relocate, PSP, segments, jump - and the child never makes another DOS
call.  The framebuffer instrument (BUILD rmmark) reads: last call in
4Bh, last call out 35h, call count frozen.  On the build before the
ECX fix the two bytes at the child's entry point were 4D 5A, which is
'MZ' - it was jumping into the .EXE header - and after the fix the
stage bits say fn4B is entered more than once and takes both the .EXE
and the .COM branch on different calls.  That is the next release,
and it is all in RMMEM.INC.

v0.49 - THE KERNEL GETS OUT OF THE WAY
--------------------------------------
PM-DOS answers Windows standard mode's INT 2Fh AX=1605h by LEAVING.
It drops paging, leaves protected mode, hands the machine to
RMDOS.SYS, and resumes the program that broadcast - which continues at
the instruction after its own INT, in real mode, on a different DOS,
with every register intact and no way to tell that anything happened.
PARKWIN.COM proves it in six lines of output.  Windows itself takes
the handover and does not yet finish; the reason is at the end of this
entry and is not a mystery.

WHAT THE VETO WAS ACTUALLY REFUSING.  v0.44 built the 1605h veto
around WIN386.EXE: it is a V86 monitor, there is one supervisor seat,
PM-DOS is in it.  All true, and all about 386 ENHANCED mode.  The
broadcast is sent by BOTH modes and DX bit 0 says which - clear for
enhanced, set for standard - and every trace since v0.44 has DX=0001
in it, in a field nobody read.  For twenty-two releases the kernel
printed a message about WIN386.EXE needing the supervisor seat to a
program that had said, in a register, that it did not want it.

DOSX.EXE IS A DOS EXTENDER AND NOT A MONITOR.  It wants to run 16-bit
protected-mode code and be given a way into that mode.  There are
three doors and it will use exactly one:

  DPMI    it never asks.  Not once - INT 2Fh AX=1687h does not appear
          anywhere in a trace of a whole standard-mode startup, and
          the only three multiplex calls DOSX makes are D200h
          (Quarterdeck), 1605h and 1606h.  PM-DOS hosts DPMI and it
          is not a road in.
  VCPI    it asks, on INT 67h AX=DE00h, after finding a manager by
          opening EMMXXXX0.  PM-DOS has no VCPI.
  itself  which is the one it wants, and it will not switch a machine
          that is already switched.

It checks with SMSW, five times, each one followed by TEST AL,1.  The
PE bit answers for the whole machine and under this kernel it is set,
because it IS set - a V86 guest is inside protected mode.  So DOSX
prints "Cannot start Windows in Standard Mode.  Make sure you are not
running other protected-mode software" and leaves.

THERE IS NO ANSWER TO THAT FROM INSIDE PROTECTED MODE.  The bit it
reads is the truth.  Setting EMS=NO to take INT 67h away changes
nothing - it still refuses, having found no manager at all - because
the manager hunt was never the question.  The only way to make the
answer no is to stop being in protected mode, which is what parking
is, and what RMDOS.SYS has been waiting since v0.45 to be underneath.

SO 1605h NOW PARKS.  vdm_winpark, on the way out of the monitor: build
a frame from the guest context, load RMDOS, hand over, and when the
excursion ends terminate the box with the exit code as though the
program had called 4Ch itself - which, one processor mode down, it
did.  Saying YES is spelled by doing nothing, because the caller sets
CX to zero itself and a resident that consents leaves it there; there
is no "accept" to write, and writing a zero would erase somebody
else's veto.  Enhanced mode is still refused, and now for a reason
that is about enhanced mode.

PARKWIN.COM, and why a test with a screen was worth writing before
one with Windows on it.  PARK.INC has said since v0.45 that the way to
test the mode switch is with something smaller than Windows on the
other end of it, and then the first thing anybody did with the finished
handover was point Windows at it - in a 640x480 graphics mode, with no
way to print, with a disk-sector trace channel that took four builds to
make work and was reading the previous run's answer for two of them.
PARKWIN.COM does the same broadcast from a program that fits on a
screen, and its output is the whole test:

    before the broadcast: protected mode or V86 (PE set)
     the DOS answering says BX = 0300
    broadcasting...
    after  the broadcast: REAL MODE (PE clear)
     the DOS answering says BX = FF00
    CX back = 0000  - allowed to start
    BP  back = BEEF  kept
    DI  back = 0A03  kept
    exiting - the DOS that answers this 4Ch unparks.
    C:\>

Two lines apart, across one INT instruction: the processor left
protected mode and the DOS underneath became a different DOS.  BX is
AH=30h's OEM byte, which is 03 for PM-DOS and FF for RMDOS, and it is
in there because the mode proves the processor changed while the OEM
proves the DOS did - and it is the second one a program would notice.
Then 4Ch unparks, PM-DOS picks the machine back up, the box ends and
the prompt comes back.

A REP MOVSB WRITES THROUGH ES, AND ONLY THAT ONE LINE DID.  The frame
never arrived.  park_fillhdr writes eleven fields into RMDOS's image
with "mov [edi+n]" through DS and copied the register frame with a REP
MOVSB, which is the one instruction in the routine that uses ES - and
ES in the monitor loop is not the flat data selector.  The copy went
somewhere else, in silence, and what it left behind was extremely
convincing: RMDOS started, checked a signature THIS ROUTINE HAD
WRITTEN, found it, ran its whole initialisation, and IRETed onto a
frame of zeroes - sending the guest to 0000:0000 to execute the
interrupt vector table.  Every symptom pointed at the guest.  It is a
loop of dword moves now, and park_fromv86's REP STOSD - which was
zeroing 48 bytes of somewhere - is gone entirely, because every byte
it was clearing is written explicitly a few instructions later.

AND THE OTHER END OF THE EXCURSION HAD THE v0.48 BUG IN IT.  Unparking
calls park_remount, which walks EVERY drive letter and mounts each
one, and mounting reads the medium: on the empty A: that is a failed
read, which is a critical error, which PROMPTS - "Not ready reading
drive A, Abort, Retry, Fail?" - on behalf of a program that asked for
none of it, at a moment when the screen may belong to Windows.  It is
the same bug v0.48 found on the way IN, at the other end, four
releases later, and it was invisible for the same reason: nothing had
ever run the unpark path on a machine with an empty drive in it.
crit_busy is the flag that makes crit_raise answer FAIL and return
without asking, and this is exactly the case it exists for -
housekeeping with no caller to ask.  Both ends of the excursion now
know that a drive which is not there is an answer and not a question.

WHERE WINDOWS STOPS, AND IT IS ARITHMETIC RATHER THAN A MYSTERY.  A
.COM is handed every byte of conventional memory DOS has, and the
handover has to LOAD RMDOS.SYS into conventional memory.  A program
that has not shrunk itself owns the only place RMDOS could go, and the
park fails with "not enough memory" on a machine with 620K free.
PARKWIN hit it first and fixed it the way a DOS program is supposed
to, with a 4Ah before anything else.

DOSX CANNOT DO THAT, BECAUSE IT SHRINKS ITSELF AFTER ASKING PERMISSION
AND NOT BEFORE.  From the trace, in order:

    2F/1E86:0036.1605=...d0001      the broadcast
    21/1E86:2AB6.4AE5=...b1CAF      SETBLOCK to 1CAFh paragraphs

The permission is asked for while it still owns the machine.  That
ordering is DOSX's and there is nothing to negotiate with, so the
memory for RMDOS has to come from somewhere that is not the box's TPA.
Three candidates, none of them free:

  reserve it at boot   simple, always works, and costs every DOS box
                       about 23K of its 620K whether it ever starts
                       Windows or not.  A CONFIG.SYS switch could buy
                       it back for people who do not want it.
  reserve it per box   the same 23K, charged only while a box exists,
                       which is nearly the same thing in practice.
  the HMA              0x100000 to 0x10FFFF is unused - the kernel
                       starts at 0x110000 - and it is REAL memory with
                       paging off, so it survives the switch and costs
                       no conventional memory at all.  It needs A20
                       forced on at park time and it needs RMDOS's ORG
                       moved to 10h, because segment FFFFh offset 0 is
                       sixteen bytes BELOW the megabyte and in the ROM.
                       This is where a real DOS puts itself and it is
                       the right answer.

AND UPPER MEMORY IS NOT ONE OF THEM, which is worth writing down
because it looks like the obvious place.  PM-DOS's UMBs exist BECAUSE
of paging: they are RAM mapped under address ranges nothing decodes.
Parking turns paging off, and at that moment every one of those
addresses goes back to decoding nothing.  A DOS loaded into a UMB
would vanish in the instruction that made it necessary.

v0.48 - THE PROMPT NOBODY COULD SEE
-----------------------------------
Windows 3.1 was never hanging after its logo.  It was WAITING FOR A
KEYSTROKE, at a critical-error prompt drawn on a screen it had already
switched to 640x480 - so the question was on the screen in the sense
that the bytes were in the frame buffer, and invisible in every sense
that matters.

The call under it is INT 21h AH=44h AL=08h, "can the media in this
drive be changed?", asked about drive A: while Windows enumerates
drives.  PM-DOS answered it by calling vol_select, which MOUNTS the
volume, which READS THE DISK.  With no readable disk in the drive that
read fails; a failed read inside a DOS call is a critical error; and a
critical error asks Abort, Retry, Fail and waits.  A real DOS answers
08h, 09h and 0Eh out of the drive parameter block and never touches
the medium, which is exactly WHY a program that is enumerating drives
uses them - they are the questions you can ask about a drive that
might be empty.

Everything those three need was already in drv_tbl, filled in by the
boot-time scan: DRV_BIOS says removable or fixed, DRVF_PRESENT says
whether the letter means anything.  f44_drive looks it up now and does
no I/O at all.

WHY TWENTY-ONE RELEASES DID NOT FIND IT.  Every test in this tree
runs on a machine with a disk in the drive, because the tests are ON
that disk - the floppy is how PM-DOS boots.  Booting from the hard
disk instead leaves an empty drive A:, and NOTHING in the machine
touches it until a program goes looking for drives.  That is the same
lesson as v0.42 and v0.43 arriving from a third direction: a feature
nobody exercises is a feature nobody is testing, and this time what
nobody exercised was not a feature but a CONFIGURATION.

AND THE 486 AND 86BOX WOULD HAVE FOUND IT ALL ALONG.  DOSBox 0.74
implements INT 13h as a callback that always succeeds, so the failing
read this whole bug is made of cannot happen there.  The first run on
86Box reproduced it immediately.

WHERE IT STOPS NOW, and it is no longer a mystery.  Windows gets
almost twice as far - 499 guest traps against 238 - loads its
extender, hooks INT 1Ch, 21h and 2Fh, and then:

    2F 1605h    "Windows is starting"   -> PM-DOS says no
    2F 1606h    "Windows is exiting"
    21 4C16h    terminate, exit code 22

It is the veto.  WINDOWS.INC still refuses the init broadcast, which
is blocker (2) of the three v0.45 wrote down, and Windows does exactly
what a well-behaved program does when told no: it unwinds and leaves.
That is not a bug to find any more, it is a piece of work to do - and
the machinery for it is already built, because accepting means parking
the kernel and handing the machine to RMDOS, which is what v0.45 and
v0.46 were for.  1687h is never called, so DOSX is not a DPMI client
and the host is not on the path at all.

v0.47 - THE CHAIN THAT DID NOT END (2026-08-29)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
WINDOWS 3.1 PUTS ITS LOGO ON THE SCREEN ON PM-DOS.  It does not run
yet - it stops after the logo, and where is written down at the end -
but the thing that stopped it before is found, understood and fixed,
and it was not in Windows.

THE HANG FROM v0.44, WHICH WAS NEVER WIN.COM'S FAULT
---------------------------------------------------------------------
v0.44 recorded that WIN.COM hangs: no output at all, never returns,
with the logo suppressed as well as with it, while WIN386.EXE run
directly reached its broadcast perfectly well.  That was as far as it
could be taken then, because the only Windows on this machine was WfW
3.11 and its WIN.COM refuses standard mode outright.

With plain Windows 3.1 media to hand it took three builds to find.
The monitor's own tools did it: "calls" showed the last thing the
guest asked - INT 21h AH=52h, the list of lists - and then silence,
and a new quiet sampler showed the guest going round four instructions
at 043C:183C for ever.  Those four instructions disassemble to this:

  les  bx,es:[bx+4]        ; the first system file table
  add  ax,es:[bx+4]        ; add this block's count
  cmp  word ptr es:[bx],-1 ; is this the last block?
  je   done
  les  bx,es:[bx]          ; no: the next one
  jmp  back

WIN.COM IS COUNTING FILE HANDLES.  It walks the system file table
chain adding up the counts, to see whether the machine has the thirty
Windows needs.  And PM-DOS published FFFF:FFFF as the HEAD of that
chain, meaning "there is no such structure here".

THAT IS NOT WHAT A CHAIN HEAD MEANS.  A walker does not read
FFFF:FFFF as "nothing here" - it LOADS ES:BX from it and follows it,
reads whatever is at the top of the first megabyte, and follows that.
The loop never ended.  Four instructions, no DOS call, nothing on the
screen, and the answer was six words in vdm_lolinit.

THE FIX, AND WHAT IT COST
---------------------------------------------------------------------
There is a real system file table now: one block at 0400:0100, with a
next pointer of FFFF:FFFF the way DOS terminates one, a count that
follows FILES=, and MAX_HANDLES entries after it in DOS 4 layout that
are all zero - which in this structure means "not open", and is true.

It cost the DOS data segment 3.8K and the DOS box the same: DOSDATA
was 256 bytes at 4000h and is four kilobytes now, and the arena starts
at 5000h rather than 4100h.  A DOS box has 620K instead of 624K.  Real
DOS spends exactly this on exactly this.

WHAT IS NOT THERE is a live mirror of the kernel's own table.  PM-DOS's
real SFT is 32-bit and above the megabyte, and copying it down on every
call is work for a reader that has not turned up yet.  A guest walking
the entries sees a table with nothing open in it - a lie only to
something looking for a file another process holds, and nothing in
Windows' startup is.

AND LOLTEST WALKS IT NOW.  The test has had a device-chain walk since
the day it was written, with a comment about unterminated chains
hanging walkers, and no file table walk at all - which is why this
lived through eleven releases of a test suite that reads this exact
structure.  Eighteen checks; the new one is bounded, prints the
pointer, and checks the total against the thirty Windows wants.

VERIFIED
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Windows 3.1 was installed under DOSBox with an unattended SETUP /H
answer file, grafted into HD16.IMG, and started with WIN /S.  It puts
up the Version 3.1 logo and stops there.  Before this release it
stopped before printing anything at all.

Regressions: fifteen tests, no failures, LOLTEST now 18 checks.  Both
park excursions still work - RMTEST 8/8 and the whole of XMSTEST on
RMDOS - which matters because the arena they adopt has moved.

WHERE IT STOPS NOW, HONESTLY
---------------------------------------------------------------------
After the logo, and it is a NEW question rather than the old one.
What is known:

  The guest is NOT spinning in its own code - the quiet sampler never
  trips, so traps keep happening.
  It is not talking to the 8042 - the keyboard transcript is empty.
  With the video mode set taken away from it (V86_NOMODE) the last
  fault is inside the BIOS at F000:1304 - but that reading is an
  ARTIFACT and is recorded here as one: WIN.COM believes it set a
  graphics mode that was not set, and the video BIOS it calls next is
  working from a state that does not exist.

That last point is the lesson of the day and it happened three times:
every probe that was loud enough to read changed what it was
measuring.  See the traps.

TRAPS
---------------------------------------------------------------------
A CHAIN HEAD OF "NOTHING" IS NOT THE SAME AS AN EMPTY CHAIN.  Five
pointers in the list of lists were set to FFFF:FFFF and called honest.
Four of them are: a program that wants the DPB array or the buffers
checks the pointer.  The fifth is a CHAIN, and the code that reads a
chain does not check the head, it follows it.  "The structure is not
here" and "the structure is here and empty" are different statements
and only one of them is safe to make with the same value.

THE INSTRUMENT CHANGED THE ANSWER, THREE TIMES.
  The loud watchdog prints through the console from inside the timer
  interrupt.  That is slow enough that the guest gets measurably fewer
  instructions per tick - and WIN.COM reached its LOGO under it and
  stopped before it without.  Two hours were spent on that difference
  before it was understood to be the probe.  A quiet sampler that
  pokes sixteen bytes into the text page reproduces the release
  behaviour exactly, and is the one to reach for.
  Drawing the sample into the GRAPHICS framebuffer instead came out
  unreadable, because the VGA's write mode, map mask and set/reset
  registers belong to the GUEST at that moment and a byte written to
  A0000 does not mean what the writer intended.
  And taking the mode set away from the guest to keep the screen in
  text mode - which does work, and is V86_NOMODE - leaves the guest
  believing in a mode the hardware is not in, so the next thing it
  asks the BIOS is answered from a state that never existed.  Useful,
  and only for the questions asked before the guest touches video.

A REGISTER THAT LOOKED FREE, IN THE ROUTINE WITH THE COMMENT ABOUT IT.
vdm_lol ends by handing the guest the list-of-lists segment in EAX,
and twenty lines above there is a comment saying so in capitals,
because the same mistake was made with DL two releases ago.  The new
FILES= refresh was written underneath that comment and used EAX.  The
symptom was a guest reading its list of lists at 0028:0002 - which is
forty, which is what FILES= says.  Fifth release running for this
family of bug.

v0.46 - AND SOMEWHERE TO PUT IT (2026-08-29)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
The first of the three things v0.45 said stood between here and
Windows: RMDOS has an XMS 3.0 driver.  DOS\RMXMS.INC, about 1,400
lines, and INT 2Fh AX=4300h answers 80h.

WHY IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS.  Windows in 386 enhanced mode does
not ask whether there is extended memory - it requires a driver, gets
every byte it uses through one, and stops with "You must have an XMS
driver" if 4300h answers anything but 80h.  v0.45 answered 0, which
was true and which ended the conversation before it started.

WHERE THE MEMORY COMES FROM, WHICH IS THE PART THAT IS NOT HIMEM
---------------------------------------------------------------------
A real HIMEM asks the BIOS how much extended memory there is and takes
all of it, because on a real DOS nothing else has a claim on it.  Here
almost all of it is spoken for: PMDOS.SYS is at 100000h, the arena
above it has live blocks in it, and the excursion has to come back to
every one of them.  Extended memory as the BIOS describes it is not
RMDOS's to give away, and a driver that worked it out for itself would
be handing Windows the kernel it has to return to.

So it is GIVEN a range.  park_xmsgrab allocates the free part of the
arena to the kernel itself - one ordinary arena block, allocated the
ordinary way - and passes it over in RMH_XMSBASE/RMH_XMSLEN.
park_release gives it back on the way up, on every exit path including
the ones that refuse to park at all.  Everything RMDOS hands out then
comes out of memory PM-DOS has already agreed to lose for the
duration, and no XMS handle in the machine can name a byte the kernel
is standing on.  On a 16MB machine that came to 13.4 megabytes.
