THE ADDRESSES IT REPORTS ARE PHYSICAL, because PM-DOS's page map is
the identity below its own ceiling.  Function 0Ch has to answer "where
is this block, really" - the caller is about to give that number to a
disk controller or a page table - and that question has a truthful
answer here only for that reason.  It is the third time the identity
map has paid for itself: v0.43 handed a bus-master controller the
caller's own pointer on the same grounds.

WHAT IS IN IT
---------------------------------------------------------------------
All nineteen of the 2.0 functions and the four 3.0 ones - 88h, 89h,
8Eh and 8Fh, which ask the same questions in EAX and are why 00h can
say 3.00.  First fit over thirty-two handles, which with that many is
the whole algorithm: the allocated blocks ARE the map and the gaps
between them are what is left.

EVERY BLOCK STARTS ON A PAGE.  HIMEM aligns to the kilobyte, because
that is the unit XMS counts in.  The customer here builds page tables
out of what it is given, and a block starting halfway through a page
is a page it cannot use.

THE A20 GATE, DONE THROUGH THE HARDWARE.  Two ways to move it - the
spare pin on the keyboard controller that IBM found going begging in
1984, and bit 1 of port 92h that every chipset since has provided
because the 8042 takes tens of microseconds - and no way to know which
this machine has.  So the driver does not decide from a model byte: it
moves the gate and LOOKS, by writing at 0000:0500 and reading at
FFFF:0510, and the method that changes the answer is this machine's
method.  If neither does, the gate is wired open and 03h has nothing
to do.  Every one of 03h to 06h ends by looking, too - a gate that
did not move has to be reported as an error, not as a success whose
caller then reads the wrong megabyte.  And bit 0 of port 92h is FAST
RESET, so that byte is read, changed and masked, never written whole.

THE BLOCK MOVE, TWICE.  0Bh is the function a real HIMEM needs
protected mode for, and there are two ways to have it:

  ITS OWN SWITCH, which is what runs.  Leave real mode, load DS and ES
  with a four-gigabyte descriptor, come back - and the descriptors
  STAY, because a 386 caches a descriptor when a segment register is
  written and uses the cache until it is written again.  The copy
  itself is then ordinary real-mode code addressing the whole machine.
  The rules it lives under are worth writing down: interrupts off,
  nothing may reload DS or ES until it is finished, and nothing in
  between may touch this file's own data, because DS no longer reaches
  it - which is why the copy DIRECTION is decided before the switch
  rather than read out of a variable afterwards.

  INT 15h AH=87h, for when LEAVING REAL MODE IS NOT OURS TO DO.  Once
  Windows is running this code is inside a virtual 8086 machine and
  CR0 belongs to somebody else.  SMSW answers that question without
  being privileged - PE is clear in real mode and set under a monitor
  - and 87h is what every monitor virtualises, because it is how
  everything moved extended memory before XMS was written.

INT 15h AH=88h HAD TO STOP TELLING THE TRUTH.  It is the other way a
program finds extended memory, and a program that finds it that way
will write on memory this driver has promised to somebody else, or on
the kernel.  Every HIMEM since the first one has hooked that vector.

WHAT IT DOES NOT OFFER, and each is a decision rather than a gap:

  THE HMA, because 100000h to 10FFEFh is PMDOS.SYS.  There is nowhere
  else the HMA can be, so 00h reports DX=0 and 01h says "does not
  exist" - which is what a machine with an immovable A20 gate looks
  like, so it is a shape DOS has always been able to present.
  DOS=HIGH is the usual customer, PM-DOS has no DOS=HIGH, and Windows
  does not need it.

  UMBs, which is what HIMEM alone answers on every machine - upper
  memory came from EMM386.  PM-DOS's own upper memory is already in
  the MCB chain RMDOS adopted and is reachable through 48h, and two
  doors onto one pool is a bug waiting for whoever opens both.

VERIFIED
---------------------------------------------------------------------
XMSTEST.COM, WHICH IS NOT A NEW TEST.  It has exercised the kernel's
own XMS host for many releases and it knows nothing about who answers
it - it finds XMS the way every DOS program does and is an ordinary
client from there.  Run through PARKTEST it lands on RMDOS instead,
and the same program now passes against BOTH providers:

  version 0300, HMA flag 0000
  request the HMA:      refused, no HMA here
  free (16-bit): largest 13744 KB of 13744 KB total
  free (32-bit): largest 13744 KB of 13744 KB total
  allocated 64 KB, locked at 00273000
  moving 32 bytes out and back: the bytes came back intact
  the handle says 64 KB
  grown to 128 KB and back, contents intact
  the whole pool, taken and given back
  INT 15h/88h: no extended memory, as it should say
  A20 on: 0000:0500 and FFFF:0510 differ
  A20 off: 0000:0500 and FFFF:0510 alias

Four of those checks are new this pass - handle information,
reallocate up and down with the contents carried across, and asking
for the whole pool - and they were written because reallocate was code
nothing had ever called.  The last one found a real bug; see below.

THE INT 15h PATH WAS RUN TOO, forced with -dRMDOS_I15MOVE, and moved
the same bytes.  It is the path a monitor would take, it cannot be
reached from here without Windows, and a switch that makes it run in
real mode - where 87h is perfectly at home - is the difference between
a fallback and a fallback nobody has tried.

Regressions: fifteen tests, WINTEST 13/13 through DEVTEST, no
failures.  RMTEST still 8/8 through the park.

WHAT IS STILL BETWEEN HERE AND WINDOWS
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Two of v0.45's three, unchanged: the 1605h accept path is written and
has never executed - WINDOWS.INC still vetoes, which is right until
the rest works - and RMDOS's own EXEC is written and has never been
called, which every DOS box needs because every DOS box is
COMMAND.COM.  And WIN.COM's own hang from v0.44 is still in front of
all of it.

TRAPS
---------------------------------------------------------------------
A NUMBER A CALLER CANNOT ACT ON IS THE WRONG NUMBER.  08h reported the
largest free block to the kilobyte, because that is the unit XMS
counts in.  Blocks are handed out on page boundaries, so a request is
rounded UP to a page - and asking for exactly as much as the manager
says is free rounded up past the end of the pool and failed.  That is
the FIRST thing Windows does.  Both ends are page-granular now: the
pool PM-DOS hands over, and the figure the driver reports.

...AND IT WAS FOUND BY A CHECK WRITTEN FOR SOMETHING ELSE, which is
the fourth release running.  The new check exists because reallocate
had never been called; it happens to ask for the whole pool on the way
past.  Sixty-four kilobytes worked perfectly and would have gone on
working perfectly right up until WIN386 asked the only question that
mattered.

WASM FOLDS CASE ACROSS FILES, AND KNOWING THAT IS NOT ENOUGH.  The
lesson was written down in v0.45 and the very next file collided five
times anyway: RMDISK.INC already had rx_ok, rx_err and rx_next,
because in that file rx_ means "read sector".  A prefix chosen to be
distinctive is only distinctive against the files you thought of.

A BUILD SWITCH IS THE CHEAPEST WAY TO TEST AN UNREACHABLE PATH.  The
INT 15h move exists for a case that cannot be produced without
Windows.  One IFDEF made it run in the case that CAN be produced, and
turned "written" into "tested" for three lines.

v0.45 - THE KERNEL LEAVES (2026-08-29)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
PM-DOS can now get out of the way.  It drops paging, leaves protected
mode for good, hands the machine to a 16-bit DOS it loaded into the
arena a moment earlier, lets a program run to completion on it, and
picks the whole machine back up afterwards.

That is phases C and D of the Windows work: the real-mode DOS, and the
handover.  What is NOT here is Windows itself - see the end.

WHY ANY OF THIS.  v0.44 answers WIN386.EXE's INT 2Fh AX=1605h with a
veto, because WIN386 is a V86 monitor and there is one supervisor seat
in a machine.  The only way to let Windows have it is to get out of
it.  And the moment PM-DOS does, every INT 21h in the machine has
nothing to answer it: the whole API is 32-bit protected-mode code and
there is no INT 21h anywhere in IO\IORM.ASM.

A STUB THAT FORWARDED THE CALLS BACK IS NOT POSSIBLE, and it is worth
writing down why once rather than rediscovering it.  While WIN386 owns
CR0, CR3, the GDT, the IDT and the TSS, there is no way to re-enter
PM-DOS's own protected mode - a V86 program under Windows reaches
protected mode only through WINDOWS' DPMI, which hands out Windows'
descriptors and Windows' page tables.  There is no thunk home.  So the
thing left behind has to IMPLEMENT DOS.

RMDOS.SYS, AND WHY IT FITS IN 20K
---------------------------------------------------------------------
DOS\RMDOS.ASM and five includes: 6,600 lines, 20,434 bytes of image.
Console, the character calls, FAT12/16/32 read and write, directories,
handles, the arena, EXEC, the swappable data area, the list of lists,
INT 20h and 22h-2Fh.  8.3 names only.

It is that small because of what it does NOT have to do, and that is
the part worth understanding: THE ARENA IS ALREADY THERE.  A DOS box's
memory is already a real-mode MCB chain in real conventional memory,
because that is the only shape a 16-bit program can walk; the PSPs in
it are real PSPs; the programs are at real segment addresses; and
below 1MB PM-DOS's page map is the identity, so when paging stops
every one of those numbers still means what it meant.

RMDOS allocates nothing, moves nothing and relocates nothing at
startup.  It ADOPTS what is there and carries on allocating out of it.
A DOS that had to build an arena would also have to decide where the
running program went, and there is no answer to that which does not
involve moving it.

What it has to supply is only what lived above 1MB and did not
survive: the handle table, the file system, and the INT 21h reaching
them.  It inherits the drive letters too - PM-DOS scanned the
partition tables and hands over the answer - but not the geometry,
which RMDOS reads out of each volume's own boot sector because that is
less code than a structure both sides would have to agree about
forever.

ONE SEGMENT, CS = DS = SS.  Code, data and all three internal stacks
are in the same 64K, which is why nothing in the file needs a segment
override to reach its own variables and why the INT 21h register frame
can be read as [bp+F_xx] with the processor's default SS and also as
ordinary data.  The frame is COPIED onto RMDOS's stack rather than
left on the caller's, and two words underneath say where the caller's
copy is so the answers can be written back into it.

THE HANDOVER, WHICH IS pm2rm WITH ITS ENDING TAKEN OFF
---------------------------------------------------------------------
IO\IORM.ASM already had the hard part.  pm2rm has gone to real mode
and back on every BIOS call since v0.06: paging off before PE off, an
identity-mapped instruction doing the switch, the BIOS IVT back, the
PICs where the BIOS put them.  Parking is that routine with its return
removed - it goes down and does not come up - and unparking is the
return on its own.  Two new fixed entries in the stub, rm_park at
0900h and rm_unpark at 0A80h, and a 32-bit wrapper in RMCALL.INC that
is rm_int with the interrupt replaced by a far jump.

From the kernel's side it is one very slow subroutine call.  RMSAVE_ESP
and RMRET are set exactly as rm_int sets them, and the return lands at
the instruction after the call - after the processor has been in real
mode and another kernel has owned the interrupt table.

WHAT IS PUT BACK ON THE WAY UP: the DOS vectors a guest reflects
through (vdm_stubs again, because RMDOS pointed them at a segment
about to be freed); every volume, remounted, because RMDOS has been
writing to the same disks and every FAT window and cluster cached
above 1MB describes them as they were; the PICs; and A20, forced on
rather than assumed, because whatever ran while we were away owned the
gate and the kernel this returns to lives above the megabyte.
Everything dirty goes out BEFORE parking, for the mirror-image reason.

AND ONE RULE, CHECKED RATHER THAN DOCUMENTED: no file may be open.
RMDOS has its own handle table and its own idea of where each file is;
two DOSes with a file open between them is a coherency problem with no
owner.  21h/F1h AL=0Bh refuses with "access denied" if any handle
above the standard five is open - which fired on its first real
outing, because the regression script redirects PARKTEST's output to a
file and that is a handle.

VERIFIED
---------------------------------------------------------------------
PARKTEST.EXE is a native 32-bit ring-3 program that asks the kernel to
leave.  RMTEST.COM is an ordinary 16-bit DOS program - the only one in
this tree that does not run on PM-DOS - and every INT 21h it makes is
answered by RMDOS.  Eight of eight, on DOSBox:

  30h says DOS 06.16 ok                    (6.22, in hex)
  19h/0Eh current drive A: 08 letters ok
  5D06h swappable data area at 0432:3F1C ok
  52h first MCB is 0410 ok
  and the arena walks: 000A blocks, ending in Z ok
  48h/49h a kilobyte, written and freed ok
  36h free space (spc/free) 0001/0052 ok
  3Dh/3Fh PMIO.SYS starts E98B ok

The last one is the interesting one: RMDOS opened a file on a real
FAT12 volume, through its own boot-sector parse, its own FAT walk and
its own directory search, and read the two bytes IORM.ASM puts at
offset zero.  And then PARKTEST printed "Back in protected mode" and
opened a file itself, through caches the excursion had invalidated.

Regressions: WINTEST 13/13, LOLTEST 17/17, APITEST, MCBTEST, FCBTEST
22/22, BUFTEST 8/8, UMBTEST 11/11, XMSTEST, EMSTEST 14/14, DPMITEST,
CFGTEST 4/4, F32TEST, UDTEST, CTRYTEST - no failures anywhere.

WHAT IS NOT DONE, PLAINLY
---------------------------------------------------------------------
This does not run Windows.  Three things stand between here and that,
and the first is the large one:

  NO XMS PROVIDER.  RMDOS answers INT 2Fh AX=4300h with "not
  installed", which is true and which Windows in 386 enhanced mode
  will not accept - it requires HIMEM and stops without it.  Writing
  one is the next piece of work and it is not small, because it has to
  report extended memory starting ABOVE PM-DOS's own image or Windows
  will allocate over the kernel this excursion has to return to.

  THE 1605h ACCEPT PATH is not wired.  WINDOWS.INC still vetoes, which
  is right until the rest works.  When it is wired, the handover is
  the OTHER branch of rd_entry - the one that does not start a program
  but IRETs to a saved frame, because WIN386 is already loaded and
  already running when it broadcasts, and what it is owed is a return
  from that interrupt which happens to land in a different processor
  mode from the one it was taken in.  That branch is written and has
  never been executed.

  EXEC IS WRITTEN AND UNTESTED.  RMDOS's 4Bh loads .EXE and .COM,
  relocates, builds a PSP and inherits handles, because every DOS box
  Windows opens is COMMAND.COM started through it.  Nothing has called
  it yet.  Same for 4Eh/4Fh, 39h/3Ah, 56h and 6Ch, all of which are
  written; 5Ah, 39h and 3Ah refuse.

  And WIN.COM's own hang, from v0.44, is still there in front of all
  of it.

TRAPS
---------------------------------------------------------------------
TWO FIXED OFFSETS WITH CODE BETWEEN THEM NEED A CHECK AT BOTH ENDS.
The stub's park entry is at 0900h and its unpark entry was at 0940h,
sixty-four bytes apart, and the park code grew to end ONE BYTE past
the second.  The ORG silently overwrote it.  What then happened is the
part worth remembering: the handover far-jumped into an instruction
stream that was half of one routine and half of another, wandered into
the unpark, went straight back to protected mode - and the machine
SURVIVED AND REPORTED SUCCESS.  There was a guard on the first
boundary and none on the second.  Both are checked now.

DEBUGGING A MODE SWITCH MEANS WRITING TO THE SCREEN, because the
screen is the only thing both sides of it agree about.  Eight markers
written straight to B8000h - the same physical bytes at 0B800h:0000 in
real mode - found the above in one run, after an hour of reasoning had
not.  Two of them were wrong at first in instructive ways: one pushed
onto a stack that had not been set up yet, and one pushed onto the
stack being handed over, whose pointer PM-DOS had set past the end of
the block it allocated.  The second was a real bug in the handover and
not only in the marker: nothing was pushed there yet, but "nothing is
pushed here" is a fragile thing for a stack pointer to rely on.

A ROUTINE THAT ANSWERS IN A REGISTER MUST NOT SAVE THAT REGISTER.
rd_path answers the directory's cluster in EBX.  Rewriting it, a copy
loop wanted a scratch register, took BX, and PUSHed and POPped it like
the others - so every caller got its own BX back instead of the
answer.  It failed on exactly one check, the one that opens a file,
and looked like a FAT bug for two builds.

AND THE FILE THAT LOOKED LIKE A FAT BUG BEFORE THAT was a segment
bug.  Every routine under rd_path reaches RMDOS's data through DS, and
the first version pointed DS at the CALLER's segment so it could read
the path string: the volume table it then read was whatever the caller
happened to have at that offset.  The path is copied into RMDOS's own
segment first now, and there is no second segment in the routine at
all.

WASM FOLDS CASE, again, and this time across FILES: RMDOS.ASM included
PMDOS.INC, whose SFT_SIZE means "how big the table is" where RMDOS's
means "how big the file is", and both are valid offsets.  Twenty
"label is already defined" errors was the lucky outcome.  RMDOS does
not include the kernel's header any more - it is a separate program
that happens to be built in the same tree - and RMDOS.INC carries the
dozen constants it needs behind IFNDEF, because PM-DOS's own side of
the park includes both.

v0.44 - INTRODUCING OURSELVES TO WINDOWS (2026-08-27)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
The smallest release in a while and the one with the longest shadow:
it is the first piece of work aimed at running Windows 3.1x, and what
it adds is not a feature so much as a set of ANSWERS.

WHAT WAS THERE BEFORE.  Nothing.  Grepping the whole kernel for the
INT 2Fh 16xx family found one passing mention in a comment.  There was
no 5D06h either - 5Dh was i21_unsup, along with the rest of its row.
So when WIN386.EXE broadcast INT 2Fh AX=1605h to ask the machine's
residents whether it could start, that broadcast reached the IRET stub
the VDM installs on 2Fh for a guest, came back with every register
exactly as Windows had set it, and Windows read its verdict out of CX
- a register it had not written for the purpose of being read.
Whatever happened next was not a decision anybody had made.

THE SWAPPABLE DATA AREA, AND WHY IT MOVED THE FLAGS.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
21h/5D06h hands out the block of DOS's own per-process state that a
multitasker saves and restores around a task switch.  Windows in 386
enhanced mode is the famous consumer - DOSMGR instances it per virtual
machine - but it is nowhere near the only one: DESQview asks, network
redirectors ask, and any TSR that wants the current drive or DTA
without disturbing them asks.

PM-DOS has had the two bytes at the head of that structure since v0.25:
the critical-error flag and the InDOS count, at 4F6h and 4F7h, in the
tail of the BIOS data area's user region.  That was a fine place for
two loose bytes and an impossible one for a STRUCTURE - 5D06h hands out
a CONTIGUOUS block whose first two bytes are exactly those flags, and
at 4F6h the block would have run into RMFRAME at 500h after six.

So they moved, into the DOS data segment, above the list of lists and
inside the same 256 bytes a guest already addresses as DOSDATA_SEG -
which is precisely where MS-DOS keeps its own.  The layout is MS-DOS
6's, field for field, and it was taken from SWAP_START in the DOS 6
source's INC\CONST2.ASM rather than from a reference book.  Both flags
are EQUs and always were, so thirty-odd use sites moved with them
without being touched, and 34h now answers the second byte of a real
structure instead of a byte that merely looked like one.

WHAT IS PUBLISHED IS SHORT AND THAT IS THE POINT.  MS-DOS 5 answers
about 1440 bytes here; PM-DOS answers 26.  The 26 are MS-DOS's own
SWAP_START through Swap_Always - error flags, DTA, PSP, drive - which
is per-process state and genuinely needs instancing.  Everything past
that point in MS-DOS is its own working storage: half-built device
request packets, directory-search state, an arena walk in progress.
PM-DOS's equivalents are 32-bit structures above 1MB, so there is
nothing there to publish, and 1414 plausible zeroes at the offsets
where a consumer expects MS-DOS's would be an invitation to read them.
Same rule as the list of lists saying FFFF:FFFF where it has nothing.

CX and DX come back equal, which is what "all of it, always" looks
like from the caller's side.  MS-DOS computes DX as the distance from
SWAP_START to Swap_Always; ours has no second half for it to stop
short of.

THE FIELDS THAT LIVE SOMEWHERE ELSE.  Drive, PSP, DTA and the extended
error have their master copies in the kernel's own 32-bit data, so the
structure has to be refreshed.  That happens at i21_r0 - the single
exit from INT 21h - and not in the four or five setters that own those
values, because forgetting one of those would produce a structure that
is right nearly always.  A consumer reads this when InDOS is zero,
which is just after a call returned, so refreshing it as the call
leaves gives the right answer at the only moment anyone is entitled to
look.  Class, action and locus are DERIVED here rather than stored, so
59h's table lookup was split out as err_classify and is called only
when the error code has actually changed.

AND TWO OF THOSE FIELDS SAY ZERO FOR A NATIVE PROGRAM, HONESTLY.  A
DOS box's PSP is in conventional memory and converts to a segment; a
32-bit program's is at 140000h or 180000h and there is no segment:
offset that names it.  The bottom sixteen bits of an address above the
megabyte is a number that means something else, and something would
follow it.

THE INT 2Fh FAMILY, AND THE ONE CALL WITH TEETH.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
1600h, 160Ah, 4680h and 1680h are questions, and the answer to all four
is no.  Every one of them is specified so that "no" is the registers
coming back UNCHANGED - AL still 00h, AX still non-zero, AL still 80h -
which means the IRET stub had been answering all four correctly since
the VDM existed, by accident.  They are claimed explicitly now anyway:
the answer stops depending on that stub still being an IRET, and a
guest TSR that hooked 2Fh can no longer answer them on PM-DOS's behalf
and get it wrong.

1605h is the one that matters.  PM-DOS vetoes it - CX non-zero - and
prints why, once per boot.  It cannot do otherwise: WIN386.EXE is
itself a V86 monitor, building its own page tables, its own GDT and
IDT, running the machine from ring 0, and there is exactly one of those
seats.  Under MS-DOS the seat is empty.  Under EMM386 it is occupied
and Windows still starts, because EMM386 answers this call by leaving
protected mode ENTIRELY and handing the whole machine over, with a
real-mode MS-DOS left underneath still able to serve INT 21h.  PM-DOS
has no real-mode DOS to leave underneath - its entire API is 32-bit
protected-mode code - and building one is a second DOS, not a shim.

THE VETO IS SET AND THE CALL IS THEN REFLECTED ANYWAY.  A broadcast is
supposed to reach every resident, and a TSR in the box that wanted to
see Windows start is entitled to see it even though the answer is
already no.  Nothing downstream can undo it - the protocol has no way
to clear CX back to zero - so setting it first and chaining second is
both polite and safe.

5D0Ah IS THE ONE THAT COULD HAVE GONE IN AND DID NOT.  Set extended
error information presets the class, action and locus that the next
59h will report, and PM-DOS does not store those three - it derives
them.  Honouring it means giving 59h an override that outranks its own
table, which is a change to the error model rather than an addition,
and it can wait for something that actually calls it.  The rest of the
5Dh row is the network server family and there is no redirector for it
to be part of.

VERIFIED AGAINST REAL WINDOWS, WHICH IS THE POINT.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
WINTEST.COM is new and passes 13 of 13: the structure is where 5D06h
says, its length and always-swap size agree, 34h answers its second
byte compared as a TWENTY-BIT ADDRESS rather than as a register pair,
both flags read zero from outside a DOS call, +02h is FFh the way
MS-DOS initialises it, and drive, PSP and DTA each match the call that
owns them.  Then all five 2Fh answers.

But the test that counts was run against Windows for Workgroups 3.11
itself.  A 15MB Windows tree was grafted into HD16.IMG, PM-DOS booted
from it, and WIN386.EXE run directly: it loaded, it broadcast 1605h,
it took the veto, it stopped, and THE MACHINE CAME BACK TO THE PROMPT.
That is the whole release working end to end on a program that has no
idea PM-DOS exists.

AND WIN.COM ITSELF HANGS, WHICH IS THE NEXT THING TO CHASE.  Started
through WIN.COM rather than WIN386.EXE directly, Windows produces no
output at all and never returns - with the startup logo suppressed as
well as with it.  Since WIN386 reaches its broadcast perfectly well
when run on its own, the hang is in WIN.COM's own startup, BEFORE it
gets as far as the thing this release fixed.  That is a separate bug
and it is now the first question for the next piece of Windows work.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO.  It does not run Windows.  Standard mode was
the cheap thing to try - it runs as a DPMI client and PM-DOS hosts
DPMI - but the only Windows on this machine is WfW 3.11, whose WIN.COM
contains the string "Windows for Workgroups 3.11 does not run in real
or standard modes" and means it.  Testing standard mode needs plain
Windows 3.1 or 3.11 media, which is not here.

TOOLS.  A fatput.pl was written to graft a host directory tree into a
FAT16 image, because there is no mtools on this machine and MKDISK.EXE
takes a flat file list.  It will be needed again: every later piece of
Windows work means putting a large tree on a test disk.

Regressions: WINTEST 13/13, LOLTEST 17/17, APITEST, MCBTEST, FCBTEST,
BUFTEST, UMBTEST, XMSTEST, EMSTEST 14/14, DPMITEST, CFGTEST, F32TEST,
UDTEST, CTRYTEST and EXECTST all clean.  ALLOCTST 1/2, R3TEST 13/14
and I24TEST needing TESTDEV are the standing DOSBox results, unchanged
from v0.42 and v0.43.

AND LOLTEST HAD BEEN LYING FOR SIX RELEASES.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
It reports 17 checks now and reported 8 before, and nothing in the
kernel changed to make the difference.  The device-chain check ended
with "jmp cpu_test" on BOTH of its exits - the passing one and the
failing one - and cpu_test is past every check in between.  So 1Bh,
1Ch, 38h, 67h, 5Ch, 63h, 6Ch and 65h ran ONLY on the path where the
device chain failed to terminate, which it never does.  Eight checks
that printed nothing, failed nothing, and were counted as neither.

This was found because the 5D06h bridge shares vd_go with 1Bh, 1Ch and
63h, so those were the checks worth watching after touching it - and
they were not in the output to watch.

Fixing it turned up a second bug in the same file rather than in the
kernel: the 65h/20h check printed the capitalised character with put2
and then compared DL against 'A'.  put2 reaches putc through put1,
which does MOV DL,AL to make the call - so by the time it returns, DL
holds the last hex digit printed and not the answer.  The check read
'1' out of "41" and called it a failure.  A scratch probe against
6520h, 6521h and 6522h showed all three working, so the kernel was
right and the test was wrong; the test now saves DL before printing it.

THE RECURRING TRAP, ARRIVING FROM A NEW DIRECTION.  "A feature nobody
exercises is a feature nobody is testing" has been the note for three
releases running, and each time the unexercised thing was in the
kernel.  This time it was in the TEST - a check that cannot fail is
worth less than no check at all, because no check does not appear in
the pass count.

v0.43 - THE CONTROLLER MOVES THE DATA (2026-08-27)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Two faster ways to get a sector off a disk, and a third thing that
came out from under them.

Until now every byte the kernel read from an IDE disk went through
REP INSW: sixteen bits a cycle, the processor doing the carrying, one
sector at a time with a status poll between them.  That is what the
driver was written with and it is what every machine can do.  It is
also two hardware generations behind the machines this kernel runs
on.  So: 32-BIT PIO, which halves the bus cycles for the same bytes,
and BUS-MASTER DMA, where the controller moves the data and the
processor is not involved at all.

THE FLAT MAP PAID FOR THE DMA, AND IT WAS ALWAYS GOING TO.  PAGING.INC
has said since v0.29 that the map is the identity everywhere, and its
third sentence says why that matters: "a linear address IS a physical
one, and a bus-master device can be handed our own pointers."  Every
other operating system doing this has to translate an address and pin
the memory behind it; here a descriptor takes the pointer the caller
gave us, unchanged.  The prediction in the roadmap was right and the
work was three quarters not-having-to.

WHAT IT COST INSTEAD WAS FINDING THE REGISTERS.  A PCI IDE controller
keeps its command block exactly where an ISA one did, at 1F0h and
170h, so the existing probe finds the drives without knowing anything
about PCI at all.  Its DMA engine is somewhere only configuration
space knows - BAR4 - and there is no probing for that.  Hence IO\PCI
.INC, which is mechanism 1, a find-by-class, and a config-space read
and write, and deliberately nothing else: no resource assignment, ever
- the BIOS did that at POST and a DOS that started moving devices
around would be taking a decision it has no way to get right.

AND THE TWO DETECTIONS FOR 32-BIT PIO ARE COMPLEMENTARY, WHICH IS THE
NICEST THING IN THIS RELEASE.  IDENTIFY word 48 was defined in ATA-1
as "can do doubleword I/O" and the VLB-era drives set it; ATA-3 made
the word obsolete, so a later drive reports zero there whatever it is
plugged into.  A PCI IDE controller handles a 32-bit access to the
data port by construction.  Word 48 covers the drives too old to be on
a PCI bus; the PCI controller covers the drives too new to set word
48; between them they cover everything.  Neither is a MEASUREMENT,
because there is no measuring this: a host adapter that cannot latch
two words does not report an error, it returns half the data.

THE ONE PLACE THIS KERNEL DECLINES TO BE CLEVER IS THE TRANSFER MODE,
and the reason is worth stating plainly because it is the difference
between fast and right.  A transfer mode is TWO settings that have to
agree: the drive's, which SET FEATURES chooses and which is
standardised, and the host adapter's timing, which is a chipset
register that PIIX spells one way, VIA another and ALi a third, and
which PM-DOS knows nothing about.  Telling a drive to run UDMA against
timing the BIOS programmed for something slower is how a disk returns
data that is almost right.  So IDEDMA=AUTO - the default - uses the
mode that is ALREADY SELECTED, which the BIOS selected at POST having
programmed its own end to match, and if nothing is selected it does
nothing and the transfers stay PIO.  That is not timidity; it is the
only version of "automatic" that cannot be wrong.  IDEDMA=ON and
IDEDMA=UDMA2 do issue SET FEATURES, because a user who writes one has
said something deliberate about their own machine.  ON stops at UDMA
mode 2 - 33 MB/s - which is the last mode a 40-conductor cable
carries and so the last one that needs no cable-detect question.

AND A BUS MASTER THAT GETS IT WRONG IS NOT TRUSTED WITH THE RETRY.
ata_dmarun separates the drive's errors from the engine's: a bad
sector is passed up as a bad sector, but an engine error, or a
transfer that never finished with the drive perfectly happy, takes
that device off DMA for the rest of the session and does the same
chunk again by PIO.  Nothing was advanced, so the retry is just a
jump back to the top of the loop.  A machine whose chipset lies gets
a slow disk rather than a wrong one.

Two 64K rules, both from the same hardware quirk.  A descriptor may
not cross a 64K boundary, so ata_prdbuild cuts the buffer at every one
it spans; and the descriptor TABLE may not cross one either, because
the engine increments only the low sixteen bits of the address it
holds, so a straddling table wraps to its own beginning.  There is no
way to ask an assembler for that, so twice the room is reserved and
ata_prdinit picks the half that does not straddle.

ata_dmaok IS FOUR COMPARISONS AND THE IDENTITY MAP IS WHY.  There are
exactly two places where a linear address is not a physical one: the
sixteen pages from 100000h that the A20 gate aliases down to zero, and
whatever UMB.INC and EMS.INC have pointed at upper memory.  Both are
below 1MB.  So everything under A0000h is itself, everything from
DOS_BASE up is itself, and a buffer in the band between goes by PIO -
which needs no physical address at all, because the processor is the
one doing the moving.  An odd address goes the same way: a descriptor
cannot name one.

TOOLS\IDETEST.ASM is the test, and its shape is the point.  Reporting
what the machine decided is the easy half, and it needs 21h/F1h AL=0Ah
because a ring-3 program has no I/O privilege and cannot read a
controller's registers even to describe them - the same argument AL=9
makes for expanded memory.  The hard half is checking, and every check
is one idea: THE SAME BYTES READ TWO DIFFERENT WAYS MUST AGREE.  32
sectors in one transfer - several descriptors, a 64K line deliberately
in the middle - against the same 32 read one at a time.  Then the same
run into an odd address, which no bus master can be pointed at, so it
is the PIO fallback proving it is live.  On 86Box all three paths -
16-bit PIO, 32-bit PIO and UDMA mode 2 - produce checksum B3C0A36B.

AND UNDERNEATH IT, TWO CONFIG.SYS BUGS, ONE OLD AND ONE AN HOUR OLD.

THE OLD ONE: CFG_BUF_SIZE HAS BEEN 4096 SINCE THE FIRST DAY AND
NOTHING CHECKED WHETHER THE FILE FITTED.  A longer CONFIG.SYS was read
as far as the buffer went and the rest was dropped IN SILENCE - no
message, no clue.  PM-DOS's own sample CONFIG.SYS grew to 5,543 bytes
over eleven releases of documenting itself, so its last third had not
been read for some time: NULLTRAP=, the whole KEYRATE block, and
anything a user added at the bottom.  All three statements it was
losing happened to be spelling out defaults, which is exactly why
nobody noticed.  The buffer is 16K now, and - the half that matters -
a file that does not fit says so.

Found by adding IDEDMA= to the end of that file and watching it do
nothing, which is the third release running where a test written for
one thing has found something else.

THE NEW ONE WAS MINE, AND IT IS THE RECURRING TRAP IN MIRROR IMAGE.
config_run read the file and then closed it, holding the read's carry
across the close in PUSHFD/POPFD - correct, and correct for as long as
nothing stood between the read and the close.  The fit check went in
between them.  "The file is shorter than the buffer" is JB, WHICH IS
CF SET, so PUSHFD started saving a carry that meant success and the
test after POPFD read it as failure: every CONFIG.SYS in the machine
was abandoned, and abandoned in silence, because a machine with no
CONFIG.SYS is not an error and never was.  Four releases have now been
bitten by a flag or a register that was still carrying an answer; this
is the first where the answer was carried into the trap rather than
out of it.  The fix is that the answer now lives in a byte and the
close preserves nothing.

VERIFIED.  86Box (Pentium-class 440BX, PIIX4 IDE, real ATA disks):
IDETEST 9 of 9 with both disks on bus-master DMA in UDMA mode 2 with
32-bit PIO, and 9 of 9 again with IDEDMA=OFF/IDE32=OFF, and again with
IDEDMA=ON forcing SET FEATURES - same checksum all three times.  The
whole suite passes with DMA doing every transfer: XMSTEST, A20TEST,
APITEST, DEVTEST, MCBTEST, FCBTEST 22/22, BUFTEST 8/8, UMBTEST 11/11,
EMSTEST, ALLOCTST 2/2, I24TEST 8/8, VFYTEST 10/10, F32TEST 10/10,
CFGTEST 4/4, IDETEST 9/9, R3TEST 14/14.

v0.42 - THE MISSING SURFACE, AND THE THREE BUGS UNDER IT (2026-08-27)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
The list this release works from was written as a roadmap of leaves:
switches a DOS user reaches for without thinking, calls a program
makes without expecting an argument about them.  VERIFY that verifies.
4Bh AL=1 and AL=3.  The rest of the FAT32 family - 7302h, 7304h,
7305h.  INT 13h's extensions inside PMIO, not just facing a guest.
DIR /S and /O, DIRCMD, DEL /S, COPY /V /A /B, FORMAT /S.  The cursor
pad, the function keys, and a typematic rate.

Every one of them went in.  What is worth the paragraphs, though, is
that three of them found bugs that had nothing to do with the feature
and everything to do with the fact that NOBODY HAD CALLED THAT CODE
SINCE THE MACHINE CHANGED UNDERNEATH IT.

New: TOOLS\VFYTEST.ASM, TOOLS\F32TEST.ASM, DISK\SWTEST.BAT, and a
KEYRATE= statement in CONFIG.INC.

INT 25h AND 26h HAD BEEN BROKEN SINCE v0.33
-------------------------------------------
This is the one to read.

int21_entry has twenty lines of comment at the top saying that an
interrupt gate does not reload DS and ES, that a native program's
pointers are offsets in its own slot, and that both of those have to
be dealt with before a handler runs.  int25_entry and int26_entry sat
forty lines below it and did neither.  The kernel ran with the
CALLER'S data segment - so every variable it touched was addressed
through a descriptor based at the program's slot - and used the
caller's buffer address as though a slot offset were a flat address.

It has been that way since v0.33 moved programs to ring 3.  Eight
releases.  It went unnoticed because these two calls have exactly two
users in the whole system, SYS and FORMAT, and the last time either
was run was v0.17 - before there was a ring 3 to get wrong.
Everything else that reads a sector does it through INT 21h.

It was found by a test that had no interest in the subject.  VFYTEST
calls 26h to write a sector it can then prove was verified, and the
machine took a page fault inside the kernel at 00110B94 writing to
00180000 - which is the transient slot's guard page, which is what a
slot offset of zero comes to once a descriptor based at the slot has
been applied to it.

The fix is int21_entry's, moved: reload DS and ES, and translate the
caller's EBX the three ways there are - flat for the kernel, r3_flat
for a native program, the client's own descriptor for a DPMI one.
The original goes in absbx and is put back before popad, because a
program that found the kernel's flat address in its EBX afterwards
would be entitled to be surprised.

THE MORAL, and it is the second time this project has learned it: A
FEATURE NOBODY EXERCISES IS A FEATURE NOBODY IS TESTING.  The v0.41
notes say the same thing about a guest's INT 24h - never reached for
twenty-one releases because R3TEST covered the other half.  Both were
found by writing a test for something else.

...AND THEY COULD NOT REACH A LOADED BLOCK DRIVER EITHER
--------------------------------------------------------
The same two calls went straight to the block layer with whatever
drive number they were given.  Since v0.40 a drive letter can name a
loaded block driver's unit instead of a disk, through a pseudo BIOS
drive number from DL_UNIT_BASE up - and dio_try makes that fork for
the filesystem's sectors.  Absolute disk I/O did not, so 25h and 26h
on a RAM disk failed with a drive number no BIOS has ever heard of.

The fork is now dio_raw, which is a routine because three callers need
it: disk_read and disk_write, VERIFY's read-back, and absolute I/O.
It was four lines inside dio_try when only one caller knew about it.

AND THE DIRECTION OF A DRIVER TRANSFER WAS THE WRONG QUESTION
-------------------------------------------------------------
dl_blkio decided read-or-write by looking at [dio_wr] - the flag that
says what the transfer disk_write is retrying was.  That is very
nearly the same thing, and was exactly the same thing while
disk_write was its only caller.

It stopped being the same thing the moment VERIFY started reading a
sector back IN THE MIDDLE OF a write: "what is this transfer" and
"what was the call" are then opposite answers, and the read-back went
out to the driver as a second write.  The direction is the SERVICE
now, out of EDX, which is what the caller was already passing.

VERIFY, ACTUALLY VERIFYING
--------------------------
21h/2Eh has set a flag since v0.31 and 54h has reported it, and for
eleven releases nothing read it.  That was said plainly in the source
rather than hidden - but "the flag is remembered" and "writes are
verified" are different claims, and a program that turns VERIFY on and
copies a file is asking for the second one.

dio_verify sits one level below every write in the system: the
filesystem's sectors go through disk_write, the raw ones through 26h
and 7305h, and all three consult the flag at the point where the
sector has just been handed to a driver.  It reads the sectors back
ONE AT A TIME through a buffer of its own - the caller's buffer is the
data being checked, and the transfer may be a whole cluster - and a
disagreement is reported as a FAILED WRITE: same status byte, same
INT 24h, same retry.  A read that fails counts as a mismatch, because
the answer the caller needs is about the write.

It costs an extra transfer per sector.  That is why it is a flag and
not the behaviour, and DOS made the same trade.

AND THE PUSH THAT WAS NOT THERE, which cost an hour.  disk_write
preserves every register its callers use, and it preserves ESI by
NEVER TOUCHING IT: there is no push for ESI, because until this
release nothing in there needed a fifth register.  Handing the buffer
to dio_verify in ESI is four instructions that read like argument
setup and are really a promise being broken - and fat_flush walks the
FAT copies with ESI as its counter, so a verified write turned its
two-copy loop into one that never stopped and wrote the FAT across the
whole disk.  The symptom was a file that came back with the media
descriptor as its first byte.

That is the third release running in which a register that looked free
already held the answer.  The pattern is worth naming: it is never the
new code that is wrong, it is what the new code assumed about the old.

TESTING A VERIFY NEEDS A SECTOR THAT LIES
-----------------------------------------
Nothing in this machine could be made to read back differently from
what was written.  A disk that reads back what it was given is what
every disk here does; one that does not is a disk with a fault in it,
and there is no way to ask for one.

So TESTBLK.SYS - the RAM disk that exists to be a block driver - has
eight bytes of test apparatus in it.  A sector written with the
signature 'POISON!!' at the front reads back ONCE with a byte changed,
and then behaves.  The data on the disk is what was written; only the
reading of it, once, is wrong.  That is precisely the fault VERIFY
exists to catch and precisely the one nothing else can produce.

VFYTEST's fourth check tests the APPARATUS before anything is tested
with it: the read after a poisoned write must come back DIFFERENT, and
the one after that must come back RIGHT.  Without it, check 5 would be
a verify that passed because there was nothing to catch.

THE REST OF THE FAT32 FAMILY
----------------------------
7303h - extended free space - went in with v0.24 because DIR needed
numbers wider than 36h can hold.  The other three are the same
widening applied to the other two things that overflowed: a DPB whose
cluster count did not fit in sixteen bits, and an INT 25h/26h whose
sector number did not.

WHAT 7302h CAN HONESTLY ANSWER is the interesting part.  PM-DOS has no
drive parameter blocks - fn52's list of lists says FFFF:FFFF where the
DPB chain would be, on purpose, because a pointer into a structure
that does not exist is an invitation to walk it.  This call is the
other direction: it COPIES a block into the caller's buffer, so there
is nothing to follow and nothing that outlives the call, and every
field in it is a fact about the mounted volume that the kernel already
knows.  The chain pointer is the one field that would have to lie, and
it refuses instead - the same sentinel, for the same reason.

7304h - set the DPB - is the one whose honest implementation is two
answers rather than one.  PM-DOS takes its idea of a volume's shape
from the BPB and cannot be told otherwise: the kernel re-reads it on
every mount, FORMAT works from it too, and F1h AL=2 exists to say
"read it again".  So a DPB that AGREES with the volume is accepted -
the caller has asked for a state the kernel is already in - and one
that DISAGREES is refused, because success would mean the kernel had
adopted a geometry it has not.

7305h HAS THE ONE POINTER NOTHING ELSE CAN CONVERT.  Every other
pointer in the DOS API arrives in a register and the bridge flattens
it on the way in; this one is INSIDE a structure, past the last point
at which anything could have looked at it.  So f7305 is the only
handler in the kernel that has to work out what kind of program called
it: a guest's packet holds a segment and an offset, a native
program's holds a slot offset, and the kernel's is flat already.  The
three tests are cbuf_ok's, which is documented at length up there.

CX = FFFFh is checked and it is not a formality: INT 25h's own escape
hatch for a volume too large to address the old way was ALSO a count
of FFFFh, so the value is what tells this call from a program that has
confused two APIs.

THE OTHER HALF OF THE INT 13h EXTENSIONS
----------------------------------------
A DOS box has had 41h, 42h, 43h and 48h since v0.27, out of
DOS\INT13.INC.  That is the kernel ANSWERING them.  This is the kernel
ASKING them, and without it every BIOS transfer was a CHS one - a
cylinder number ten bits wide, which stops at 1024 cylinders and, with
sixteen heads and 63 sectors, at 504 megabytes.

It matters only where ATA.INC is not already doing the work: an IDE
disk that answered IDENTIFY is addressed directly and in LBA and
always has been.  This is the machine whose controller PM-DOS does not
drive - a SCSI card with an INT 13h ROM, a BIOS-only build, DOSBox -
carrying a disk larger than its CHS geometry can name.

AND THE BUG THAT WAS ALREADY THERE: a sector past cylinder 1023 has no
CHS address at all, and until this release it got one anyway, the high
bits quietly dropped.  That reads or WRITES some entirely different
part of the disk and reports success.  Either the extensions can name
it or nobody can, and "nobody can" is now an error (04h, sector not
found) rather than a silent lie.

The two EDD structures live in the globals block at the top of the
real-mode stub, which had two hundred spare bytes in it and is already
addressed both ways.  A disk address packet has to be somewhere a
real-mode segment and offset can name; everything else the block layer
owns is above 1MB.

4Bh AL=1 AND AL=3, AND WHOSE THEY ARE
-------------------------------------
The roadmap suspected AL=3 might never be implementable, and that
suspicion was about the wrong caller.  An overlay is loaded into
memory the caller already owns at an address the caller picks; a D32
image is linked for one absolute offset in its own slot, and a slot is
the whole of a program's address space.  Neither sentence can be
finished about a native program - there is no other program's memory
to load into, and no way to jump to an entry point in a slot that is
not yours.

A SIXTEEN-BIT GUEST HAS NEITHER RESTRICTION, which is why the same two
functions are ordinary work over there and impossible here.  Every
program that ever used an overlay was sixteen-bit.  So both went into
vdm_child and fn4B refuses them with the reason written down.

AL=1's hard part is not the loading, it is the CALLER.  vdm_load
writes the loaded program's registers straight into vdm_ctx, which for
AL=0 is exactly right - the box is about to become that program - and
for AL=1 is the caller's live context being overwritten by a program
that is not going to run.  So the whole frame is parked in the shape
vdm_push and vdm_pop already agreed on, the entry point is read out of
vdm_ctx in between, and the frame is put back.  No nesting level is
used and the child's memory is not freed: there is no child as far as
the box is concerned, only a caller and some memory with a program in
it that the caller now owns the problem of.  Real DOS says the same
thing in the same words.

DIR /S AND DIR /O
-----------------
/S needs the pattern SPLIT ONCE - into the directory it lives in and
the pattern within it - and then "list *.TXT here" and "and in every
directory under here" are the same operation with the directory half
changed.  dir_resolve does the splitting with 7160h; nothing below it
knows or cares which directory it is being run in.

THE FIND IS NOT HELD OPEN ACROSS THE RECURSION, and it cannot be:
under LFN=OFF the wrapper falls back to 4Eh/4Fh, which resume out of
ONE DTA, so a second search started inside the first would take the
first one's place.  So a directory's subdirectory NAMES are collected
into a block first, the find is closed, and the walk goes down the
list.  One allocation per level, and it works the same whether long
names are on or off.

ONE WALKER, TWO COMMANDS.  DIR /S and DEL /S are the same traversal
with a different verb at each stop, and the traversal is the part with
the difficulties in it - so tree_walk takes the verb in walk_act, and
dir_one lists where del_one deletes.

/O collects the directory, sorts an index over it, and puts each
record BACK INTO find_data to draw it - so one piece of code draws
every row in either order.  A find record is 318 bytes and a directory
can hold thousands, so what is kept is the six fields the listing
prints.  No memory means no order, not no listing: a directory too big
to collect is listed unsorted, because what was asked for was to see
it.

EVERY KEY AGREEING MEANS THE NAME DECIDES.  Without that tie-break the
order of equal entries is whatever the directory happened to hold -
/O:E puts three directories in front, all with no extension, and they
come out in no order at all.  It is also what makes a sorted listing
REPRODUCIBLE, which a sorted listing had better be.

AND A LEADING DOT IS NOT A SEPARATOR: "." and ".." are directory
entries and DOS stores them with a blank extension, so reading the
second dot of ".." as one gave them an extension nothing else had and
put them in the middle of a /O:E listing.

DIRCMD, AND WHY "/-W" HAD TO EXIST
----------------------------------
MS-DOS reads DIRCMD and puts its contents in front of the command
line, which is a description of the effect rather than of the
mechanism: what is in it is switches, and switches are already lifted
out of the line and turned into a mask before anything else happens.
So the merge is done on the MASKS, where the rule can be stated
exactly - the command line wins - instead of on text, where it would
depend on which of two /O switches came first.

That rule is the whole reason "/-x" exists.  A DIRCMD of /W with no
way to say "not this time" is a variable nobody would set.  sw_scan
returns the negatives separately from the positives, because a caller
merging two sources has to be able to tell "asked for off" from "did
not ask" - which is the entire difference between the two sources.

sw_scan also lifts a switch's ARGUMENT with it now, into eight bytes
per letter, because /O:GN and /A:-D are switches that carry text.  It
runs to the next blank or the next '/', which is what makes
"DIR /O *.TXT" the pattern it looks like and not a sort order called
"*.TXT".

COPY /A AND /B ARE POSITIONAL, WHICH IS WHY sw_scan CANNOT DO THEM
------------------------------------------------------------------
"/A applies to the file it FOLLOWS and to every file after it until
another /A or /B" is a rule about where in the line the switch was
written, and a bit in a mask has forgotten that by the time anybody
reads it.  So COPY parses its own three switches, and each item
records the mode in force where it was written - with the switch
reaching backwards one item, which is the half that makes it
positional.

The defaults are not arbitrary.  A plain copy is BINARY: the point of
it is that the file at the far end is the same file, and a byte that
happens to be 1Ah is a byte.  A CONCATENATION is ASCII, because
joining files is a text operation - it exists so that three text files
become one, and a text file of that era ended at its first Ctrl-Z
whatever came after.

/V turns VERIFY on for the length of the copy and puts it back
afterwards, which is what it has always meant - and which means
something now that the kernel reads the flag.  It goes back however
the copy ended: a /V that left the flag standing would make every
write in the machine twice as slow until the next reboot, which is a
thing nobody would connect to a COPY they typed an hour ago.

FORMAT /S RUNS SYS RATHER THAN BEING IT
---------------------------------------
Making a disk bootable is three jobs - a boot sector with the target's
own BPB spliced into it, the stage-2 loader in the reserved sectors,
and three files copied and re-attributed - and SYS.ASM does all three
already, correctly, on every FAT type.  A second implementation inside
FORMAT would be a second thing to keep right, and the one that got it
wrong would be the one nobody ran.  Real FORMAT carried the code
because real DOS had no nested EXEC worth the name; this one has had
one since v0.18.

WHERE SYS.COM IS is the only question, and COMSPEC answers it: the
interpreter is on the system disk by definition, so the directory it
came from is the directory the system came from.

Two things went wrong writing it and both are worth keeping.  The
COMSPEC scan stepped over the '=' twice - fm_comspec carries it, so
the comparison had already consumed it - and left ":\SYS.COM".  And
the parameter block was built in the EP_* shape, which is the SIXTEEN-
BIT one: a D32 program's block is two flat dwords, an environment and
a tail, and nothing else, because there are no FCBs to parse for a
program that has no PSP fields to put them in.  SYS came up and
printed its usage.

THE KEYBOARD: THE PREFIX THAT WAS TRACKED AND NEVER READ
--------------------------------------------------------
An E0 prefix means the key is the one on the CURSOR PAD rather than
the one on the numeric keypad, and the two send THE SAME SCAN CODE.
The prefix was tracked, cleared, and never once consulted - so the
arrow keys went through the ordinary table and came out as the digits
printed on the keypad.  Pressing Left typed a four.

THE FAKE SHIFTS ARE NOT KEYS.  A keyboard sends E0 2A in front of a
grey key and E0 AA behind it, so that a program reading 40:17 sees the
shift state the key was pressed with rather than the one the keypad
would have needed.  Taking them for shift presses means the shift
state LATCHES ON the first time an arrow key is touched.

Ctrl gives each cursor key a code of its own and they are not adjacent
to anything - Ctrl-Left is 73h, Ctrl-Home 77h - so they are a table
rather than a rule.  A text editor reads exactly those.

THE FUNCTION KEYS ARE FOUR KEYS EACH: F1 is 3Bh, Shift-F1 54h, Ctrl-F1
5Eh, Alt-F1 68h.  A program that offers Alt-F4 is reading for that
last one and not for 3Bh with a flag set, because the flags are gone
by the time it looks.  F11 and F12 were reported as 57h and 58h, which
are the codes a 101-key BIOS never sends and nothing looks for; they
are 85h..8Ch now.

ALT AND A KEY IS AN EXTENDED KEY.  Alt-F is how half the DOS software
ever written opens its File menu, and it arrives as ASCII zero with
the scan code, because "F" and "Alt-F" would otherwise be the same
byte.  The keypad is left out on purpose: Alt with a keypad digit is
how a character is entered by number, and giving those keys an
extended code would be inventing a third behaviour.

AND A FUNCTION KEY IS TWO CALLS, which is the half that reaches a
program.  DOS reports a key with no ASCII of its own as a ZERO and the
program asks again to be told WHICH.  std_in has always handed back
the scan code in AH alongside the zero, which is more information than
DOS gives and no use at all - because the program that wants it is
looking in AL on its SECOND call, and what it got there was the NEXT
KEY.  Every menu that offers a function key was reading a keystroke
behind.  con_extin parks the scan code in the same one-byte pending
slot the raw 3Fh path has used since the console got a raw mode; 0Bh
reports it as a key waiting and 0Ch flushes it, because it is a
keystroke that has been typed and not yet collected.

KEYRATE=rate[,delay], AND AN EMULATOR THAT CANNOT TAKE THE FASTEST
------------------------------------------------------------------
The numbers are MODE CON's, because MODE is what a person would reach
for and MODE is a program PM-DOS does not have.  RATE runs 1 to 32 and
counts upwards to faster; DELAY is 1 to 4 quarter-seconds.  The 8042
wants the rate the other way up in five bits and the delay in two,
which is a conversion and not a decision, so it happens in CONFIG.INC
and the kernel's side speaks the hardware's units.

A COMMAND TO THE KEYBOARD IS A CONVERSATION - F3h, an ACK, the
argument, another ACK - and it is held with interrupts off, with the
ACKs swallowed here rather than left for the decoder.  They are
harmless when the decoder gets them (FAh has bit 7 set, so it reads as
a break code for a key nobody pressed), but a HALF-DELIVERED
conversation is not harmless at all: a keyboard left waiting for its
argument treats the next thing it is sent as one.

RATE=32 DELAY=1 IS THE BYTE ZERO, and it is legal - it is what "as
fast as the keyboard goes, after the shortest pause" comes to.  It is
also the one value DOSBox 0.74 cannot take: that emulator does not
implement F3h's argument state, reads the zero as a COMMAND instead,
and stops delivering keystrokes altogether.  Nothing is done about it
in the kernel, because the byte is correct and the emulator is not.
KEYRATE=31,1 is as fast as makes any difference; DISK\CONFIG.SYS says
so where somebody will read it.

AND THE REDIRECTION BUG UNDERNEATH THE TESTS
--------------------------------------------
"TYPE FILE > OUT" compacts to "TYPE FILE " - the space in front of the
'>' is ordinary text and was copied through - and a command that takes
its argument raw then opens a name with a space on the end of it.  DIR
and DEL never saw it because sw_scan trims for them; TYPE, MD, CD and
RD do not call sw_scan, so every one of them failed the moment its
line was redirected.  Found because the switch tests could not read
back what they had just written.  Real DOS trims the tail for the same
reason and redir_parse does now.

AND LASTDRIVE COULD BE RAISED AFTER IT WAS SET
----------------------------------------------
cfg_lastdrv already clamps the number up to the drives that exist when
the line is read - "never fewer than there really are" - but a
DEVICE= block driver further down the file adds a letter after that,
and a CONFIG.SYS with LASTDRIVE= above its DEVICE= lines is the
ordinary way round.  The only place that rule can be true at the
moment somebody asks is the moment somebody asks, so the list of lists
raises it again when it is filled in.

VERIFIED
--------
DOSBox 0.74, floppy: F32TEST 10/10, VFYTEST 10/10, UMBTEST 11/11,
EMSTEST 14/14, MCBTEST 5/5, FCBTEST 22/22, BUFTEST 8/8, APITEST,
DEVTEST, CFGTEST 4/4, XMSTEST, I24TEST 7/8 (check 8 reports "no
failing drive": a one-floppy machine gives B: to the same drive, which
is the same environmental skip as v0.41).  R3TEST 13/14 and ALLOCTST
1/2 fail there for the same kind of reason and always have - R3TEST's
fourteenth check needs a B: that will not read, and ALLOCTST EXECs
itself from C:, which on that machine is the RAM disk.

86Box on real ATA hardware: ALL OF IT.  F32TEST 10/10, VFYTEST 10/10,
UMBTEST 11/11, EMSTEST 14/14, MCBTEST, FCBTEST 22/22, BUFTEST 8/8,
APITEST, CFGTEST 4/4 (LASTDRIVE 8 with the RAM disk loaded), DEVTEST,
I24TEST 8/8, ALLOCTST 2/2, XMSTEST, R3TEST 14/14.

The switches, on both: DIR /S descending three levels with per-
directory totals and a grand total; /O:N, /O:-N, /O:S, /O:-S, /OGN and
/O:E each in the right order; DIRCMD=/W and /-W cancelling it; COPY
/B, COPY /V, and a concatenation whose result is the two files plus
one Ctrl-Z; VERIFY ON and OFF reported; DEL /S deleting three .DAT
files across three directories and naming each in full.

FORMAT /Q /S formats, finds SYS.COM through COMSPEC, and runs it with
the right drive - and SYS then correctly refuses, because the target
partition has one reserved sector and stage 2 needs nine.  That is
SYS's own check doing its job and is as far as this hardware can go:
no partition on the test disks is a valid SYS target, since the only
one with room for stage 2 is the drive being booted from.

NOT run on the 486, and not committed.

v0.41 - EXPANDED MEMORY, AND THE CONSOLE MOVES (2026-08-26)
----------------------------------------------------------
INT 67h, LIM EMS 3.2, out of the kernel rather than out of a driver.
CTTY does what it says.  A character device that reports an error now
gets asked about.  New DOS\EMS.INC, TOOLS\EMSTEST.ASM,
TOOLS\DEVCRIT.ASM.

WHAT WAS LEFT OF EMM386 ONCE THE HARD PART WAS ALREADY BUILT
------------------------------------------------------------
Expanded memory is a 64K PAGE FRAME somewhere in upper memory, cut
into four 16K WINDOWS, each of which can be pointed at any 16K page of
a pool that may be many megabytes.  A real-mode program addresses the
frame with an ordinary far pointer and changes what is behind it by
asking the manager.  In 1985 that meant a card with bank-switch
registers on it.  In 1988 it meant a 386 pretending to be one, and
EMM386 - which had to put the machine into V86 mode, take over the
page tables, and then run the whole of DOS underneath itself, for the
sake of remapping four windows.

PM-DOS has been paging since v0.29 and has run its guests under a V86
monitor since v0.30.  A WINDOW IS FOUR PAGE TABLE ENTRIES AND A CR3
RELOAD, which is pg_map with a different caller.  Everything EMM386
was mostly made of was already here and had been for a dozen releases;
what was left to write was the API, the handle table, and the
bookkeeping - and that is the whole of DOS\EMS.INC.

That is the second time this has happened.  v0.38's upper memory was
the same observation about the same file: a real-mode memory manager
can only offer upper memory some chipset has been persuaded to put RAM
behind, and a paging kernel can simply point a page table entry at
one.  EMS is that argument a second time, and it is worth noticing
that the second time cost less than the first, because the first one
left pg_map and pg_umbprobe behind it.

THE FRAME AND THE UMBs ARE ONE RESOURCE, AND ONE MEASUREMENT
------------------------------------------------------------
Both want 16K pages of C0000h-EFFFFh that nothing decodes.  Both find
them with pg_umbprobe, which is not a lookup but a MEASUREMENT OF
HARDWARE - write a pattern into a page and see whether anything stores
it - and a measurement made twice gives a different answer the second
time, because by then some of those pages have a page out of the arena
underneath them and measure as RAM that was always there.  So the
probe became umb_probe, which runs once and remembers, and both
callers get the first one's answer.

THE FRAME IS RESERVED BEFORE THE CHAIN IS BUILT, and that ordering is
the whole of the arrangement between the two.  EMS= runs first,
picks its 64K, marks those pages TAKEN in umb_state with umb_reserve,
and leaves umb_init to lay its MCB chain over what is left.  Carving
the frame out of the UMB pool afterwards would have been worse in two
ways: nothing guarantees 64K of it is still contiguous once programs
have been loaded high, and a UMB that has been handed to a program is
a page this file must never remap.

The search goes HIGHEST FIRST and 64K aligned.  The alignment is
convention rather than a rule - the specification asks only for 16K -
but every EMM ever shipped put its frame at C000h, D000h or E000h, and
there is software that quietly assumes the frame paragraph looks like
one of those.  Highest first because what is left over stays in one
piece: taking the top 64K of the region leaves the rest contiguous,
where taking a frame out of the middle would split one UMB run into
two and cost a filler block to describe the gap.  On both emulators
and on the shipped CONFIG.SYS the frame lands at E000h and the UMB
pool keeps C800h-DFFFh.

EMS= IS PM-DOS'S OWN STATEMENT, WHICH IS WORTH SAYING RATHER THAN
HIDING.  On a real DOS expanded memory arrives through
DEVICE=EMM386.EXE and there is no statement for it, because the
manager is a driver and the driver is the manager.  Here it is
neither: there is nothing to load, and the only thing left to ask for
is permission and an address.

    EMS=NO      no expanded memory, which is also what an absent
                statement means
    EMS=AUTO    on, and the kernel picks the frame.  A bare "EMS="
                means this too
    EMS=D000    on, with the frame at that segment

IT WAS A WORD IN DOS= FIRST, and the address is why it stopped being
one.  DOS= is a list of yes-or-no words about how the machine uses
memory; "where the page frame goes" is not one of those, and hanging
a four-digit number off one of the words would have been the wrong
shape - DOS=HIGH,UMB,EMS=D000 is not a statement anybody would want
to parse or read.  Real DOS asks the same question as a parameter on
DEVICE=EMM386.EXE (FRAME=D000), which is that DOS saying the same
thing its own way round: the manager is a driver there, so its
statement is DEVICE=.  Here the manager is the kernel, so its
statement is EMS=.

AN EXPLICIT SEGMENT OVERRULES THE PROBE, ON PURPOSE, and does not
consult it at all.  Choosing the frame automatically means writing to
an address and seeing whether anything stores it, and that
measurement can be wrong in BOTH directions on hardware nobody here
has: an adapter with a window and no option ROM in front of it looks
exactly like shadow RAM, and shadow RAM already switched on over a
ROM looks exactly like memory somebody owns.  A user who knows their
machine can say so, and being overruled is the entire point of being
able to name an address.  What is NOT overruled is the format - 64K
of frame, on a 16K boundary, between C000h and F000h - because that
is the specification rather than an opinion about the hardware.

The automatic search insists on 64K alignment as well; an explicit
request is held only to the 16K the specification asks for, because a
user naming C400h has said something deliberate.  EMSTEST had to be
loosened to match: it was asserting the convention, which is a test
asserting the default rather than the contract.

ONE POOL, THREE DOORS
---------------------
The pages behind a handle come out of the same arena that 48h and XMS
allocate from, for the reason XMS.INC states about itself: two doors
onto one pool is correct and two pools is a bug waiting for whoever
opens both.  EMS is the third.

A handle's pages are ONE CONTIGUOUS ARENA BLOCK, page aligned, so
logical page N is base plus N times 16K - one rounding per handle
rather than one per page, which matters because the only way to get a
page-aligned address out of a sixteen-byte-granular heap is to ask for
a page more and round up.  Per page that would have been 25% waste.

It also decides what 42h reports.  "Unallocated pages" is the LARGEST
FREE BLOCK and not the total free space, because what a program can
actually get is what will fit in one block; reporting the sum of the
fragments would be a number no allocation could ever reach.  The
system total is measured once at init and capped at 512 pages, which
is the LIM 3.2 ceiling of 8MB - a statement about the specification
rather than about the machine, since page counts travel in 16-bit
registers and 512 is what the API can describe.

Handles are released by OWNER when a program ends, alongside
xms_relown and immediately after arena_freeown - which is why
ems_relown drops the windows and the rows and deliberately frees
nothing.  The memory has already gone; freeing it twice would hand the
arena an address that is now inside somebody else's block.

46h ANSWERS 32h AND MEANS IT
----------------------------
LIM 3.2, not 4.0.  4.0's additions are mostly about mapping pages
OUTSIDE the frame - anywhere in conventional memory, on demand, so
that Windows and DESQview could give a whole DOS box its own bank -
and a manager that claims 4.0 will be asked for 5Ah, 57h and 58h by
programs that will not take an error for an answer.  Claiming what is
implemented is the honest version, and every 3.2 program works against
it.  40h-4Eh are all there, including the two holes: 49h and 4Ah were
"get page map" and "set page map" in EMS 3.0 and the 3.2 specification
withdrew both, so they answer 84h.

BX=FFFFh on 44h unmaps a window, which is a 4.0 spelling this manager
honours anyway.  It costs one comparison, a 3.2 program cannot ask for
it by accident (no handle has 65535 pages), and without it there is no
way at all to take a window down again.

An unmapped window is pointed BACK AT ITSELF, which is not nothing and
is exactly right: the frame was chosen because nothing decodes it, so
a window with its own address in the page table has no memory behind
it.  Reads come back FFh and writes go nowhere, which is what an
unmapped EMS window does on a machine with a real card in it.

HOW A PROGRAM FINDS IT
----------------------
It reads the segment of the INT 67h vector and looks for EMMXXXX0 at
offset 0Ah of that segment, which is where a character device driver
keeps its name.  So two paragraphs of conventional memory are dressed
up as a device header and the vector points into them - the detection
the LIM specification recommends.  The alternative, opening the device
by name, is served too, through a row in dev_tab that holds eight FFh
bytes until ems_init writes the name into it: a name no path component
can be, so a machine with no manager cannot be told it has one.

The header is deliberately NOT linked into the device chain.  A
program that found it there would be entitled to call its strategy and
interrupt entries with a request packet, and there is no real-mode
code behind them to fill one in.  Not being in the chain is a gap;
being in it and answering with an untouched status word would be a
lie.

67h JOINED vdm_stublist ON THE WAY PAST, and that is a fix rather than
a detail.  It is not a DOS vector, so it was not on the list, so on a
machine with no manager it held whatever the BIOS left - which on most
BIOSes is nothing at all.  A program that probes for EMS by CALLING
the vector rather than by reading it therefore jumped to 0000:0000 and
started executing the interrupt vector table.  Programs that do this
are wrong and they exist.

The trap bit for 67h is set ONLY WHEN THERE IS A MANAGER.  Claiming
the vector otherwise would mean answering as though there were one,
and the honest reply to "is EMS here" is the IRET.  A DEVICE= driver's
INIT gets the same bit in its excursion, because a driver is entitled
to ask: RAMDRIVE.SYS /A allocates its handle before it reports its
unit count.

MEM ASKS THE KERNEL, BECAUSE MEM CANNOT CALL INT 67h
----------------------------------------------------
MEM.EXE is a native program at ring 3 and expanded memory is served to
V86 guests, so it cannot make the call it would be reporting.
21h/F1h AL=9 hands it the frame segment and the two page counts
instead.  That is the argument the whole F1h family exists to make and
which MEM.ASM's own header has carried since it stopped reading the
MCB chain directly: a report that has to reach inside the kernel is a
report proving the kernel has no way to ask.

CTTY, AND WHAT IT TURNED OUT TO BE
----------------------------------
The roadmap entry said "CTTY properly, once there is a device chain to
redirect onto" and it said it for eight releases.  The chain arrived in
v0.37.  What CTTY needed after that was THREE DOS CALLS AND NOTHING
FROM THE KERNEL AT ALL: open the device, force the handle over 0, 1
and 2 with 46h, close the original.  Standard input and output are SFT
slots, every console call in the kernel goes through those slots, and
pointing them somewhere else is the whole of what CTTY has ever meant.

Real DOS does exactly this and reaches handle 0 the long way round -
tcmd2b.asm closes the three standard handles and dups three times, so
that the new handle lands in the lowest free slot - which does not
work here, because PM-DOS refuses to close the standard handles on
purpose.  46h says the same thing without the trick.

44h IS THE CHECK THAT MATTERS.  A name that is not a device opens
perfectly well as a file, and "CTTY AUTOEXEC.BAT" would otherwise
install a file as the console: reads coming back as the text of the
batch file, writes appending to it.  Bit 7 of DL is the answer and
real DOS tests the same bit in the same place.

AND THE NAME HAD TO BE REMEMBERED, which was not obvious until the
grep.  Two places in COMMAND.COM open the console BY NAME rather than
using handle 1 - the ^C handler, putting the standard handles back
after a redirection, and the critical-error prompt, which deliberately
asks its question somewhere that cannot have been redirected into the
file on the disk that just failed.  Both opened the literal string
"CON".  After a CTTY, both would have quietly moved the console back,
and a ^C would have looked like the console spontaneously deciding
where it lived.  ctty_name is what they open now.

What it cannot do is undo itself.  "CTTY AUX" on a machine with
nothing on the serial port leaves an interpreter reading a device that
has nothing to say and no keyboard to type "CTTY CON" on.  That is
authentic - it is the oldest joke in DOS - and the answer is the same
as it was in 1983.

A CHARACTER DEVICE THAT SAYS NO
-------------------------------
"CTTY and a character-device critical error both wait on this" appears
twice in the roadmap against the device chain.  The second half is
this.

dl_out called the driver, the driver set DEVS_ERROR and a reason in
the request packet, and dl_out threw the reason away.  A printer
driver reporting out of paper and one reporting success were the same
event from the kernel's side - which is the exact situation INT 24h
was invented for, and the reason the character half of it had never
been reachable: CON and NUL cannot fail, and PRN and AUX are reached
through a BIOS that answers by not answering.  A DEVICE= driver is the
first character device in this kernel that can report a reason.

crit_dev raises it with bit 7 of AH set, which is DOS for "not a
disk", and NO TRANSLATION TABLE - unlike crit_disk, which has to map
INT 13h status bytes.  A character driver's status byte IS a DOS error
code, because the request packet was designed to carry one; the
numbering in the packet and the numbering INT 24h publishes are the
same numbering and have been since DOS 2.0.

FAIL IS NOT OFFERED, and that is a statement about the call rather
than about the device.  dev_out has no error return and never had one:
02h, 09h and the rest of the DOS character-output calls cannot report
that a byte did not go anywhere.  A handler answering Fail would get
exactly what Ignore gives it, and offering a choice with no
consequence is worse than not offering it.  Retry, Ignore and Abort
all mean different things here and those three are what AH allows.

The handler is also shown the REAL driver's header rather than the
block-device stand-in crit_devhdr, because there is one and because
the attribute word is the field a handler reads: showing it the
stand-in would be telling it the printer was a disk.

AND THE HOLE THAT OPENED UNDER IT: A GUEST'S INT 24h
----------------------------------------------------
Testing the character-device critical error is what found this, and
it is not about character devices at all.  It is EVERY critical error
a DOS box can cause.

A 16-bit guest's 21h/25h writes the REAL-MODE IVT at 0:0, which is
where the monitor reflects an untrapped interrupt.  crit_raise
executes INT 24h from 32-bit kernel code, which goes through the IDT.
TWO TABLES, AND ONLY THE SECOND WAS EVER CONSULTED - so a DOS program
that hooked 24h to handle its own disk errors quietly got COMMAND's
"Abort, Retry, Fail?" prompt instead, and a program that meant to
fail silently asked the user a question.  R3TEST's fourteenth check
has covered the ring-3 half since the ring-3 release, which is
exactly why this went unnoticed for twenty-one releases: the
mechanism works perfectly for the caller it was written for, and
there was no test that could have been written in a native program.

NOTHING NEW HAD TO BE BUILT, which is the pleasant part.  dpmi_simint
parks the current V86 context, points the guest at an INT instruction
with the vector byte patched, and borrows the box's own loop; the
monitor reflects 24h through the guest's table; the handler's IRET
lands on a HLT the host planted, and dpmi_rmdone hands the registers
back.  dos_int28 has been using that path for INT 28h since v0.30.
So crit_guest is a register set, four refusals and a call.

THE FOURTH REFUSAL IS THE ONE THAT CANNOT BE SKIPPED.  The other
three are ordinary - no box, an excursion already holding vdm_ctx, no
callback paragraph - but "has the guest hooked 24h AT ALL" is a
question with a trap in it.  The vector always points at SOMETHING:
this same release put an IRET on 67h and the DOS vectors already had
one, so a box that never hooked 24h would run that IRET and come back
with whatever was in AL.  AL IS THE DRIVE NUMBER.  Drive 0 reads as
Ignore.  Comparing the vector against the stub we planted is what
tells "nobody is listening" from "somebody is", and without it every
unhandled disk error on drive A: would have been silently ignored -
which is the worst answer of the four and would have looked like
success.

BP:SI NEEDED A SECOND POINTER.  The handler is shown the failing
device's header, and for a guest that has to be a real-mode far
pointer.  A loaded character driver has one, because drivers live
below 1MB; crit_devhdr - the stand-in for a block device - is inside
PMDOS.SYS at 110000h and no segment:offset can name it.  So crit_init
copies eighteen bytes into conventional memory at boot, owner 8, the
way the XMS callback paragraph and the DPMI landing pads are.  Two
pointers to one header, because there are two kinds of handler and
they cannot hold the same thing.

THE GUEST'S OWN STACK, and not the 256-byte scratch one dpmi_simint
would otherwise lend.  A handler is the program's code and the
program sized its own stack; the DPMI scratch stack is tight for one
