that prints a message and reads a key, and running out there would be
very hard to recognise afterwards.  It is also what a real INT 24h
looks like from inside: an interrupt taken on the stack that was
current.

And one flag that had been leaking since v0.30 without anybody
noticing: dpmi_rmact is set by dpmi_simint and cleared by
dpmi_rmdone, which covers every case where the guest comes back - but
a guest CAN end without coming back, and an INT 24h handler that
answers by calling 4Ch is the obvious way to do it.  The flag would
then stand for the life of the machine and refuse every simulated
interrupt in every box after that one.  vdm_done clears it now: the
box is over, nothing can still be in it.

I24TEST.COM IS SIXTEEN-BIT AND HAS TO BE, and its failure is
TESTDEV rather than a dead disk.  The obvious choice is a read of
drive B:, which is what R3TEST uses - and on the floppy build B:
READS THE BOOT DISK AND SUCCEEDS, because a machine with one floppy
drive gives both letters to it.  The first version of the test
reported five failures for that reason and every one of them was the
test's fault.  A test whose premise depends on how many drives are
fitted passes for the wrong reason somewhere; TESTDEV refuses a '!'
on every machine, always.  Check 8 tries the disk anyway and reports
"no failing drive" where there is nothing to fail, which is what
DOSBox says and 86Box does not.

CHECKS 6 AND 7 ARE A COUNTING ARGUMENT rather than a report, and that
is the part worth keeping.  TESTDEV alternates, so three rounds of
one '!' answering Retry, then Ignore, then anything must call the
handler exactly ONCE, ONCE and NOT AT ALL.  A kernel that ignored the
answer and always retried gives 1,1,1; one that ignored it and never
retried gives 1,0,x.  Only obeying both produces 1,1,0, and no single
round could have told the three apart.
WHAT TESTING IT NEEDED, AND THE THING IT FOUND
----------------------------------------------
Nothing in the machine could fail on purpose, so TESTDEV.SYS learned
to.  It REFUSES A '!' EVERY OTHER TIME, with "printer out of paper" -
alternate rather than permanent refusals, because a driver that always
failed could only ever test Ignore: a Retry would go round for ever.
Alternation means the SAME byte offered twice succeeds the second
time, so Retry has somewhere to arrive.

DEVCRIT.EXE IS NATIVE AND IT HAS TO BE, and the first version was not
and hung the machine.  A 16-bit guest's 21h/25h writes the REAL-MODE
IVT at 0:0, which is where the monitor reflects an untrapped
interrupt; crit_raise executes INT 24h from 32-bit kernel code, which
goes through the IDT.  Those are two different tables.  So a guest's
INT 24h handler was not reached at all - COMMAND's own handler
answered instead, and COMMAND's handler asks the user, so a test with
nobody at the keyboard waited for ever.  A native program's 25h
installs the gate the kernel actually enters, which is the mechanism
R3TEST's fourteenth check has proved since the ring-3 release.

That hole is FIXED, later in the same release and in the section
below, which is why DEVCRIT stays native anyway: it is now the test of
the ring-3 half of a character-device error, and I24TEST is the test
of the other half.  Two callers, two tables, two tests.

And an hour went into a hang that was neither of those things: the
rename from DEVCRIT.COM to DEVCRIT.EXE missed the MKDISK line in
BUILD.CMD, so the image kept carrying the stale 16-bit binary while
the .EXE built beside it and was never copied.  Every run reproduced
the original bug perfectly.  The tell was that DCMARK.TXT - a
breadcrumb file the test opens and closes on every step, precisely so
that a run which does not finish still says how far it got - was never
created at all, which meant the program under test was not the program
being built.

VERIFIED, BOTH EMULATORS, AND THEY DISAGREE ABOUT THE FRAME ON
PURPOSE.  DOSBox 0.74 floppy puts it at E000h; 86Box FAT16 over real
ATA puts it at D000h, because on that machine EC00h upwards is spoken
for and E000h therefore has only 48K of clear space behind it - so the
search falls through to the next 64K-aligned block that is wholly
empty.  THE SAME RULE ANSWERING A DIFFERENT MACHINE, which is what a
measurement is supposed to do, and 86Box is also the case the "highest
first keeps the rest in one piece" argument does not get: the frame
lands in the middle, splits the region, and costs exactly one filler
block to describe (CFFFh, 1000h paragraphs, 'SC') with the UMB run
carrying on above it at E000h.  That is the arrangement working, not
failing.

EMSTEST 14/14 on both, 512 pages on both; UMBTEST 11/11 and MCBTEST
5/5, which is what says the frame reservation costs upper memory
exactly 64K and nothing else; DEVCRIT 6/6 with TESTDEV loaded; CFGTEST
4/4 (LASTDRIVE 5 on the floppy machine, 7 on the one with seven real
volumes - the same rule again); DEVTEST 9/9; FCBTEST 22/22.

I24TEST 7/8 on DOSBox and 8/8 on 86Box, the difference being the one
check that is allowed to be skipped: DOSBox's B: reads the boot disk
and there is nothing to fail.  On 86Box the disk round reaches the
guest's handler with AH=18h and DI=0002h - fail and retry permitted,
bit 7 clear, "drive not ready" - and the driver round reaches it with
AH=B0h and DI=0009h, which is character device, retry and ignore
permitted, out of paper.  Those are the two register sets the whole
mechanism exists to deliver, and they arrive exactly.

ALL THREE FORMS OF EMS= EXERCISED, each on its own boot.  EMS=AUTO
puts the frame at E000h on the floppy machine; EMS=D000 moves it and
the MCB chain rearranges round it, the UMB run now reaching F000h with
a 64K hole in the middle; EMS=NO gives the pool its 64K back - upper
memory goes from 256K to 320K, EMSTEST reports no expanded memory and
stops, and MEM drops the row entirely.  That last one is also the
cleanest measurement there is of what the reservation costs, because
it is the same machine with and without it.

The two ways EMS= can be refused - a value that is not hex, and a
segment that cannot hold a frame - are read out of the code and not
out of a run: they print at boot, and a boot message is the one thing
this headless arrangement cannot capture.

CTTY
refuses a name that is no device and refuses AUTOEXEC.BAT, and then
"CTTY TESTDEV / ECHO HELLO-THROUGH-CTTY / CTTY CON" leaves TESTDEV
reporting exactly 20 bytes more than it had - eighteen characters and
a CRLF, through dev_out, dl_out and a request packet, with no
redirection on the line at all.  A count that is exactly right is a
better result than a count that is merely different.

EMSTEST's ninth check is the one that cannot be faked: four windows,
four different logical pages, four different patterns, all readable at
once.  A manager that keeps a handle table, hands out handles,
remembers what 44h was told and reports it faithfully through 4Ch and
4Eh passes every test built out of return codes and maps nothing at
all.  Nothing but four separate mappings produces four patterns.

v0.40 - BLOCK DEVICE DRIVERS (2026-08-26)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
DEVICE= loads a block driver and each of its units becomes a drive
letter.  New TOOLS\TESTBLK.ASM; the block half of DOS\DEVLOAD.INC.

A CHARACTER DRIVER IS A NAME; A BLOCK DRIVER IS A DRIVE LETTER
--------------------------------------------------------------
That sentence is the whole of the extra work, and it is why v0.37
shipped one half and refused the other with a message rather than
half-obeying it.  ANSI.SYS joins the device chain and dev_find starts
finding it.  RAMDRIVE.SYS hands back a unit count and a BPB per unit,
and every one of those units has to become a letter in a volume table
that until now got its letters by scanning partitions on real disks.

Three things a block driver needs that a character one does not.

A ROW IN drv_tbl, which is keyed by BIOS drive number - something a
driver unit does not have.  So it is given one: DL_UNIT_BASE upwards,
a range no BIOS uses (this machine's real disks are 80h and 81h).  The
number then flows through fat_mount, disk_read, bios2log and the
volume table untouched, and the only place that has to know what it
means is dio_try, where one comparison sends the transfer to a request
packet instead of to the block layer.  Inventing a key was cheaper
than threading a second one through nine routines, and it means the
retry, the critical error and the answer INT 24h's handler gives are
the same code for both kinds of drive.

A STAGING BUFFER.  A driver is 16-bit real-mode code and takes the
address of its transfer as a segment and an offset; the buffers the
filesystem hands down are sec_buf and clus_buf inside PMDOS.SYS at
110000h, which no segment:offset can name.  So every transfer is
copied through conventional memory in chunks, exactly as the floppy
path has staged through XFER_BUF since v0.9.  It costs a memcpy per
sector and it is the only arrangement that works.

AND A SECTOR NUMBER THAT FITS.  The request packet's sector field is a
WORD - the format is from 1983, when 32MB was a large disk - so a
volume past 65535 sectors needs the DOS 4 form: FFFFh in the word and
a dword after the packet.  A driver says it understands that by
setting bit 1 of its attribute word, and one that does not is refused
the transfer rather than being handed a sector number it would
silently truncate.  That is the difference between a failed read and a
successful read of the wrong sector.

WHAT THE UNIT COUNT IS
----------------------
The driver's answer in the INIT packet, not the one in its header.  A
block header carries a unit count in the first byte of its name field
and that is the count BEFORE init - the driver may find less hardware
than it hoped - so DOS reads the packet's, which was written after the
driver looked.  TESTBLK reports one either way; a driver for real
hardware would not.

The BPB array is where the size comes from: a far pointer to N far
pointers, one per unit, and the total-sectors field of each is what
drv_tbl records.  A BLOCK DRIVER'S BPB IS NOT A BOOT SECTOR and does
not have a boot sector's offsets - it starts at what a boot sector
calls BPB_BPS, so every field is 0Bh lower.  The DBPB_* equates spell
that out rather than biasing the existing ones, because a bias applied
once too often is a number that still looks plausible.

THREE BUGS, ALL OF THEM IN THE TEST DRIVER
------------------------------------------
Which is worth saying: the kernel side worked the first time it ran,
and every failure was in the 16-bit driver written to exercise it.
That is the shape of this kind of work.

THE IMAGE WAS ABOVE endres, in a file whose header comment warns at
length that it must not be.  A driver tells DOS where its resident
part ends and every paragraph above that goes back to the arena, so
the RAM disk's storage would have been handed to the next program that
asked for memory and would then have been quietly full of it.  Writing
the warning did not prevent making the mistake in the same file.

THE TRANSFER DIRECTION was a tangle of a flag that was never set and a
pushf/popf around a comparison that did nothing.  Rewritten so that
the two cases load DS:SI and ES:DI the two ways round and share one
REP MOVSW, which is what it should have been.

AND THE ONE THAT COST A BOOT: "mov bx,cs" as scratch inside INIT.
ES:BX is the request packet for the whole of that routine, so the unit
count went somewhere in the code segment, INIT reported nothing, and
the kernel refused the driver for having no units - correctly, and
with a message that named the real problem.

VERIFIED, both emulators.  DOSBox 0.74 floppy: DEVICE=\TESTBLK.SYS
gives C:, DIR reads its volume label through the driver, and
"ECHO ... > C:\TEST.TXT" then TYPE writes a file and reads it back -
which is the FAT, the directory and the data area all going through
request packets to 16-bit real-mode code called from a 32-bit
protected-mode kernel.  86Box FAT16 over real ATA, where seven real
volumes already exist: the same driver gets H:, DRIVES shows it as
"driver" with no partition type and FAT12 beside it, and the same
file round-trips.  FCBTEST 22/22 and CFGTEST 4/4 with the driver
loaded, which is what says the new comparison in dio_try costs the
real drives nothing.

v0.39 - CONFIG.SYS MEANS SOMETHING (2026-08-26)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Five statements stopped being decoration: SET=, INSTALL=,
INSTALLHIGH=, FILES= and LASTDRIVE=.  New TOOLS\CFGTEST.ASM.

THE MASTER ENVIRONMENT, WHICH DID NOT EXIST
-------------------------------------------
COMMAND.COM started with an empty block and put COMSPEC in it, and
nothing the machine had been configured with could reach the shell at
all.  That is the whole of what SET= in CONFIG.SYS is for: PATH and
TEMP and PROMPT set before AUTOEXEC.BAT runs, and set for every
program in the machine rather than for one interpreter.

It reaches the shell the way an environment reaches any program -
copied into its slot behind its PSP with PSP_ENV pointing at it, which
is exactly what exec_setenv has done for a child of 4Bh since v0.33.
The interpreter reads it there and seeds its own block from it.  A
second mechanism would have been a second thing to get wrong.

The chain is four copies and three address spaces: the kernel's
master_env, the shell's slot, COMMAND's env_blk, and conventional
memory again for a DOS box.  CFGTEST looks for the variable at the far
end of all four, because a link missing anywhere in it does not
announce itself - the variable is simply not there.

AND ds: IS LOAD-BEARING.  The first version of the interpreter's end
read PSP_ENV as "[SLOT_PSP + PSP_ENV]" and got nothing, every time.
Without the segment override wasm makes that a reference INTO _CMD,
and wlink's "option offset=0x2000" then biases it - so the read lands
two pages inside COMMAND's own image, finds whatever is there, and the
environment silently does not exist.  R3TEST.ASM writes every one of
its PSP reads with the override and has done since v0.33; this is the
same trap the D32 link offset has set twice before.

INSTALL=, AND A THIRD WALK OVER THE FILE
----------------------------------------
What INSTALL= is for is TSRs - SHARE, FASTOPEN, KEYB - programs that
install themselves and stay, and that a real DOS runs here rather than
from AUTOEXEC.BAT because they cost less memory when nothing else has
been loaded yet.

It runs AFTER EVERY DEVICE= LINE wherever it sits in the file, because
an INSTALL= program is entitled to the drivers and a real DOS makes
the same guarantee.  That is the third walk: v0.38 added a first walk
for DOS= so that upper memory existed before a DEVICEHIGH could ask
for it, and the same argument produces the same answer one statement
further on.  cfg_phaseof is the list of exceptions - two statements
early, two late, and the other twenty-odd genuinely do not care.

SIXTEEN-BIT PROGRAMS ONLY, and the refusal is an admission about what
a native program is here rather than a limitation.  vdm_exec sets up a
DOS box, runs the guest and RETURNS, which is what lets CONFIG.SYS
carry on to the next line; the native path jumps into the program at
ring 3 and never comes back to its caller.  A native program installed
here could not return to finish reading the file it was named in, and
there is no such thing as a native TSR to make it worth solving.

INSTALLHIGH= is INSTALL= with the strategy set to "upper first" round
it, which is the same three lines DEVICEHIGH= got in v0.38.  On the
86Box machine that puts TSRTEST at CA05 with its environment at CA00
and costs conventional memory nothing.

FILES= AND THE TABLE THAT WAS ALWAYS 32
---------------------------------------
FILES= is the system file table and not a per-program limit, here as
in real DOS: one table, shared, and a handle is an index into it.
PM-DOS gave thirty-two entries whatever the line said, which was more
than DOS's own default of eight and therefore looked generous - and
was a promise it could not keep for the FILES=40 that half the
CONFIG.SYS files in the world contain.

The table is sixty-four now and the statement chooses how much of it
to hand out, clamped to eight at the bottom and to what exists at the
top.  Raising the ceiling mattered more than making the statement
adjustable: at thirty-two, FILES=40 was silently short.

LASTDRIVE=, AND WHY THE TEST WAS WRONG FIRST
--------------------------------------------
It says how far a program should bother looking for drives, so it can
never be fewer than there really are: a machine with seven volumes and
LASTDRIVE=E would be hiding two of its own disks from anything that
asked politely.  Real DOS raises it for the same reason.

CFGTEST's first version asserted the number in CONFIG.SYS and passed
on the floppy machine, which has two drives, and failed on the 86Box
one, which has seven.  The test now expresses the RULE - five, or the
block-device count if that is more - and the two machines agree
because the rule is what both of them implement.

IT ALSO HAD TO MOVE.  The list of lists is built at boot by
vdm_lolinit, before CONFIG.SYS has been read at all, so a LASTDRIVE=
written there would be the default every time.  It is filled in by the
52h handler now, beside the two drive counts, which were moved there
in v0.35 for the same reason and left a comment saying so.

THE REGISTER THAT LOOKED FREE, FOR THE THIRD TIME THIS MONTH
------------------------------------------------------------
Moving LASTDRIVE into the 52h handler was four instructions and one of
them was "mov eax,[lastdrive_n]".  EAX held the list-of-lists SEGMENT
and was handed to the guest two lines further down, so a guest read
its LASTDRIVE out of whatever segment that number happened to name.

That is the third instance in three releases: v0.38's XMS function 10h
restored the allocation strategy through EAX and destroyed the segment
lm_alloc had just returned, and lm_alloc's own comment has described
the shape since v0.32.  A return value arrives early, the register
carries it a long way, and the instruction that overwrites it reads as
housekeeping.

VERIFIED, both emulators.  CFGTEST is four checks and none of them
asks the kernel what it did - they measure what a program can see: the
list of lists for LASTDRIVE, handles opened until the table says no
for FILES, the environment block for SET=, and the multiplex interface
for the TSR.  DOSBox 0.74 floppy: 4/4 with LASTDRIVE 5 and 36 handles.
86Box FAT16 over real ATA: 4/4 with LASTDRIVE 7, which is the same
rule answering a different machine.  Regressions on 86Box: UMBTEST
11/11, MCBTEST 5/5 with the INSTALLHIGH TSR resident in upper memory,
FCBTEST 22/22 including forty FCBs open at once, APITEST 14/14,
BUFTEST 8/8, EXECTST including four-level nesting - and EXECTST's
environment dump shows PMDOSTEST and TEMP reaching a grandchild, which
is the SET= chain proved a second time by a test written for something
else.  LOLTEST reads 02/05 for block devices and LASTDRIVE on the
floppy machine.  The shipped CONFIG.SYS still boots in total silence.

v0.38 - UPPER MEMORY (2026-08-25)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
DEVICEHIGH= and LOADHIGH mean what they say.  New files DOS\UMB.INC
and TOOLS\UMBTEST.ASM; pg_map and pg_umbprobe at the foot of
IO\PAGING.INC; a rewritten lm_alloc; LH and LOADHIGH in COMMAND.COM.

FINDING THE MEMORY IS THE EASY HALF, AND ONLY HERE
--------------------------------------------------
A real-mode DOS can only hand out upper memory that some chipset has
already been talked into putting RAM behind.  That is what EMM386
spent its life doing and why it needed V86 mode to do it: with the CPU
in real mode there is nothing to be done about an address nothing
answers to.

PM-DOS has been paging since v0.29, for the A20 gate.  An address in
C0000h-EFFFFh that nothing decodes is a page table entry pointing at
itself with no memory on the other end, and pointing it somewhere else
costs one dword.  Upper memory stops being a scarce accident of the
hardware and becomes ordinary memory that happens to live at an
address a real-mode program can reach.  pg_map is thirty instructions.

The probe is the part that has to be careful, and the question it asks
is NOT "is there memory here".  It is "does anything at all answer to
this address", which is a different question with different
consequences: memory that answers is memory somebody may be using,
and an address nothing answers to is free by definition.  Two passes.
First the option ROMs by their own declaration - 55 AA on a 2K
boundary and a length at offset 2 - because the tail of a ROM is very
often FFh padding and is indistinguishable from nothing at all by
measurement.  Then a write test on what is left: the pattern comes
back, something is storing it and it is left alone; it does not, and a
page goes underneath.

On the 86Box machine that finds the video BIOS at C0000-C7FFF, an
adapter ROM at C8000-C9FFF and something at EC000-EFFFF, and hands
back 136K between them.  On DOSBox, where the whole region is plain
RAM, it hands back all 160K of C8000-EFFFF without mapping anything.
Both are right, and they exercise different halves of the code.

DESCRIBING IT IS THE HARD HALF, BECAUSE AN MCB CHAIN IS CONTIGUOUS
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Every block's header sits one paragraph before its data and the next
block begins exactly where this one ends.  A chain cannot skip over
the display, or the video BIOS, or a gap between two runs of usable
pages - it has to COVER them, with blocks owned by the system so that
nothing allocates them.  Those filler blocks are the whole of the
complication.

And a filler's header cannot live in the hole it describes.  Sixteen
bytes have to be stored somewhere and the first paragraph of a hole is
by definition a paragraph nothing will store anything in.  So each
filler's header goes in the LAST PARAGRAPH OF THE RUN BELOW IT.  That
is why umb_head points at the last paragraph of CONVENTIONAL memory
rather than at the first upper block: the first filler covers the
display and the ROMs, and its header is the top sixteen bytes of the
transient program area, which lm_shrinktop takes off the end of the
arena properly rather than by moving a number and hoping.

MS-DOS does precisely this - sysconf.asm, LinkFirstUMB, "cx = ax - 1"
where ax is the size of memory in paragraphs - and it reads like an
off-by-one in that source too.

Linking is then ONE BYTE.  The last conventional block's signature is
'Z' when the upper chain is detached and 'M' when it is joined on, and
everything that walks the chain follows it or stops at it without
knowing a decision was made.  Real DOS does exactly and only this
(alloc.asm, LinkUmbs) and it is worth admiring: the state is stored in
the same place that acts on it, so the two cannot disagree.

WHAT "LOAD IT HIGH" ACTUALLY IS
-------------------------------
Four calls to 58h and no more.  Set the strategy to "upper first",
join the chains, run the command exactly as it would have run anyway,
put both back.  DEVICEHIGH= is the same three lines round dl_load.
The kernel does the rest in lm_alloc, which is where the decision
belongs: a shell that tried to place a program itself would have to
know how big the program was before loading it.

That works only because 58h stopped being a polite fiction.  The high
bits of the strategy were accepted and dropped on the floor, and the
link state was always 0 and refused to become 1 - both of which were
the honest answers on a machine with no upper memory, and neither of
which survives one having some.  lm_alloc now takes the region from
bits 6 and 7 and the fit from bits 0 and 1, and honours all of them;
it used to be first fit into conventional memory whatever anybody
asked for, the strategy having been stored for the KERNEL's arena.

AND "GIVE IT EVERYTHING" IS A REGIONAL QUESTION
-----------------------------------------------
This is the one that would have made the whole release a no-op.

A .COM is handed every free paragraph there is, and the way that has
always been written - here and in MS-DOS both - is to ask for FFFFh
paragraphs, be refused, and then allocate whatever size the refusal
reported.  With one region that is exact.  With two it is not: the
refusal reports the largest block ANYWHERE, which is the conventional
one, so the second ask finds it low and puts the program there.  Every
LOADHIGH would have succeeded, said nothing, and loaded low - and the
only way to notice would have been to go looking.

lm_allocbig asks the question one region at a time, in the order the
strategy names, and the first region with a block big enough wins the
whole of it.  It also takes a MINIMUM, which nothing in the .COM path
had ever needed: with one region there was never a block too small to
be the largest, and handing a 40K program the 8K that happened to be
free up there would have loaded it over whatever came next.

MEM, AND THE TWO BUGS IN THE MEASURING
--------------------------------------
21h/F1h AL=8 walks a chain by index for MEM, which cannot read either
arena for itself now that it runs at ring 3 in a segment of its own.
Conventional and upper are ONE chain, so the region became the
selector and the kernel does the classifying: F8_CONV and F8_UPPER
walk the same blocks and count different ones.  MEM grew an Upper row,
printed only when there is any, and MEM /D grew a listing of the DOS
chain - which is the listing that answers "did it load high?", and
which the arena listing above it never could, being a report about
memory no DEVICEHIGH ever touches.

Two things went wrong in the writing and both were the same shape.
lm_alloc returns the segment in AX; XMS function 10h restored the
saved allocation strategy through EAX afterwards and destroyed it,
which is the trap lm_alloc's own comment has described since v0.32 -
the register looks free and the value has already arrived.  And 42h
hands a DOS program back DX:AX but hands the KERNEL back a flat 32-bit
position in EAX, so recombining a DX that nothing had written made the
size of every .COM in the machine a large number and stopped all of
them loading.  "Bad command or file name", for every program.

MCBTEST HAD THE OLD ASSUMPTION IN IT
------------------------------------
Its fourth check was that the chain ends at the top of conventional
memory, which was arithmetic when there was one region and is a fact
about a machine when there are two.  It now reads umb_head and asks
the right question either way: with no upper memory, the old test
unchanged; with upper memory, that the walk passed THROUGH umb_head,
that umb_head is the last paragraph of the TPA, and that the chain
ends above it.  Its fifth check bounded a block's owner by the top of
conventional memory, which a program loaded high fails by definition -
its PSP is up there.  A test that shares an assumption with the code
cannot find out that the assumption changed.

VERIFIED, both emulators.  UMBTEST is eleven checks and every one that
says a block was allocated goes on to WRITE TO IT AND READ IT BACK: a
UMB is the one allocation here whose address is not backed by whatever
lives at that address on a real machine, and "the page tables were
never touched" looks exactly like success until the first store.  The
check that cannot be faked is number seven - with the chains detached
there is no path to a UMB at all, so an upper-only allocation that
succeeds proves the strategy bits were never read.

86Box, FAT16 over real ATA, 128MB: UMBTEST 11/11, 136K of upper memory
found between the ROMs.  DEVICEHIGH=\TESTDEV.SYS puts the driver at
CA53 and "LH TSRTEST" puts the program at CA77 with its environment at
CA73, both still there afterwards, with conventional memory unchanged
at 637,264 bytes free.  MCBTEST 5/5 with that TSR resident.  DOSBox
0.74 floppy: UMBTEST 11/11, 160K found, BUFTEST 8/8, FCBTEST 22/22,
DEVTEST 9/9.  Regressions on 86Box: ALLOCTST, APITEST 14/14, EXECTST
including four-level nesting, XMSTEST including the A20 wrap, HELLOX
relocating.

AND WITH DOS=UMB TAKEN OUT, nothing changed: MCBTEST 5/5 with the
chain ending at 9FC0 exactly as it always did, MEM with no Upper row
at all, and DEVICEHIGH loading the driver low without a word - which
is what a real DOS with no upper-memory provider does, and is the
regression that mattered most.  The statement is the escape hatch on
purpose.  Deciding what a machine has at D800h by writing to it is a
measurement, measurements can be wrong on hardware nobody here has,
and the only useful answer to a machine that will not boot is a line
the user can take out of CONFIG.SYS.  Real DOS has the same
arrangement for the same reason and calls it EMM386.

v0.37 - THE BUFFER GUARD, AND DEVICE= (2026-08-25)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Two things: a hole in INT 21h closed, and DEVICE= made real for
character drivers.  New files DOS\DEVLOAD.INC, TOOLS\BUFTEST.ASM and
TOOLS\TESTDEV.ASM.

THE LENGTH WAS THE HOLE, NOT THE POINTER
----------------------------------------
v0.36 left a note on the roadmap saying a guest's INT 21h pointers
were unbounded.  Reading it properly, the pointer was never the
problem: a segment:offset stops at 10FFEFh, PMDOS.SYS starts at
110000h, and the sixty-four kilobytes between them are the HMA, which
belongs to the guest on purpose.  A DOS box cannot POINT at this
kernel however hard it tries.

It can ask for FFFFh bytes to be read into FFFF:FF00.  Sixteen of them
land in the guest's own HMA and the rest land in PMDOS.SYS, and the
read reports success, because from inside a copy loop the second half
of a buffer looks exactly like the first.  The machine dies later and
somewhere else, and the only evidence is that a file was read.

buf_ok is the guard, and the rule it enforces is deliberately NOT
"this belongs to the caller" but "this is not OURS".  Which program's
memory a DOS program corrupts is DOS behaving normally and always was;
what cannot be allowed is the kernel being overwritten while it is
running the very call doing the overwriting.  Three ranges - the low
scaffolding at 4E8h-3FFFh, PMDOS.SYS, and PMIO with the IDT and the
stacks and the page tables - and the gaps between them are deliberate:
the IVT and the BIOS data area are the guest's to ruin, the DOS data
segment holds the list of lists and a program is invited to read it,
and the program slots belong to a PROGRAM rather than to the kernel,
which is what r3_xlat is for.

The same argument as i13_bufok in v0.27, one API further up.  It is
asked at the five places where a caller supplies a buffer AND a
length - 3Fh, 40h, 0Ah, 60h, and the DTA that 4Eh/4Fh and the FCB
block calls fill - and, as a pointer-only check, in the two bridges
that had none.  The DPMI host also puts the client's registers back
before refusing: a flat kernel address in DX is both a wrong answer
and one the client had no way to ask for.

AND THE HARD PART WAS NOT THE RULE, IT WAS "WHOSE BUFFER IS THIS?"
The kernel calls its own INT 21h - CONFIG.SYS is opened with 3Dh and
read with 3Fh into a buffer inside PMDOS.SYS - so a guard that cannot
tell the kernel from a guest either refuses the boot or protects
nothing.  Three answers were needed and the first two are each a
correct answer to a question that turns out not to be the whole
question:

  - the frame's CS is not enough.  A DOS box's calls arrive through
    k21, and k21 manufactures a frame with SEL_CODE32 in it ON
    PURPOSE, so that anything asking "was this a DPMI client?" gets
    the right answer.  Believing the CS exempts every guest in the
    machine: the check ran, passed everything, and BUFTEST walked
    into PMDOS.SYS on the next line.
  - the frame's DS beside it is not enough either.  An interrupt gate
    does not reload DS, so a real INT 21h carries the caller's own -
    SEL_DATA32 from kernel code - while a manufactured frame has none
    and k21 pushes zero.  That identifies the kernel's own INT 21h
    correctly and says nothing about k21 frames, BECAUSE THE KERNEL
    USES k21 TOO: exec_kind reads eight bytes of a program's header
    through exactly that door, and every EXEC in the machine failed
    the first time this was got wrong.
  - so k21 grew a second door.  k21u marks the frame as a guest's and
    k21 does not, and the mark travels in the frame rather than in a
    global because these calls NEST - a guest's 4Bh runs exec_kind,
    which calls k21 for itself while the guest's own call is still
    open.  A flag would have to be saved and restored at every one of
    those points; a frame field is already per-call, and stacks.

BUFTEST is eight checks and two of them cannot be faked: a read whose
COUNT reaches the kernel (any guard that looks only at pointers passes
it), and a DTA sixteen bytes below PMDOS.SYS being ACCEPTED while the
4Eh that would write forty-three bytes there is not - because that is
a different call from the one that was given the pointer, which is the
whole reason the measurement cannot live in the bridge.  The test file
is eight kilobytes on purpose: FFFF:FF00 is 1110h bytes short of the
kernel, so a shorter file overruns nothing and an unguarded kernel
passes a test it should have died on.

DEVICE= AND DEVICEHIGH=
-----------------------
The device chain has been there since v0.30 with four real headers
below 1MB and NUL first.  What was missing was the loading, and it is
five pieces: read the .SYS into conventional memory, call INIT through
strategy and interrupt with a request packet, keep what INIT says to
keep and link the header behind NUL, make dev_find look at the loaded
drivers BEFORE the built-in table, and route dev_in/dev_out through
packets for anything loaded.

THE ONLY GENUINELY NEW MACHINERY IS THE EXCURSION.  Calling a driver
means running 16-bit real-mode code from a 32-bit kernel, with no
program, no PSP and no DOS box around it.  A far RETURN is how a
driver finishes and there is nowhere here for it to return to, so it
returns to a HLT the kernel planted and the monitor stopping on that
byte at that address is the signal - the same trick the XMS and DPMI
entries use, and for the same reason: a HLT is the one instruction
whose only possible meaning here is "we are done".

INT 21h is trapped and everything else reflects to the ROM, because a
driver talking to its hardware through the BIOS is a driver doing its
job.  A driver's INIT is entitled to make DOS calls and it makes them
before there is a shell - which nothing in this kernel had ever done -
and they are serviced by vdm_do21, the same routine a DOS box's calls
go through.  That is why vdm_do21 exists at all: it was the middle of
vdm_loop until this release, and a DOS box is no longer the only thing
that makes 16-bit DOS calls.

NESTING IS NOT A CORNER CASE.  A loaded CON driver - which is what
ANSI.SYS is - means every character the kernel prints goes through a
driver call, so a driver's INIT printing its own banner is a driver
call made from inside a driver call.  ANSI.SYS prints a banner.  Four
levels of packet and stack, and the live V86 context parked on the
kernel stack for the duration of each.

BLOCK DRIVERS ARE REFUSED WITH A MESSAGE rather than half-loaded.
Their units have to become drive letters in a volume table that gets
its letters by scanning partitions, which is a different piece of work
and wants its own release.  The character half is where the programs
are.

DEVICEHIGH= is accepted and means DEVICE=.  A real DOS with no
upper-memory provider loads a DEVICEHIGH driver low and says nothing
about it, because the statement asks for a preference and not a
guarantee; PM-DOS has no UMBs to offer yet and gives the same answer
for the same reason.

TWO BUGS THE TEST DRIVER FOUND, AND ONE OF THEM WAS NOT MINE
------------------------------------------------------------
THE DIRECTION FLAG IS THE GUEST'S AND THE MONITOR WAS STANDING IN IT.
v86_leave saves the guest's eight general registers with a REP MOVSD
and does it with whatever DF the guest left set, so a guest that traps
with STD in force has them written BACKWARDS, off the front of the
context.  EIP and CS come back correct because they are stored one at
a time; AX and DX come back as whatever they were before the guest
ran.  That is a bug in the V86 monitor and not in this release's code:
a DOS program that calls INT 21h in the middle of a string copy is not
exotic, it is a REP MOVSB with a CALL in the loop, and it has been
there since v0.30 waiting for somebody to look.  One CLD in v86_fault.

It surfaced here because the excursion set the guest's flags to
V86_UFLAGS, which is a MASK and not a value - as a value it sets OF,
DF, SF, ZF, AF, PF and CF all at once.  The DOS box path starts a
guest with EFL_IF and had never tripped it.

AND LINKING A HEADER INTO THE CHAIN DESTROYS THE FIELD YOU ARE WALKING
IT BY.  One .SYS may hold several drivers chained by the NEXT field
inside the file, and dl_chain writes that very field - it puts NUL's
old next pointer in it.  Asking afterwards where the file's next
header is gets the answer "the console", and the loader walks off into
the middle of the driver it has just installed and tries to initialise
whatever it finds there.  Read it before you write it.

VERIFIED, DOSBox 0.74 floppy: BUFTEST 8/8, and TESTDEV.SYS loading
from CONFIG.SYS with its INIT banner printed through INT 21h, then
"TYPE TESTDEV" reading its reply through a request packet and
"ECHO HI > TESTDEV" counting five bytes into it - which is a round
trip through dev_find, the SFT, dev_out, dev_in and a packet in each
direction, and cannot be faked by a driver that merely loaded.
Regressions: FCBTEST 22/22, APITEST 14/14, DEVTEST 9/9 - and FCBTEST
matters most of the three, because every call in it goes through the
vdm_do21 that was lifted out of vdm_loop.

v0.36 - THE FCB SET, AND A NAME THAT MEANT ANOTHER FILE (2026-08-24)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Two things, and the second one is the smaller change and the worse
bug.  New file DOS\FCB.INC; new test TOOLS\FCBTEST.ASM.

THE FILE CONTROL BLOCK API - 0Fh-17h, 21h-24h, 27h-29h - is in, all
sixteen calls, and with it the last thing a pre-1983 program could ask
PM-DOS for and be told did not exist.  It has been on the roadmap
since v0.31 waiting for ring 3, and ring 3 landed in v0.33.

THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY IS THAT THE STRUCTURE IS THE CALLER'S.  A handle
is a number the kernel chose and can look up in a table it owns; an
FCB is thirty-seven bytes of the PROGRAM's memory, which it may copy,
hand to a child, forget about, or still be holding long after the
kernel has given the table entry to somebody else.  So the kernel
cannot put a pointer in it and believe what comes back.  What goes in
the eight reserved bytes instead is an INDEX AND A CLAIM ID:

    SFT_STAMP is a number never handed out twice, assigned at the one
    place an entry is ever claimed.  An FCB carries the stamp of the
    entry it was opened on, and an entry that has since been closed
    and re-used answers "not yours" instead of handing over somebody
    else's file.  A bare index cannot do that: index 7 is index 7
    whoever is in it.

    When the id does not match, THE FILE IS OPENED AGAIN from the name
    the FCB is still carrying.  That is not a workaround for a small
    table - it is what real DOS does, and its FCBS= statement exists
    to size the pool the recycling runs over.  A CP/M-era program
    opens FCBs and never closes them; that is not a leak, it is how
    the API was meant to be used, and a kernel that refuses the
    thirty-third is a kernel those programs do not run on.  So when
    the table is full, the FCB that has waited longest is closed and
    its entry taken (SFT_FCBLRU, fcb_evict).  A HANDLE is never a
    candidate, because a handle cannot be re-opened from anything.

MS-DOS keeps the first cluster and the directory sector and position
in those eight bytes instead, and re-opens only when it has to.  Those
fields are sixteen bits wide, which is a FAT16 answer to a FAT16
question, and this kernel mounts FAT32 volumes where none of the three
fit.  Re-opening by name always fits, and is the same answer arrived
at from a wider disk.

WHAT WAS BUILT ON, RATHER THAN COPIED.  Four routines came out of the
handle API so that both doors reach one implementation, and that is
the whole reason the FCB code is as short as it is:

    open_core / create_core   3Dh and 3Ch minus their frames
    file_read / file_write    3Fh and 40h minus their frames
    file_trunc                40h's ECX = 0 case, which is also 28h's
                              CX = 0 case - the same operation reached
                              through two APIs a decade apart

A record read IS a byte read with the position worked out beforehand,
and that is the entire difference between the two file APIs.

fcb_io is the six I/O calls in one engine, and the order of operations
in it is real DOS's step for step, because the order is observable:
the extent and record fields are written back BEFORE the transfer as
well as after it, a random call leaves them pointing at the record it
just did, a block call also updates the random record field, and a
write stamps the FCB with the time whether or not anything reached the
disk.  A program that mixes sequential and random calls on one FCB
knows where it is only because of those four.

29h IS THE ONE WORTH GETTING EXACTLY RIGHT, because every DOS program
that ever read a command line called it and inherited its quirks.  Two
are reproduced deliberately:

  - A NAME LONGER THAN THE FIELD IS NOT AN ERROR AND NOT A STOP.  DOS
    keeps scanning and throws the extra characters away, so
    "LONGFILENAME.TXT" parses to LONGFILE.TXT with SI left after the
    whole thing.  The DOS 6 source calls this a "horrible bug" in a
    comment and then ships it, because by 1993 far too much depended
    on it.  A parser that stopped at the eighth character would leave
    SI in the middle of a name and every caller would read the
    remainder as the next argument.
  - '*' FILLS THE REST OF THE FIELD WITH '?' AND NOTHING ELSE, which
    is why "*.*" is eleven question marks and why "A*B.TXT" loses
    the B.

AND 29h IS THE ONLY DOS CALL WHOSE ANSWER IS A POINTER REGISTER.  SI
comes back past what was parsed - and all three bridges into this
kernel were built on the assumption that pointers travel INWARDS only.
The DOS box's flattens them on the way in and never looks again; the
DPMI host's puts back what the client passed.  Handing a guest the
kernel's flat address there would send it walking off above 1MB with
it.  So the answer leaves as a DISTANCE rather than an address
(p29_adv), which is the one form a V86 guest, a DPMI client and a
native ring-3 program can all use.  The native bridge needed nothing:
r3_unxlat converts the CURRENT value back rather than restoring the
old one, which turns out to be the only one of the three that was
already right.

FOUND BY THE TEST, AND WORTH THE PARAGRAPH: AN FCB FULL OF ZEROES MUST
NOT LOOK LIKE A BINDING.  It is the commonest FCB there is - a program
clears a buffer and fills in the name - and index zero is a real,
in-use table entry: it is the standard input.  The stamp agreed too,
because the three standard entries are planted by sft_init and never
go through sft_new, so nothing ever gave them one and theirs is zero
as well.  A freshly cleared FCB therefore bound itself to CON and the
first record read sat waiting for somebody to type ninety-six bytes.
The screen showed the test's name printed and no verdict after it,
which from outside is indistinguishable from a kernel loop.  Two tests
are cheaper than one: the standard handles are never an FCB's, and a
claim id of zero was never handed out.

SWEPT UP ON THE WAY: 41h called lfn_tomb BEFORE deciding whether it
was allowed to delete the file, so "DEL <a read-only file with a long
name>" printed "access denied", left the file where it was, and had
already thrown its long name away.  Same two calls, opposite order,
and only one of the orders can be undone.  Found because the FCB
delete has the same two tests and therefore had to decide which order
they went in.

A LOSSY NAME MAY NOT OPEN WHAT IT TRUNCATES TO
----------------------------------------------
Asking for "SUBQ.CMDCMDTEST.CMD" opened SUBQ.CMD.

fn_conv renders that to the 8.3 pattern "SUBQ    CMD" and flags the
rendering as LOSSY, and the resolver then arms a long-name match for
the raw text - but fat_search treated the long match as an EXTRA way
to hit rather than a REPLACEMENT for the 8.3 one.  No long name
matched, the mangled pattern still did, and the open succeeded and
handed back a different file with no error anywhere.

v0.11 fixed the half of this where the truncated name was silently
CREATED.  This is the half where it is silently FOUND, and it is the
worse half: creating the wrong name leaves evidence on the disk and
opening the wrong file leaves none.

The fix is one flag, srch_lonly, set beside srch_long by whoever armed
it and cleared everywhere srch_long is cleared - because a leftover
would refuse an ordinary lookup, and "file not found" for a file that
is plainly there points nowhere near this byte.  When it is set, an
8.3 hit falls through to the same comparison a miss does.

UNDER LFN=OFF IT STANDS, deliberately.  LFN=OFF means "behave like a
DOS that has never heard of long names", and such a DOS parses that
name to SUBQ.CMD and opens SUBQ.CMD - exactly as 29h above does with
the same string.  Refusing there would be neither the old behaviour
nor the new one.

VERIFIED, DOSBox 0.74 floppy: FCBTEST 22/22 with no failures - the
five 29h cases, create/open/close, sequential and random and block
I/O in both directions, the size and relative-record calls, the short
last record answering 3 with the rest zeroed, past-the-end answering
1, find first and find next, wildcard rename and wildcard delete, and
FORTY FCBs OPEN AT ONCE on a table of thirty-two with the first one
still reading its own data afterwards - which is the only check in the
file that would notice if the recycling broke.  Regressions: APITEST
14/14, MCBTEST 5/5, LFNTEST end to end (long names created, aliases
distinct, copy, rename, delete, a long-named directory walked through
and entered), COPY/TYPE/DEL/redirection, and the lossy-name case now
in LFNTEST.BAT.  ALLOCTST's second check fails here and fails
identically on the v0.35 kernel built from a clean tree - it is
DOSBox, not this release, and it passed on 86Box at v0.35.

NOT YET RUN ON 86BOX OR ON IRON.  The VDM is developed against 86Box
for good reasons written up under v0.32; this is a regression check
away from being finished, not a new unknown.

v0.35 - AN EXCEPTION BELONGS TO THE PROGRAM (2026-08-15)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
The 486 came back a second time with three sentences, and every one of
them was a different bug: "KBTEST worked" (v0.34 holds), "QCONFIG
crashed with guest faulted, vector 06 at 0653:D2EE", and "MEM locked up
the system".  A fourth turned up on the way, hiding behind the first
one that got fixed.

QCONFIG DID NOT CRASH.  IT ASKED A QUESTION.
Vector 06 is #UD, an undefined opcode, and on an 8086 that is not a
crash - it is how the CPU talks to the program.  Vectors 0 to 7 are
delivered through the interrupt vector table like anything else:
divide by zero to INT 00h, BOUND to INT 05h, an instruction the chip
has never heard of to INT 06h.  A program that wants to know whether
the CPU it is on HAS an instruction hooks INT 06h, runs it, and sees
whether it comes back.  That is how every CPU detector written before
CPUID was universal asks, and QCONFIG on a 486 is one of them.

The monitor emulated #GP and treated every other vector as the end of
the DOS box.  So the program had its own handler installed, one
instruction away, and never found out it had been given its answer.

Vectors 0,1,3,4,5,6,7 now go to v86_reflect, which already existed for
software interrupts and does exactly what the 8086 does.  Two guards,
because reflecting blind is worse than not reflecting: a vector whose
IVT slot is 0000:0000 is still a crash, and A HANDLER THAT MAKES NO
PROGRESS IS COUNTED.  A fault pushes the address of the instruction
that faulted, so a handler which IRETs without stepping over it takes
the same fault for ever - and that is what the ROM's own dummy INT 06h
does.  Real hardware hangs there.  After 32 identical faults at one
address the box ends with "the guest is stuck on its own handler for
vector NN" instead, because a spinning guest makes no DOS call, so
nothing ever looks at the ^C flag and the only way out is the power
switch.  UDTEST.COM tests all of it; UDTEST /HANG tests the guard, and
a pass there is the machine still being alive.

INTO fell out of the same reading.  Opcode CEh was not in the #GP
dispatcher's list at all, so a guest that used the overflow trap was
killed and told it had "faulted".

MEM.EXE: OWNER 8 IS A PROMISE ABOUT THE CONTENTS.
The lockup reproduced on 86Box first go, and finding it needed a tool
that did not exist.  A guest that CRASHES says so; a guest that SPINS
says nothing, and the monitor's fault trace is no help because a
program going round its own loop makes no calls and causes no faults -
the trace simply stops, which is what the screen was already doing.
So: BUILD watch, a sampler on the timer tick that prints where the
guest is if the monitor has not been entered for two seconds.  It
answered in one boot - 0437:1460 to 14DC, round and round - and
disassembling MEM there showed a walk over sixteen-byte headers,
stepping by the length at offset 3.

That walk is INSIDE a DOS-owned block.  MS-DOS keeps what CONFIG.SYS
asked for - the device drivers, the buffers, FILES, FCBS, STACKS -
each behind a header laid out exactly like an MCB with a letter in
place of the 'M', and every memory reporter walks them.  PM-DOS marked
its own low-memory blocks owner 8, which is the correct way to say
"this is the system's", without knowing it was also promising that
shape.  The list of lists begins with the first-MCB word and then
FFFF:FFFF, the "no drive parameter block" sentinel - so MEM read a
length of FFFFh, added one to step over the header, and got ZERO.  It
never moved again.

lm_sysalloc now puts one paragraph in front of every system block with
a header of the shape the walk expects and a length that tiles the
block exactly, so the walk lands on the end and stops.  The letter is
deliberately one DOS does not define: claiming 'D' to be counted would
be inventing a device driver, which is the lie the list of lists
already refuses to tell with its pointers.  MCBTEST.COM walks the
chain the way MEM does and counts, so an endless walk is reported
rather than performed.

NOT FINISHED: MEM runs, returns, and prints the wrong numbers.  It
reports two regions below 1MB where there is one - the "Upper" row
holds the correct conventional figures (15K used, 623K free) and the
byte counts in brackets are its own thousands off ("549 bytes" for
548,864).  A lockup is fixed; the arithmetic is not, and it is a
reporting bug now rather than a machine that has stopped.

AND THE ONE THAT WAS HIDING: v0.34 ONLY HALF-FIXED THE AUTOEXEC BUG.
"Whenever there is a crash, AUTOEXEC.BAT gets re-run" was reported at
v0.33 and answered at v0.34 for a fault inside a DOS BOX, verified by
injecting one.  A fault in a native 32-bit program still did it, and
CRASHTST was called green because the screen it produces when it goes
wrong is a scrolling mess that looks like the test running.

The ring-0 stack is ONE stack shared by every EXEC level: 4Bh hands
the child the parent's frame base as its ceiling and the child works
downwards, so a program at depth 1 has its parent's unfinished 4Bh
frame immediately above it.  r3_fault set ESP to R3_KSTACK - the
SHELL's level, above all of that - and then made a dozen nested calls
to print the report, writing their return addresses straight down
through the waiting frame.  The report came out perfectly; the EXIT
died, on the IRETD at the end of int21_entry, returning through a
frame the reporting had just overwritten.  From outside: a program
faults, the fault is reported correctly, and THEN the machine says
"CPU exception" on its own account and reloads the interpreter.

It is r3_esp0, the running program's own level, and at depth 0 that IS
R3_KSTACK - which is why the shell's own crashes always looked fine
and hid it.  v0.34 fixed this exact mistake in r3_abandon, four
hundred lines away in the same file, and did not think to look here.
THE LESSON IS THE SHAPE OF THE MISTAKE, NOT THE LINE IT WAS ON: when a
fix is "use the level, not the top", every other place that touches
the same stack is suspect until it has been read.

Also: lm_resize orphaned a paragraph.  Shrinking a block to leave
exactly one paragraph over set the new length first and then refused
to split, so the block claimed to end one paragraph before the next
header really began and a walker landed on the last sixteen bytes of
somebody's data.  A zero-length MCB is legal and real DOS makes them;
the header IS the paragraph.  Found by reading, not by a test - which
means nothing was testing it.

And MKDISK's FAT32 root was four clusters, 64 entries, which the test
image list walked past the day MCBTEST and MEM622 were added.  Loud
("root full", non-zero exit) rather than silent, at least.

Verified on 86Box: R3TEST 14/14, UDTEST 4/4 and /HANG ending the box
and not the machine, MCBTEST 5/5, CRASHTST all five crashes caught
with the shell intact and no re-run, LOLTEST, DEVTEST, APITEST,
VDMTEST with DPMITEST inside it, EXEHDR, NMAKE, and MEM622 running to
the end.  MSD stops at "Not ready reading drive A - Abort, Retry,
Fail?", which is the v0.34 critical-error fix working and needs a
keystroke nobody was there to give.

NOT VERIFIED ON IRON.  All of it wants the 486.

v0.34 - A 16-BIT PROGRAM CAN GET A KEYSTROKE (2026-08-15)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
The 486 came back with "we seem to have lost the ability to run 16-bit
DOS programs": QCONFIG crashed, QCONFIG piped into MORE locked up, and
MS-DOS 6.22's MEM.EXE locked up.  Four bugs came out of chasing that,
and the last one is not a v0.33 regression at all - it has been there
since the VDM's first evening and nothing had ever asked.

THE KEYBOARD BUFFER BELONGS TO THE MACHINE.  PM-DOS owns IRQ 1, so the
ROM's INT 09h never runs, so nothing wrote 40:1A, 40:1C or the sixteen
words between them.  A 16-bit program asking for a key does it through
INT 16h, which the monitor reflects to the ROM, which reads exactly
those bytes - finds head equal to tail, concludes that nothing has been
typed, and waits.  It waits for ever.  EVERY FULL-SCREEN DOS PROGRAM
STOPPED AT ITS FIRST KEYSTROKE, and from outside that is a machine
that has locked up.  Programs reading 40:17 for the shift state, or
peeking at 40:1A themselves rather than calling anybody, were being
lied to by the same silence.

  This is v0.32's timer lesson wearing different clothes and it is
  worth saying in the general form: OWNING AN INTERRUPT MEANS OWNING
  WHAT THE BIOS'S HANDLER DID.  v0.32 learned it for IRQ 0 - the
  floppy motor countdown at 40:40 and the tick count at 40:6C - and
  fixed those two without asking what ELSE the kernel had taken over
  by claiming an IRQ.  IRQ 1 was the answer and it was sitting right
  there.  When this kernel takes a vector away from the ROM it
  inherits the ROM's bookkeeping, all of it, and the bookkeeping is
  the half that is invisible until somebody reflects a call back.

  So the private ring is DELETED, not mirrored, for the same reason
  tick_count was deleted: a copy is a thing that can drift, and a
  keyboard the shell and a DOS box disagree about is worse than
  either.  kb_put and kb_getchar work the ring at 40:1E, honouring the
  bounds at 40:80 and 40:82 rather than assuming them, and the
  modifier keys publish shift, ctrl, alt and caps into 40:17 on every
  make and break.  KBTEST.COM is new and checks all four ways of
  asking; it is interactive on purpose, because a keystroke test needs
  a keystroke, and every wait in it is bounded by the tick count so
  that it REPORTS the hang instead of becoming it.

  STILL MISSING, and named here rather than discovered again: a guest
  that hooks INT 09h ITSELF still never sees a key.  IRQ 1 is not
  reflected into the DOS box, so the kernel's handler has already
  taken the scan code off port 60h by the time the guest could look.
  MSD's menus are the test case - it comes up, reports the machine
  correctly, and will not take a keystroke.  That is the next piece of
  work and it is a real one: delivering a hardware interrupt into V86
  at a point where the guest can survive it.

EVERY CRITICAL ERROR OFFERED ONLY "ABORT".  crit_disk builds the set of
answers the handler may give in AH - abort, retry, fail - and then
calls bios2log to turn a BIOS drive number into a letter.  bios2log
counted the scan in EAX and started with `xor eax,eax`, which is the
whole register: AH arrived at the handler as zero, so no retry and no
fail, on every disk error there has ever been.  "Not ready reading
drive A" with a chance to put a disk in and press R is the oldest
reason INT 24h exists, and crit_disk's own comment says so four lines
above the call that was throwing it away.  It matters more than it
looks: a program that merely LOOKS at an empty floppy - which every
system-information program does - could not be told to carry on.  The
only key that did anything killed it.

A FAULT INSIDE A DOS BOX RESTARTED THE SESSION.  A 16-bit EXEC does not
nest - the guest lives below 1MB, nothing above it is disturbed, and
vdm_exec RETURNS to the 4Bh that called it - so it pushes no nesting
record and leaves exec_depth alone.  dos_fault handed the unwind to
4Ch, which found a depth of zero, concluded the INTERPRETER had
faulted, and reloaded it: AUTOEXEC.BAT round again and any batch file
in progress gone, because one 16-bit utility crashed.  That is exactly
the complaint v0.30 fixed for a 32-bit program without noticing that a
DOS box is the other half of the same thing.  It goes through
vdm_abort now - the unwind ^C and Abort already use - and 4Dh reports
a system error, the nearest true thing DOS has a code for.

r3_abandon RESET THE RING-0 STACK WHERE IT SHOULD HAVE RESTORED IT.
Found by reading rather than by crashing, which is worth recording
because the scenario SURVIVES: a disk fails under a child program,
COMMAND's INT 24h handler answers Abort and terminates the child with
4Ch - and the shell's own 4Bh is still open, its frame at the top of
that stack, waiting for the 4Ch to return through it.  Starting the
4Ch at the top writes the new frame exactly over the old one.  It
survived because the frame it left behind happened to describe a
legitimate resume point and the code after COMMAND's 4Ch happened to
be harmless; an A/B with the old code back in place confirmed both
builds reach a prompt.  Accidental survival is not survival.  What the
level should be is what it was before the excursion, which is the one
thing r3_thunk already writes down.

AND TWO THINGS FOR DIR, both asked for directly.  The free-space total
is indented to sit under the byte total rather than under the file
count - two numbers that have nothing to do with each other were lined
up, and the one it wants to be read against was ten columns to the
right.  And "DIR," works: MS-DOS's undocumented "show me everything",
which survives because it is quicker to type than /A:HS.  A comma is a
DOS delimiter like any other, so the mechanism is one line in the verb
parser and the shell hands the comma over as an argument instead of
looking for a command called "DIR,".

  THE COMMA IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT OR IT IS NOTHING, and the first
  version here got that wrong: it stripped a leading comma and let
  whatever followed be the pattern, which quietly invented "DIR,/P"
  and "DIR,*.SYS" - forms no MS-DOS ever had.  6.x takes the comma
  alone and nothing else.  Charlie caught it in the diff.  Being
  generous with a syntax is the same mistake as being wrong about it:
  the point of matching 6.22 is that a thing which works here works
  there, and a thing that works here and NOT there is a lie in the
  more expensive direction.

WHAT THE TEST SUITE COULD NOT SAY.  Every 16-bit guest in TOOLS\ was
written to exercise one thing and is a few hundred bytes long, and all
of them passed on both emulators while a 486 could not run a program
anybody would actually use.  That is v0.32's other lesson - a limit no
test can reach is not covered by having tests - arriving from the
direction of what the tests are made OF.  So the test disks now carry
REAL 16-bit programs: MSD, EXEHDR and NMAKE off this machine's MASM
6.11, and REVEAL and DISKSTAT out of the Dobson Utilities.  Tens to
hundreds of kilobytes, large model, hundreds of relocations each, and
MSD asks the machine every question a system-information program asks.
None of them is built here, none is redistributed, and MKHD leaves
them out silently if they are not in BIN\.  DISK\BIG16.BAT runs the
ones that can run unattended.

VERIFIED on 86Box AND DOSBox 0.74, which agree throughout: KBTEST 5 of 5 with a real keystroke arriving through
INT 16h and shift showing in 40:17; "Abort, Retry, Fail?" in full, and
Fail letting MSD carry on past an empty A: and B: to its main screen,
where it reports the BIOS, a 486DX, VGA, the mouse, five drive letters
and "Non MS-DOS 6.22"; EXEHDR straight and through a pipe into SORT;
NMAKE; DIR's four comma forms and the totals; R3TEST 14 of 14;
LOLTEST; DEVTEST; APITEST; VDMTEST with DPMITEST inside it; CRASHTST.

AND THE DOS-BOX FAULT RECOVERY, A/B'd, because it was the one fix with
no way to reach it from outside: a scratch build with a divide by zero
planted in vdm_lol, so that LOLTEST's 52h faults the kernel with a box
running.  With the fix, "exception 00", the recovery line, and the
prompt.  Without it, the same two lines and then "Hello from AUTOEXEC"
- the 486's symptom exactly, reproduced and then removed.  Both
scratch patches are out; grep for SCRATCH says so.

NOT REPRODUCED EITHER: a floppy written from PMDOS.IMG that boots the
486 and then says "Bad or missing command interpreter".  That message
is shell_restart's, so PMIO and PMDOS both LOADED off the floppy and
what failed was exec_load on the interpreter.  Ruled out from here:
the boot sector and BPB (byte-identical to BOOT.BIN, 55AA, a correct
1.44M BPB); the disk being full (420 clusters of 2847); the drive
letter, because A: and B: are slots 0 and 1 of drv_tbl whatever else
is in the machine and bios2log cannot answer anything else; reads
crossing a track boundary, which the block layer has clamped for since
it was written; and the image itself, which boots in DOSBox with a
hard disk attached and without one.

  What is left is the 486's own floppy path, and the thing to run
  there is a BUILD fdd image - BIN\PMDOSFDD.IMG - which prints what
  INT 13h/08h said the geometry was and the status of every INT
  13h/02h.  A failing read shows a nonzero AH and names the problem.
  That build is what proved the 86Box floppy was an EMPTY DRIVE rather
  than a bug in the thunk, and this is the same question again: an
  emulator that cannot fail the way the hardware fails cannot be asked
  about it.

STILL NOT REPRODUCED: the QCONFIG crash itself.  MSD is the nearest
thing available here and it does not fault.  The fault line QCONFIG
printed on the 486 would settle it - the EIP maps straight through the
build's .lst files - and until then the three fixes above are the
honest account of what WAS found, not a claim to have found that.

v0.33 - NATIVE PROGRAMS RUN AT RING 3 (2026-08-14)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
The release the roadmap has been pointing at since v0.30, taken up
after the 486 confirmed everything v0.32 and v0.32b owed it: C: mounts
off an MS-DOS-formatted 850MB disk, the floppy light goes out, CRASH /N
fires the null guard, and QCONFIG runs.  DOS\RING3.INC is the new file
and the argument is in its head comment.

WHAT WAS WRONG WITH RING 0.  A D32 program ran in the kernel's own
code segment at the kernel's own privilege.  Everything worked and
nothing was protected: a program's wild pointer and the kernel's were
the same event, its bugs and the kernel's arrived at the same handler,
and the recovery v0.30 built could only ever be a best effort - the
program might have scribbled on the kernel before it faulted and there
was no way from inside to know.  The least protected thing in PM-DOS
was PM-DOS's own software.

A SLOT IS A SEGMENT NOW.  Two GDT descriptors, DPL 3, based at the
running slot with a limit of its size, rewritten by EXEC.  A program
can address its own slot and nothing else in the machine - not the
kernel, not the interrupt vector table, not the arena, not the other
slot.  There is no address it can form that names any of them.

AND ITS ADDRESS ZERO IS A PAGE THAT IS NOT THERE, which is the real
null-pointer guard and the one v0.31 could not build.  Page zero of
the MACHINE is load-bearing - the IVT, the BIOS data area, InDOS at
4F7h, the real-mode frame at 500h - so it could not be unmapped, and
four debug registers watching sixteen bytes for writes were what was
left.  Page zero of a PROGRAM is nothing at all.  Two cleared bits in
pg_init, and a null store is now an ordinary page fault at a known
address: any width, any offset within the page, reads as well as
writes.  It can also be TESTED HERE, which the DR7 guard never could
be on either emulator.  The debug registers stay armed and now guard
what they are the right size for - the kernel's own null pointers.

THE LAYOUT IS THE SAME IN BOTH SLOTS, so one linked image runs as the
interpreter or as a transient program: guard page at 0, PSP at 1000h,
the environment behind it, image at 2000h, stack at the top.  Every
D32 program is linked for offset 2000h now and COMMAND's
SHELL_PSP+PSP_TAIL and MEM's PROG_PSP+PSP_TAIL have become the same
constant.  D32H_BASE and D32H_ENTRY are slot offsets; D32H_STACK,
informational for eight releases, is load-bearing at last - it divides
what is above the BSS between the stack and the heap.

THE THREE THINGS THE RELEASE HAD TO PAY FOR, and each of them is the
same bill: a pointer nobody can follow is worse than no pointer.

  48h ALLOCATES INSIDE THE SLOT.  The kernel's arena is above 2MB and
  a program cannot see it, so an address out of it would fault the
  first time it was used - and the program would carry it around until
  the damage was somewhere else.  A small first-fit heap lives between
  the BSS and the stack reservation, with the arena's own header
  format because two block formats in one kernel is one too many.
  That is also what DOS did: a .COM owned its segment and allocated
  from inside it, which is why 4Ah "shrink yourself" ever existed.  It
  parks correctly too - a nested program's heap travels in the park
  copy and needs neither an owner nor a sweep.

  THE ENVIRONMENT IS COPIED INTO THE CHILD rather than pointed at,
  because a child cannot reach its parent's slot.  The VDM has done
  exactly this for a 16-bit guest since v0.25 and for exactly this
  reason.  Note the copy is taken into KERNEL memory at the top of
  4Bh, beside the path and the tail and for the same reason: for a
  nested EXEC the parent's memory is the slot about to be overwritten.

  MEM.EXE ASKS INSTEAD OF READING.  It walked both arenas itself - the
  kernel's from the pointer 52h hands out, the conventional one where
  it lies below 1MB - which is what MEM did under real DOS and worked
  here for the same reason: one address space.  New call 21h/F1h AL=8
  answers one block of one arena by INDEX, in a record that does not
  depend on which arena it came from.  This is the v0.19 lesson one
  level deeper: a report that has to reach inside the kernel is a
  report proving the kernel has no way to ask.  Walking by index
  rather than by chain is the other half - a damaged chain now stops
  the kernel's walk instead of spinning the caller's.

AN INTERRUPT GATE CANNOT REACH RING 3, and that is the piece of this
release with no precedent in it.  A program hooks INT 23h and INT 24h
with the ordinary 25h call, and until now the handler was just an
address in an IDT gate, because a program's code and the kernel's were
the same code at the same privilege.  `int 24h` from inside the disk
layer cannot arrive at a handler that lives in a program: control does
not travel outward through a gate.

  So a hooked vector gets a KERNEL stub, the offset is remembered, and
  the stub does what everything else that enters ring 3 does - builds
  a frame and IRETDs.  The way BACK is two bytes at PSP+54h: the
  handler ends in the IRET its specification demands, that IRET
  returns to a bare INT 21h, and the kernel recognises the call by the
  EIP it arrives from.  DPMI's real-mode callbacks solve the identical
  problem the identical way, and the reason the trampoline carries NO
  function number is the same one: by then the registers are the
  handler's answer, and loading AX would destroy what the trampoline
  exists to carry.  int24_hand's existing `iretd` with the answer in
  EAX needed no change at all.

  A HANDLER BELONGS TO A SLOT, not just to an offset, and the case
  that proves it is the commonest critical error there is: a disk
  failing under a CHILD program, where the handler that has to answer
  is the interpreter's, one slot over.  So each hooked vector also
  records the EXEC depth it was installed at.  Same depth, run it
  where we are; depth 0 while a child runs, switch the descriptors to
  the shell's slot and run it on the shell's own stack, exactly where
  the shell was when it called EXEC - which is where DOS ran one.  Any
  OTHER depth is refused, and the refusal is the honest answer rather
  than a cautious one: nesting is done by PARKING the occupant, so a
  program at depth 1 with a child running has had its code copied into
  the arena and overwritten.  There is nothing at that offset to call.
  THE RING-0 BUILD HAD THE SAME HOLE AND NO WAY TO NOTICE IT - it
  would have jumped into whatever the child had at that address.

  Only six vectors get a stub - 1Bh, 1Ch, 22h, 23h, 24h and 28h, the
  ones DOS raises INTO a program.  Any other vector a program sets is
  remembered so that 35h answers what 25h stored, and no gate is
  installed: hooking the keyboard interrupt from a program is the
  thing this release exists to stop, and a program that tries has not
  been lied to, it has been ignored.

  WHAT A REFUSED CALL-OUT ANSWERS IS "FAIL", explicitly.  Returning
  with the registers untouched looks harmless and is not: crit_raise
  masks EAX to two bits and would have taken the drive number it
  passed IN as the answer, which is a coin toss between retrying for
  ever and terminating the program.

NO TAG IS NEEDED TO TELL THE TWO KINDS OF HANDLER ADDRESS APART, and
that fell out rather than being designed: a program's handler is an
offset in its own slot and every kernel address is above 1MB, so the
ranges cannot overlap.  One rule - below the slot size means the
program's, anything else means a kernel address being put back -
serves 25h, 35h, the PSP save, the PSP restore and the kernel's own
installation.  A vector that went in one way and came out another is
how a restored handler ends up pointing at nothing.

POINTER TRANSLATION IS THE BRIDGE'S OWN TABLE, read by a third caller
now: a native program's pointers are offsets, which is the same
question with a different arrow.  Two things about it are worth
keeping:

  IT SUBTRACTS RATHER THAN REMEMBERING THE ORIGINALS.  The DPMI host
  keeps copies because a selector:offset pair cannot be recovered from
  a flat address; here the conversion is one addition.  A register is
  put back only if it still holds what the call put there, so a
  handler that answered in one of them keeps its answer.

  WHICH REGISTERS, THOUGH, HAS TO BE REMEMBERED, and that is not the
  same thing.  r3_pflags reads the function out of AH and by the time
  a call returns AH is the ANSWER - the trap vdm_result's comment
  describes, arrived at from the other side.  It is kept per (EXEC
  depth, handler depth) pair, because these calls nest two ways: a
  critical error runs a handler that makes DOS calls of its own, and a
  program that EXECs another leaves its own call open for the whole of
  the child's life.  Nothing has to unwind it - the next call at that
  level writes over it.

  38h AND 65h ARE NOT IN THE TABLE AND CANNOT BE, and they are not in
  it for the DOS box either: 38h's DS:DX is a sentinel when DX is
  FFFFh, and 65h's subfunctions disagree about which register holds
  the pointer.  The bridge answers both by hand in vdm_country and
  vdm_ctryext; the ring-3 path answers them the same way, in
  r3_pflags, rather than growing a table row that would have to be
  wrong for one of the cases.

CLI, STI, IN AND OUT STILL WORK, and are not privileges: they fault
into pm3_fault and are emulated there, exactly as they are for a DPMI
client.  IOPL stays 0 because that is what keeps the A20 ports out of
a program's hands, and the interrupt flag a program believes in has to
be a fiction or a program could stop the machine's timer.  The only
thing pm3_fault needed was the arrow from a selector to a base for
GDT selectors as well as LDT ones; the six emulated cases are
untouched.

A FAULT NOW SAYS SOMETHING IT COULD NOT SAY BEFORE.  v0.30's recovery
was honest about being a best effort - the program had had the run of
the machine right up to the instant it faulted.  This one is contained
by construction, so the report can say the program is gone and nothing
else is affected, and mean it.  IOS_EXCHOOK stays, for the case it was
always really about: a fault in the kernel itself.

TESTS.  TOOLS\R3TEST.ASM, fourteen checks: the ring it is running at
and the selectors it holds, the PSP where it should be and the parent
field that says it cannot be reached, the DTA in the program's own
terms both ways, a null pointer and an out-of-range offset REFUSED by
DOS rather than followed, 48h allocating inside the slot and the
memory it hands back working and freeing and coming back, 25h/35h
round-tripping a handler of ours AND a kernel address put back, and -
the one that exercises the whole call-out - a critical error on B:
reaching a handler at ring 3 whose answer reaches the kernel.  CRASH
gained /K, which reads the kernel and used to succeed.

THREE BUGS THAT ONLY RUNNING IT COULD FIND, and all three were in the
new machinery rather than in anything it touched.  It assembled clean,
it had been desk-checked instruction by instruction - including reading
the generated bytes of r3_enter out of PMDOS.SYS to confirm the segment
loads and the IRETD frame - and it was still wrong three times.

  NT WAS SET, SO THE IRETD WAS A TASK SWITCH.  Exception 0Ah, error
  code 0, at the IRETD in r3_enter: with NT set, IRET follows the
  back-link at the front of the TSS, finds the zero there and raises
  invalid-TSS.  This is the SECOND time this project has met that
  instruction wearing the other hat - the first was the IRETD that
  should have entered V86 mode, on the VDM's first evening, and
  v86_run has cleared NT ever since.  The bit is never set on purpose;
  it comes from whatever the BIOS left in FLAGS.
    WHAT MADE IT WORSE THAN IT LOOKS: taking an interrupt gate is
  itself what clears NT, so the FIRST entry to ring 3 faulted, the
  recovery ran, and the SECOND entry worked.  The machine came up to a
  prompt with one exception printed above it.  A bug that fixes itself
  after one failure is a bug that gets shipped.

  A CHILD'S FIRST DOS CALL LANDED ON ITS PARENT'S FRAME.  Programs
  used to run at ring 0 and the kernel ran their DOS calls on their own
  stacks - so a parent's open 4Bh frame lived in the parent's slot,
  where a child could not reach it.  At ring 3 there is ONE kernel
  stack for every program, and r3_start reset it to the top: the
  child's first INT 21h frame was written exactly over the 4Bh frame
  its parent was waiting in, and 4Ch then returned the parent to a
  frame full of the child's DOS call.  The shell resumed in the middle
  of its own message table.  The ring-0 stack now DESCENDS with the
  nesting - 4Bh moves it below the caller's frame and records the old
  level in XN_ESP0 for 4Ch to put back.
    It presented as "every child program's exit crashes the shell",
  which sounds like the exit path and was nothing of the kind.  What
  found it was mapping the faulting EIP through the .lst symbol table:
  both faults were in COMMAND's data, and code faulting in a message
  table is not code that arrived there on purpose.

  RING-3 CODE WAS RESUMED WITH THE KERNEL'S DATA SELECTORS.  #GP with
  error code 0 at a perfectly correct instruction, which is what a
  NULL DS looks like.  exc_common replaces all four segment registers
  with the kernel's to be able to run at all, and pm3_fault - which
  emulates CLI, STI, IN and OUT and then RESUMES the faulting code -
  IRETDs back without putting them back.  An inter-privilege IRET
  nulls every data selector whose DPL is too low, so the client came
  back holding four nulls and died on its next memory reference.
    THIS BUG WAS OLDER THAN THE RELEASE.  A DPMI client executing CLI
  or STI had exactly the same fate, and nothing had ever done it:
  DPMITEST does descriptors, memory, DOS calls and callbacks, and
  never a privileged instruction.  It took COMMAND's break handler,
  which does STI on its way home, and it took a ^C to get there.

VERIFIED, 2026-08-15, 86Box (P-II/440BX, real ATA, FAT16) and DOSBox
0.74 (FAT12 floppy):
  - boots to a prompt with the interpreter at ring 3, AUTOEXEC and all
  - R3TEST 14 of 14, twice, exiting cleanly both times
  - CRASH /K: exception 0Dh.  The read of the kernel does not happen -
    no value is printed, because the instruction never completes.
    THAT READ SUCCEEDED IN EVERY RELEASE BEFORE THIS ONE
  - CRASH /N: exception 0Eh with err 06 and the null-pointer line, on
    BOTH emulators.  The guard v0.31 could not exercise anywhere is
    now exercised everywhere
  - CRASHTST: all five faults caught, errorlevel 255 each, the batch
    file running throughout, DIR and VER working afterwards
  - ^C at a PAUSE inside a batch file: the batch aborts, the prompt
    returns, and the interpreter does NOT reload - which is the whole
    ring-3 call-out, including the handler that never returns
  - VDMTEST end to end, DPMITEST included: the DOS box, the bridge and
    a ring-3 DPMI client all still work with a ring-3 shell above them
  - APITEST, LOLTEST, NULTEST, BATTEST, REDTEST, CMDTEST, LFNTEST,
    DISKTEST (multi-volume), NESTTEST (free memory identical either
    side), and DIR | SORT | MORE through two native programs
  - MEM through the new enumeration call, totals adding up

AND ONE THING THE TWO EMULATORS DISAGREE ABOUT, which is worth more
than the tests they agree on: CRASH /K faults on 86Box and does NOT
fault on DOSBox, where it returns zero and prints "it did not fault -
nothing was tested".  DOSBox does not enforce the segment limit.  It is
not reading the kernel either - the base saves it - but it would have
let a program walk off the end of its slot without a word.  86Box is
the one telling the truth here, and this is the standing rule arrived
at from the other direction: develop against 86Box, regression-check on
DOSBox, and when they differ do not average them.

v0.32b - THE NULL GUARD'S FIRST FIRING WAS A FALSE POSITIVE
