    orphaned fragments the way plain-DOS deletes on Win95 disks did.
  - Creation stays 8.3: 3Ch (fresh entry), 39h, 56h destination
    refuse a lossy final component until phase 2 writes chains.
    3Ch onto an EXISTING long-named file truncates in place though -
    that needs no new name and works today.
  - DIR walks 714Eh/714Fh now and prints the long name in a right-
    hand column when an entry has one - the Win95 look.  The label
    line and the directory-probe stay classic 4Eh.
  - VOL fix folded in structurally: LFN fragments are peeled off
    before the label test can see them, so a fragment can no longer
    print as 13 bytes of UCS-2 garbage pretending to be the label.
  - MKDISK plants an LFN test set (the C code is the reference for
    the phase-2 assembly: checksum, fragment layout, FFFF padding):
    two long-named files and, on the floppy, a long-named directory
    with a nested file.  The HD test files crosslink onto the last
    real file's chain - no new cluster machinery for a read test.
  - Verified in DOSBox (floppy AND FAT32 hard disk) and 86Box
    (FAT16 over ATA): DIR's long column on all three; TYPE by alias,
    by spaceless long name, by long name WITH spaces (TYPE takes its
    whole tail as the path, so no quoting needed); TYPE through a
    long-named directory component; CD into one and back, prompt
    canonicalized; all-lowercase typing matching mixed-case names;
    VER 0.11; REDTEST regression green throughout.

v0.10: redirection and pipes.
  - The kernel half is 21h/45h (DUP) and 46h (FORCEDUP), plus one
    structural change that is the actual mechanism: the CP/M-era
    console functions (01h 02h 06h-0Ch) no longer talk to the screen
    and keyboard - they go through HANDLES 0 and 1.  That is what
    real DOS does, and it is the entire trick of redirection: point
    handle 1 at a file and every 02h and 09h in every program lands
    in the file, with the program none the wiser.  std_in/std_out/
    std_write in INT21.INC are that routing; a device slot goes to
    IOS_CONIN/CONOUT exactly as before, so an unredirected system
    runs the same instructions it always did.
  - Handles are global-table slots here, so DUP cannot be DOS's
    shared-SFT-entry refcount.  It is a full COPY of the slot: the
    pair track the file independently afterwards.  Less than DOS
    promises, but redirection only ever uses DUP to PARK a standard
    handle while 46h lends the slot out, and a parked handle is not
    used - so the difference cannot be observed from where we stand.
    Revisit if JFT-per-PSP ever becomes real.
  - COMMAND's half is CMD\REDIR.INC: exec_line became a layer that
    peels < file, > file, >> file and | off the line (compacting it
    in place) before exec_core ever parses the verb.  Setup is the
    classic sequence: open/create the target, 45h to park the real
    handle 0 or 1 in a spare slot, 46h to install the file over it,
    close the opening handle.  Restore is 46h back the other way -
    and THAT close is what flushes the file and writes its directory
    entry.  The parked handles live on the exec stack, not statics:
    IF and FOR re-enter exec_line, and an inner run must not disturb
    an outer restore.
  - Tokens are stripped at the OUTERMOST level of a line, which is
    DOS's own ordering with DOS's own consequences, both verified:
    a false IF still creates its empty > target, and FOR's
    iterations all land in ONE open file rather than each reopening
    and truncating it.  Redirecting a .BAT invocation redirects only
    the launch, not the lines that later run from its frame - also
    what MS-DOS does.
  - Pipes are DOS pipes: sequential, through %PIPE1.$$$/%PIPE2.$$$
    in the current directory, alternating for multi-stage lines,
    deleted when the line is done.  Nothing runs concurrently;
    nothing ever did in DOS either.  ECHO Y | CHOICE /C:YN works
    end to end - CHOICE polls 06h and blocks on 08h, both of which
    now read the pipe file through handle 0.
  - 09h to a redirected stdout writes the whole '$' string as ONE
    block, because file_wchunk writes its cluster through on every
    call and DIR at a cluster write per character would be felt on
    real iron.  02h stays per-character write-through - correct
    first; a stdout buffer is future work if it ever matters.
  - EXIT > FILE ends the shell INSIDE the redirected run, so the
    restore never happens.  fn4C's shell path now closes whatever
    the standard slots hold (flushing that file) and re-marks them
    as CON before reloading the interpreter; the parked copies were
    shell-owned and go in the ordinary owner sweep.
  - TYPE < FILE answers "Required parameter missing" - authentic:
    TYPE takes its name from the command line and does not read
    stdin, in MS-DOS 6.22 just the same.  The input-redirection
    test that actually proves something is CHOICE < FILE.
  - wasm note: a dword access to a db-declared label needs an
    explicit size - "mov edx,[sft_tbl+SFT_POS]" is E039 until it
    says "dword ptr".  The EQU offset does not carry a size; the
    label's db does, and it wins.
  - COMMAND label prefixes rn_ rd_ pp_ el_ were already taken
    (RENAME, RD, put_prompt, exec_core's own lines) - REDIR.INC
    uses xl_ rdp_ rda_ rdr_ pip_ rx_.  With case-insensitive
    symbols, grep before you name.
  - Verified on all three platforms - DOSBox floppy (FAT12), DOSBox
    FAT32 hard disk, 86Box FAT16 over ATA: > >> creating and
    appending, DIR > FILE, CHOICE < FILE taking its answer from a
    file, ECHO Y | CHOICE, TYPE FILE | CHOICE, pipe temp files
    cleaned up, and VER reporting 0.10 from the kernel.

Renamed from DOS32 to PM-DOS on 2026-08-07, for Protected Mode DOS.
The tree is S:\CPP\PM-DOS, but the shared header, the floppy image and
the assembler identifiers are PMDOS.INC, PMDOS.IMG, PMDOS_DEBUG and
PMDOS_MAJOR/PMDOS_MINOR: a hyphen cannot appear in a symbol, and the
8.3 names read better without one.  The FAT OEM name and volume label
are "PM-DOS", which happened to fit the 8- and 11-byte fields exactly.
Re-verified after the rename: DOSBox 0.74 booting the floppy, the FAT16
hard disk and the FAT32 hard disk, and 86Box booting the FAT16 disk
over ATA - plus VER, DIR, VOL, and CHTEST.BAT running the external
CHOICE.COM and continuing afterwards.

v0.9: CONFIG.SYS, the first external command, and handle ownership.
  - CHOICE left COMMAND.COM and became CMD\CHOICE.ASM, a real
    external.  MS-DOS ships CHOICE.COM rather than building it in,
    and a command that needs no interpreter state has no business
    living in the shell.  It is also the first ordinary PM-DOS
    program: loaded into the transient slot by 21h/4Bh, arguments
    from the PSP command tail, exit through 21h/4Ch.
  - Making it external immediately exposed a real kernel bug.  PM-DOS
    has ONE global handle table and 4Ch closed every open handle in
    it, so a child terminating closed the SHELL's open batch file and
    the batch simply stopped after the first external command.  Every
    SFT entry now carries SFT_OWNER, stamped in sft_new - the single
    place a handle is ever claimed - and 4Ch closes only what the
    terminating PSP opened.  This is the JFT-per-PSP idea, minus the
    indirection: with one table, ownership has to be recorded
    somewhere, and pretending a shared table is private is how the
    bug happened.
  - DOS\CONFIG.INC processes CONFIG.SYS from the root of the boot
    drive, in the KERNEL, once, before the interpreter is loaded.
    That is the only place it can go: a SHELL= line decides which
    interpreter to load, so nothing running after the shell could
    honour it.  MS-DOS put this in IO.SYS for exactly the same
    reason.  The order falls out of it - CONFIG.SYS configures the
    system, the shell starts, the shell runs AUTOEXEC.BAT.
  - The file is read through our own INT 21h.  Everything in PM-DOS
    runs at ring 0 through one flat code selector, so an INT from
    kernel code builds the same frame a program's would: no stack
    switch, no special case, and no second copy of the file logic.
  - Statements are a table (cfg_table): a name and a handler taking
    ESI -> the value text.  Adding a statement is a row and a
    handler, with no second mechanism beside it.
  - EVERY statement a real DOS understands is recognised, and almost
    all of them do nothing.  The goal is compatibility: a CONFIG.SYS
    carried over from a real install must boot without a word of
    complaint, and a release build printing NOTHING for a full DOS
    CONFIG.SYS is the test.  Only an unrecognised statement is an
    error, which is what keeps a typo in a PM-DOS statement visible.
      SHELL=      real, and the one with teeth: replaces both the
                  interpreter path and its command tail.  Leaving
                  "/P" off is meaningful rather than a mistake - it
                  is how you get a shell that skips AUTOEXEC.BAT and
                  that EXIT can terminate.  shell_name and shell_tail
                  became buffers in DOSMAIN for this.
      BREAK=      remembered; nothing consults it until Ctrl-C exists
      REM, ;      comments; [blocks] are skipped, so a multi-config
                  file is read rather than rejected (every block is
                  read, none is chosen from - there is no menu yet)
      BUFFERS FILES LASTDRIVE FCBS STACKS COUNTRY SWITCHES NUMLOCK
      DOS DRIVPARM DEVICE DEVICEHIGH INSTALL INSTALLHIGH SET INCLUDE
      MENUITEM MENUDEFAULT MENUCOLOR SUBMENU COMMENT MULTITRACK
                  recognised, and doing nothing.  They describe
                  machinery PM-DOS does not have and mostly does not
                  want: it caches per volume rather than in BUFFERS,
                  has no FCBs, and is flat and unpaged, which makes
                  DOS=HIGH,UMB a statement about a memory model that
                  does not exist here.  A debug build lists them as
                  "(recognised, no effect)" so the silence is
                  checkable.
      anything else  "Unrecognized command in CONFIG.SYS", after
                  echoing the offending line.

    [DEVICE= and DEVICEHIGH= were in the inert list when this was
    written, "for now", and it says they will not stay.  They left it
    in v0.38: DEVICE= loads the driver it names (DEVLOAD.INC, v0.37)
    and DEVICEHIGH= loads it into upper memory (UMB.INC, v0.38).  DOS=
    left it in the same release and is now the statement that decides
    whether there IS any upper memory.  What is left in the list is
    genuinely inert and mostly always will be - BUFFERS and FCBS and
    STACKS describe machinery this kernel does not have.]

  - PM-DOS's own statements, parsed and RECORDED but not acted on -
    there is no paging subsystem yet, so paging_on / swap_kb /
    swap_perm are the settings, not the state.  The statement that
    turns a feature on is worth having before the feature does,
    rather than being retrofitted around it afterwards:

    [SUPERSEDED in v0.19: both statements are REMOVED.  The reasoning
    below was sound about swap files and wrong about CONFIG.SYS - a
    statement that accepts a setting nothing will ever read is a
    promise, not a record.  Kept here because it is the argument that
    v0.19 answers.]

      PAGING=ON|OFF
      SWAPFILESIZE=kilobytes[,PERMANENT|TEMPORARY]

    A permanent swap file is allocated once and kept - the
    386SPART.PAR idea, and the only way to guarantee the space is
    contiguous and actually there.  A temporary one is created at
    boot and deleted at shutdown, which is friendlier to a shared
    disk; it is the default, being the one that cannot strand disk
    space if the machine never comes back.  SWAPFILESIZE=0 is
    rejected rather than treated as OFF - that is what PAGING=OFF is
    for, and a size of zero is far more likely to be a mistake.
    Nothing is committed until the whole statement has parsed, so a
    bad qualifier cannot leave a size behind from a rejected line.
    A debug build reports the settled configuration.
  - TOOLS\MKDISK.C: the FAT32 root directory is now a real cluster
    CHAIN rather than a single cluster.  One cluster held spc*16 = 16
    entries, which a boot disk outgrows immediately (it did, mid-
    build).  Allocated contiguously from cluster 2 so a directory
    entry's byte offset still maps straight onto datalba.

  Verified in DOSBox 0.74 (floppy) and on 86Box (hard disk, ATA): a
  full DOS CONFIG.SYS - the whole inherited set plus multi-config
  blocks - processed in complete silence, with a lone typo the only
  thing reported; PAGING and SWAPFILESIZE parsed and recorded, both
  qualifiers and the unqualified default, with four bad parameter
  forms each rejected and nothing left behind by them; SHELL= without
  /P suppressing AUTOEXEC.BAT AND re-enabling EXIT; SHELL= naming a
  missing file giving "Bad or missing command interpreter";
  CHOICE.COM run from the prompt and from a batch file, with the
  batch CONTINUING afterwards and ERRORLEVEL arriving through the
  genuine 4Bh/4Dh path; FAT32 booting with a 14-entry root,
  fragmented and not.

v0.8: batch files, and a VER that tells the truth.
  - VER now asks the KERNEL what version the system is, through a new
    21h/F1h.  30h has to go on claiming DOS 5 so that ordinary
    programs recognise us, which left nothing there to report what
    IBMDOS.SYS actually is; and COMMAND.COM reporting its own number
    was answering a different question from the one asked.  They are
    separately built binaries and can differ, so when they do, VER
    says so on a second line.
  - CMD\BATCH.INC is the batch interpreter, to MS-DOS 6.22 parity:
    @, ECHO/ECHO., REM, PAUSE, :labels and GOTO, IF with ERRORLEVEL /
    EXIST / str1==str2 / NOT, FOR %v IN (set) DO (wildcards in the set
    expand), SHIFT, CALL, CHOICE, CTTY, %0-%9 and %VAR% substitution,
    and AUTOEXEC.BAT at startup.
  - The read-eval loop was split into get_line and exec_line.  That is
    the whole structural change: get_line takes a line from the batch
    file or the keyboard indifferently, and exec_line runs one command
    from anywhere - which is what lets IF and FOR feed a line straight
    back in, and CALL run a whole file, without a second parser.
  - A batch file's state is a frame: handle, file position, and its
    arguments.  The file POSITION is the program counter, so GOTO is
    just a store to it after a scan from the top - which is why a
    batch file can jump backwards as freely as forwards, and why the
    :ARGLOOP / SHIFT / GOTO ARGLOOP idiom works.
  - CALL stacks a frame; running a batch file WITHOUT call replaces
    the current one and never returns.  That difference is the entire
    reason CALL had to be invented, so both behaviours are real here
    rather than CALL being a synonym.
  - Every argument is kept, not just ten, and SHIFT moves a window
    over them.  MS-DOS lets SHIFT reach an eleventh argument that %9
    could never name, and sliding a ten-entry array down would have
    quietly thrown it away.
  - The kernel starts the shell with a "/P" tail, exactly as
    CONFIG.SYS's SHELL= line did.  It means run AUTOEXEC.BAT, and it
    means ignore EXIT - the permanent shell has nothing underneath it
    to go back to, which is what MS-DOS does too.
  - COMMAND keeps its OWN copy of the last exit code.  21h/4Dh clears
    the code as it reads it, but a run of consecutive IF ERRORLEVEL
    lines - the entire idiom - has to see the same number each time.
  - ECHO measures its text from one delimiter past the verb, not from
    the first non-blank, because batch files indent their output with
    leading spaces and eating them is not a kindness.

  Not at parity, and why: CTTY accepts CON and refuses anything else,
  because there is no device chain to move the console onto yet (it
  says so rather than pretending).  [STALE as of v0.41: the chain
  arrived in v0.37 and CTTY moves the console onto anything on it.
  The rest of this paragraph was overtaken release by release too -
  Ctrl-C in v0.22, redirection and pipes in v0.25 - and it is left
  standing because it is what the parity list looked like at v0.21.]
  CHOICE is internal here; in 6.22
  it is CHOICE.COM, an external, and PM-DOS has no external command set
  to put it in yet.  There is no Ctrl-C, so no "Terminate batch job
  (Y/N)?" prompt.  Redirection and pipes are not implemented anywhere
  in COMMAND yet, batch or otherwise.

  Verified in DOSBox 0.74 (floppy, BIOS path) and on 86Box (hard disk,
  ATA path), with the same results on both: AUTOEXEC.BAT runs at boot;
  argument and environment substitution; forward and backward GOTO;
  the label-not-found case ending the file; IF in all three forms and
  negated; FOR over a list and over a wildcard, from a batch file and
  from the prompt; SHIFT reaching a twelfth argument; CALL returning
  and recursing; chaining NOT returning; CHOICE setting ERRORLEVEL for
  IF to read; and EXIT ignored by the permanent shell.  DISK\*.BAT are
  the test files and are written onto both the floppy and hard-disk
  images.

v0.7: an IDE/ATA driver, with the BIOS kept as a fallback.
  - IO\ATA.INC talks to the drive controller directly from protected
    mode.  That removes, per request: a switch to real mode, a PIC
    reprogram to 08h/70h, the INT 13h call, a reprogram back to
    50h/58h and a switch home - plus the XFER_BUF bounce and its
    16-sector chunking, because PIO reads land straight in the
    caller's flat 32-bit buffer.
  - Detection is by IDENTIFY DEVICE across both channels, master and
    slave.  Anything that does not answer is left to BLOCK.INC's BIOS
    path, which is what keeps DOSBox 0.74 - no IDE controller at all -
    working unchanged.  blk_read/blk_write ask ata_owns FIRST, so a
    genuine ATA failure is reported as a failure rather than being
    mistaken for "ask the BIOS instead".
  - LBA28/LBA48 when the drive offers it, plain CHS when it does not.
    CHS is not legacy decoration: the drive 86Box presents reports no
    LBA at all, and neither do real pre-1994 disks - which are
    squarely PM-DOS's target.
  - Interrupts are suppressed at the drive (nIEN) and transfers are
    polled, so no IRQ 14/15 handlers are needed.
  - BUILD ata builds with the probe tracing: a stage letter per slot,
    the IDENTIFY geometry, and an LBA 0 read-back self-test.

  Verified on 86Box (Pentium II / 440BX / PIIX4 IDE): boots to C:\>
  through the driver, MD/COPY/TYPE work, and the writes were then
  confirmed present in the raw image file on the host.  DOSBox 0.74
  still boots and does cross-drive copies on the BIOS path.

v0.6: a FAT-walking loader, and a FAT32 boot sector.
  - BOOT\FATLOAD.INC is one real-mode FAT12/16/32 file loader, shared
    by the hard-disk stage 2 (which loads IBMIO.SYS) and by IBMIO
    itself (which loads IBMDOS.SYS).  It finds a file by name in the
    root - fixed area or FAT32 root chain, whichever the volume has -
    and follows its cluster chain.  NOTHING has to be contiguous any
    more, on any filesystem.
  - The FAT is windowed TWO sectors at a time.  Two rather than one
    because a FAT12 entry can straddle a sector boundary: with the
    next sector already in the buffer, the word read at offset 511
    simply spills into it and needs no special case at all.  The
    same window then serves FAT16 and FAT32 unchanged.
  - The volume boot record became STAGE 1 and does nothing but read
    stage 2 out of the partition's reserved sectors and jump to it.
    This is not a shortcut, it is arithmetic: a FAT32 VBR has 420
    bytes left after its 5Ah-byte BPB, and the walker measured 690.
    Microsoft hit the same wall and put their FAT32 boot record's
    continuation in sector 2 of the reserved area.  Stage 2 lives in
    reserved sectors rather than in a file so that nothing has to be
    found before the FAT walker exists.
  - BOOT\BOOTHD.ASM assembles twice - plain for FAT16 (code at 3Eh,
    stage 2 at reserved sector 1, rsvd raised to 9) and with
    -dFAT32BOOT for FAT32 (code at 5Ah, stage 2 at reserved sector 9,
    clear of FSInfo at 1 and the backup boot sector at 6).  Stage 2
    (BOOT\BOOT2.ASM) is ONE binary for both: FATLOAD works the FAT
    width out from the cluster count at run time.
  - IBMIO's load_dos is now ~60 lines around the same include, and
    handles FAT12/16/32 identically; the old hand-rolled FAT12 chain
    walk and its contiguous-FAT16 special case are gone.
  - MKDISK grew -s2 (install stage 2), FAT32 -vbr (splicing at 5Ah
    instead of 3Eh), and -frag, which deliberately scatters every
    file across ALTERNATE clusters.  MKHD.CMD frag builds such a
    disk; a loader that reads straight through cannot survive it.

  Verified in DOSBox: FAT16 and FAT32 hard disks both boot to C:\>
  with no floppy attached; both still boot when built with -frag, so
  the walker is genuinely following 2 -> 4 -> 6 -> 8 chains; the
  floppy still boots (its FAT12 chain now goes through the shared
  loader too); and from a FAT32 boot, a FAT16 second disk mounts,
  reads and takes cross-drive copies.

v0.5: booting from a hard disk.
  - BOOT\MBRBOOT.ASM: a real master boot record.  Relocates itself to
    0060:0000 (so the volume boot record can load at 7C00 where it
    expects to be), finds the active partition entry, reads its first
    sector with the CHS values from the entry itself, and chains to it.
  - BOOT\BOOT16.ASM: a FAT16 volume boot record.  It does NOT walk the
    FAT - a FAT16 FAT is up to 128 sectors and there is nowhere in low
    memory to put it - so it finds IBMIO.SYS in the root directory by
    name and reads it CONTIGUOUSLY from its start cluster.  MKDISK
    writes files sequentially into a freshly formatted image, so that
    holds by construction; it is the same bargain IO.SYS always made.
    Full CHS packing (cylinder bits 8-9 into CL bits 6-7) and the
    partition's hidden-sector count folded into every LBA.
  - IBMIO's load_dos grew a hard-disk path on the same terms: for
    drives 80h+ it reads IBMDOS.SYS contiguously in XFER_SIZE chunks
    instead of walking a FAT12 chain, and every LBA now includes the
    BPB's hidden-sector count.  Floppies keep the FAT12 chain walk.
  - MKDISK: -mbr <file> and -vbr <file> install boot code into a hard
    disk image (the MBR's first 1BEh bytes; the VBR's jump plus its
    code from 3Eh up, so the BPB stays MKDISK's), mark the partition
    active, write a real CHS end field, add a volume label entry, and
    flag the first two files System+Hidden+ReadOnly.  MKHD.CMD now
    builds HD16.IMG bootable, with the system files on it.
  - 4Eh/4Fh finally honour the DOS attribute rule: hidden and system
    files stay out of a directory search unless asked for, so DIR no
    longer lists IBMIO.SYS and IBMDOS.SYS.  Lookups by name (open,
    exec, path walking) are unaffected - they pass srch_attr without
    the internal SRCH_FILTER bit and still see everything.

  Verified in DOSBox: "boot -l c" reaches C:\> with no floppy present
  at all; MD/CD/COPY/TYPE on the boot volume; EXIT reloads
  C:\COMMAND.COM; A: and D: still mount and take cross-drive copies;
  and a later floppy boot reads back what the hard-disk boot wrote.

v0.4: per-drive state and quiet release boots.
  - Every drive (A: B: C: D:) keeps its own live volume: the mount
    state, FAT caches (dirty flags included) and current directory
    live in a single vol_state block that vol_select swaps in and out
    of per-drive slots (vol_slots, 4 x 8872 bytes inside IBMDOS.SYS).
    Caches keyed by absolute LBA / cluster number (sec_buf, clus_buf,
    the dir-walk cache) are invalidated on a swap instead of saved -
    two disks can answer to the same LBA.  A parked volume's dirty
    FAT sectors are NOT flushed by the swap; they come back exactly
    as they were, the same as if no switch had happened.
  - resolve_core maps a "C:" prefix (or its absence, meaning the
    default drive) through vol_select, mounting on first touch and
    retrying failed mounts, so a path reaches the right disk no
    matter where you stand.  cwd is per volume: CD C:\WORK from A:
    changes where C: will land when you switch to it.
  - The SFT grew a drive field (SFT_DRIVE, SFT_LEN now 40).  Opens
    and creates stamp it; reads, writes and closes vol_select it
    first.  COPY A:\X C:\Y therefore just works - the two handles
    pull the volumes back and forth per chunk, dirty caches and all
    (verified with a 64K file A: -> C: -> D:, byte-identical).
  - 56h rename refuses to cross volumes (ERR_NOTSAME, 11h) - a
    rename never copies data.  36h and 47h take the drive in DL
    (0 = default, 1 = A:) like real DOS.  0Eh mounts before it
    adopts, so a dead drive leaves the default alone.
  - The shell reload path is "X:\COMMAND.COM" with the boot drive
    letter patched in at startup - EXIT on D: still finds it.
  - Release builds boot like the real thing: ONE line, "Starting
    PM-DOS...", and nothing else.  As of 0.29 the two that came before
    it are gone - the boot sector's "PM-DOS loading... ok" and PMIO's
    real-mode copy of the banner - because con_init clears the screen
    the moment protected mode is entered, so both were lines the user
    watched scroll away.  COMMAND.COM's banner went with them: it is
    printed by cmd_entry, which runs again on every reload of the
    shell slot, so it appeared on every EXIT as well as at boot.  VER
    reports the version, which is where a version belongs.  BUILD.CMD
    debug (-dPMDOS_DEBUG) brings back the stub and kernel banners and
    the mount messages.  Errors print in both: a boot sector that
    fails, or a machine that never reaches protected mode, still has
    its own voice.
  - COMMAND: DIR/VOL take a drive argument for the label, free-space
    and header lines ("Directory of C:\..." now names the LISTED
    drive and its cwd); put_cwd passes DL=0 explicitly - 47h reads
    DL now, and a stale register there is an invalid-drive error.

v0.3: subdirectories and FAT16/FAT32.
  - FAT.INC rewritten for all three FAT widths.  Cluster numbers are
    32-bit everywhere.  FAT12 keeps its whole-FAT cache (entries
    straddle sectors); FAT16/32 go through a one-sector FAT cache
    with lazy write-back to every copy (fatsec_buf).
  - Directories are enumerated through a context (dc_isroot/dc_start)
    that hides "fixed FAT12/16 root area" vs "cluster chain" (subdirs
    everywhere, and the FAT32 root).  dir_seek caches its chain walk;
    chain directories grow a zeroed cluster when they fill.
  - PATH.INC: paths normalize into an array of 8.3 components
    (absolute vs cwd-relative, "." / ".." folded), then walk from the
    root.  resolve_parent / resolve_dir / cwd_install / cwd_string.
    Current directory is per-mount, reset on drive change.
  - New INT 21h: 39h MKDIR (builds "." / ".." dot entries), 3Ah RMDIR
    (empty check, refuses the cwd), 3Bh CHDIR, real 47h.  4Eh/4Fh
    carry the searched directory in the DTA (start dd at +0Fh, isroot
    at +13h).  56h can move files between directories (directories
    rename in place only - moving one would orphan its "..").  0Eh
    accepts A: B: C: D: and falls back to the old volume if the new
    one will not mount.
  - Drives 80h+ read an MBR and mount the first used partition.
    FAT type is picked by cluster count (the MS rule), not the label.
  - COMMAND.COM: MD/CD/RD wired to 39h/3Bh/3Ah, CD alone prints the
    cwd, $P renders the real path, DIR of a directory name lists its
    contents (arg + "\*.*"), DEL glues the argument's directory part
    onto the names findfirst returns, volume labels looked up with
    an absolute "\*.*".
  - MKDISK grew -hd16/-hd32 modes: MBR + formatted FAT16/FAT32
    hard-disk images (63 spt, 16 heads); MKHD.CMD builds the two
    test images and NOTES the imgmount lines.
  Verified in DOSBox on all three: nested MD/CD, COPY across dirs
  and drives' paths, TYPE, DEL with paths, RD guards, persistence
  across remounts.  One-volume-at-a-time still (no cross-drive COPY).

v0.2 (same day): the shell moved out of IBMDOS into a real external
COMMAND.COM, which required growing the kernel three ways:
  - D32 executable format + INT 21h/4Bh EXEC, PSP, program slots
    (see "Programs" below)
  - FAT12 WRITE support: 3Ch create/truncate, 40h file writes (and
    the CX=0 truncate-at-position rule), 41h delete, 56h rename,
    close-time directory/FAT flush
  - 2Bh/2Dh set date/time (RTC via the thunk), 4Eh/4Fh attribute
    filtering (CX=08h finds the volume label), AH=F0h console
    extension (AL=0 CLS, 1/2 get/set cursor)
CMD\COMMAND.ASM implements: BREAK CD CLS COPY DATE DEL DIR ECHO ERASE
EXIT MD MEM PATH PAUSE PROMPT RD REM REN RENAME SET TIME TYPE VER
VERIFY VOL, drive changes, $-code PROMPT rendering, a 1K environment
block, and EXEC fallback (VERB.COM then VERB.EXE) for externals.
MD/CD/RD print an honest "not supported yet" (no subdirectories).

Programs (the D32 format)
-------------------------
A D32 IMAGE is a memory image: a 32-byte header ('CD', INT 20h, a
version and a type byte, load base, entry, bss size, stack) followed
by the code; the loader streams the whole image to the base and
zeroes BSS after it.  A FILE is either that image and nothing else -
what the linker writes - or an MS-DOS .EXE with the image behind it
and the image's offset in the dword at 3Ch of its MZ header, which is
what TOOLS\D32BIND makes of every command that ships.  Real MS-DOS
runs the program in front: TOOLS\D32STUB.ASM, which says the file
needs 32-bit DOS mode and exits, or a 16-bit version of the program
itself.  See "'CD', AND AN MS-DOS PROGRAM IN FRONT OF EVERY COMMAND"
(2026-10-10) and, for what it replaced, v0.29.
WHERE A PROGRAM RUNS, as of 2026-10-01 (the paragraph that was here
described v0.2's two fixed slots and one level of EXEC).  At ring 3,
in a segment based at its SLOT: a guard page at 0, the PSP at 1000h,
the image at 2000h (SLOT_IMAGE) - so every native program is linked
at offset 2000h and its header's load base says so, whatever linear
address the slot is at.  The interpreter's slot is the fixed 256K at
140000h.  Every other program's is a block of the arena, 512K to
start with and grown by 48h when the heap runs short, one per nesting
level, EXEC_MAX (8) deep.  The PSP starts with INT 20h and a plain
RET still ends a program.  Tail at PSP+80h, DOS format.  Termination
closes and flushes every handle the program opened and frees what it
owned.  When the SHELL ends, the kernel loads it again from disk
("Bad or missing command interpreter" + retry if it cannot).

Two kernel files in the classic PC-DOS split, but the API runs in
32-bit flat protected mode:

  PMIO.SYS   hardware layer.  Real-mode stub (A20, memory sizing,
             loads PMDOS above 1M through unreal mode, enters
             protected mode) + 32-bit body (console at B8000h, PS/2
             keyboard, PIC, IDT, BIOS disk I/O through a PM->RM
             thunk).  Exports a flat call table at IOSVC, 200010h.
  PMDOS.SYS  DOS layer: the arena, FAT12/16/32 with long names,
             INT 21h, the DOS box and its XMS, EMS and DPMI, the
             disk cache.  (v0.1's was a read-only FAT12 driver, 28
             functions and a built-in shell.)  The shell is CMD.EXE,
             a program like any other.

Everything PMDOS knows about hardware goes through the PMIO service
table; the two binaries are linked independently.

Layout
------
  BOOT\BOOT.ASM     FAT12 floppy boot sector (CHS INT 13h).  Finds
                    PMIO.SYS in the root dir, loads it at 2000:0000.
  BOOT\MBRBOOT.ASM  master boot record: relocate, find the active
                    partition, chain to its boot sector.
  BOOT\BOOTHD.ASM   hard-disk volume boot record, stage 1.  Assembles
                    twice: FAT16, and FAT32 with -dFAT32BOOT.  Loads
                    stage 2 out of the reserved sectors.
  BOOT\BOOT2.ASM    hard-disk stage 2: loads PMIO.SYS by chain.
                    One binary for FAT16 and FAT32.
  BOOT\FATLOAD.INC  the shared real-mode FAT12/16/32 file loader,
                    included by BOOT2.ASM and by IO\IORM.ASM.
  IO\IORM.ASM       real-mode stub, first 8K of PMIO.SYS exactly.
                    Owns the GDT (offset C00h) and globals (F00h).
                    pm2rm thunk entry is at fixed offset 0010h.
                    Loaded at 2000:0000, relocates itself to 0B00:0000
                    and blits IOPM above 1MB before entering PM.
  IO\IOPM.ASM       32-bit body (+ EXCEPT/PAGING/NULLTRAP/VM86/CONSOLE
                    /KEYBD/RMCALL/ATA/BLOCK .INC), linked at 200000h
                    and concatenated after IORM - loaded low, run high.
  IO\NULLTRAP.INC   the null-pointer guard: four debug registers, not
                    a guard page.  The comment at the top is the
                    argument for why page zero cannot be unmapped in
                    a kernel that shares an address space with the
                    BIOS data area, InDOS and the real-mode IVT.  A
                    native program has had a real guard page since
                    v0.33 - the first page of its slot, taken out of
                    the map and put back by IOS_PGPRES.
  DOS\DOSMAIN.ASM   PMDOS.SYS (+ ARENA/FAT/INT21 .INC and the rest),
                    linked at 110000h, its _KBSS at 1C9000h.
  DOS\RING3.INC     native programs at ring 3: their descriptors, the
                    heap inside a slot, and the slots themselves -
                    slot_new, slot_grow, slot_trim, slot_free.
  DOS\CONFIG.INC    CONFIG.SYS: reader, parser and statement table.
                    Add PM-DOS's own statements to cfg_table.
  DOS\CACHE.INC     the disk cache, between disk_read/disk_write and
                    the drive.  Four-kilobyte blocks keyed by physical
                    drive and absolute LBA, lazy writing on fixed
                    disks only, memory taken from and given back to
                    the arena, and INT 2Fh AX=4A10h answered so that
                    no second cache loads on top of it.  The header is
                    the argument for all of that AND for the register
                    contract cache_io has to keep, which is the one
                    thing about this file that is not optional.
  CMD\CMD.ASM       CMD.EXE, the native shell: a D32 program linked
                    at 2000h like every other, run in the fixed slot
                    at 140000h.
  CMD\COMMAND\      COMMAND.COM, the 16-bit interpreter COMSPEC names,
                    for DOS programs that shell out.
  CMD\BATCH.INC     the batch interpreter: frames, line fetch and
                    substitution, GOTO/IF/FOR/SHIFT/CALL/CTTY.
  CMD\REDIR.INC     redirection and pipes: exec_line, the layer that
                    strips < > >> | off a line and points handles
                    0/1 before exec_core sees the verb.
  CMD\<name>\       one directory per EXTERNAL command (2026-09-25):
                    ATTRIB CACHE CDEX CHKDSK CHOICE DISKCOMP DISKCOPY
                    DRIVES EDIT FC FDISK FIND FORMAT LABEL LFNAPI MEM
                    MORE MOUNT MOVE SORT SYS UNDELETE XCOPY.
                    CMD\ itself keeps only the native shell.  BUILD.CMD
                    cds into each, so its paths there are ..\..\INC
                    and ..\..\BIN; a new command's directory must also
                    go in the stale-object sweep near the top.
                    CHKDSK\, EDIT\, LABEL\ and XCOPY\ are C (Open
                    Watcom, no C library): SYS_D32.C is all they know
                    of PM-DOS, and DOSINT.ASM -dD32 is the header and
                    startup, FIRST on the link line.  See the
                    2026-09-25 entry for why their wlink line differs
                    from the rest.  FC\ is C as well, one file with a
                    DOSINT.ASM of its own.  The others are one
                    <name>.ASM.
  CMD\CHOICE\CHOICE.ASM
                    CHOICE.COM, the first EXTERNAL command.  Every
                    native program links at 2000h, an offset in its
                    own segment, so they no longer have to take turns
                    in one slot.
  CMD\MEM\MEM.ASM   MEM.EXE, the memory report.  The one program that
                    reads kernel structures directly - it walks the
                    arena from the header 52h hands it, which is what
                    MEM always did and why 52h exists.  It walks the
                    conventional chain at V86_TPA too, which is where
                    the 588K figure can be seen from a running system.
  DISK\CONFIG.SYS   the CONFIG.SYS every disk ships with: settings
                    only, no help text.  A release build boots it
                    without a word.  SHELL= is not in it: the same
                    file goes on the floppy (A:) and both hard disks
                    (C:).  CFGTEST expects its FILES=, LASTDRIVE= and
                    SET PMDOSTEST lines.
  DISK\CONFIG.TXT   the user's guide to every CONFIG.SYS statement,
                    on every disk next to CONFIG.SYS (2026-10-02).
                    The help moved out of CONFIG.SYS itself, which had
                    grown to 14K of a 16K read buffer.  A new
                    statement gets its entry here.
  DISK\*.BAT        batch test files, written into \TESTS on the
                    test floppy by BUILD.CMD and on the hard disks by
                    MKHD.CMD.  BATTEST is the broad
                    one; GOTOTEST, LOOPTEST, SHIFT12, CHAIN1/CHAIN2
                    and NOLABEL each pin down one behaviour.
  INC\PMDOS.INC     the one shared header: memory map, selectors,
                    service table offsets, SFT layout, error codes.
  TOOLS\MKDISK.C    builds the bootable 1.44M FAT12 image, and the
                    FAT16/FAT32 hard disks (bootable with -mbr/-vbr).
  TOOLS\MKCD.PL     builds the CD-ROM test discs nothing on this
                    machine could make: Rock Ridge, two sessions,
                    audio tracks, a file in several extents.
  TOOLS\MKUDF.PS1   ...and the one it could, through IMAPI2FS: a UDF
                    disc with NO ISO9660 bridge on it, which is the
                    only kind DOS\UDF.INC is for.
  BUILD.CMD         assembles, links, checks sizes, makes PMDOS.IMG
                    (the boot floppy) and TESTS.IMG (the test floppy).
  MKHD.CMD          makes IMAGES\HD16.IMG (bootable FAT16) + HD32.IMG.
  IMAGES\           every finished disk image.  BIN\ is what a disk is
                    MADE OF, BIN\TESTS\ is what proves it, IMAGES\ is
                    the media itself - entries dated before 2026-09-11
                    say BIN\HD16.IMG and mean this.

Memory map: see the big comment at the top of INC\PMDOS.INC.

Build
-----
  BUILD.CMD        release: boots with "Starting PM-DOS..." only
  BUILD.CMD debug  defines PMDOS_DEBUG: chatty stub/kernel banners,
                   mount and load messages (errors print either way)
  (Open Watcom 1.9 wasm+wlink+wcl386 on PATH)

Raw binaries come from  wlink form raw bin option offset=<base>.
Watch out: wlink silently rounds a non-4K-aligned offset UP (that is
why the boot sector addresses everything through DS=07C0h and links
at offset 0).  The sources use MASM-compatible syntax and should
assemble with ML 6.1x as well, but that path is untested - no MASM
on this machine.

Testing
-------
DOSBox 0.74 boots the image:  dosbox -conf <conf with:
  [cpu] core=normal cycles=30000
  [autoexec] imgmount a IMAGES\PMDOS.IMG -t floppy /
             imgmount b IMAGES\TESTS.IMG -t floppy / boot -l a >
cycles=max starves DOSBox's event pump (window goes Not Responding);
use fixed cycles.  Verified 2026-08-06 in DOSBox: boot, VER, DIR,
MEM, TYPE README.TXT - i.e. keyboard IRQ, INT 21h, FAT12 reads and
the PM->RM BIOS thunk all live.  86Box (C:\86Box) is the closer-to-
hardware second opinion when needed.  NOT YET TRIED ON REAL IRON, and
as of the v0.30 audit that is the largest single unknown left in the
project: two emulators agreeing is two opinions, not a fact.  SYS16.COM
is the way in - it runs on an ordinary MS-DOS and writes a bootable
PM-DOS disk - and it was confirmed current in v0.29 by finding all four
boot blobs in the built binary.

v0.31 SHARPENED THAT FROM A PRINCIPLE INTO A SPECIFIC DEBT.  The null
guard is four debug registers, and neither emulator implements data
breakpoints - not DOSBox 0.74, not 86Box 4.2.1 in either of its cores.
DR7 reads back exactly as written on both and nothing ever fires.  So
there is now a feature in the kernel that no amount of emulator work
can test, and CRASH /N on iron is the first thing to run.  Note the
shape of that: the emulators did not disagree, they were both missing
the same thing, which is the failure mode "two opinions" was always
about.

ALSO WORTH RUNNING ON IRON, for the same reason - they touch hardware
the emulators model loosely or not at all:
  - 21h/03h, 04h and 05h against a machine with a REAL serial port and
    a REAL printer.  Both emulators here have neither, so all v0.31
    proved is that the calls return rather than hang, which is the
    less interesting half
  - IDLETEST, because the INT 28h excursion rate is set by how fast
    the machine can go round a V86 exit and re-entry, and that is a
    number an emulator has no reason to get right
  - the raw-mode console (4401h), because it changes how keys arrive
    and a real keyboard controller is the one that matters

Every release is checked on BOTH: DOSBox for the FAT12 floppy path
and 86Box for the FAT16 hard disk over real ATA.  v0.20 added a third
kind of check that neither emulator can be talked into on demand -
a DISK THAT WILL NOT READ - and got it for free from the drives
neither of them has: DIR B: under DOSBox (no second floppy), DIR D:
and DIR A: under 86Box (no second hard disk, and a floppy controller
whose unit 00h has never worked here).  Between them they cover both
sides of the FFh rule and all four answers.
v0.21 added a fourth: the 40MB FAT32 image mounted as a DATA drive
(imgmount 2 IMAGES\HD32.IMG -size 512,63,16,81 then boot the floppy)
is the only volume here with more than 65535 clusters, so it is the
only place 7303h can be told apart from 36h - it reports 40,962,048
bytes free where 36h saturates at 33,553,920.  A fix nobody can see
fail without it is a fix nobody has tested.
SYS16 added a fifth kind of check, and the only one that needs an OS
other than ours: a REAL MS-DOS, booted from the MSDOS6 disk in the
PRESARIO backups.  DOSBox's own DOS cannot stand in for it - see the
SYS16 section - so anything that leans on INT 25h/26h or on file
attributes has to be run there.
The regression set is BATTEST, CHTEST, REDTEST, CMDTEST, LFNTEST,
LFNAPI, CTRLC.BAT and DIR | SORT | MORE, plus whichever throwaway
prober the release needed
(scratchpad EXECTEST.ASM for v0.18's nesting, PSPTEST.ASM for v0.19's
PSP and memory work).  Both probers earned their keep by finding
things a build cannot: EXECTEST the i21_fail stack bug, PSPTEST
nothing in the kernel but its own immediate-vs-dereference mistake -
and MEM.EXE, just by existing, the MORE page-boundary bug.

v0.30 added three that are PERMANENT rather than throwaway, because
what they cover is foundation and will keep needing to be true:
DEVTEST.COM (the device namespace, InDOS, extended error and file
stamps, all from inside a DOS box so the VDM bridge is exercised
too), NULTEST.BAT (the same devices through COMMAND's own
redirection, which is where "> NUL" actually goes) and CRASHTST.BAT
with CRASH.EXE (a native program faulting three different ways inside
a batch file that has to survive it).  DEVTEST found a bug in this
release's own code within an hour of being written - see the v0.30
notes - which is the argument for spending the hour.

v0.31 added two more of the same kind.  APITEST.COM covers the whole
release from inside a DOS box - both version calls, six IOCTL
subfunctions, 5Ah, 5Bh, 60h, 68h, 2Eh/54h and 05h - and is worth
running BOTH WAYS, because "APITEST > FILE" makes stdout a file and
4400h/4401h are the two calls whose answer is supposed to change when
it is.  APITEST.BAT does both.  IDLETEST.COM hooks INT 28h and counts
how often its handler runs while it waits for a key, which is the only
way to see the idle hook at all; it is interactive by nature, so it is
not in a batch file.

Both earned their keep immediately.  APITEST found the ".."-at-the-
root bug in a resolver four releases old, and CRASH's new /N found
that the whole null-guard question needed rethinking (see v0.31).

SINCE 2026-10-01 THE REGRESSION RUN IS TOOLS\RUNTESTS.PS1 -All, and
the regression set above is what a person still runs by hand.  It
builds a disk of every program and test, boots it headless in
DOSBox-X on seven machines - a 4MB 386, a 32MB 486, and Pentiums with
252MB, 256MB, 260MB, 1GB and 3GB - and compares each test's output
with BASELINE\<machine>\<test>.OUT; it exits 0 only if every machine
matched.  -Update records a new baseline, which goes in the same
commit as the change that moved it.  IDLETEST runs there as
"IDLETEST /T", which needs no key.  The header of RUNTESTS.PS1 is
the manual, and the 2026-10-01 entry is what it was built for.

Design notes / traps hit
------------------------

* THE TWO HALVES OF A REGISTER ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE AND THE COMMENT
  WILL NOT TELL YOU.  rdbg_flush said "mov dx,8100h  ; head 0, drive
  81h".  DH is the head, DL is the drive; that line asks for head 129
  of drive 0.  The comment was right, the code was its mirror image,
  and the two were read together as agreeing for three releases while
  every theory about the missing trace assumed the write was at least
  addressed to the right disk.  A constant that contains both operands
  can be exactly backwards and still look like the comment.

* A SILENCE IS NOT A MEASUREMENT UNTIL SOMETHING HAS BEEN SEEN TO
  ARRIVE.  v0.51's notes said this and left it undone.  Doing it -
  PROBE13.COM, one write, one read back, both sides of the park -
  cost one boot and destroyed three releases of accumulated theory in
  it.  Build the positive control FIRST; it is cheaper than the
  reasoning it replaces.

* A WORKAROUND HIDES THE SECOND CAUSE FOR AS LONG AS THE SYMPTOM IS
  THE SAME.  The first BIOS disk call after every park has failed
  since v0.45.  RMDISK retries once through a reset on any error -
  written for floppies, which genuinely need it - so every read RMDOS
  has ever done was the second attempt and nobody could tell.  The
  trace had no retry behind it, which is the only reason it was ever
  visible.  When a retry exists, ask what fraction of first attempts
  it is covering.

* A ROUTINE THAT TWO CALLERS SHARE WAS WRITTEN FOR THE FIRST OF THEM.
  pic_to_rm masks IRQ 14 because rm_call is a short trip into the BIOS
  and this kernel polls its own disk.  rm_park reuses it and then
  never comes back, leaving a whole DOS on a BIOS that wants the
  drive's interrupt.  Same shape: ATA.INC sets nIEN once at IDENTIFY
  because it polls - and nIEN lives IN THE DRIVE, so it outlives the
  mode switch, the park, and the kernel that set it.  State written
  into hardware is not undone by leaving.

* AN EXIT CODE OF ZERO IS NOT A BUILD.  BUILD.CMD printed
  "iorm.asm(337): Error! E551: Symbol ATA_DC_NIEN is not defined",
  carried on, and exited zero, leaving the PREVIOUS PMIO.SYS in BIN.
  Four experiments then ran against a kernel containing neither of the
  fixes they were testing, and both were written off as ineffective.
  The tail of the log was clean because the error was four hundred
  lines up.  Grep the log, not the status.

* AND THE SYMBOL WAS MISSING BECAUSE THE FILE IS ASSEMBLED ALONE.
  ATA_DC_NIEN is defined in ATA.INC, which IOPM.ASM includes; IORM.ASM
  is a separate assembly and shares nothing with it.  A constant used
  in the real-mode stub has to be spelt out or defined there.

* A RING BUFFER THROWS AWAY THE OPENING MOVES, WHICH ARE THE ONES THAT
  SAY WHAT THE PROGRAM IS TRYING TO DO.  Ten opens of CON in a row
  pushed the name of every file Windows had opened before them out of
  an eight-slot ring - including the one that would have said which
  kernel it went looking for.  Keeping the FIRST N is the choice
  rdbg_i2frec already made about INT 2Fh, for the same reason.

* A TRACE OF THE QUESTION CANNOT TELL A WRONG ANSWER FROM A MISSING
  ONE.  The channel logged what every INT 21h ASKED and not what came
  back, so "KRNL386 asked for the DOS version and then complained
  about it" left the version itself unmeasured - and the release spent
  a while on AH=30h, which had been returning 6.22 correctly all
  along.  Recording the result as well took eleven instructions and
  named the real fault in one run: ten opens of CON, ten times
  ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND.

* THE ERROR MESSAGE IS THE PROGRAM'S OPINION, NOT A DIAGNOSIS.
  "Incorrect MS-DOS version.  MS-DOS 3.1 or greater required." is what
  the Windows kernel says when the DOS underneath is unusable, and the
  version was never the reason.  Read it as "this DOS did not work"
  and look at what it did immediately before.

* A FEATURE EVERY TEST STANDS ON IS A FEATURE NO TEST TOUCHES.  RMDOS
  could not open CON, NUL, PRN or AUX by name, and had not been able
  to since v0.45 - while dev_read, dev_write, the 44h that reports a
  character device and the five inherited handles all worked, so the
  machine looked like it had devices.  Every test in this suite gets
  its handles from its parent and so never asks.  This is the old
  lesson from a new direction: not something nobody exercises, but
  something everybody depends on without ever naming.

* AND THE TEST WRITTEN FOR IT FAILED FOR THE OLDEST REASON IN THE
  FILE.  RMTEST's new check read 44h's answer out of DX and then
  printed it before testing it - and put4 ends in putc, which passes
  the character to DOS in DL.  Printing the answer destroyed half of
  it.  Fifth release running: a return value already in a register,
  destroyed by an instruction that reads as housekeeping.

* TWO BUGS THAT CANCEL ARE ONE BUG THAT CANNOT BE FIXED HALFWAY.
  sft_get destroyed DX, so every EXEC read went to offset zero of its
  destination; the .COM loader asked for offset 0100h when it wanted
  0000h.  Wrong plus wrong was right, on the only branch anything ever
  took, for five releases - and the branch that did NOT have the
  second error simply did not work at all, which is how RMDOS came to
  be unable to load an .EXE without anybody noticing.  Fixing either
  one alone breaks the machine.  When a fix makes things worse, the
  thing it broke may be what was holding it up.

* LDS IS AN ASSIGNMENT TO DS, AND EVERYTHING AFTER IT IS IN A
  DIFFERENT WORLD.  exec_psp loaded DS:SI from the parameter block and
  THEN read its own destination out of a variable - a variable in a
  segment DS no longer pointed at.  The address it got happened to be
  zero, so 128 bytes of the parent's command line went to 0000:0080:
  the interrupt vector table, from INT 20h to INT 3Fh.  Fetch every
  argument before the instruction that takes the segment register
  away, not after.

* AND THE SYMPTOM WAS A PROGRAM THAT RAN PERFECTLY AND SAID NOTHING.
  The child was loaded right and jumped to right; it marked the screen
  and the BIOS answered it, because INT 10h's vector is at 0000:0040
  and the damage started at 0000:0080.  Its first INT 21h went to four
  bytes of its parent's command tail.  From outside, "the loader is
  broken" and "the loader is perfect and the table under it is not"
  look identical - and the loader is where you look.  A child that
  reports before it asks DOS anything separates them in one boot; that
  is what PEKID.COM is for, and it should have existed five releases
  ago.

* A CLAMP THAT WRITES TO THE CALLER'S COUNTER.  file_io limits each
  transfer to the tail of the current sector - and did it by clamping
  ECX, which is not the size of the chunk but what is left of the
  whole request.  So it moved one sector, subtracted that from itself,
  reached zero, and returned success.  It had never moved more than
  512 bytes in its life and nothing had noticed, because until the
  .EXE loader nothing had ever asked it for a second sector.  A
  variable that means "how much is left" and a variable that means
  "how much this time" are two variables.

* THE INSTRUMENT MUST NOT SHARE A CHANNEL WITH WHAT IT IS BEING
  COMPARED AGAINST.  The markers painted through i21's prologue fired
  on the PARENT's calls as well as the child's, so a screen full of
  letters said nothing about which of the two had painted them - and
  one of those readings was then used as evidence that the child's
  call had arrived.  It had not.  This is v0.50's "one row, one
  meaning" arriving again with the roles swapped: not two facts
  sharing a row, but two callers sharing a fact.

* AN INSTRUMENT THAT HAS ONLY EVER REPORTED A SILENCE HAS NOT BEEN
  SHOWN TO WORK.  The same markers were gated off until the moment
  they were needed, so their first ever reading was the absence they
  were built to detect, which is exactly the reading a broken probe
  gives.  Arming them early enough to catch a call whose answer is
  already known cost one boot and made every later silence mean
  something.

* AND THEN THE SILENCE WAS REAL AND STILL PROVED NOTHING.  RMDBG's
  disk channel has been dead since v0.50; the HMA was the obvious
  cause - INT 13h writes from up there move nothing - and a low bounce
  buffer was the obvious fix.  The buffer is demonstrably allocated
  and the trace still does not land, and neither does PM-DOS's own
  sink in the same build.  So the fix may be correct and irrelevant.
  Until one deliberate write to that gap has been SEEN, "the trace is
  missing" is a statement about the instrument, not about the machine.

* A TEST CAN BE DESTRUCTIVE WITHOUT BEING WRONG WHEN IT WAS WRITTEN.
  XMSTEST proves the 1MB wrap by writing a byte to FFFF:0510.  That
  was empty memory until v0.50 put a DOS in the HMA; afterwards the
  byte lands in the code answering the call the test is making, and
  the run that follows is a DOS printing its own message table.  The
  question the test must ask is not "is there an HMA" - PM-DOS refuses
  that too, while keeping it safely empty - but "does the driver LIVE
  there", and the driver answers that about itself: its own entry
  point, which RMXMS gives as FFFF:4306 and PM-DOS's as 0502:0000.

* A ROUTINE THAT ENDS THE WORLD INSTEAD OF RETURNING.  RMDOS's 4Bh
  gave the machine back to PM-DOS when the child exited, because v0.45
  believed the caller's frame had been unwound.  It had not - the
  return path had just restored SS:SP to exactly where it was.  A
  shortcut taken on a path nothing exercises is a shortcut nobody
  checks, and this one was written five releases before anything
  called it.

* MEMORY THAT EXISTS BECAUSE OF PAGING STOPS EXISTING WHEN PAGING
  DOES, AND THE STRUCTURE THAT DESCRIBES IT DOES NOT.  v0.49 already
  knew upper memory was no place to put RMDOS - the UMBs vanish in
  the instruction that made them necessary - and stopped one step
  short of the consequence: the MCB CHAIN still runs through them.
  A walk from the head goes off the top of conventional memory into
  the VGA frame buffer and reads whatever it answers with as a block
  header.  Windows counts its conventional memory that way and quit.
  When a resource disappears, look for the thing that still points
  at it.

* AND PUTTING IT BACK IS NOT THE SAME AS REMEMBERING WHERE IT WAS.
  The first park_chainjoin restored the 'M' to the block park_chaincut
  had turned into a 'Z'.  But RMDOS allocates out of that arena the
  whole time it is parked, and a SPLIT gives the tail block the marker
  the original carried - so the real end of the chain had moved, the
  restore wrote 'M' over an 'M', and upper memory stayed orphaned
  behind a 'Z' in the middle.  RMTEST passed and UMBTEST failed three
  checks.  Undo by finding the current state, not by replaying the
  change.

* A COUNT IN CX FOR A ROUTINE THAT READS ECX.  Three reads in fn4B -
  the .EXE header, each relocation entry, and the whole .COM image -
  loaded CX and left the top half of ECX as whatever the caller
  happened to have there.  file_io compares all thirty-two bits.  It
  survives only because a READ is clamped to the end of the file, so
  the damage is "reads more than asked for" rather than a crash, and
  a write on the same path would have been unrecoverable.

* A CALL THAT DOES NOT RETURN STILL HAS TO PUT ITS COUNTERS DOWN.
  i21 raises the InDOS flag and the internal stack depth on the way
  in and lowers them at i21_out.  4Bh with AL=0 never reaches
  i21_out - the whole point of it is that control leaves through a
  far jump - so every program RMDOS has ever started began life
  looking at a DOS that was permanently mid-call.  InDOS is the byte
  every well-behaved program watches to decide whether it may talk to
  DOS, and what a program does about a DOS that is always busy is
  WAIT, quietly, making no calls at all.  From outside that is
  indistinguishable from a crash and is not one.

* ONE ROW, ONE MEANING.  The framebuffer instrument paints a bar per
  fact.  Borrowing the two rows that hold "last call in" and "last
  call out" to show the child's entry bytes worked once - 4D 5A,
  'MZ', which was the finding of the day - and then went on reading
  4D 5A on a later build where the probe had never executed, because
  4Dh and 5Ah are also perfectly plausible DOS function numbers for
  the bars that own those rows.  An instrument that shares a channel
  is an instrument that can only be believed when you already know
  the answer.

* A MARKER THAT OVERWRITES ITS PREDECESSOR ANSWERS THE WRONG
  QUESTION.  The EXEC stage markers were a number painted per stage,
  so the screen showed the LAST stage reached - and the thing worth
  knowing was which BRANCH was taken three stages earlier.  One bit
  per stage, OR'd together, says both.

* THE INSTRUMENT HAS TO BE PUT WHERE THE PICTURE IS NOT.  The first
  bars went at screen row 400, which is inside the Windows logo, and
  measured the artwork; moved to row 20 of the text page they were
  scrolled away by the output they were measuring.  This is the
  fourth release running in which reading an instrument has cost more
  than building it.

* THE IDENTITY MAP HAS EXACTLY ONE HOLE IN IT AND IT IS THE ONE THIS
  RELEASE MOVED INTO.  PM-DOS emulates the A20 gate in the page
  tables - sixteen entries covering 100000h, pointing at themselves
  when the gate is open and at 00000h when it is shut - and THE
  KERNEL IS NOT EXEMPT FROM ITS OWN PAGE TABLES.  A DOS box starts
  with the gate shut, because that is what a real machine does, so
  the kernel's write of RMDOS to linear 100000h went to physical
  zero: onto the interrupt vector table.  Then the far jump to
  FFFF:0010 - which the processor makes with the REAL gate, and the
  real gate is open - found nothing there.  Reset.  park_run forces
  the alias to the identity for the length of the excursion and
  park_release hands the guest's own idea of the gate back.  The
  file header says the map is the identity "with two exceptions,
  both below 1MB and both deliberate"; it was right, and the
  exception was the address I had chosen to live at.

* TWO ARGUMENTS THAT HAD ALWAYS BOTH BEEN ZERO, SO IT HAD NEVER
  MATTERED WHICH ONE CARRIED THE VALUE.  k21's 42h takes its offset
  in ECX and does not look at EDX at all.  Every LSEEK in park_loadrm
  until now asked for position zero and zeroed both registers.  The
  first call that wanted a non-zero position put it in EDX, got a
  silent successful seek to the beginning, and loaded the whole image
  sixteen bytes too high - which is a working DOS at the wrong
  address, so the header validated, the signature matched, and the
  far jump landed on sixteen bytes of padding.  When a convention has
  never been exercised, reading the callers proves nothing: they all
  agree because they are all zero.

* A TRIPLE FAULT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE AN EMULATOR THAT NEVER FINISHED
  POST.  Three boots in a row stopped at "Detecting Secondary Slave"
  and I spent them on the emulator - restoring CMOS, detaching a
  disk, pressing F4 - before running the machine with the test taken
  out of AUTOEXEC and watching it reach a prompt in forty seconds.
  It had been booting all along: booting, running, faulting,
  resetting, and hanging in the SECOND POST.  The screen I was
  reading as "never started" was the one after the crash.  When a
  machine appears not to boot, take the payload out before touching
  the machine.

* THE BUILD THAT DID NOT RUN, AND ANSWERED ANYWAY.  `cmd //c
  "BUILD.CMD rmbisect"` from bash does not pass the argument through
  this shell, and the build silently left the previous binary in
  place.  The run that followed produced a screen consistent with
  every belief I had, because it WAS the previous run.  The tell was
  a rebuild of unchanged source that came out 26 bytes bigger than
  the binary I had just tested.  Build through the shell that owns
  the build, and check the size when it matters.

* A CALL THAT RETURNS SUCCESS AND MOVES NOTHING.  INT 13h AH=42h -
  the extended packet read - comes back with carry clear and AH zero
  on this BIOS and transfers no data.  RMDOS read boot sectors for
  five releases into a buffer that still held its assembled zeroes,
  and reported "cannot mount" about a BPB it had never seen.  The
  same discovery had already been made in this tree, about AH=43h,
  in v0.48 - written down in RMDBG.INC, next to the code that
  switched to CHS because of it, and never carried across to the
  file that does the actual disk I/O.  A note in the file where you
  found the bug is not a fix in the file that has it.

* A TEST THAT STOPS AT THE FIRST FAILURE HIDES THE STATE OF
  EVERYTHING BEHIND IT.  RMTEST's bad: printed FAILED, incremented a
  counter and RET'd - and every site reaches it with a JUMP, so the
  RET unwound out of the run.  Seven checks after the first failure
  had not been executed in five releases.  What made it costly was
  not the missing coverage but the missing SHAPE: one early check
  failing for a trivial reason made the whole DOS look broken, and
  three of the four "failures" I set out to fix did not exist.

* ...AND THE TEST WAS BREAKING THE THING IT THEN MEASURED.  0Eh is
  SELECT DISK.  RMTEST asked it "how many drive letters are there"
  with DL=0, which also moved it to A:, and then failed every
  remaining check against an empty floppy.  A test that changes the
  state it is about to inspect is not an instrument, and this one had
  been lying about a whole file system.

* THE CONTROL HAS TO BE READ WITH THE SAME INSTRUMENT.  The low-RMDOS
  run that exonerated the HMA was made before RMTEST was fixed, so it
  was a comparison between two different questions.  It happened to
  give the right answer.  Re-running it afterwards was three minutes
  and turned a coincidence into evidence.

* AN INSTRUMENT PUT WHERE THE OUTPUT GOES MEASURES THE OUTPUT.  The
  RMDOS markers went to row 20 and the screen scrolled them away;
  moved to row 0 column 30 they collided with PM-DOS's own probe, and
  the tail of one read as the tail of the other for two runs.  This
  is the fourth release in which reading an instrument has cost more
  than building it.

* A STRING INSTRUCTION WRITES THROUGH ES AND EVERYTHING ELSE IN THE
  ROUTINE WRITES THROUGH DS.  park_fillhdr fills eleven fields of
  RMDOS's handoff block with "mov [edi+n]" and copied the register
  frame with one REP MOVSB.  Ten fields arrived and one did not, in
  silence, and the silence was the problem: RMDOS came up, checked a
  signature THIS ROUTINE HAD JUST WRITTEN, found it, initialised
  completely, and IRETed onto a frame of zeroes - so the guest went to
  0000:0000 and executed the interrupt vector table.  Every symptom
  said "the guest died"; nothing said "segment register".  When one
  line out of a dozen does not arrive, ask what is different about
  that line before asking what is wrong with the far end.

* THE SAME BUG AT THE OTHER END OF THE SAME FEATURE, FOUR RELEASES
  APART.  v0.48 found that answering an informational IOCTL by
  MOUNTING the volume raises a critical error on an empty drive, and
  prompts where nobody can see it.  v0.49 found park_remount doing the
  identical thing on the way back from an excursion, for the identical
  reason - nothing had ever run that path with an empty drive in the
  machine.  Fixing a bug of this shape is a prompt to go looking for
  its twin, and the place to look is the OTHER direction of whatever
  the fixed code was half of.

* AN INSTRUMENT THAT READS LAST RUN'S ANSWER IS WORSE THAN NO
  INSTRUMENT.  The RMDOS trace lands in the gap on the second disk and
  the clear-before-run zeroed sectors 1 upwards; the trace was landing
  on sector 0.  So two consecutive runs "confirmed" a result that had
  been written before either of them started, and one of those runs
  was the one that was supposed to prove the ES fix.  Clear exactly
  what you read, read exactly what you clear, and make an empty
  channel say "empty" rather than saying nothing.

* A LABEL AND A CONSTANT DIFFERING ONLY IN CASE, AGAIN, IN THE FILE
  THAT DOCUMENTS THE RULE.  RMDBG.INC was written the same afternoon
  the v0.48 note about dbg_ring/DBG_RING went into this file, and it
  was written with rdbg_2fn next to RDBG_2FN.  This time wasm said
  something - "invalid instruction operands" on an INC - which is luck
  and not protection: the v0.48 instance assembled clean and rewrote
  the interrupt vector table.  Knowing a trap is not the same as being
  proof against it.

* A .COM OWNS ALL OF CONVENTIONAL MEMORY UNTIL IT SAYS OTHERWISE, and
  anything the kernel needs to put in conventional memory ON ITS
  BEHALF has to come from somewhere else.  The handover loads a 23K
  DOS into the arena and failed with "not enough memory" on a machine
  with 620K free, because the program that asked for the handover had
  not yet shrunk itself.  A test program can fix that with a 4Ah;
  DOSX.EXE cannot, because it does its 4Ah AFTER the broadcast rather
  than before.

* BACKSLASHES EATEN BY BASH-QUOTED PERL AND SED, twice more, and once
  it reached a build script: "..\BIN\PARKWIN.COM" was written as
  "..BINPARKWIN.COM" and the link silently produced a file with that
  name in the wrong directory.  perl -pi -e and sed -i BOTH did
  nothing at all on this share when the pattern contained a backslash,
  reporting success.  Write the script to a file with the editor and
  run it; or build the string with chr(92), which does work.

* A LABEL AND A CONSTANT THAT DIFFER ONLY IN CASE ARE ONE SYMBOL, and
  the constant wins in silence.  The new trace buffer was dbg_ring and
  the count of entries in it was DBG_RING, so "add edi,OFFSET
  dbg_ring" assembled to "add edi,512" - no warning, no error, a
  clean build.  Every guest trap then wrote eight bytes over the
  interrupt vector table and the machine reset so fast it never
  printed anything to say so: a black screen and a window the
  emulator kept resizing.  wasm folding case across FILES is written
  down twice already, from v0.45 and from XMS; this is the same trap
  INSIDE ONE FILE, between two things it is completely natural to
  name the same.  There is no assembly-time check for it - OFFSET of
  a relocatable label is not a constant, so IF cannot weigh it - so
  the rule has to be kept by naming.
* AN OFF-SCREEN WINDOW SCREENSHOTS AS PURE BLACK.  CopyFromScreen
  reads the desktop, not the window, and 86Box remembers where it was
  last used - which was another monitor, at x = -1013.  That is
  indistinguishable from an emulated machine drawing nothing, and it
  cost a round of "the kernel broke the boot" before a window list
  showed where the thing actually was.  The capture script moves the
  window on-screen first now.
* AND KILLING AN EMULATOR DOES NOT FLUSH WHAT IT WAS WRITING.  Every
  "the trace produced nothing" result during the printer experiments
  was a file that had been written to and never closed, because the
  runs ended with Stop-Process -Force.  A run script that closes the
  window and waits is not tidiness, it is the difference between no
  output and no evidence.
* A DEBUG CHANNEL THROUGH SOMEBODY ELSE'S DEVICE IS A SECOND THING TO
  DEBUG.  The trace went to the parallel port first, on the sound
  reasoning that the guest is not using it and cannot corrupt it.  It
  never delivered a byte - and neither did the machine's own BIOS
  through INT 17h, which is the reference implementation and settled
  that the driver was not the problem.  86Box drops lpt1_enabled out
  of the configuration file every time it rewrites it on exit.  The
  sink is the DISK now: the trace accumulates in RAM and is written in
  one transfer to the sectors between the master boot record and the
  first partition, through the kernel's own ATA driver, which is port
  I/O and nothing else and therefore safe to call with a guest hung
  underneath.  Nothing to configure, and it works on real hardware.
* A WATCHDOG THAT WAITS FOR SILENCE NEVER FIRES ON A GUEST THAT SPINS
  THROUGH THE MONITOR.  The first version dumped the ring after five
  seconds with no guest trap, which is the right trigger for a guest
  looping in its own code and useless for one going round a loop of
  DOS calls: every turn clears the counter.  There are two triggers
  now and the second is a deadline that nothing can defeat.
* A CHAIN HEAD OF "NOTHING" IS NOT THE SAME AS AN EMPTY CHAIN.  The
  list of lists had five pointers set to FFFF:FFFF and called honest,
  and four of them are - a program wanting the DPB array or the disk
  buffers checks the pointer before using it.  The fifth was the
  system file table, which is a CHAIN, and code that reads a chain
  does not check the head: it FOLLOWS it.  WIN.COM walks that chain
  adding up file handle counts, went round four instructions for ever
  on PM-DOS, and that was the "WIN.COM hangs" of v0.44 - eleven
  releases of a test suite that reads this structure, and none of them
  walked it.
* THE INSTRUMENT CHANGED THE ANSWER, THREE TIMES IN ONE AFTERNOON.
  The monitor's watchdog prints through the console from inside the
  timer interrupt, which is slow enough to change how many
  instructions the guest gets per tick - and Windows reached its LOGO
  under the watchdog and stopped before it without one.  Two hours
  went on that difference before it was understood to BE the probe.
  Drawing the sample into the graphics framebuffer instead came out
  unreadable, because the VGA's write mode, map mask and set/reset
  registers belong to the guest at that moment.  And holding the
  screen in text mode by swallowing the guest's mode set leaves it
  believing in a mode the hardware is not in, so the next BIOS call
  it makes is answered from a state that never existed.  A quiet
  probe - sixteen bytes poked into the text page - is the only one
  that reproduced the release behaviour exactly.
* AND THE REGISTER-THAT-LOOKED-FREE FAMILY REACHED FIVE RELEASES, this
  time in the routine that already carries a comment about it in
  capitals.  vdm_lol ends by handing the guest the list-of-lists
  segment in EAX; twenty lines above, a comment says exactly that,
  because the same mistake was made with DL two releases ago.  The new
  code was written underneath that comment and used EAX.  The symptom
  was a guest reading its list of lists at 0028:0002 - forty, which is
  what FILES= says.  Reading the warning is not the same as heeding it;
  the only thing that catches this is running the test.
* A NUMBER A CALLER CANNOT ACT ON IS THE WRONG NUMBER.  RMDOS's XMS
  driver reported free extended memory to the kilobyte, which is the
  unit XMS counts in, and handed out blocks on page boundaries, which
  is what a customer that builds page tables needs.  Both were right
  and together they were a bug: a request is rounded UP to a page, so
  asking for exactly as much as the manager says is free rounded past
  the end of the pool and failed - and asking for exactly that is the
  first thing Windows does.  A figure that is reported has to be a
  figure that can be acted on, in the same units the acting uses.
* AND IT WAS A CHECK WRITTEN FOR SOMETHING ELSE THAT FOUND IT, for
  the fourth release running.  The new checks went in because
  reallocate was code nothing had ever called; one of them asks for
  the whole pool on the way past.  Sixty-four kilobytes worked
  perfectly and would have gone on working perfectly.
* A BUILD SWITCH IS THE CHEAPEST WAY TO TEST AN UNREACHABLE PATH.  The
  block move has a second implementation for the case where protected
  mode belongs to somebody else, which cannot happen without Windows.
  Three lines of IFDEF made it run in the case that CAN be produced,
  and turned written into tested.
* AND KNOWING A TRAP IS NOT THE SAME AS AVOIDING IT.  "wasm folds case
  across files" was written down in v0.45, and the next file added
  collided five times: RMDISK.INC already had rx_ok, rx_err and
  rx_next, because in that file rx_ means "read sector".  A prefix
  chosen to be distinctive is only distinctive against the files you
  thought of.
* TWO FIXED OFFSETS WITH CODE BETWEEN THEM NEED A CHECK AT BOTH ENDS.
  The real-mode stub's park entry is at 0900h and its unpark entry was
  at 0940h; the park code grew to end ONE BYTE past the second, and the
  ORG silently overwrote it.  There was a guard on the first boundary
  and none on the second.  What happened next is the part to remember:
  the handover far-jumped into an instruction stream that was half of
  one routine and half of another, wandered into the unpark, went
  straight back to protected mode - and THE MACHINE SURVIVED AND
  REPORTED SUCCESS.  A silent overwrite that produces a working
  machine is worse than a crash.
* A ROUTINE THAT ANSWERS IN A REGISTER MUST NOT SAVE THAT REGISTER.
  rd_path answers a directory's cluster in EBX; a copy loop added
  later wanted a scratch register, took BX, and PUSHed and POPped it
  along with the others - so every caller got its own BX back instead
  of the answer.  It failed on exactly one check out of eight, the one
  that opens a file, and looked like a FAT bug for two builds.
* AND THE SAME CHECK, ONE BUILD EARLIER, WAS A SEGMENT BUG WEARING THE
  SAME COSTUME.  Every routine under rd_path reaches RMDOS's own data
  through DS, and the first version pointed DS at the CALLER's segment
  so it could read the path string - so the volume table it read was
  whatever the caller happened to have at that offset.  A routine that
  changes DS and then calls anything is a routine that has to be read
  twice.  The string is copied into our own segment now and there is
  no second segment in it at all.
* DEBUGGING A MODE SWITCH MEANS WRITING TO THE SCREEN, because the
  screen is the only thing both sides of it agree about: B8000h in
  protected mode and 0B800h:0000 in real mode are the same bytes.
  Eight markers found the ORG collision above in one run, after an
  hour of reading the source had not.  Two markers were themselves
  wrong in instructive ways - one pushed onto a stack not yet set up,
  one onto the stack being handed over - and the second was a real
  bug: PM-DOS was setting that stack pointer past the end of the block
  it had allocated.  Nothing was pushed there yet, and "nothing is
  pushed here" is a fragile thing for a stack pointer to rely on.
* WASM FOLDS CASE ACROSS FILES TOO.  RMDOS.ASM included PMDOS.INC,
  where SFT_SIZE means "how big the table is" and in RMDOS means "how
  big the file is" - both valid offsets into different structures.
  Twenty "label is already defined" errors was the lucky outcome; the
  unlucky one is a program that assembles.  A separate program does
  not include the kernel's header, even when it is built in the same
  tree.
* A CHECK THAT CANNOT FAIL IS WORTH LESS THAN NO CHECK AT ALL, because
  no check does not appear in the pass count.  LOLTEST's device-chain
  test ended with "jmp cpu_test" on BOTH exits, the passing one and the
  failing one, and cpu_test is past everything in between - so eight
  checks (1Bh, 1Ch, 38h, 67h, 5Ch, 63h, 6Ch, 65h) ran only on the path
  where the device chain fails to terminate, which it never does.  The
  file reported 8 checks and looked like a clean run for six releases.
  The recurring note - a feature nobody exercises is a feature nobody
  is testing - arriving from inside the test suite this time.
* AND FIXING IT BROKE NOTHING AND FAILED ANYWAY, in the test.  The
  revived 65h/20h check printed the capitalised character with put2 and
  then compared DL against 'A'.  put2 reaches putc through put1, which
  does MOV DL,AL to make the call, so DL held the last hex digit
  printed by the time it returned - the check read '1' out of "41".
  The output it had already printed was the proof the kernel was right.
  A HELPER THAT TAKES ITS ARGUMENT IN A REGISTER OWNS THAT REGISTER,
  and printing a value is not a read-only operation on it.
* WHEN A STRUCTURE HAS TO BE CONTIGUOUS, WHERE ITS FIRST FIELD LIVES
  STOPS BEING FREE.  The InDOS and critical-error flags sat at 4F6h in
  the BIOS data area for nineteen releases, which cost nothing while
  they were two loose bytes.  5D06h hands out a block whose first two
  bytes ARE those flags, and at 4F6h that block ran into RMFRAME at
  500h after six.  Both were EQUs, so moving them into the DOS data
  segment touched thirty-odd use sites without editing any of them -
  which is the whole argument for the EQU having been there.
* THE RIGHT ANSWER BY ACCIDENT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE THE RIGHT ANSWER.
  INT 2Fh 1600h, 160Ah, 4680h and 1680h are all specified so that "no"
  is the registers coming back unchanged, and the VDM's IRET stub on
  2Fh had therefore been answering all four correctly since the VDM
  existed, without a line of code for any of them.  They are claimed
  explicitly now: the correctness stops depending on that stub still
  being an IRET, and a guest TSR hooking 2Fh can no longer answer for
  PM-DOS and get it wrong.
* A FLAG SAVED ACROSS A CALL IS SAVED FROM WHATEVER RAN LAST, and what
  ran last is not fixed by the code that saves it.  config_run held
  the read's carry across the file close in PUSHFD/POPFD, which was
  right for as long as the read and the close were adjacent.  Putting
  one comparison between them changed what PUSHFD was saving - "the
  file is shorter than the buffer" is JB, which is CF SET - so the
  close preserved a carry meaning SUCCESS and the test after POPFD
  read it as FAILURE.  Every CONFIG.SYS in the machine was then
  abandoned, in silence, because an absent CONFIG.SYS is not an error.
  PUSHFD names no flag and no source; a byte does both.
* AND THE SILENCE IS THE OTHER HALF OF THAT BUG.  It took four boots
  to find because nothing said anything: statements did not complain,
  unknown statements did not complain, and the machine came up
  perfectly - just without its configuration.  The lesson is not about
  carry.  A path that is allowed to do nothing (no CONFIG.SYS is
  legal) must not be reachable by accident from a path that failed.
* A LIMIT THAT IS NOT CHECKED IS NOT A LIMIT, IT IS A CLIFF.
  CFG_BUF_SIZE was 4096 from the first day and nothing compared the
  file against it: a longer CONFIG.SYS was read as far as the buffer
  went and the rest vanished without a word.  PM-DOS's own sample
  CONFIG.SYS passed 4K somewhere around v0.39, so three of its own
